ladies and gentlemen, as you know, a terrible tragedy has occurred since then. i ask that we collectively pay tribute to the victims, to the families of the victims of the tsunami in the indian ocean. i ask you to observe a moment of silence. (the sitting was suspended at 1.30 p.m. and resumed at 3 p.m.) ladies and gentlemen, before we start our agenda i would like to draw your attention to something which i think we are all fully aware of: the way in which we react will perhaps allow us to draw some positive consequences from this terrible disaster. in addition to the actions undertaken on an individual basis, we can do a great deal as a european parliament, from the european parliament. i should like to inform you that last week the president of the commission, mr barroso, called me to inform me of the developments and of his intention to propose at the jakarta summit the mobilisation of the resources provided for in our budget to deal with this kind of disasters. mr barroso stressed in jakarta the need for the european parliament, as one of the two arms of the budgetary authority, to approve the commission's proposals. i have sent a message on behalf of parliament to the jakarta summit, assuring it that this institution will do everything possible to ensure that the european union's contribution to the immediate relief of the consequences of this catastrophe is not delayed by the procedures laid down in our rules. i must inform you that the committee on budgets will decide tomorrow on the transfer of eur 100 million from the reserve for aid. parliament will also examine the proposals put forward by the commission to help with reconstruction as soon as we receive them. but i think that parliament must make it clear from now on that this is a new problem and that new resources are needed to deal with it. i mean, we can't dress one saint by stripping another. we cannot devote to mitigating the consequences of this catastrophe the resources we have already committed to earlier. last week i also the whole world are on this catastrophe.

the next item is the statement by the commission on the outcome of the 10th conference of the parties to the united nations framework convention on climate change, held in buenos aires.
mr president, i believe that the european commission has been the one that has fought the most and the one that has raised the world's awareness of the problem of climate change. but i also think that responsibility and the glory of having been the ones to raise this problem has to go along with a great scientific effort to ensure the veracity of the claims. we must move from a very declarative europe to a more efficient and more scientific europe. in this sense, i believe that, after the meetings that have taken place successively in kyoto and elsewhere, it is necessary, and i believe it is urgent, to develop comprehensive work on climate change. we've studied a lot of what's bad for you, but not what's good for you. in this connection, i would like to see one of the proposals of this parliament to be to look more closely at the relationship between agriculture and the environment. i include reforestation within agriculture. for example, if one hectare of orange trees produces 40,000 kilos a year or 4 tonnes of greenery and firewood, is this beneficial or not for climate change? what is mediterranean agriculture contributing to climate change, for example? this confrontation between agriculture and the environment must end, and one of the ways to do that is to see the benefits of agriculture in the co2 sinks it is creating, as well as to see which reforestation is the most appropriate and which is the best for the environment, and in this way to set up positive policies that serve to meet all activities, not only industrial, but also agricultural. i think we're way behind schedule there. for the same reason, if, as the latest report says, spain, greece and the mediterranean are the countries that will suffer the most from the impact of climate change, i believe it is the commission's responsibility to put studies and solutions on the table.
commission. mr president, very many useful suggestions have been made tonight. in the forthcoming spring european council, which will be the first important step in the european union's discussion on our future climate change strategy, the commission will make a communication, which my colleagues and i are currently preparing. this communication will be very important for the spring council discussions. in this communication, i expect to set a series of specific recommendations and will include quite a few of the suggestions that have been made tonight. i thank those members who made those constructive suggestions. as regards buenos aires, the degree of its success can be measured by objective criteria and, as i said, our objective expectations were not great, but this does not mean that we do not have high targets and that our wishes are not ambitious. we shall work towards those targets because this is what the world needs. we made some progress in buenos aires. the decision to hold a seminar in may to discuss current and new responses to climate change provides a promising opening to the dialogue and the debate for a global climate policy after 2012. the agreement to establish a work programme for adaptation is also a very important breakthrough, not only for the developed countries but also, and even more so, for the developing countries. overall i think we had a successful conference of the parties. however, i agree that we need to strengthen our dialogue with key countries such as india, china, the united states of course, and russia. the united states says it is following a different approach, investing a lot in research and development, but i saw a small breakthrough in its agreement to participate in this seminar and to have presentations about the future. we need to continue and strengthen our dialogue – as was suggested by many honourable members – with these countries, both in the multilateral and bilateral contexts. as mrs frassoni mentioned, with the troika, we are going to have quite a few meetings with countries such as the united states, china, india and developing countries. we also need to continue to show that we are serious about it and that we are taking the fight against climate change seriously. we should lead by example, as mrs corbey suggested. the european union trading scheme and its success will be very important in this regard and we need to continue to emphasise the need for others to join us in these efforts. as i mentioned previously, norway, canada and japan have shown interest and we should see how we can cooperate with the united states which – except the nine north-eastern states and california – have trading systems for other greenhouse gases, but not for carbon dioxide. but the problem there is that they have not signed the kyoto protocol. let us see how we overcome this obstacle. cooperation with local and regional authorities could be very interesting, especially to get support for fighting climate change in countries around the world, and in terms of our contacts with developing countries, such as india and china – and here i must acknowledge, as someone has already said, that the small island states were our allies. it is also very important that they fully support us in what we are trying to do. in our contacts with these countries, it is important to place the benefits of addressing climate change in the broader context of sustainable development. on local air pollution, mr blokland suggested that we stress the benefits in other sectors, and addressing climate change will bring important benefits to these countries. it is very important to stress the eco-innovation and environmental technologies which could be very competitive and could give the benefit of first-mover advantage to european industry and to the industries of those countries, so that they really innovate in an environmentally friendly way. it was suggested that we did not help the least-developed countries as much as we could. i must stress that almost half of the funds for these countries are provided by the european union. the united states is not participating at all, because it considers that to be part of the kyoto protocol. we have to finance projects, that is to say planned projects, not one-off, isolated projects which are ineffective. there were so many questions, so i will answer certain very ones. mr blokland asked whether the chemical industry would be included in the eu emissions trading directive. that is not possible at present. however, we are holding discussions on what will happen after the end of the first phase of emissions trading. we shall probably include it. the combustion used in chemical plants is included. mr davies asked about the uk and the national allocation plan. the decision regarding the uk plan was taken on 7 july 2004, and the uk can avoid prolonging uncertainty for uk companies by proceeding on the basis of that decision. it sent us a letter dated 23 december providing certain information regarding the two questions of gibraltar and new entrants and also asking us for additional, higher amounts of allocations. we are still looking at the technical and legal details of this. in principle, the commission considers that a member state can only present a single national allocation plan. regarding biomass and biofuels, we have a number of instruments already in place to stimulate the use of biomass. this includes a biofuels directive and a directive on electricity from renewable energy sources. last year's commission communication on renewable energy announced a biomass action plan, which should be submitted by the end of 2005. biomass emissions are neutral. there are no allowances for emissions caused by the consumption of biomass. in the time allotted to me, i am unable to answer all the questions and the suggestions that i have noted down during the debate. however, i must stress again how important it is to include in the cooperation developing countries such as china and india. they are worried about their future and very concerned about any limitations or reductions. we have to give them incentives so that they will know that their development will not be hindered by any future agreement. we have to find a way to cooperate and reach the targets that we mentioned before: a maximum of a 2c increase in temperature. with regard to the united states, it is investing a great deal in research. even there – i have heard certain people say that there are questions about the scientific proof of the anthropogenic causes of climate change and its impact – there are very recent reports, published in 2004, proving beyond doubt that climate change is caused by human activity. in the united states they say that their approach is different. they have not and are not going to sign the kyoto protocol. however, we have to find a way to include them in our endeavour to fight climate change. it is not a problem for one country alone or merely for the mediterranean, where the effects will be worse than for other areas of the world: scientists say that the temperature there, by the end of 2100, will have increased by more than five degrees. that is a large increase. one can imagine how this will affect agriculture and tourism, for example, and have an impact on the way in which people live. i heard that there will be positive effects in siberia. that is not true. we do not know what impact climate change will have, nor what areas of the world it will affect. science has proven that climate change caused by human activity should be fought against. that is what we should do and will attempt to do. with your cooperation, the european union will continue to play a leading role in the fight against climate change. the rapporteur. mr president, in the european union parlance, the directive we are discussing today is called the 'fifth motor insurance directive'. it is a directive which amends five other directives, namely four council directives and one european parliament and council directive. the car insurance sector has become a very important sector from an economic and social point of view, as a result of the impact of the car on our lives. from the economic point of view, it is because of the importance of insurance companies and, from the point of view of citizens, because of the possible consequences. in general, it is a sector in which there has been considerable state intervention, with the creation of minimum compulsory services to which everyone must subscribe and with state compensation for cases where insurance coverage is not provided. the commission presented the proposal on 7 june 2002. it was discussed in this parliament under the rapporteur, mr rothley - who is no longer a member of this house - and after parliament's approval at first reading in 2003, the commission and the council made an amendment which led to a common position of the council which at this stage is quite close to the amendments proposed by parliament at first reading. we are now at the second reading. in particular, the committee on the internal market adopted a text at second reading on 14 december, and we hope that a final vote on the text will be taken on wednesday. there are still differences between parliament's position and the council's common position on certain points. first of all, with regard to trailers: what do we do with these vehicles which may or may not be identified with the main vehicle? this is also a sector in which vehicles which were previously not insurable could become so, which would have a number of legal and economic consequences. secondly, as regards legal costs, parliament wants them to be included in the payment of compensation to victims. thirdly, as regards the amount of compensation, i think that at the moment we are discussing the wording rather than a dispute over the amount itself, so that parliament's proposal cannot be interpreted as a limitation on the amount, but on the contrary, the principle of compensation. fourth, there is direct action against the insurer. parliament wants the insured, the victim, to be able to sue the insurer in the courts of his own domicile, without having to go to the insurer's domicile. and fifthly, we have the issue of the importation of vehicles, where parliament is trying to impose the state of destination of the vehicle as the competent state for the insurance of imported vehicles and not the state of the place of dispatch. i think that when this debate is over parliament will have an idea of the situation. we are very interested in hearing from the commission representative to see to what extent parliament maintains these amendments or accepts any other compromise which might bring us closer to an agreement. the rapporteur hopes, in any event, that parliament and the council will soon agree to adopt the directive, which would avoid us having to go through a long formal codecision process and would allow us to solve this problem in a very short time through an informal codecision process.
commission. the proposal for a regulation on sales promotions that was strongly supported by this house two years ago is a key internal market initiative linked to the achievement of a smooth-running internal market for services. i am therefore pleased to see that parliament has maintained its interest in this text in spite of the fact that the council is still considering it. sales promotions are key tools to market goods and services. they cover discounts of all forms: premium offers, free gifts, promotional contests and promotional games. they are a tool for entering into new markets with innovative products or services, for encouraging customer loyalty, for stimulating competitive actions, or for efficiently managing stocks, to name just a few areas in which sales promotions are crucial. their design, execution and communication accounts for a large number of jobs in the eu, with investments representing billions of euro. sales promotions are essential to the development of cross-border trade in products and services within the internal market. this is particularly true for small- and medium-sized enterprises in their development of new markets. yet the free movement of goods and services is seriously hindered due to a myriad of different national rules governing sales promotions. i wish to assure you that the commission has made its best efforts to assist the successive presidencies-in-office of the council to achieve a political agreement. in particular, the commission has shown great flexibility in terms of the two key remaining issues, which are the choice of the legal instrument and the inclusion of a mutual recognition clause in the text. as regards the implications of the lisbon strategy, it is clear that if the current position were not to alter, then this impasse would suggest that the council would be unable to achieve the internal market commitments it has set itself in that context. however, the commission does not believe that the negotiations on this text are over. the alternative to harmonisation will be court rulings that would lift the identified disproportionate restrictions, but this will not harmonise provisions that achieve a high level of consumer protection, including the protection of minors. the commission trusts that the council will not find this a satisfactory proposition. the commission will therefore continue work with the incoming presidency with a view to finding a solution that brings about a genuine single market for sales promotions.
the next item is the report (a6-0070/2004) by mr richard corbett and mr íñigo méndez de vigo, on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs, on the treaty establishing a constitution for europe 2004/2129 (ini).
the rapporteur. mr president, when my group gave me the honour of speaking at the last plenary session of the last parliament at an event we organised in this house to honour monnet, schuman and spinelli, i wondered what the founding fathers, the visionaries of europe, would have thought of the moment we were in in the process of european construction and what they would have thought of the european constitution. i think - i said it then and i repeat it today - that they would not believe that the moment we are living in is real, because, leaving behind a europe divided by fratricidal struggles, this constitution sanctions peace on our continent and, to use a beautiful expression of mr geremek, this constitution sews the two europes together. we are moving from a europe that was ravaged by totalitarian regimes to a europe - and this constitution sanctions this - based on democratic regimes where fundamental rights are respected. after a europe of ration cards, this constitution sanctions a europe of prosperity and material well-being. the european parliament has been a great help to the people of europe, and it is a great help to the people of europe, and it is a great help to the people of europe. this constitution will have and does have the means to make europe count more in the world. i believe that the constitution marks a point of no return and, just as in not too distant times the constitution of my country was the constitution of concord, the one that allowed us to move forward into the future, this european constitution will allow all of us europeans to move forward together in a common project of civilization. the value of the european constitution is to banish ambiguities; it is the first document that defines what the european union is as a union of states and citizens, and it does not weaken the states in the least, because the powers of the union are the powers that come from the states, and it does not weaken the national constitutions, on the contrary: it strengthens them, because the strength of the european constitution derives from the strength of the national constitutions. with this constitution, europe shows that it is much more than a market; it is also, and it is important, but it is much more: it is a project of common civilization based on the religious, cultural and humanist heritage. it is recognised in the first sentence of the preamble, rooted in the values of freedom and human dignity, rooted in the charter of fundamental rights of the person. it is a constitution which also advocates a particular economic system: a capitalist system with a social dimension. if we look at the history of europe, we see that, that was not so obvious fifty years ago. today it is. for all these reasons, mr president, i believe that many of the flags that this parliament has unfurled over the past few years are as high today as those we have back there. i entered this parliament 13 years ago when it was a consultative assembly; it is no longer a consultative assembly. i entered this parliament when the democratic deficit of the european union was being discussed; i believe that with the european constitution we will put an end to the term democratic deficit, because this constitution introduces more democracy, more efficiency, more clarity and more transparency, as my friend richard corbett has very well pointed out. mr president, that is a task for many people over many years. i want to remember them here today. i would like to mention the names of emilio colombo, marcelino oreja, fernand herman, giorgio napolitano, olivier duhamel, antonio seguro, dimitris tsatsos, antoinette spaak, and so many others who, sitting on the benches of this parliament, have defended what is going to be a reality today. they have often been called utopians or dreamers; well, today those dreams, those utopias, are becoming reality. we in this parliament can be very proud of the work we have done. mr president, eight years ago, in this very room, a young member defended the opinion on the amsterdam treaty and said that it was not perfect, we knew that, but it was not the last station, and he recalled, as i shall recall today, a certain miguel de cervantes, disillusioned with life in his last days, who said that there were times when you had to choose between being a road or an inn. that was a path, and that path has led us to where we are today, and i believe that today, in the comfortable inn of the european constitution, europeans will find in the coming years an effective instrument for making europe progress in peace, freedom, justice and solidarity. that is why i would like this parliament to vote very strongly in favour of this document tomorrow, which opens up a new era for our continent. i would like to thank mr schmit for his presence and express our sympathy to him and to the people of luxembourg, who are in a state of national mourning following the death of the former grand duchess.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. mr president, the committee on development of the european parliament expressed its strong support for the constitutional text, considering that it represents historic progress precisely because it assumes, as defining features of the european union, solidarity with those who need it most, development cooperation and responsibility for humanitarian intervention wherever it is required. the committee on development calls for action to ensure that the constitution is ratified and comes into force as soon as possible, and for the involvement of those institutions, ngos and individuals who have made north-south solidarity a fundamental cause of our political activism and social commitment in europe. let us remember that the constitution elevates these values of solidarity, cooperation and humanitarian responsibility to the status of the european union's hallmark, and that they must therefore transcend all policies and guide all community action. the constitution also assumes that the european union will henceforth have the legal personality that we lacked and that will enable it to act as such on the international stage and, more precisely, in the universe of the united nations. we shall thus be making a considerable advance in terms of representativeness, responsibility, effectiveness and potential, which is particularly important for the presence and work of the european union in the third world countries and in the field of cooperation for their development. let us not forget that the eradication of poverty in the world is explicitly included as one of the constitutional objectives of the european union. the european union has a duty to help the victims of the conflict in the region, and the european union has a duty to help the victims of the conflict in the region.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. mr president, for those of us who are working to ensure that the union's financial resources are well spent, this is a good day: all spending will be subject to greater democratic control by parliament and the council, and it will also increase the efficiency of spending, because it increases governance: we are changing vetoes for democracy. that means that we will be able to spend better; and that if the resources given to us by the citizens are spent better, we will have more authority to ask for more resources to develop the policies that the citizens demand from the european union. it is therefore a great day, a day to say a happy 'yes', in these days when we are putting an end to the european project after fifty years with this constitution. there are many advances in this constitution, but as our group chairman, mr poettering, rightly said, there are some things missing. we've been timid in acknowledging our christian roots, we've been timid in acknowledging the obvious. we have just celebrated christmas; this parliament will be sitting in holy week; here in strasbourg the most important building is not a building like this, but a medieval building, a cathedral. we may have been victims of a certain intolerant secularism, but christmas, holy week, strasbourg cathedral will remain, and there are many areas where we have been able to improve. we must therefore say 'yes', because we believe in europe and we are aware that this european project is going to solve the everyday problems of the citizens. we will do it in the best way possible: by spending better, by controlling our expenditure better and by having more democratic and effective policies. our group and i personally say yes to the constitution.
opinion of the committee on regional development i would like to begin, mr president, by congratulating the rapporteurs on their excellent work. i had the honour of being the rapporteur on this report in the committee on regional development and i would like to say that the debate on this subject was very positive and intense, because, among other things, it is necessary to recall the fundamental role of regional and local authorities in the construction of europe. it is also essential to remember that the european constitution recognises local and regional autonomy as an integral part of the national identity of the member states. this means, among other things, that the european constitution guarantees the inviolability of the present borders of the states which make up the present european union. but today, speaking of the constitution and the regions, i also want to denounce the fact that in a region of europe, in a spanish region like the basque country, the nationalist government, which excludes the autonomous community, wants to put in place a plan of rupture, secession and independence, such as the ibarretxe plan, which is a frontal attack on the spanish constitution and the european constitution. because ibarretxe and his government, who call themselves democrats, have made a pact with the murderers of eta and batasuna to carry out this plan; they have made a pact with an organization which is on the european union's list of terrorists, such as batasuna, and the pnv is making a pact and is allying itself with the executioners, with the murderers: in short, with the enemies of europe. i am convinced that this european constitution will also help to put an end to separatist, rupturist and secessionist approaches such as those of the ibarretxe plan, and i am sure that the new european constitution will be an impassable wall to that ibarretxe plan and to all that seeks to dismember the european union.
mr president, madam vice-president of the commission, mr president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to speak in support of the corbett-mendez de vigo report, which is the culmination of a historic process, on behalf of myself and the spanish socialists. there have been two constituent debates in the european union. the first was the debate at the congress of the european movement in 1948, where churchill, reynaud, ramadier, van zeeland, madariaga and adenauer had the opportunity to begin debating a constitution for europe. the second is the one we are concluding today, which has changed the history of a continent where more than a hundred million people died violently between 1914 and 1945 and where, in the present reality, peace is the rule, thanks to a process to which we are giving its true dimension with this constitution, in which fundamental, shared values are expressed, enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights, with a common citizenship and a union based on citizens and states: a secular union and a union with ambitious objectives that have already been mentioned here. mr president, let me refer to my country, which is the first to hold a referendum on ratification of the constitution, with a public and open debate which we believe is important for everyone. it is true that the zapatero government, by winning the elections on 14 march, unblocked the process of adopting the constitution, but i want to say here - and i do not see any member of the spanish popular party, so i ask the vice-president of the commission, mrs grossetête, to convey this to her on my behalf - that the convention began with a presidency of the spanish council of government by mr aznar, and it was he who called for the referendum. i therefore believe and hope that the spanish people's party will also give decisive support to this whole process - the epp's support is guaranteed. i believe that this will enable us to have a referendum which will really set a positive pace for other referendums in the other states which have called them and that there will be a real public and open debate. i would like to conclude by saying that this is the culmination of a process in which europe has been built with passion and with reason, and that has led it to change history.
mr president, any position on the european constitution must be based on a balance between what this constitution says and what it does not say – something that is not perhaps properly underlined in the report we are voting on at this part-session. this leads me to say 'yes' to this constitution because of what it represents and because it means a new step forward on the way to a stronger and more efficient, more transparent, more democratic europe. with this constitution, europe will have a stronger voice in the world. citizens will get better protection of their fundamental rights. their freedom and security will be better defended. moreover, our values, including those which are behind our social and economic model, will be strongly proclaimed and protected to allow europe's growth and, simultaneously, to protect europe's social cohesion. but that does not prevent me from acknowledging that the text reflects the unfortunate bias of some political majorities that existed in europe at the time when it was drafted. i particularly regret that it reflects a virtual europe, a europe that is not the real europe, a europe that does not exist in political terms, where everything that lies between individual citizens and states is just ignored. peoples in europe, regions, and their political role in the construction of a diverse and plural europe have simply been neglected, have been passed over in silence in this text. but this is just not the reality of the europe we are all building here together. what is worse, some languages, such as my own – catalan – which are mr president, as this report very well shows, the draft constitution has three basic aspects: firstly, the values and objectives of the union, the unity and equality of its peoples, and the protection of the diversity of its cultures, identities and languages; secondly, the rights, interests and duties of citizens; and thirdly, rules for the institutions and for the european political game. the first two aspects - values and rights - define the european democracy we want, based on the diversity and freedom of peoples, their progress and equality. the third aspect - and this must be clear: the rules of the game - is the result of compromises between the right and the left, between federalists and intergovernmentalists; it must be clear that it refers to these rules, not to the policies that must be developed. in this sense, the constitution is not an endpoint but a starting point for overcoming europe's economic and social weakness, its weak capacity for innovation, research and development and its insufficient international weight. we must move towards a european government, overcoming the currently dominant method of intergovernmental coordination and its impotence, as shown by the failure to implement the lisbon strategy or the divisions in the face of the invasion of iraq. with this prospect of future progress we will call for a vote in favour of the european constitution.

vice-president of the commission. according to article 34 of the treaty on european union, framework decisions are binding upon the member states as to the result to be achieved but leave to the national authorities the choice of form and methods. however, framework decisions 'shall not entail direct effect'. whereas, within the first pillar, the commission has the authority to initiate an infringement procedure against a member state, this possibility does not exist within the treaty on european union. the situation described by the honourable member certainly does not facilitate the commission's role, but it does not prevent it from producing a broad range of policy initiatives, which have been the basis for the policy definition of the union in the important area of the fight against terrorism. the commission has been playing this role very actively in establishing in june 2004 the revised action plan on combating terrorism, in updating it in december 2004 and in implementing more than half of the respective measures. this is also evident from the submission, in october 2004, of four communications covering different aspects of the prevention, preparedness and response to terrorist attacks and from the adoption, in the same year, of a communication on mutual access to data relevant to the fight against terrorism and of several classified documents in the field of consequence management and the protection of critical infrastructures. the commission in general and president barroso and i in particular are determined to work in close cooperation with council presidencies to maintain the fight against terrorism. this is very high on the agenda of the council, including that of the jha council and the european council comprising the heads of state and government.

the next item is the statements by the council and the commission on the consequences of the tsunami of 26 december 2004.
counsel. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr president of the commission, the unprecedented disaster of 26 december last has affected 12 countries and has so far caused the death of more than 160 000 people, not to mention the thousands of missing, the many injured and the millions - we are talking about five - of displaced or homeless people. children, now orphaned or isolated from their families, are particularly vulnerable in this environment. the health situation is very worrying and the damage to property is beyond calculation. the luxembourg presidency, in close cooperation with the dutch presidency, reacted to the scale of the disaster as soon as 26 december, visiting the site with the commission on 1 january. the luxembourg minister for health contacted and met with officials of the who and the international red cross on 1 january. on the basis of these initial contacts with the united nations and the countries concerned, and also following the enlarged extraordinary summit in jakarta, the presidency called for a general affairs and external relations council on 7 january, which brought together a large number of ministers for foreign affairs, ministers for cooperation and ministers for health. the council of 7 january reaffirmed the european union's solidarity with the countries affected and with the people of those countries, thanking them - this is very important - for the support they have given to the european nationals on the ground at the time of the disaster. the council also paid tribute to the general spirit of solidarity shown by civil society and citizens. the council took stock of the many initiatives taken by the commission and the member states, and of the coordination of the european union's vital assistance. together we have considered how best to respond to the urgent financial, material and health situation and the necessary and sufficient financial and operational resources for the successive phases of rehabilitation and reconstruction. officials from the un agencies were invited to participate in the council: they were members of ocha, who and also unicef. they provided the council with additional information on the situation on the ground, on the measures taken and on the assessment of future needs. the united nations' leading role in coordinating aid in this context was loudly reaffirmed on this occasion. the council's immediate main results are as follows: on the financial side, the council announced that the combined official assistance of the european union and the member states to the tsunami victims - emergency aid and reconstruction aid - currently amounts to around eur 1.5 billion. however, the council also stressed that this effort must not lead to the general problem of humanitarian aid development and the millennium development goals, particularly in africa, being forgotten, nor must it reduce resources for this purpose. on the health front, the member states were invited to join forces under the auspices of the who to prevent the risk of epidemics and to set up health infrastructures by sending appropriate medical equipment and teams. the european union and its member states will support the who. turning now to longer-term measures, the council expressed the wish that the european union's capacity to cope with major disasters should be strengthened and indicated its willingness to provide itself with the following instruments. firstly, a prevention strategy, an early warning system and a rapid response to disasters, in preparation for the world conference on disaster reduction, to be held in kobe, japan, from 18 to 22 january. secondly, improvement of the civil protection and humanitarian aid mechanism and of analytical capacities. the council wishes to develop the european union's rapid response capabilities by establishing appropriate planning, coordination and resource mobilisation structures. thirdly, the strengthening of consular cooperation. fourthly, there are other measures which the council will have to consider, in particular the development of a rapid response capacity of the european union, namely a rapid early warning system. secondly, it will assess the setting up of a european voluntary humanitarian aid corps and, thirdly, it will strengthen the coordination of the european union in the areas of rescue, evacuation and the delivery of food and medical care. i am also thinking of trade support measures and bilateral partnerships, including twinning of cities, hospitals, etc. and finally, an adjustment of the debt service of the affected countries who wish to do so. this should be on the agenda of the ecofin council next week. the general affairs council on 31 january will review all the measures and paths envisaged by the union and the member states in the medium and long term with a view to drawing up an operational action plan for the union. on the evening of 7 january, mrs benita ferrero-waldmer, the european commissioner responsible, and the ministers responsible for health and cooperation, as well as myself, briefed a very important delegation from your parliament. this week the presidency and the commission will continue to engage in intensive dialogue with the competent bodies of the european parliament with a view to implementing the union's financial commitments, and i hope that we will be able to put into practice some of the lines we outlined at the general affairs council on 7 january at the general affairs council on 31 january. (applause) i would like to thank
president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the scale of the disaster in south asia makes us reflect seriously on the fragility of human life in the face of the forces of nature and on how irrelevant other issues become when compared with a human tragedy of this magnitude. it also calls into question the essence of political action at national and european level to deal with the consequences of natural disasters such as this one. and this is the right time to reflect on our instruments and our policies, on the ways in which we coordinate our efforts and on how we allocate responsibilities between national authorities and european institutions. my trip to jakarta last week brought me into contact with the true scale of the tragedy caused by this earthquake and the tsunami that followed. i was also able to confirm that the international community, including the european union and the european commission, were able to respond quickly by raising substantial amounts of aid and other support. what commissioner michel saw when he was on the ground was shocking. the giant wave completely wiped out human presence along 500 kilometers of coast, destroying everything in its path, even reaching places more than five kilometers inland, and the most tragic thing is that most of the population lived exactly in this coastal area that was completely wiped out. equally disturbing stories come from sri lanka, thailand, india, the maldives, not to mention the devastation in other less accessible countries that are only now becoming known, and the fact that this tragedy has reached the shores of africa. this huge natural disaster leaves behind 150,000 dead, over five million homeless, traumatized people who now face the challenge of reuniting what is left of their devastated families, rebuilding their homes, rebuilding their economic activities, trying to finally start their lives over again.
i am grateful to both the council and the commission for the complete information they have given us on this tragic event; in particular, i would like to expressly acknowledge the perfect coordination which the president of the commission has maintained with the presidency of parliament during the meetings which have followed, and in particular, i would also like to thank him for having added two members of this parliament to the delegation to the geneva conference, which will undoubtedly help us to carry out the work of each institution in a more coordinated and rapid manner.

mr president, i would like to record our dismay, our grief, our solidarity and our commitment to help alleviate the consequences of the catastrophe. the main points of the socialist group are contained in the joint resolution, which we shall vote for with conviction and which can be summed up in seven points. firstly, the positive assessment of the correct action of the council and the commission, which reacted immediately to the disaster and committed the necessary resources and informed parliament - although there is a lack of information, a lack of communication with society, which may lead some of our colleagues to say that there has been no one on the ground, when it has been acting admirably. secondly, the resources committed by all must be made effective immediately and within a fixed timetable. thirdly, all the resources of the european union must be fresh money, in no way detracted from other programmes; we have not been convinced by president barroso's arguments in this respect. fourthly, the commitment to combine emergency action with essential reconstruction action, in agreement with the main actors, the countries concerned. fifthly, the commitment to set up an early warning system which is actually capable of preventing disasters like this. sixthly, the commitment also to set up a permanent and professional disaster response mechanism which is able to intervene when prevention is out of date. and an important reference point in the constitution is the creation of the humanitarian aid volunteer corps. seventhly, all these actions cannot be the result of one-off actions, of coalitions led by one or another country, but must be the result of mobilization within the framework of the united nations, with the active participation of the european union and with visibility of that participation. the european union, mr president, must rise to the occasion of the tragedy and the mobilization that has taken place in our societies.
mr president, the high number of fatalities resulting from the disaster is undoubtedly due to the enormous vulnerability of the people in the region. i therefore believe that we have a responsibility which is also an opportunity. it is a question of dealing seriously with the question of the debt to the countries concerned. in some cases, moreover, this debt was contracted by dictatorial and corrupt governments, such as suharto's indonesia, to whom money was left unscrupulously, giving rise to what is now called odious debt. there is therefore a responsibility on the part of certain donors which should be investigated first and then taken up. the opportunity here is twofold: if on the one hand it is absolutely urgent to proceed to the immediate cancellation of this debt - not as an act of compassion, but as a recognition that people who have already suffered because of irresponsible regimes should not suffer twice as much by having to pay their debts in addition - on the other hand it is necessary that international aid be based mainly on donations and not consist of new credits that increase the weight of this debt even more.
mr president, i think the first thing to do - as i said at the meeting of the joint committees on foreign affairs, development and budgets - is to express our appreciation for the reaction of the european institutions and, in particular, of the commission, which we so often criticise and which i believe has lived up to the serious circumstances and the example set by civil society. i think the most urgent thing at the moment is to try to help the victims who still need water, food and hospitals and who need communications restored. on the other hand, as commissioner benita ferrero-waldner said in her speech, we must have a plan for rehabilitation and reconstruction in which a whole series of budgetary resources must be mobilised, especially in the form of additional resources, as mr van den berg rightly said a moment ago. i think the european union has done the right thing; now it is a matter of establishing an effective aid package for the victims. it is particularly important to me, mr president, and i would ask the commission representative to convey this to his colleague, the commissioner responsible for transport, that it is incredible that there is still no common system for preventing tidal waves at european union level. this is a very cheap system and i believe that the european union, in the field of aid to developing countries, to the countries of the african, caribbean and pacific convention and to the countries of the mediterranean basin, could offer it under really very interesting conditions to prevent this kind of catastrophe. i believe, mr president, that the resolution which this parliament is going to adopt tomorrow is a good one, because it refers to the solidarity shown by the local populations, to the witness of solidarity and support they have given to the families of the european union who have been victims of this tragedy.
counsel. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european security strategy confirms the unique and irreplaceable nature of the transatlantic relationship. the european union and the united states, acting together, can be a formidable force for our common values in the world. the november european council conclusions recall the shared responsibility of the european union and the united states in the face of the most important challenges, such as terrorism, the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, the middle east peace process and the eradication of poverty in the world. the luxembourg presidency is firmly committed to implementing these conclusions. i am sure that the debate taking place today in this parliament will help us to achieve this. relations between europe and america are based on shared interests and the promotion of common values, such as freedom, democracy and human rights. they also benefit from the unique interdependence of their economies. all these factors explain why, even at the worst of the recent crisis over iraq, transatlantic cooperation has continued on most major issues, whether the balkans, the middle east peace process, the fight against terrorism or non-proliferation. despite some pointed differences, economic relations have continued to develop. the united states and the european union share a great responsibility for international economic and monetary stability. the very recent agreement on aircraft construction shows that we can resolve our differences in this spirit of cooperation and partnership. the balance sheet of the relationship has been and remains extremely positive, but it is nevertheless true that it must adapt to a threefold evolution. the president of the european council insisted this morning that the status quo was not a credible option. first, the end of the cold war fundamentally changed the international situation. in the face of the soviet threat, transatlantic unity was dictated by considerations of mere survival. today there is a greater element of choice and political will. the tragedy of 9/11 changed the way america perceives the world. it also requires us to revise our definition of collective security. this obviously affects relations between the united states and the rest of the world, including the european union. the internal transformation of the european union towards a more political union with a common foreign and security policy, a common currency and an area of justice and freedom is inevitably reflected in the relationship with america. it changes the quality and intensity of our relationships. the combination of these factors means that of the three major components of the relationship with the us - nato, bilateral relations and eu-us relations - it is the third which is gaining momentum. president bush's visit to the european union on 22 february is of particular importance in this context. the presidency intends to use this opportunity to union. this visit must be well prepared and i will listen very carefully to the suggestions of the honourable members on this subject. we are advocating a pragmatic and constructive approach, but also middle east. resolving it is a vital issue for the parties to the conflict, but also for europe and the united states. we are working on this, as part of the quartet, with the americans, the united if their methods and approaches differ: to prevent that country from developing nuclear weapons. the european union has entered into more comprehensive negotiations with iran, which we hope will be very successful, and not just in the nuclear field. the results that emerge will be or can be a great success of european foreign policy and its approach. finally, the disaster in asia, which we have just discussed, has clearly illustrated the need for good cooperation between the european union and the united states in the face of such disasters. the recognition of the central role of the united nations in coordinating aid, which many of you have noted and which was immediately championed by the european union, was an encouraging signal because the americans were quick to agree. there are many areas where washington and brussels share broadly the same views, whether on the lasting stabilisation of the balkans, afghanistan, the main aspects of the fight against terrorism, which must reconcile the requirements of freedom and security, the relaunch of the doha round, etc. in other areas - we have to accept this - shared objectives coexist with different approaches, as in the case relationship over the coming years. this debate today is both timely and welcome. i would like to start by stating two simple and irrefutable facts. first, eu-us relations are truly unique and irreplaceable. second, the balance sheet of the transatlantic relationship is fundamentally positive. on the economic front, we have the largest trade and investment relationship in the world, with global priorities. it must also adapt to changes within the european union. we are convinced that as the enlarged eu's foreign policy strengthens, so too will the scope and intensity of our relations with the united states. in essence, the european union and the united states are both founded on the same principles and values: respect for the rule of law, democracy, human rights and of course free market economies. we also share many common interests, such as the fight against terrorism, promoting solutions to regional conflicts, dealing with third countries, improving transatlantic economic relations, concluding the wto doha round, and creating global prosperity. in many cases, we share the same strategy for implementing those goals. in others, although we share the same goals, we have together to help put iraq on the road to democracy, peace, prosperity and stability. third, we share the objective of preventing iran from developing nuclear weapons capability and we should both do our best to ensure that iran fully implements the paris agreement. doubtless many of you have the feeling that we could do more and work better together. the commission shares that feeling. in order on behalf of the group. mr president, i think that this debate on transatlantic relations should be stripped of all its ideological foliage and focused, as the representative of the presidency-in-office has rightly said, on trying to transform the discord of the past into the harmony of the present. the european union and the united states share a common history, common values and a common passion for freedom, and that is because the transatlantic bond is written into the european union's genetic code. it is clear - and the commission and the council have both said so - that there are differences between us, such as the international criminal court, the kyoto protocol, laws with extraterritorial effect or trade policy, to which the commissioner referred a moment ago. but i think we need to put a lot more emphasis on what unites us than what divides us. and it is clear that the objectives which we are pursuing as the european union - and the president-in-office of the council said so - in terms of peace, stability, the fight against terrorism, weapons of mass destruction, and so on, we can achieve much better in cooperation with the united states than by standing up against them - as commissioner patten said in one of his last speeches - in the same way that the united states can achieve its objectives better in cooperation with the european union than in contradiction to it. the united states is an admirable people; it represents 3% of the world's population and is capable of producing 30% of the world's goods and services, and has succeeded in becoming a political, economic and military superpower today, unlike anything since the roman empire. i believe that president bush's forthcoming visit is a great opportunity to restore this strategic alliance, this harmonious tandem between the european union and the united states, and to ensure that the values we both defend - human rights and fundamental freedoms, among others - are upheld in all regions of the world, can be consolidated and can be really effective.
counsel. the honourable member will recall that the council has already expressed on several occasions its emotion at the human tragedies that result from certain attempts to enter the european union illegally. the hague programme, adopted by the european council on 4 and 5 november 2004, also addresses this problem and calls for increased cooperation between member states. in this connection, the council would like to mention the european agency for the management of operational cooperation at the external borders of the member states of the european union. on 26 october 2004, the council adopted a regulation establishing the agency, which will start its activities on 1 may 2005. the agency shall facilitate the application of existing and future community provisions on the management of the external borders by ensuring coordination of the actions of the member states in the implementation of those provisions. in addition, in 2002 the council adopted a comprehensive plan to combat illegal immigration and trafficking in human beings in the european union and an integrated management plan for the external borders of the member states of the european union. the implementation of these plans is a priority for the council and the member states, which have intensified their operational cooperation through a series of joint operations and pilot projects. a key role was given to the joint body of external border officials, which coordinated the implementation of the operations provided for in the plans. two centres have been set up under this joint body to coordinate operations and joint measures to be implemented at sea and in ports: the western and the eastern maritime frontiers centres, located in spain and greece respectively. both centres have carried out operations to combat illegal immigration by sea. the council would also like to draw the attention of the honourable member to the programme of measures to combat illegal immigration by sea in the member states of the european union, which was adopted on 27 november 2003. this programme comprises a series of measures aimed at developing as rapidly as possible a coordinated and effective management of maritime borders. it also stressed the importance of strengthening international relations with third countries of origin or transit for illegal immigrant flows. i would also like to draw your attention to the fact that the informal meeting of the jha council will be mainly concerned with these questions. on 2 december 2004, the council adopted conclusions on the evaluation of the progress made in the implementation of the programme of measures to combat illegal immigration by sea in the member states of the union. the council noted that progress had been made in implementing this programme, but it also concluded that further progress was needed in the operational and legislative measures. the council also confirmed the need to strengthen cooperation with third countries, drawing on the experience gained by the various member states. the council suggested that this cooperation cover all aspects of illegal immigration, such as return and readmission, the fight against trafficking in human beings and networks linked to it, as well as all forms of illegal immigration, border management and capacity building in immigration control.

commission. mr president, in the framework of its political dialogue with china, and more recently on the occasion of the 7th bilateral eu-china summit held in the hague on 8 december 2004, the eu has constantly addressed the issue of the safeguard of the rights of minorities, especially as regards tibet. it has, in particular, urged the chinese authorities to preserve the cultural, religious and linguistic identity of the tibetan people. these issues have also been systematically dealt with in the context of the eu-china bilateral dialogue on human rights. during this dialogue, the eu has regularly brought to the attention of the chinese authorities, at every session, and most recently in beijing on 24 september 2004, the situation of individuals who have been sentenced for having expressed their opinion or their beliefs. the case of tenzin deleg rinpoche is one such case. at the beginning of 2004, the eu made an official démarche in beijing to request information on his whereabouts and state of health, expressed the hope that the death sentence would not be upheld and asked for judicial review of the case. more recently, on 15 november, the eu troika made a new ad hoc démarche in beijing, during which the case of tenzin deleg rinpoche was again highlighted. the eu is fully committed to urging china not to carry out the sentence and is prepared to contribute, in this respect, to finding an acceptable solution to the case under examination. it takes the view that the application of the death penalty to tenzin deleg rinpoche would send out a very negative signal and would have an adverse impact on relations with china. we have just learned that the luxembourg presidency - and the commission immediately contacted it - is currently preparing a démarche that would also associate the commission. the démarche will be sent to china asking it not to administer the death penalty and to re-examine the case. on a more general level, the eu has called for years, and will continue to call, as part of its overall policies vis-à-vis tibet, for the establishment of a direct dialogue between the dalai lama and the chinese authorities as the only realistic way of finding a lasting solution to the question of tibet. in this context, we consider the recent third visit to china of the dalai lama’s special envoys to be an encouraging sign of progress. in the dialogue with china, the eu has regularly expressed concern over the extensive use of the death penalty. while reaffirming our longstanding position in favour of abolition, we have continued to press hard for at least the introduction of a moratorium. we have also stressed the need to comply, in the fight against terrorism, with the basic principles governing international relations and safeguarding human rights.

interviews were fundamental in trying to put the future of palestine in perspective and to find out, in the best possible way, how europeans can contribute to the solution of the historical problems ladies and gentlemen, on three points: firstly, how i see the situation in palestine; secondly, how i see it from the israeli perspective; and thirdly, how it seems to me that we should move forward, from the european perspective, to support a peace process which, in my view, must acquire a faster pace, a greater speed and a greater determination. ladies and gentlemen, from the palestinian point of view i would like to be able to show you, or share with you, the mood of the palestinian people on the day of the vote and in the days that followed. if i may, i would sum up the feeling i had in those days there, in palestine, whether in ramallah or in gaza, in two words. the first word is pride: pride in having been able to manage a difficult crisis very well; a crisis that when it started, with the arrival of president arafat in paris, they really did not know how it would end. they have done it extraordinarily well and with great maturity, and i think that the international community and we europeans must take note of the capacity and the good work of a society which is proudly capable of doing things well. and, alongside this feeling of pride, there is a normal feeling of hope; hope that we must be able to nurture, that we cannot allow to be lost through lack of political action, either by israel or by the international community. ladies and gentlemen, the most difficult time we are going to have to live through is probably from now until the months of july, august, or maybe even september. during that time period very important events are yet to be celebrated. perhaps the most important from the palestinian point of view are the legislative elections. the presidency elections are perhaps sometimes the easiest; the legislative elections are going to be more complex, they are going to require perhaps more detailed preparation on our part, and, as you know, they are going to be held with an electoral law which has a majority component and a proportional component as well. the various political groups in palestinian political life as a whole will therefore be able to participate. it would be very important for all of us, especially for us and for the palestinian people, that those who want the peace process, those who want to move forward along the path that president abu mazen made very clear in the election campaign, should be in the majority. during the election campaign, president abu mazen said some very courageous things, which we have heard and applauded: issues relating to the violent intifada, the peace process and his willingness to dialogue. we must recognize that what president abu mazen has done, both during the election campaign and in the first days after taking office, is truly extraordinary. he had the courage to say the things that had to be said and he said it well, and he has not only said it, but he has done it; he has begun to implement the measures that he said he would apply during the election campaign. the need for support for this process on the part of the international community and the european union is therefore absolutely essential. let me tell you that this feeling, which i want to share with you, is not only found in the hierarchy, in the presidency or in the men who lead the palestinian authority at this hour. civil society has the same feeling. i had the opportunity to meet with civil society leaders in ramallah and see that they had and shared the same feelings, the feeling of hope and the feeling of pride, that goes from entrepreneurs to teachers, from doctors to people who work in the administration. so we have an obligation to do our best to maintain these feelings of pride and hope. ladies and gentlemen, in order to give you an idea of the situation in the territories and the amount of work that needs to be done, let me tell you a very small anecdote from a meeting i had with a group of businessmen, businessmen who are honestly working in ramallah or gaza and who are trying to help economic development, in very difficult conditions. one of them said to me, "if i have to take a container of tomatoes and take it, for example, from ramallah to gaza, it costs me twice as much as it costs to import the same container from hamburg, germany, to gaza, and it costs me half the time: two and a half weeks late to take the container from ramallah to gaza, and practically in a day or a day and a half it arrives from hamburg to gaza". that is the economic situation that even those people who want to help the economic recovery of the country are experiencing. so there is a lot to be done from all points of view, from the political to the economic. and let this be an example so that those of you who have not visited the area can see the situation. in gaza, ladies and gentlemen, the situation is much more serious. very few people have been to gaza lately; i spent a whole day in gaza, meeting with the political forces as well as with civil society and, now that we are talking about disengagement, withdrawal from gaza, we have to know that gaza is practically at this moment a zone, i would not say totally destroyed, but a zone that, since the last time i was, six months ago, has changed radically. it's a situation of very deep poverty, a situation of very great destruction, visiting either the northern part, the part that borders israel, the southern part, the so-called "philadelphia corridor", or the city itself, the capital gaza, the historic city of gaza. so this is the situation we find ourselves in. but he said it's going to be a very important time between now and summer. why would you do that? the palestinians themselves have decided to hold elections in the fundamental organization, the organization which is the heart of the palestine liberation organization, which is fatah. fatah will also hold elections in the summer, which will undoubtedly mean a change in the palestinian representative structures and, certainly, a generational change also in the palestinian authorities themselves. ladies and gentlemen, it is worthwhile to take these brushstrokes to get a handle on the situation we find ourselves in from the palestinian point of view. if i wanted you to remember one expression, i would like it to be the one i said before: pride in what has been done and hope for what remains to be done. ladies and gentlemen, let me now briefly tell you what i found in israel after having interviewed all the political leaders, from prime minister sharon, the foreign minister, the minister of defence, the defence services and also society itself. as you know, on the same day as the elections in palestine, there was a change of government in israel; a change of government which, as you know, was elected practically "by the hair", in the spanish expression of chastity; two votes of difference were in favour of prime minister sharon for the government to leave. so, although there is a pro-peace majority in palestinian society and in israeli society, which is gradually growing, in the knesset, the parliament, there is still such a deep division that prime minister sharon did not have the fourteen votes of the majority party, his likud party, and the new government had to be elected with the votes of a separate minority party, the party of yosi beilin, and with the abstention of two members of an arab party, who abstained in order to help the government go. that is the situation of potential governmental instability that israel finds itself in. but the most important issue, which we also have before us from israel's point of view, is what we might call the abandonment of gaza. the abandonment of gaza, which we europeans have already said on what conditions we would support, and on those conditions we will support it, and i think the conditions will become clearer in these circumstances. as you know, the conditions we have put for a long time are that this process which is called the disengagement from gaza, to use the english word, has to be part of the final peace agreement that we all have in our dreams and in our minds and that it must end with the two states. the exit from gaza must not be the end of a process, but the beginning of a process that must lead to its completion, which is to end the occupation of the territories. from that point of view, it is also very important to know the timetable along which this disengagement from gaza will take place. the timing is almost identical to the palestinian election calendar. what we have yet to vote on - we shall see if it comes to fruition by the end of march - is the approval of the budget; we have to see whether there is a sufficient majority for the budget to be approved by the knesset and, if approved by the knesset, the disengagement process, the exit from gaza would take place at the end of august or the beginning of september. so, ladies and gentlemen, if you could overlap the situation in palestine and the situation in israel on a map, from the point of view of their respective calendars, the two calendars would practically overlap. we are therefore facing a situation of great delicacy, of great difficulty, but at the same time, as i said earlier, full of hope and goodwill on the part of the majority of the political actors who have a definitive role to play. ladies and gentlemen, you can imagine that in order to maintain the hope expressed by the palestinians, in order to maintain this sense of pride, it is absolutely necessary that things start to move, and this means that there is action on the part of the palestinians, which has already been taken, and president abu mazen has taken very important decisions in recent days to try to stop those acts of violence which prevented the resumption of negotiations and dialogue between palestinians and israelis. thanks to these measures, there has been a first meeting today, after the previous ones were suspended, between the heads of the cabinets of prime minister sharon and minister erekat, a meeting which, as i have just been told, was a positive one and which gives some hope that there is a possibility of resuming contacts between the palestinians and the israelis. if all goes well, there will be a new palestinian government in two weeks, prime minister abu allah has it practically finished, and the agreement between president abu mazen and prime minister sharon to have a first high-level meeting once the government is formed. that is also the position of the friends of israel, who are prepared to remain in the security situation in which we are living. the efforts of president abu mazen have made it possible to hold this meeting and to open a dialogue between the two parties, which will lead to a somewhat clearer political horizon than we have had so far. why is it essential that there be a political horizon? without a political horizon it will be very difficult for the citizens of palestine to maintain the feeling of hope and pride in what they have done, and that it is useful. for this, as i said earlier, there must be a political horizon which the israeli leaders must offer. ladies and gentlemen, i do not think that a window of hope has been opened, nor a door of hope. i would go further: i believe that a path of hope has been opened, an avenue of hope that we must make possible so that it can be walked, walked, taken to the end. and the end we all know what it is: the end is two states, a viable, democratic palestinian state that can live side by side with the state of israel, so that there is not only peace between israel and palestine, but also influence over the whole region. i can tell you that this is the dream of every palestinian citizen, i believe it is the dream of many israelis and certainly the dream of all european citizens, and in particular of all those who have devoted much of their lives to trying to find a final solution to this terrible problem, which has consequences not only for those who suffer most directly but also for those who live farther away. i would like to say, and i want to say it again, that for some countries the problems of the middle east are considered strategic problems. for us, these are not just strategic problems. for europeans, they are also neighbourhood problems; what is happening in the middle east concerns us, and not only for strategic reasons, as i said, but also for reasons of proximity. the middle east is our neighborhood, they are our neighbors, as well as being our friends. we must therefore stress once again that we europeans have a great responsibility. we are already working from day one, both with the team of prime minister abu allah and president abu mazen, and with the team of prime minister sharon, to see how we can do the two things i told you earlier, which are fundamental: to change the situation on the ground and to try to give a political perspective, which cannot be other than to return as quickly as possible to the roadmap, which is what we all agreed, the international community, to be able to move towards that dream. what of sad remembrance for all mankind. on a day like today in 1945, red army soldiers liberated the nazi death camp whose name has been etched in the collective memory of mankind. it has been etched in our collective memory as the name of absolute horror, of evil in its most extreme form, of planned, industrialized and documented crime. how that could happen still amazes us all today. but it did. it's unimaginable, but it was real. today a delegation from this parliament, comprising the chairmen of all the political groups, the largest of the delegations to auschwitz, will take part in the ceremony of homage to those victims, together with former prisoners, heads of state and government from many countries and some of the soldiers who liberated the camp. in this way we will pay tribute to the victims, but above all we will remember that evil which led to the death of millions of jews for the simple fact of being jews, of ethnic minorities, of homosexuals and of political prisoners of various nationalities. it's an evil that affects us all. of course to the victims and their descendants, but also to those who were not there, who cannot remember because they did not meet him. auschwitz must bring to our minds the battle of memory against oblivion, the battle of memory against what we wish had never happened, because people who forget their history are doomed to repeat it. the holocaust is a great problem of all mankind. not just a problem of the nazi murderer and the jewish victim. it has its roots deeply rooted in some of the characteristics that have, many times, given rise to its horrible image in human history. today, 60 years later, we have to continue to fight against everything that made it possible: racism, anti-semitism, xenophobia, inter-racial hatred, the indifference of a part of our society, which thinks that it is not good for it, until it realizes that it is, that it also affects it, but then it is too late. that is why, and so as not to forget, we shall also be voting today on a resolution on the memory of the holocaust and anti-semitism. ladies and gentlemen, we have an obligation to work every day, not just when the magic of round figures, 60 years - why 60 and not 59? - brings back memories, every day, so that the values of our constitution - peace, human rights, respect and tolerance - the complete opposite of what was lived in auschwitz, are propagated and defended in schools, at work, on the stairs, on the street, in the bar, in the permanent coexistence of one another. remembering auschwitz gives us an opportunity to defend the values of our constitution and, by taking this opportunity, to defend human dignity, so terribly sullied in that place. ladies and gentlemen, i would ask you to gather for a minute of silence.
