mr president, the rapporteur, mr goebbels, laments the lack of coordination of economic policies, a complaint which i agree with, but which leads to a different conclusion. without these coordination rules, the flexibility of the stability pact is tantamount to its breaking down, and breaking down the stability pact will mean sterilising the efforts of the central bank to maintain prices, it will mean raising interest rates, it will mean a delay in growth, which is what we all want, a delay in the implementation of structural reforms and, what is more dangerous, a serious attack on the welfare state. the resources we allocate to paying interest and paying off the public debt will be less than the resources we have to guarantee finances. what is needed at the moment is more employment and more productivity. more employment means, above all, paying attention to those groups who are having the most difficulty, and we know that these are women, young people between 15 and 25 years of age and those over 55. and more productivity means more investment, more effort in investment and development and more effort in education and vocational training to increase productivity of labor. the commissioner's speech also reminds me - and i quote mr goebbels again - of those speeches from the soviet union, which said that the transition to socialism would inevitably end the following year. when they realized that this transition was possible, they concluded that the transition was over and they had reached communism. a few years later, the iron curtain fell. there is no need to weaken macroeconomic stability, but there is a great need to continue to insist more strongly, more vigorously, on structural reforms which are the only guarantee, the only serious recipe, for growth.
mr president, i agree with the analysis you have made here this morning that europe needs more growth and more jobs. more growth to meet the challenges we face as europeans: the challenge of enlargement, the challenge of providing jobs for our young people and women. more growth so that europe can play its rightful leading role in the world economy, otherwise the world economy will not have balanced growth. that means, as mr rasmussen has just stressed, that european consumers, european investors, need more confidence, they need confidence policies, policies, in short, on which to base their consumption and investment decisions. that confidence, in turn, requires a clean-up of public finances and a balanced budget. balanced budgets mean less taxation for workers and for small and mediumsized enterprises, less taxation to compete successfully in the globalised world economy. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we need structural reforms alongside this firm stability pact. we need a more flexible economy, which is not, in short, an economy that is betting on the few, but a balanced economy that supports our growth on flexibility and competitiveness.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the protection of biodiversity is undoubtedly a political priority for the commission and the successful implementation of the natura 2000 framework is the cornerstone of the european union's efforts to achieve this objective. as mr florenz has pointed out, securing adequate funding for natura 2000 is therefore one of our first priorities. i fully agree with the objectives and priorities of the european parliament. i would also like to point out that this priority is shared by many of my colleagues in the commission who agreed and adapted the regional, agricultural and other funds to include natura 2000 in the funding. member states have a legal obligation and commitment to manage natura 2000 sites exclusively. the provision of financial resources for this management is the responsibility of the member states but, in addition, the commission, precisely because of the special nature of natura 2000, has community co-financing. the use of these community funds is the responsibility of the member states, but we are prepared to offer all possible assistance to facilitate access to them. if it is found that the management of the areas is not sufficiently supported, the commission is prepared to refer the member state concerned to the european court of justice. in view of this, the commission adopted, as mr florenz said, last year, on 15 july 2004, a communication on the financing of natura 2000. it examined all possible scenarios, including the creation of a separate fund, and concluded that the most effective approach was to integrate natura 2000 funding into existing community financial instruments. the new structural fund regulations, which are now being discussed in the council, will be implemented by the member states and the regions on a decentralised basis. there is therefore no possibility of setting a specific amount within any fund. it is also not possible at present to know what amounts may be allocated per year for the co-financing of natura 2000 sites in the period 2007-2013. this is because, under the principle of subsidiarity, it is up to each member state to decide on the needs of these areas when drawing up its national programme. the commission does, however, have the means to ensure that natura 2000 is given priority within these national programmes. i shall come back to this at the end of my speech. first, a few comments on the new regulations under discussion: the commission's proposal for a regulation on the european regional development fund, which is to be adopted by the council in december, is to be based on the principle of subsidiarity, and is to be based on the principle of subsidiarity. there are also possibilities for co-financing from the cohesion fund and european social fund regulations, in particular to strengthen administrative capacity in relation to natura 2000. natura 2000 is also included - and this is important - in the second axis for land management of the new rural development regulation, which will have 25% of its total. the commission proposes a total of €22 billion for land management over the period 2007-13. it is necessary - and here, mr florenz, i would like the support of the european parliament - to preserve this amount and, if possible, to increase it. the european parliament's support in this matter is therefore of paramount importance. the new regulations contain mechanisms which allow the commission, as i said earlier, to provide guidance and to control to some extent the content of the programmes to be submitted by the member states. immediately after the adoption of the proposed regulations on the structural funds, which is likely to take place towards the end of the spring, the commission will set out in detail its specific priorities for funding all the funds in a document on strategic guidelines. in accordance with the practice followed, the contents of this document will be the subject of consultations with all the departments concerned, including the directorate-general for the environment. this consultation will ensure that natura 2000 co-financing is included as a priority. following the strategic guidelines, member states should prepare national strategic frameworks, around the second half of 2005 or early 2006, as well as operational programmes to be submitted to the commission. all the commission departments concerned will be involved in the consultation on the content of these programmes. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment and the environment of natural habitats is a very good one. in particular, with regard to the national rural development programmes, for which mr florenz said earlier that there would be a competitive relationship, each programme submitted will be examined in detail to ensure that it takes account of both the community legislative framework and policy priorities on issues such as biodiversity, the management of natura 2000 sites, climate change, the implementation of water resources ideas and other issues. if it is found that a national programme does not provide sufficient financial coverage for the above, the commission services are always entitled to reject it. this is another guarantee that natura 2000 will remain a priority in the member states' programmes, but it is not an absolute guarantee. it is therefore a key obligation for all those concerned with natura 2000 funding to press for member states not only to propose ambitious targets in their national and operational programmes but also to ensure a permanent and continuous action to prepare valid natura 2000 programmes. thank you very much for your attention.
on behalf of the group. mr president, we are all pleased that the commission has addressed the natura 2000 network, which is linked to the life programme of which i am the alternative rapporteur. however, i think we are very frustrated because the issue has been tackled against the comprehensive concepts that all sustainability requires and, moreover, we have fallen back into the old problem of considering natura 2000 as a crystallized territory, without life or activity. since the beginning of the declaration of protected areas, natura 2000 has become a problem rather than a joy for society. nobody wants to be declared a protected area, because there is no parallel policy of support. it's become a constant struggle. there has been no pedagogy of the exploitation of natural resources, nor of the real surplus value of this nature network, which generates and awakens the illusion. on the other hand, there has been a covert expropriation, since the use of land is much more limited than before and in many cases decreases the value of land ownership. so he has become a burden. what, then, of the document before us? first of all, it doesn't recognize typologies. we cannot introduce the concept of natura 2000 without visualising the large families of biodiversity, because each requires different financial instruments. for example, the seabed, which is not there, how are they going to be managed through rural development? we'll have to create a separate nature. nor are rivers listed as being important, when, in my view, they are an essential project. nor is it easy to distinguish forest areas from other areas. at the very least, there should have been an intention to diversify policy. finally, i would say that if we do not bring nature into the market economy, we have achieved nothing, because nature is life, economy and sustainability.
mr president, commissioner, the timing of mr florenz's question is that the natura 2000 network is the most important initiative the european union has undertaken in the field of the protection of natural areas and that is how the member states have understood it. my country, which represents 16% of the territory of the european union, contributes 40% of the entire natura 2000 network: 25% of the spanish territory is included in it. but natura 2000 has a cost which, to date, has not yet been precisely calculated. the commission's estimate of eur 6.1 billion may be far from reality, because this figure does not take sufficient account of the cost of compensation that might have to be paid to landowners and farmers who are in fact being expropriated of the use and rights they have over their agricultural land. and it must be remembered that, in addition to the management of natural resources, they must be compensated for lost profits, as laid down in article 17 of the charter of fundamental rights, included in the european constitution. the natura 2000 network is a community initiative, so the european union has to be responsible for the cost of not only managing the areas, but also for the lost profits of farmers. the proposal by commissioner wallström to finance part of this cost through rural development policy means that the commission does not take natura 2000 seriously or that it disregards rural development, or both. member states have to choose between these two objectives, always one to the detriment of the other. if the proposal we have on the table for the new european agricultural fund for rural development, with an annual budget of eur 11 billion, is adopted, 20% of that amount would have to be deducted to finance a substantial part of the cost of natura 2000. the cap reform of september 2003 also extended the list of actions to be financed under rural development, adding to it improvements in quality, food safety and livestock welfare. the natura 2000 network is therefore very important and needs to have an instrument to finance itself, either exclusively or through an increase in the rural development budget.
the inclusion of natura 2000 in the rural development regulation, as proposed by the commission, is tantamount to throwing this ambitious nature protection initiative into the trash. we all know that, following the current discussions on the financial perspective, there may not be enough funds to cover even the lines which have been financed to date under rural development policy, let alone the new measures planned, following the september 2003 reform, to improve safety, food quality and livestock welfare. it is therefore a dream to think that there will be money in this context to meet the immense cost of natura 2000. the uncertainty about the funding of this network is growing, but we must admit that it has always been there. the evidence is that the designation of natura 2000 sites has been delayed for at least 12 years since the adoption of the habitats directive. in the consultation that the european commission once held with civil society, all actors - from farmers to environmental organisations - were in favour of funding this initiative through a separate and single fund, as this would be the only possible formula to oblige the european union to make a funding effort. the commission, however, turned a deaf ear to all the actors concerned by this initiative. the financing of a substantial part of the cost of natura 2000 through rural development is not only a pipe dream, but its inclusion within the axis of agri-environmental measures could call into question the efforts made by european farmers to respect the eco-conditionality to which the recently launched cap reform obliges them. the european commission says that it has priority for nature conservation, but when it comes to the truth, it is stingy with money and wants farmers and landowners to bear the financial cost.

most important in the world, rotterdam, only 7% of the ships that call there deposit their waste from bilge tanks at the port collection facilities. where does he pour the other 93%? probably mostly at sea. we must adopt as soon as possible more effective control regulations to prevent the more than 77 000 deaths of birds per year from oil spills and the unquantified deaths of cetaceans, sea monitoring instruments, a kind of black box, which can provide reliable evidence of illegal dumping. it is necessary, in the development of the accompanying measures set out in article 10 of the regional groups. however important the union's action in the hrc is, it is not the only means at its disposal to promote human rights. the common guidelines on human rights, cooperation with other organisations such as the council of europe or the organisation for security and cooperation in europe, and the human rights dialogues with china and iran are all instruments for the promotion of human rights. discussions are still ongoing on the initiatives to be taken by the european union in the context of the human rights council this year. some decisions have already been taken. the union will present thematic resolutions on religious intolerance, the death penalty and the rights of the child. these are three main themes. in the face of manifestations of intolerance towards believers of whatever religion they profess, the union wishes to reaffirm its determination to combat all intolerance. the union considers that the abolition of the death penalty contributes to the strengthening of human dignity and works towards its universal abolition. it considers that the commission on human rights is an appropriate framework for promoting this objective. the promotion and protection of the rights of the child is an important part of the european union's human rights policy. the european union has decided to present resolutions on the human rights situation in myanmar, the democratic people's republic of korea and the israeli settlements in the occupied territories. discussions on further initiatives to be presented by the union will continue at the next meetings of the human rights group to be held before the session of the hrc. at its march meeting, the council will formally define the union's priorities for the 61st session of the hrc. beyond its own initiatives, the union intends to cooperate with third countries which take initiatives to promote human rights, in particular in the context of the fight against terrorism or in the context of transnational corporations. as in the past, it will endeavour to encourage the spirit of dialogue which is essential to the joint search for solutions to common problems. the european union hopes to have the support of parliament, whose resolution is much more ambitious than our programme for the 61st session of the hrc. the union shares the concerns expressed by parliament and i can assure you try to find the most appropriate and effective tool for each situation.

acting president of the council. mr president, mrs morgantini, mr barón crespo, i think that the question you have asked is indeed related to the debate we have just had. if there is one sector that is in some ways at the forefront of globalisation, it is the textile sector. the extent to which the international division of labour has changed, particularly in the textile sector, has been evident for decades. you are indeed raising important issues which affect not only europe but also its partners, particularly those on the southern shore of the mediterranean, as evidenced by this morning's debate on the constant evolution of production and the relocation of textile production. i think this is a very important question. in recent years, the council has also been closely monitoring the situation of the european textile and clothing industry as it has developed following the abolition of quotas for imports of textiles and clothing from wto member countries. two sets of council conclusions, adopted in response to two communications presented by the commission in 2003 and 2004, bear witness to this concern. as regards, in general, the gradual transition to a quota-free environment, it should be noted that this is not an unforeseen event. in fact, as parliament certainly knows, the end of four decades of regulated trade in textiles and clothing is not at all a surprise. the establishment and expiry of the agreement on textiles and clothing is an integral part of the outcome of the uruguay round concluded in 1994. since then, it has been clear that as of 1 january 2005, the textiles and clothing sector would be fully integrated into the gatt 1994 article 9. all the players in the world, including of course the european textile and clothing industry, knew what to expect. the commission has adopted a series of seven actions to deal with this new environment without quotas. as the commissioner responsible for enterprise said when this plan was adopted, whether at union level or at national or regional level, we must provide the sector with the right conditions to strengthen its competitiveness and remain a key industry in the union, which is what you, mr president, have also asked for. in its conclusions of 25 and 26 november 2004, the council stated that it supported the strategy adopted by the commission with regard to the textile and clothing sector. this is mainly focused on competitiveness factors related to research and innovation, training and skills development, protection of intellectual property rights, access to third country markets and support for the development of strategies for the textile industry in the euro-mediterranean region. the council considers the commission's package of measures to be appropriate. the council also asked the commission to allow the high level group on textiles and clothing to continue its work. it also called on the commission to keep the council regularly informed of developments in the eu textile and clothing sector after the abolition of import quotas on 1 january 2005. it also invited the commission to report on the outcome of future discussions within the high level group. with regard to the recommendations of the high level group on the development of imports from china, which is indeed a primary concern, the council noted that the commission has stated its readiness to use the trade defence instruments at its disposal if the legal conditions are met and if such recourse is indeed necessary. i would add that our relations with china are indeed important in this particular area as well. we are concerned about integrating china into the rules of international trade. that is why we have done everything we can to get it to join the wto. it is now necessary to ensure that it respects these rules, but also other less formal rules, such as social protection or social standards. this is a matter we must discuss with this country. these legal conditions have recently been amended to translate the abolition of quotas into community law. the council adopted a regulation to that effect on 13 december 2004. council regulation 2200/2004 therefore marks the end of the agreement on textiles and clothing as far as the european union is concerned. the regulation also provides for a surveillance system to be set up as from 1 january 2005 to monitor imports of the most sensitive textiles and clothing. this system will provide for customs-based surveillance of imports of liberalised goods from all origins and will include the obligation to issue an import surveillance document for imports of certain products from china. this obligation will be lifted in 2005, once the surveillance system based on customs data is fully operational. this information will be made public at least once a month. as regards the use of safeguard measures, parliament considered in its resolution of january 2004 on the future of the textile and clothing sector in the union that a clear, rapid and transparent procedure was needed for the wto general safeguard clauses and the specific clauses applicable to china under the protocol of accession of china to the wto. the high level group also requested the commission to provide further clarifications on this matter. the commission seems to be ready to meet the expectations in this respect, as it will be drawing up guidelines for safeguard procedures. finally, as regards the consequences of the expiry of the agreement on textiles and clothing for developing countries and the measures that the european union could take under articles 177 and 178 of the treaty, let me first mention two of the three objectives of our development cooperation as set out in the treaty: the sustainable development of developing countries - and particularly the most disadvantaged among them - and the integration of the poorest countries into the world economy. the european union's trade policy clearly takes account of these objectives, as required by article 178 of the treaty. the design of the doha development round and the way the doha development agenda is being implemented are just another example. let me also remind you, more specifically with regard to the expiry of the agreement on textiles and clothing, that the end of quotas and the integration of trade in textiles and clothing into gatt was one of the main demands of the developing countries during the uruguay round. it is true that since joining the wto, china has seen its share of the world textile and clothing trade steadily increase. the continued growth of the already considerable chinese share could be at the expense of a number of weak and vulnerable developing countries, as was stressed by the honourable members. in this respect, the council has a clear line and i quote again the conclusions mentioned above: 'the council supports a gsp scheme which concentrates its effects on those countries which need it most, such as the least developed countries and the most vulnerable developing countries, in order to enable them to play a greater role in international trade.' in this context, the situation resulting from the exit from the quota system for textiles will also be examined in the context of the discussion of the new gsp scheme. the new gsp, known as gsp+, should in principle be finalised by the end of march and enter into force in anticipation at the beginning of april. this issue is also constantly addressed in the framework of the china-eu dialogue on textile trade, which was launched on 6 may 2004. at the last session of this dialogue in december 2004, the impression was first given that the chinese authorities had begun to understand the problem and the message of the european union, as they announced measures in favour of a number of developing countries. the degree of effectiveness of these measures remains to be seen. the council will continue to monitor closely all developments in this market. as regards measures to assist the european union's textile and clothing industry, the council urged the commission to focus more on the strategic sectors, namely innovation, including non-technological innovation, and the development of industrial cooperation with partners in the euro-mediterranean region. the emphasis should be on high value-added products on the one hand and on industrial cooperation with complementary partners in developing countries on the other. i would also add the opening up of markets, particularly the chinese market, for this type of european products. to complement this general approach, a certain degree of flexibility in the area of rules of origin should be envisaged. it would improve the situation of developing countries exporting textiles and clothing. the commission presented to the council, at the beginning of january 2004, a green paper entitled 'the future of rules of origin in preferential trade regimes'. the council will examine any legislative proposal which the commission may submit to it in due course in this field.

the state of emergency declared by king gyanendra on 1 february is a clear threat to human rights in nepal, as it has strengthened the power of the security forces and reduced the prospects for a political peace process. but it should also be remembered that although the european union's code of conduct on arms exports explicitly prohibits sales to countries in armed conflict, some european governments, such as the uk, have sold arms to the nepalese government over the past three years. ladies and gentlemen, the resolution we are voting on today is of vital importance in clarifying the european union's position on the peace process and human rights in nepal. given the gravity of the situation, the decision of london and the indian government to suspend all military aid to the present nepalese government should be welcomed. the european union also calls on the government of sri lanka to take all necessary measures to ensure that the situation in sri lanka is brought under control. the european union must also urge the maoist guerrillas to commit themselves to respecting international humanitarian law and to sign a humanitarian and human rights agreement with the government security forces. fourthly, in accordance with the resolution we adopted this morning on the forthcoming session of the united nations commission on human rights, we must also urge the commission to adopt a specific resolution on nepal and to appoint a special rapporteur to monitor the human rights situation in that country. finally, echoing mr mann's invitation - with which i fully agree - we must not forget that the situation in nepal has a regional dimension, particularly in relation to neighbouring tibet. in this connection, we must demand that the nepalese government reopen the office for the welfare of tibetan refugees and the representation of the dalai lama in kathmandu.
member of the commission. mr president, the european commission is gravely concerned about the sharp deterioration in the political situation in nepal since 1 february. i do not have to tell members of this parliament how important the respect for human rights, democracy and the rule of law are in our relations with third countries. the presidency’s declaration of 2 february is very clear: the european union views the king's move as a serious setback for the prospect of a negotiated and democratically-based solution to the current conflict. the european union troika, which visited nepal only two months ago, expressed at that time its grave concerns at the rapidly deteriorating human rights situation. since 1 february, nepal has been experiencing a profound human rights crisis, as many parliamentarians have now underlined. the united nations has recorded more than 340 detentions of political leaders, journalists, human rights defenders and civil society activists. we, the european union, will continue to press for the release of all those who remain arbitrarily detained, and we will use the opportunity of the forthcoming session of the united nations commission on human rights in geneva to remind both sides to the conflict of their obligations under international law. as members may be aware, no european union position has yet been taken on the issue of continued external assistance to nepal, because the situation is very complex. the commission's global approach to conflict prevention calls for us to ensure that community instruments and programmes are directed towards achieving political and social stability and democracy. as we have frequently stated, development policy and other cooperation programmes provide the most powerful instruments at the community's disposal for treating the root causes of conflict. we have learned that conflict countries sometimes require more, rather than less, assistance, and applying blunt political conditions risks penalising the weakest in society. that is why we think that the basic objectives of ec cooperation remain achievable. indeed, the priorities of support to poverty reduction, human rights and conflict mitigation are more urgent in the new environment. now is not the time for us, for instance, to cancel our support to nepal's national human rights commission, provided this institution continues to operate as an autonomous and independent technical body, seeking to promote the rule of law. however, this does not mean that it is 'business as usual' in terms of donor support to nepal, not least because of the new constraints faced in ensuring that all sides respect the donors' basic operational guidelines in the state of emergency as the conflict escalates. therefore, the commission has taken the following position. the delegation of the european commission in kathmandu will not accept any high level invitations from the king or from any of his cabinet ministers unless instructed otherwise by its headquarters. all ongoing ec cooperation activities are carefully reviewed and the situation in the field is constantly monitored. for the time being, activities continue but new appraisals or identification missions will not be launched for the preparation of the 2005 cooperation pipeline until further notice. the commission maintains extensive contacts on this issue with member states and with other donors on the ground, and will participate in a meeting of like-minded donors during the week of 7 march in europe to continue to seek a coordinated line. as ever in such situations, the cost of conflict falls heaviest on the weakest in nepalese society. i am thinking of the children denied schooling or forcibly recruited, the poor deprived of basic healthcare and shelter and the many victims of brutal violence. whilst the primary responsibility for resolving the conflict in nepal rests with the local actors, we must not abandon them now. working closely with the european union member states and especially with successive european union council presidencies, the commission remains committed to pursuing all diplomatic, political, and developmental efforts that might facilitate the peace process and a return to democracy in nepal.

gentlemen, last thursday the conference of presidents of the political groups unanimously adopted a statement on the situation of journalists in iraq which i was to read to you today. this statement to enable the media to carry out their mission, in particular in areas of armed conflict, including iraq. and after this statement on these current events, both painful and happy, i must make another statement on what we can call historical commemorations. as you know, centuries of fratricidal wars between our countries have marked our memory. as president of the european parliament i am often asked for a minute's silence to commemorate events which remind us of the saddest part of our past. just a few days ago, our polish colleagues asked me to remember, through a minute of silence, the massacre at katyn, miednoye and kharkov, where 14 000 polish officers were executed in cold blood by stalin's regime on 5 march 1940. this is a legitimate request and it is our duty not to forget these events or their victims. but every day, the history of our continent - a tragic and tormented history - will bring us, at random on the calendar, the memory of sad events for each of our victims of gender discrimination and all kinds of abuse every day, in times of peace and in times of war. they continue to be victims of physical, psychological, sexual and economic violence, sometimes from their immediate emotional environment. only a few days ago we saw the tremendous footage of turkish riot police against a demonstration of women who were celebrating today in advance. i had the opportunity yesterday to express in plenary the condemnation that these acts deserve. i have asked the turkish government to punish the perpetrators of these unqualified acts and i would like to remind you that this is certainly not the best presentation letter for turkey in the face of its hypothetical accession. ladies and gentlemen, the united nations is hosting the world conference on gender equality until 11 march to review the progress made since the beijing conference in 1995, ten years ago. as you know, a delegation from our parliament is taking a very active part in this conference, as it did in 1995. since then, there is no doubt that progress has been made. kofi annan acknowledged this in his opening speech at the beijing + 10 conference, but there are still enormous problems, enormous challenges, which should not be considered as unsolvable, nor should we regard today's celebration as a symbolic day to wash our bad conscience. this afternoon we'll be holding a debate on "cultural and domestic violence" with personalities and specialized press. i would like to invite you all to this seminar/debate, and when i say "everyone" i mean in the masculine, because normally, at events dealing with women's issues, men are usually apparently absent. we must be aware that the problem of gender equality is not a women's problem, it is a problem for women and for society as a whole, and men need to be more involved in solving it. today, in europe, one in five women claims to have been the victim of ill-treatment, one in five. and this proportion, unfortunately, is increasing in many countries. in the rich, democratic, developed and cohesive european union, poverty is becoming more and more feminized. there are worrying signs of a feminization of poverty. women still receive, on average, 16% less pay than their male colleagues for the same work. this point must also be dealt with in the so-called lisbon strategy, which does not offer too positive figures either. for this reason, in this parliament we have introduced a member in each parliamentary committee responsible for monitoring gender issues, which cannot be dealt with in isolation, in a kind of conceptual ghetto, but must affect all policies horizontally. this term will also be marked by the ratification of the constitution, which includes, with great success, gender equality as one of the objectives and values of the union. but, above all texts and declarations, let us be aware that equality will not be effective as long as male mentality does not radically evolve, overcoming anthropological inheritances that sometimes sink deep into customs and consciences, as long as employers do not propose equal wages, as long as concrete advantages are not offered to make it easier for women to exercise a professional activity or to prevent or compensate for the disadvantages that in their professional careers are associated with the fulfillment of a function that only they can do, human reproduction. we will not solve the demographic problems in europe if we do not solve the problems of equality with women, for women. the day when all the member states implement the declaration on article iii-116 of the constitution and take the necessary measures to punish criminal acts, because we are dealing with criminal acts of gender-based violence, we will have taken a great step forward. i would like this parliament to have absolute gender parity. but i would like it to be so, not because a rule imposes it, but because the equal distribution of capacities between men and women is reflected in our social and political practices. nor do we think that the best indicator for measuring equality between men and women is the percentage of women in the national parliaments. inequality is most vicious and severe in the lowest strata of society, where the accumulation of painful working conditions with family burdens is most difficult for women. i therefore reiterate my invitation to you to follow the events taking place today in the european parliament, which is joining in the commemoration of this day with the greatest enthusiasm. member of the commission. mr president, thank you for inviting me to address parliament on the subject of the generalised system of preferences and its reform. the gsp is a key instrument to put trade at the service of development by helping stimulate developing country exports to the european union. the current system will be improved in four principal ways. first, the gsp will be simplified. second, the product coverage will be expanded. third, the benefits will be focused on those developing countries that are most in need. fourth, additional gsp benefits – gsp+ – will be available for the first time to those countries that encourage sustainable development. the new gsp scheme is simpler to comprehend. it comes in only three forms: the general arrangement; everything but arms for less-developed countries, which remains unchanged; and a new special arrangement to promote sustainable development and good governance. the graduation process will be clearer, simpler and fairer. graduation – the exclusion of competitive products from gsp benefits – will not be applied annually any more, but over the three-and-a-half year period of the regulation. this will bring greater stability and much more predictability. the new gsp scheme is a clear example of an integrated approach to trade policy and sustainable development and i am sure will be welcomed by members here for that reason. the new incentive for sustainable development and governance will support our commitment to core human and labour rights and environmental protection in the framework of our existing trade policy. the reformed gsp will be a more effective tool to foster export diversification and economic growth for countries most in need: for example, vulnerable countries like honduras; poorly diversified economies like georgia; small islands like sri lanka; and landlocked countries like mongolia. my aim is to get this simpler, better scheme into force more rapidly. following the tsunami, the commission has been keen to act quickly to provide relief for the countries affected in the indian ocean. the new gsp will provide better access for some of the countries worst affected by the tsunami, and we want to accelerate its entry into force on 1 april. the countries that bore the brunt of the tsunami disaster will benefit most from the new scheme. sri lanka will receive duty-free access to the eu for almost all its exports, including vital textile and clothing exports. india, indonesia and thailand will benefit from reduced duties and wider product coverage, especially on crucial seafood exports. in parallel, the commission is working on simplifying and, where appropriate, relaxing the rules of origin in order to make gsp preferences provide the poorest with more benefit. the commission will complete the revision of the gsp rules of origin as soon as possible. let me turn to the amendments proposed by parliament commission’s position on amendments by parliament: see annex.. overall, i wish to thank the rapporteur, mr sánchez presedo, and the committee on international trade, for the excellent work done in a tight timeframe. i welcome the fact that the conclusions in the report adopted by that committee on 22 february are broadly supportive of the commission proposal. more specifically, the committee has highlighted the need for an evaluation of the functioning and impact of the current gsp scheme. the commission is currently working on an impact assessment of the gsp on beneficiary countries during the five-year period from 1999 to 2003 and we should deliver a final report to parliament by the end of the summer. furthermore, i am also ready to report to the european parliament annually on the impact assessment of the new gsp. let me turn to some detailed points. the commission is ready to accept amendment 47, tabled by the committee on international trade, according to which ‘the commission shall, in close cooperation with member states, monitor the imports of [some sensitive tuna] products’. however, i am not persuaded by the committee’s proposal to lower the graduation threshold for textiles and clothing products. this would exclude india from the gsp for those products. india is one of the countries that bore the brunt of the indian ocean tsunami disaster and where 300 million people still live on a dollar a day or less. the time and circumstances are not right to make this change, as it would adversely affect india. in this context, therefore, a decision such as this does not seem justified. member states are divided on the issue: some wish to decrease this threshold, others support a higher one. the commission proposal for a 12.5% threshold is a fair compromise between these two positions. then there are proposals that affect the eligibility of specific countries. the committee proposes a specific clause for el salvador. this would imply granting gsp+ to a country that has not ratified a maximum of two ilo conventions due to constitutional constraints, but undertakes to ratify and implement them as quickly as possible. i think you will agree that any ad hoc clause which downgrades two ilo conventions runs counter to the eu policy of promoting core labour standards. on 4 march this year the council adopted its conclusions on the social dimension of globalisation, which ‘recall its commitment to promote core labour standards and note the importance of the revision of the gsp in this context’. furthermore, up to now, el salvador has not shown any movement towards the ratification and implementation of the two missing ilo conventions – on freedom of association and the right to collective bargaining. the committee also recommends a revised definition of the gsp+ vulnerability criterion, which would make pakistan eligible. let me remind members of this house of some of the history of this. in the wake of 9/11 we decided to grant the benefits of the gsp drug regime to pakistan. following the wto panel launched by india against the gsp drug regime, additional tariff preferences can only be granted to countries facing specific trade, financial, or development needs. accordingly, the selection of gsp+ beneficiaries is to be based on clear, transparent and non-discriminatory criteria. any specific clause for pakistan would represent a de facto discrimination. it would therefore make us vulnerable to challenge and i do not want to risk triggering another wto case against the new gsp scheme that would not only affect pakistan, but every other developing country that was a beneficiary of gsp+. we should also bear in mind that pakistan is one of the largest gsp beneficiaries, whereas gsp+ is targeted at the most vulnerable countries, in particular the smallest ones which represent less than 1% of gsp-covered trade flows. but i would like to stress that pakistan will not be disadvantaged. it will enjoy favourable treatment in the new scheme, as it will benefit from reduced duties for all its exports to the eu market. in conclusion, i believe that the new gsp scheme opens good market access opportunities for developing countries. it is simpler, it is more predictable and covers a broader range of products. by ensuring its wto compatibility, it will provide legal security to our trading partners and on that basis i commend it to this house.
the european union has been a pioneer in establishing the generalized system of preferences. since 1971, following the recommendation of the united nations conference on trade and development, it has been granting non-reciprocal preferential treatment to developing countries, which currently benefits 177 countries, 50 of which are among the least developed. the european union imports more gsp-covered products than all other developed countries combined and three times as much as the second. the first gsp regulation of the 21st century should reaffirm the european union's leadership in promoting trade and sustainable development in the world. the declaration of the fourth ministerial conference of the world trade organisation, held in doha in 2001, recognised that international trade could play a greater role in promoting economic development and poverty reduction. the new regulation is the first to be adopted by the european union of 25. it gives access to a market of more than 450 million people, which can be even larger with the accession of two new member states. the opportunity arises from the need to revise the special drug regime, taking into account the requirements of the world trade organisation's april 2004 report, which should become effective on 1 july this year. the rapporteur welcomes the council's consultation of parliament in a procedure where codecision is not yet applied. it considers that the new initiative should have been preceded by a study assessing the impact of the system in the beneficiary countries and by more time available for hearings of experts, specialised organisations, beneficiary countries and representatives of civil society. this would have allowed the report of the committee on development to be accompanied by those of other parliamentary committees. the report envisages that the future revision of the system will be more structured and participatory and will strengthen the role of the parliament, without altering the balance of powers, while improving good european governance. we support the initiative of commissioner mandelson to present a revised proposal to bring forward the application of the regulation to 1 april so that the countries affected by the tsunami can receive its benefits as soon as possible. it seems appropriate, in the interests of legal certainty, good administration and legitimate expectations, to ensure that the countries not included in the list may temporarily continue to enjoy the advantages granted to them until the end of the current year. i would like to stress that the requirements for access to the new special incentive must be in line with the requirements of the rule of law and the case of el salvador will put this to the test. the end of violence and the pacification of el salvador have been encouraged and supported by the granting of a preferential system by the union. if the current salvadoran constitution, which has created a delicate balance of concord, does not allow a literal and immediate response to the new requirements, although it does meet its essential objectives, it should not prevent the search for formulas such as the one envisaged in the report on compliance by equivalence. an overly restrictive definition of the vulnerability requirement for access to the special incentive scheme should also be avoided. the report envisages the provision of technical assistance to build institutional and regulatory capacity to enable beneficiary states to increase the currently low system utilisation rate. from the sectoral point of view, i would like to stress the acceptance of the compromise amendment, tabled with the development rapporteur, to link the sugar liberalisation deadlines with those set out in the reform of the common organization of the market, as well as the amendments on textiles and fishery products. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'commercial vehicle' to cover vehicles with a maximum mass of less than 100 tonnes. the report has dealt with other aspects of the future, such as the preservation of the calculation base, the expansion of sensitive products and the attention to the interests of acp countries which are not able to build an epa. i conclude by pointing out that the new gsp+, by placing human development at the heart of any development strategy, must become the backbone of the future gsp and by thanking you for your attention and the collaboration of all those who have contributed to the outcome of my report. mr president, the proliferation of nuclear weapons in iraq and north korea is a threat not only to the regions in which these states are located, but to the whole of the planet, especially when we are talking about developing countries which could devote their resources to other purposes. furthermore, if we continue along this line, they could be emulated by other countries in the region, by neighbouring countries, which would therefore break the non-proliferation trend adopted in recent years by some twenty countries. mr president, there is a disturbing fact, namely that the international atomic energy agency has detected more than a dozen cases of nuclear material disappearing, which now represents a potential danger of the use of these weapons. as mr wiersma said in his speech, if terrorist organisations such as al qaeda could acquire nuclear weapons or totalitarian states such as those mentioned could have access to such weapons, it would be very difficult to control their use. the path indicated by mr schmit for the continuation of the dialogue is an interesting one, and i think we must follow it, but we must not forget that in the case of iran, on 1 march last, iaea inspectors were denied access to the parchin military complex and that, in turn, the international atomic energy agency has confirmed that iran is building underground tunnels for the storage of nuclear material and equipment, and that north korea has between 20 and 30 kilos of plutonium in the yongbyon nuclear reactor, in addition to one of the largest nuclear arsenals in the world. i think we must therefore accept the recommendation of the council presidency that we should be vigilant and watchful, and at the same time we must try to follow the path of dialogue, as the president said, in order to put a stop to the proliferation of nuclear weapons, which is, of course, a threat, as i said at the beginning, not only to the region but to the whole planet.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of my colleague, mrs ferrero-waldner, commissioner for external relations and european neighbourhood policy, i have the honour to address you on the situation in lebanon. we were shocked and saddened by the horrific terrorist attack in beirut on 14 february, which took the lives of former lebanese prime minister hariri and many others, and seriously injured more than 100 others. this is the most devastating attack on lebanon since the civil war of 1975-1990. mr hariri was one of the main architects of the 1989 taëf accords, which ended the civil war in lebanon. he was a champion of reconstruction in his war-torn country and became a symbol of peace and reconciliation based on a delicate balance between the 18 religious communities that make up the country. we have worked closely with mr hariri and his government. during his term of office, negotiations on an association agreement were successfully concluded and an interim agreement on trade entered into force in march 2003. mr hariri also fully supported the dialogue on the european neighbourhood policy, which also includes lebanon. in the weeks since hariri's death, thousands of protesters have protested against the syrian military presence in their country, defying the government's ban. in the face of relentless pressure following the assassination of mr hariri, lebanese prime minister omar karamé and his government resigned on 28 february following an extraordinary parliamentary debate on the political situation following mr hariri's death. the next few weeks will obviously be decisive for the country and it is important that the parliamentary elections in lebanon take place as scheduled in may. the commission hopes that calm will prevail in the period ahead and that the channels of dialogue between the various political groups will remain open. the elections must be held in accordance with a free and fair electoral process, without any foreign interference or influence, and under the sovereign control of the lebanese authorities. these elections could be a turning point in lebanon's return to full independence question no 23 by jan andersson (h-0134/05) subject: impact of eu agricultural policy on world trade eu agricultural policy is an obstacle to world trade. because of eu agricultural subsidies, the world's poorest countries are excluded from the possibility of competing on the world market and the eu market. does the commission share this view on the impact of the eu's agricultural policy? if so, what action will it take?
member of the commission. i agree that the agricultural policy of the european communities was for a long time an obstacle to world trade, but since 1992 a successful reform of the common agricultural policy has remarkably changed the situation. the most recent agricultural reform packages adopted by the agriculture ministers in 2003 and 2004 have to a large extent eliminated the trade-distorting nature of the common agricultural policy and contributed to more market-oriented agricultural trade. eu trade statistics show that eu agricultural imports from the developing countries totalled more than eur 37 billion in 2003. that is more or less equal to the combined imports of the united states, canada, japan, australia and new zealand. the european union alone absorbs 85% of total agricultural exports from africa and 45% of total agricultural exports from latin america. in the doha negotiations, the eu committed itself to a substantial reduction in trade-distorting subsidies, eliminating export refunds and offering improved market access. for the benefit of the poorest or less developed countries, the european community, as well as other major agricultural producers, should introduce similar reforms. the eu makes efforts to persuade other countries to provide quota-free and duty-free market access for agricultural products for less developed countries.
member of the commission. mr. representative, i share your views and concerns. the commission has also been asked to provide information on the implementation of the new rules on competition. it is well known that the 10 new accession countries receive substantially less support from the cap than the 15 former member states, and this puts farmers and producers in the 10 new member states at a competitive disadvantage. of course, i know that developing countries, and especially the poorest countries, have much bigger problems to deal with. but seeing how serious the problems of the 10 new countries are, i can feel and understand the problems of the poorest countries. further steps are needed to make the eu market accessible to the poorest countries.

quality. that is why the directive stops short of dealing with the issue of payment, and simply expresses the spirit and philosophy of non-payment that should be implemented and followed by the member states. however, it is not a binding rule. the commission has limits on how much it can do in this respect. for example, it cannot initiate infringement proceedings against a member state, because the principle of subsidiarity applies and this is a matter for the member states. i repeat that this does not mean that because we do not have legal competence we cannot adopt political positions or take mr president, i agree with the diagnosis made by the president of the commission. i think europe is at a crossroads at the moment. europe may enter into crisis if the constitutional treaty is not ratified, either now or in a few years' time, if we are unable to define a european power which affirms our political and economic identity abroad. that is what we have to do now and it will coincide with the mandate of this commission and with the mandate of this parliament. and to do that, from an economic point of view, which is what we are talking about here today, there is a necessary condition, macroeconomic stability, and a sufficient condition, to accelerate the lisbon reform process, to create more jobs, to be more productive, in short, more competitive, and thus to shorten the distances that separate us from the united states and to face the competition of the emerging countries. we have discussed the lisbon reforms this morning, so i will now return to the necessary condition, the stability pact. i think we have to be very honest with each other on this issue. we are going to reform the stability pact, not because it has lost its internal logic, the foundations on which it was based, but simply because there have been too many breaches, mostly by the large countries. and if it is the big countries that are forcing us to reform the pact, we must know what they are prepared to do, and we have just learned that. they are willing to accept reform of the preventive aspect of the pact, to make efforts in times of prosperity, simply because they know that there will be no power in the world to force them to comply with those rules. and in matters of prevention, they want to sweeten, to break the rules, to the point that 'as some source in german social democracy has said', there are no rules at all. in this respect, there are only two solutions - and only two: either we move towards economic governance, economic coordination, an impartial arbiter incapable of imposing action, or we maintain automaticity. we have not wanted to make any progress on economic coordination. the intergovernmental conference has undone the timid steps taken by the convention in the field of coordination, so we are as before. and we also don't want to keep the automation. all we're going to do in this and the next councils is backtrack. the problem is to what extent and at what speed. the exemptions granted in respect of compliance with the rules we have given ourselves are a weakening, a concession, of the stability pact. the extent to which you give in will determine our future credibility, our economic strength and, in short, the avoidance of the economic crisis which i have predicted in the years ahead.

on behalf of the pse group. mr president, commissioner, no one in this parliament is questioning the need for reform in the sugar sector. you have described very well in your speech the reasons why it is necessary. we are opposed to the commission's proposal, and in my case for two fundamental reasons: firstly, because it creates an imbalance in the distribution of the reduction effort within the european union, burdening it on the most disadvantaged areas; and secondly, because it does not guarantee the maintenance of the incomes of beet growers. in my country, spain, the application of this directive would mean the disappearance of a large part of the 118 000 hectares of arable land in castile and león, andalusia and castile-la mancha, and would affect 23 000 producers. the commission is proposing a new system of farm prices, which is not yet in force, and the impact of the reductions in prices and quotas on the incomes of family farms, the loss of jobs in industry and the impact on the rural environment of the member states concerned are not taken into account in the impact study. we believe, madam commissioner, that the price reductions should be smaller and more spread over time, with a significant part of the aid being tied up, so as not to disrupt the economic and social fabric of the producing areas in my country, which are located in the less prosperous regions. in addition, the reduction of quotas should begin with the surplus quantities and those intended for export, which are the most harmful to the international market for this product. we are totally against - and i have to say it this way - the transfer of quotas between member states. we believe that this would or could lead to a relocation of employment and economic activity within the european union, which would create greater imbalances the less competitive the states are, and would create a dangerous precedent within the cap. as regards the external scope of the proposal, the 'everything but arms' (eba) initiative should include quantitative import control instruments similar to those already in place for acps. this is what the acp and ldc representatives are asking for and it is thus amply reflected in our resolution. in conclusion, commissioner, i would ask you to take into account what has already been said to you by both mr daul and mr fruteau, my two colleagues who have tabled this proposal: this resolution was adopted by a broad consensus in the committee on agriculture and rural development; so it is now appropriate to put forward legislative proposals which reflect the observations contained in it.
mr president, the european industrial beet-growing sector has unanimously said 'no' to the european commission's proposal and has spoken out against a reduction in institutional prices, a cut in production quotas and the possibility of transferring quotas, a measure which would clearly benefit the most competitive countries to the detriment of others, such as spain. spanish beet growers alone will suffer losses that could amount to 60 million euros a year. the possibility of transferring quotas from one country to another would lead to the concentration of european production in a few regions and the impoverishment of the rural world in many areas where sugar beet production plays a very important social and economic role. the european commission itself acknowledges in its communication that this reform will also lead to the closure of sugar production units, that is, it assumes that its reform will have disastrous consequences. the commission does not take into account the situation of countries such as spain, whose sugar production quota has always been in deficit. the draft resolution by the committee on agriculture and rural development of the european parliament should, in my view, be regarded as a minimum document, which should serve as a basis for the negotiations to be held by the council of ministers of the european union. the commission should not, once again, turn a deaf ear to the concerns of the sector and should take careful note of the rejection which i hope this parliament will express to its proposal in the vote which will take place today. i also hope that this house will reject the package of measures put forward by a socialist member, whose line is in contradiction with the negotiations that have already taken place between different political groups.
ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, one year ago, at the initiative of the european parliament, our union decided that 11 march would be the european day of the victims of terrorism. and we did so, because tomorrow will be the one year anniversary of madrid waking up to the sound of the bombs that took the lives of 192 citizens from different countries. spain has unfortunately been a country accustomed to the terrorist threat. for many years we endured it. many dead were left behind. but even in the hardest times of the fight against the terrorist group eta, spanish society never renounced its freedom. however, that march 11, that new and even more terrible attack, was part of the dynamic created by another attack, that of september 11, 2001 in new york and washington, which awakened the western world from its calm confidence and changed the course of world geopolitics. that 9/11 we said we were all americans. then in march, in madrid, we said we were all going on the atocha trains. today, in atocha square, the candles that made it a shrine of remembrance are no longer there, but the memory is still there, the memory of some victims who, as a sign of our respect, should be a symbol of our unity and not flags of our political confrontation. the first tribute to the victims is to make them a symbol of the unity of democrats, a symbol of the unity of those of us who believe in the rule of law and human rights. on 11 march, europeans were confronted with a global perspective on the problem of terrorism. until then, each country had its terrorists, but after 9/11, first, and then march 11, terrorism reached a global dimension that required a global response. we europeans then realised that our values, and not just our lives, were threatened and therefore reacted together without forgetting that the fight for democracy was and will be at the heart of our political project. let us remember that democracy has never succumbed to terrorism, but that more than military instruments are needed to implement it. first, we must look back and appreciate the response we have been able to give to those events. the first conclusion to be drawn is that perhaps the deaths in madrid were not in vain because, shortly afterwards, europe reached an agreement to unblock its constitution, now subject to ratification. maybe that was a big push that allowed us to overcome a lot of our differences. secondly, we must know whether we have really implemented the commitments we made then, whether we have fulfilled the agreements we made with ourselves and whether we have really implemented the measures we committed ourselves to implement. in this respect, perhaps, we should acknowledge that we have not applied all that the emotion of the moment has impelled us to agree. a large part of the measures provided for in the action plan adopted by the council after 11 march have not yet been fully implemented, which should remind us that the fight against terrorism also requires more europe, because we are now aware that the traditional forms of judicial and police cooperation are not working. the european parliament has always been at the forefront of the fight against terrorism, despite the limited role that the treaties give us in this area. it is not, of course, the time to give a long account of all that parliament has done, but it is the time to express our deep conviction that police effectiveness will be greater the greater the capacity of the member states to exchange police and security information and that is why we must ask ourselves now, now that we are remembering the victims: what are still the underlying problems that prevent europol from being fully operational? when will we have a european public prosecutor's office? when will we have european legislation to prevent money laundering...{protests)... a basic element in the fight against organised crime and its links to terrorism? there is some positive progress in these areas, but some of the decisions that were taken - i am not talking about anything other than what was decided to be done after 11 september - have not yet seen the light of day. i do not understand the expressions of indignation, because that is what many political leaders from all over the world are talking about in madrid today. that is what is being discussed in madrid today at the international conference attended by many dignitaries and experts from all over the world, and which i myself will be attending at the end of this solemn event, together with the secretary-general of the united nations, mr kofi annan, and the president of the commission, mr barroso, who will be presenting an action plan drawn up by the commission to combat terrorism, which refers to some of the measures i have just mentioned. yes, in madrid, as before yesterday here in brussels and strasbourg, there is talk of the need to fight terrorism from a global, comprehensive perspective, starting with full respect for the rule of law and not forgetting to examine the causes of terrorism and the instruments that allow it to grow and spread throughout the world. let us not forget that to ensure our security it is essential to promote dialogue and integration between cultures and religions, not forgetting development cooperation. it is not a comfortable or easy debate, but we cannot avoid it. terrorists have no explanation or justification, but there are causes which produce them and we must also pay attention to them in our analysis. an analysis which takes into account the need not only to respect the values and fundamental rights which are the basis of our community, but to apply preventive measures which not only prevent having to regret everything, but also avoid having to regret it. obviously, i am not just talking about prevention of war. i am talking about prevention in the broadest sense of the word. internal and external prevention, internally in our societies, to ensure the integration of migrants, tolerance, religious and cultural pluralism, the fight against discrimination, cooperation between intelligence services and judicial systems... (applause)... and external action also on many fronts: war, poverty, the proliferation of nuclear, biological or chemical weapons; a global framework to combat terrorism, without forgetting, ladies and gentlemen who represent the citizens of europe here, that the most effective way, the basis of all forms of combating terrorism, is respect for the fundamental values of our union. thank you very much, ladies and gentlemen of the house. (loud applause) and now, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, in memory of those victims, who must be, as i said, the symbol of our democratic union, i ask you to observe a minute's silence. vice-president of the commission. mr president, let me start by saying that i very much share the sentiments expressed in your motion for a resolution on belarus, about which we share many of the same concerns. the eu's goal is to have close relations with all of our neighbours, including belarus. we want to see belarus as a democratic, stable and prosperous country, fully benefiting from our neighbourhood policy. unfortunately, its government's policies prevent it from taking its rightful place in the family of european nations. the seriously flawed conduct of the parliamentary elections and the referendum in october 2004, show how far belarus is lagging behind in terms of democratic development. it is deeply worrying for us all that democratization, respect for fundamental freedoms and respect for the rule of law are deteriorating rather than improving, as the regime continues to tighten its grip on democratic forces, the independent media and opposition forces. in november 2004, following the elections in belarus, eu foreign ministers adopted conclusions setting out a clear eu policy. we confirmed the restrictions on ministerial-level contacts with belarusian authorities, but at the same time sent a clear message to the population that they are not forgotten and that we are trying to support civil society and democratic forces in belarus. we are closely monitoring the human rights situation in the country and, as a result, the eu imposed a visa ban last year on certain high-ranking belarusian officials, on the basis of the findings of the council of europe's pourgourides report on politically motivated disappearances. we then extended this visa ban to the officials considered responsible for the rigged election and the referendum, as well as those responsible for the repression of the peaceful demonstrations that followed. the cases of mr marinich and other imprisoned political opponents are of great concern to us. we believe that his trial was politically motivated and have issued a statement calling for his disproportionate sentence to be reconsidered. we have serious concerns in general about the independence of the judiciary in belarus and continue to follow these cases closely. the eu issued the statement on mr marinich's case in january. as regards your call on the commission to step up our assistance efforts to belarus, i am pleased to report that we have already done so in response to the eu foreign ministers' conclusions last november. the commission is playing the lead role in coordinating and delivering eu assistance in support of civil society and democratisation in belarus. a conference will be held in vilnius next week on that very important subject. in difficult situations such as that of belarus, where a country is isolating itself from the world, this is particularly difficult and we are working on the appropriate division of labour between the community member states and other donors. we very much welcome the role that the european parliament can play in encouraging democratic changes and supporting democratic forces in belarus. we are currently carefully examining the action plan which your delegation for relations with belarus has prepared, to see how this can mesh with our own efforts in that regard. there is much to be done and we look forward to working with parliament and with the democratic forces inside belarus. you raised some questions in your contributions that i should like to answer. the first was whether belarus was discussed at high-level meetings between the eu and russia. the answer is yes; the issue is always raised during those meetings. the question of how to channel the funds and how to assist civil society in belarus financially was also raised. the main question is the ability of the relevant organisations to absorb the funds. the commission is ready to examine all possible ways of supporting belarusian civil society financially so that the funds can be used efficiently.
