the six motions for resolutions on saudi arabia are now under debate.
mr president, mr commissioner, the holding of municipal elections in saudi arabia is indeed a significant and important event in favour of the political reforms that this country is undertaking; this must be recognized and this is also recognized in the resolution we are presenting today. however, the fact that the state of segregation still persists, in these terms, against women, who have not been able to vote or stand for office, is a clear anachronism. women face incomprehensible and unacceptable restrictions on freedom of movement - including the right to drive - employment opportunities, legal personality and legal representation in court proceedings. it is also regrettable that the whole immigrant population lives in precarious conditions, especially women. if saudi arabia wants to be internationally recognised as a modern state that respects human rights, it must at least respect the rights set out in the convention on the elimination of all forms of discrimination against women, to which saudi arabia is a state party. in particular, article 7 of the convention provides that states parties shall take all appropriate measures to eliminate discrimination against women in the political and public life of their country and shall in particular guarantee the right of women to vote in all elections and to be elected and to take part in the formulation of state policy and its implementation. it is clear that this article was not respected in the recent municipal elections. it should also be recalled that according to amnesty international data, at least 31 people were executed under the death penalty in 2004. it is therefore necessary to reiterate the call for the abolition of the death penalty, as the european union has been doing for some time. maintaining good relations with saudi arabia is important and provides an opportunity for both sides to contribute to a better understanding between peoples and cultures. however, it is precisely for the sake of these good relations that saudi arabia should not be another example of the double standard with which the european union sometimes measures the democratization and respect for human rights in the world. the credibility of the european union is again at stake here.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, the european commission thanks parliament for bringing forward this resolution on saudi arabia. it is a well-drafted and balanced resolution, which has the merit of pointing out the positive and less positive aspects of the saudi elections and the on-going reform process. the commission also welcomes the visit to saudi arabia by the european parliament's delegation for relations with the gulf cooperation council, and encourages it to pursue its efforts. the commission shares the parliament's view on the need to promote a substantial strengthening of eu-saudi relations. in june 2004, the european council adopted an eu strategic partnership for the mediterranean and the middle east. that document reflected the eu's political will to intensify efforts to resolve conflicts, ease tension, build trust, strengthen governance and improve the lives of the people living on the shores of the mediterranean and in the middle east, and not least to address the situation faced by women in some of these countries. our current eu-gulf cooperation council agreement and our future free trade area agreement - which will include human rights as an essential element - will remain the framework for our cooperation. however, we will be further developing our relations with each gulf country according to its particular needs, capacities and will to move towards. the european union's determination to promote both stability and change throughout the region is at the core of this process. indeed, we must pursue stability through change and reform: political and economic reforms are needed for the region's development and the well-being of its peoples. the commission, as you know, is keen that an initiative for reform should come from within the region itself. this requires that the region speak out clearly in favour of political, economic and social reform. while reforms cannot be imposed from the outside, they can be encouraged. for example, the eu should encourage the saudi government to accelerate the pace of reforms that contribute towards women's empowerment. the eu will continue to raise such issues in its official contacts with the saudis, not least at the next eu-gulf cooperation council ministerial meeting to be held in bahrain on 5 april. in addition, saudi arabia has now been included as one of the countries on which the european initiative for democracy and human rights can focus. that means we will assess initiatives from ngos willing to support the efforts made in the region.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. the new european reality has a very particular impact on territories such as spain and others, which have become peripheral in relation to the situation of the main european markets. for these peripheral countries, the likelihood of having to travel longer distances is much higher than for the central countries, which have a greater proximity between the centres of production and consumption. in order to try to alleviate these circumstances, we believe that it is fair to establish flexibility schemes to prevent adverse geography from progressively reducing the competitiveness of transport in the union. in this situation, the legislative effort is excessive and rigid rules may lead to an imbalance in the conditions faced by carriers in peripheral countries rather than to harmonization. the obligation to take a new rest period after six consecutive driving periods means that long-distance drivers are often unable to return to their places of origin and therefore have to take weekly rest breaks along the route. this is a real shame, because the conditions of rest are often far from those necessary to maintain a reasonable level of quality of life: confinement and isolation in a motorway rest area, without adequate housing or hygiene conditions, in a distant country and, moreover, without the possibility of moving away from vehicles for fear of being robbed. the situation is all the more bleeding because, in theory, these are measures which are said to be aimed at guaranteeing them adequate resting conditions. the recognition of the long distance concept has been picked up in other sectors, such as high-altitude fishing. in the field of transport, french legislation also distinguishes between short-distance and long-distance drivers. it is essential to distinguish between these two cases in order not to penalise long-distance drivers or the legitimate interests of peripheral countries.

on behalf of the verts/ale group.– mr president, in order to eradicate famine in the world, many things must be changed in the european union. the common agricultural policy, which is not very accurate in the allocation of funds, has made things difficult in europe and in many developing countries, especially in acp countries. on the one hand, europe should guarantee that the common agricultural policy is not being used to increase the benefits of large producers while small producers are in a very complicated situation. on the other hand, it should be guaranteed that product subsidies by the eu will not be an obstacle for the developing and acp countries. theoretically, the eu could help to eradicate poverty and famine in the world if it changed its agricultural policy. better conditions in the developing countries should mean benefits for europe and for the whole world. but before that, we also need to eradicate the very clear discrimination in the eu, which favours the big producers while small ones and thousands of farmers have to leave agriculture every year.
member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, malaria remains a disease closely linked to poverty. each year, more than a million people die from malaria, the vast majority of them children under five years of age. thus, malaria remains the leading cause of death among children in africa. the disease is most prevalent in africa, although other continents are also affected. the fight against malaria remains underfunded, even though the global fund to fight hiv/aids, tuberculosis and malaria, of which the european union is the main donor, has increased the resources available to countries in recent years. despite these global efforts and the efforts of the global south, the annual global resource shortfall is likely to reach usd 2.6 billion in 2007. as the countries most affected by this disease are also among the poorest, the majority of the resources needed will have to come from external partners, if countries are to be able to combat the disease and achieve the sixth millennium development goal. the european union must therefore increase its contribution through bilateral programmes and through the global fund. yet, we have effective tools to fight malaria. in 2001, the commission formulated a policy and action programme to combat the three main diseases of poverty, namely hiv/aids, malaria and tuberculosis. in 2004, the commission presented an overview of its work, which shows, among other things, that it has quadrupled its financial contribution to the fight against these diseases. this contribution includes an increased allocation for research. the commission's annual contribution to the global fund is eur 259 million for the period 2003-2006. it should enable it to support programmes proposed by countries for the production of insecticide-impregnated nets with sustainable efficacy and medicines. the commission also adopted a new policy framework to continue the fight against these diseases beyond 2007. this policy will be implemented in cooperation with the member states of the european union, with multilateral partners such as the world health organisation, the roll back malaria programme, and with the countries of the south, including the african union, civil society and the private sector. the main actions remain essentially the same. a strong focus on prevention measures, including insecticide-impregnated nets with long-term efficacy and the introduction of new anti-malarial drugs such as artemisinin-based combination drug formulations in countries experiencing resistance to current drugs. the commission will also continue to invest in research and development of preventive vaccines, diagnostic tools and new curative medicines. in order for the development of new tools and medicines to be equitable for those who need them, the social sectors, especially the health sector, obviously need to be strengthened through increased investment and human resources in health services.
i welcome this declaration by the commission on malaria because three years ago, when approving our contribution to the budget of the global fund to fight malaria, tuberculosis and aids, the commission accepted parliament's request to inform us regularly, and the previous commission did not always do so. also, in the fight against the infectious diseases linked to poverty, aids often takes center stage when tuberculosis and malaria claim more lives each year and the chances of success in their eradication are higher. just a few years ago, malaria seemed close to eradication in many countries; today it is the leading cause of death in sub-saharan africa, affecting more people and regions where it had already been eradicated. recent figures put the number of direct and indirect victims of malaria at over three million annually. it is good that the commission is encouraging debate on national protocols for the treatment of malaria, but this is not the most important thing if the aim is to include new therapeutic combinations, such as artemisinin and some other chemotherapeutic. insecticide-treated bed nets and intermittent preventive treatments significantly reduce morbidity and mortality, but to date only vietnam and some countries in latin america offer encouraging results. in africa, less than 10% of exposed children sleep protected by mosquito nets and systematic use of these nets protects only 1% of the population at risk. the commission, as a member of the governing council of the united nations fund for the fight against these diseases, should increase its attention to malaria and, in the light of experience, should do the same with the sixth and seventh framework programmes for research and technological development, to which we are contributing eur 400 million for research on these diseases, and thus relieve more people at a lower economic cost, although this brings less benefits to the pharmaceutical industry.
mr president, i support what the commissioner has said in his statement, and i believe that this is a debate on a colossal scandal that is taking place in the world and in our societies. the figures my colleagues have given are quite clear: 3,000 children die every day, particularly in sub-saharan countries, from a disease which has been perfectly studied and for which there are absolutely no shortcuts in terms of prevention and treatment. the challenge posed to our countries by this disease is a question on which the european union and the developed north in general are playing with their coherence, their credibility and, of course, their dignity. i therefore believe that if we are not able to deal with this problem effectively, we will have no moral authority to go and talk about values or human rights, specifically to talk about human rights in geneva to a country like cuba, which has been able to eradicate the evil on its territory and which has more doctors in sub-saharan africa fighting this evil than the 25 states of the european union put together.

the rapporteur. mr president, the european parliament's report, which was adopted unanimously last night, has two fundamental origins. firstly, the council's finding in march 2004 that the financial package proposed by the commission for bulgaria and romania is fair and balanced, completely excluding the other arm of the budgetary authority. secondly, the council intends to include in the annex to the accession treaty, for the years 2007 to 2009, fixed amounts of non-compulsory expenditure which become compulsory, thus undermining the institutional and budgetary powers of the european parliament. the european parliament deeply regrets that the council has systematically refused to agree to the drawing up of a joint declaration with parliament on the financial implications of the accession of these two countries. the council's lack of will means a lack of loyal cooperation in the spirit of the interinstitutional agreement. parliament strongly rejects this infringement of its budgetary powers. in this annex, where the figures will be fixed, parts of the annex which are the sole responsibility of the european parliament become mandatory. parliament therefore calls on the council to adopt this joint declaration. we leave this door open before the signing of the accession: that the council should put this joint declaration into effect. it should also be stressed that the council should be very clear that by its refusal it is sending a very bad signal to the future negotiations on the financial perspective.
president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the founding fathers of the community clearly stated in the treaty of rome in 1957 that they were 'determined to lay the foundations of an ever closer union between the peoples of europe'. in the preamble to the treaty, the member states call on the other peoples of europe - including those who were then divided - who share the same ideals of peace and freedom to join them in their project of building a united europe. tomorrow, by adopting the relevant opinions on the completion of the fifth enlargement of the union, which includes bulgaria and romania, the european parliament will enable the union to take a decisive step in the process of unifying our continent. it is a new step in the unification process, as the bulgarian and romanian nations are finding their place in a europe with a common history, heritage and culture. the two countries thus find their true place in a continent open to culture, knowledge and social progress, as the preamble to the constitution emphasizes. by your assent, you are making a crucial contribution to a europe without dividing lines, a europe of democracy, freedom, peace and progress, sharing the same values as those enshrined in the constitution for europe. moreover, the accession of these two countries to the union is first and foremost an adherence to these values, to this european model to which european citizens, all european citizens, are attached. our noblest ambition, shared by the citizens of these two countries, who have regained their freedom after nearly five decades of sometimes terrible oppression, is precisely to anchor these countries in these values. i would like to ask the honourable member a simple question: what convinced european, who wants to move europe forward along the path of democracy and human rights, but also social rights, can reasonably take the risk of rejecting the charter of fundamental rights, which is an integral part of the constitution and which marks a fundamental step in the construction of our europe, a europe based on common values? (applause) i would like to thank the two countries were also fully involved in the drafting of this constitution, which will provide a stronger basis for europe. the success of this enlargement depends not only on the concrete efforts of bulgaria and romania in the process of reforming their societies. it also needs the support of our citizens, who must understand the significance of this enlargement for the stability of our continent. the european parliament has a vital role to play in giving political legitimacy and credibility to this process. this fifth enlargement process, launched in 1997 by the luxembourg european council, has been a global, inclusive and evolving process. the twelve states involved have all done so under the same conditions and have been called upon to join the european union on the basis of the same criteria. it was carried out in stages, at the pace of each candidate country, depending on its level of preparation. this has ensured that each state is able to join the european union with equal opportunities but also with the same obligations. at the european council in december 2002, which decided on the accession of the 10 new member states, the one europe declaration underlined the continuity, inclusiveness and irreversibility of the enlargement process, clearly announcing our aim to welcome bulgaria and romania as new member states in 2007. the accession negotiations have not always been easy - the commission certainly knows something about this - but i think that the results contained in the accession treaty are fair and appropriate and are broadly comparable to those of the negotiations with the ten new member states. bulgaria and romania now have about 20 months to complete their preparations for accession. in its last regular reports, the commission considered that, in view of the progress made by these two countries, the results obtained in implementing their commitments and the preparatory work under way, these two countries should be ready to join the union on 1 january 2007. the commission confirmed this conclusion in its favourable opinion of 22 february on the accession of the two countries. the european council considered that bulgaria and romania will be able to meet all the obligations of accession, provided that both countries continue their efforts within the time limits, complete all the necessary reforms and honour all the commitments made in each of the areas of the acquis. you are aware of the legitimate questions about the correct and timely implementation of the acquis, particularly in the field of justice and home affairs, as regards romania, and in particular competition and environment policy. there are no shortcuts to membership. the credibility of the process depends on the fact that each country can only join on the basis of the same political and economic criteria and on its ability to fulfil all the obligations arising from membership. this implies the existence of the administrative and judicial capacity necessary to carry out this task. bulgaria and romania are fully aware of what is expected of them as future member states. from the very beginning of the accession negotiations, the union has emphasized what accession to the european union implies: full acceptance of all the actual and potential rights and obligations of the union system and its institutional framework, including the constitution, in which i have the greatest confidence, and the effective and real implementation of the acquis. in the light of the reports by mr moscovici and mr van orden on the applications for accession of bulgaria and romania, i am convinced that we share the same analysis that these two countries should be able to join the union in january 2007 and to fulfil fully the obligations arising from their membership. in the meantime, the union will continue to support bulgaria and romania in their preparations by all means at its disposal. until accession, the europe agreements concluded in 1994 will continue to apply. they have worked well and have been a key element in preparing bulgaria and romania for accession. but it is clear that it is up to bulgaria and romania to do everything possible to be ready. we cannot underestimate the economic, social and political implications of this and the work done so far certainly deserves our respect. the european union will continue to follow closely the preparations made by both countries and the results achieved, including the effective implementation of the commitments. i can assure you that the luxembourg presidency takes the monitoring work - the so-called monitoring - very seriously. it is in the vital interest of both countries to be truly prepared. otherwise, they risk not being able to take full advantage of membership, for example if the implementation of sectoral safeguard clauses should prove necessary. we know the respective roles of the institutions in this context. let me get this straight: having regard to the assent opinions of the european parliament on the application for accession to the european union of the republic of bulgaria and romania, the council, if the commission submits to it a recommendation for the implementation of one of the safeguard clauses contained in the treaty of accession, shall act in this regard, taking due account of the position of the european parliament. the council is giving this assurance to parliament today, which is right to want to follow developments in both countries closely. a letter was sent in this connection by the president of the european council to the president of the european parliament, as has been pointed out. i repeat that enlargement can only succeed if it enjoys the broad support of the peoples of the union. you represent these people. you represent the citizens of europe. your voice must be heard, your appreciation should be fully taken into account when decisions should be enlargement process will continue to be valuable. we are grateful for the political support you have given to the process throughout its development, in particular through the open and constructive dialogue with your elected parliamentary partners in the bulgarian and romanian parliaments. in conclusion, let me remind you that the historic project you are discussing today is the accession of bulgaria and romania. they all agree that the accession of these two countries will be a decisive step towards overcoming the injustice and artificial division of europe. i would now like to say a word about the financial implications. as regards the financing of the enlargement to 27 with bulgaria and romania, i would like to point out that the negotiations with these two countries were conducted on the same basis and in accordance with the same principles as those applied to the 10 new member states. on the basis of a commission proposal, the member states approved a financial envelope for these two countries, which will cover a period of three years, as was the case for the ten. after that, the acquis will apply, including the next financial perspective. it's a matter of justice, of fair treatment, but also of predictability for both countries. we cannot negotiate without putting the cards on the table, especially with regard to the financial aspects in their first difficult steps as member states. it is clear that, given the date envisaged for the accession of these two countries, we are in a different context from that experienced by the ten new member states. critical conditions when we evaluate romania’s progress towards accession. romania has started to tackle the accession requirements seriously, especially in the field of justice reform and the fight against corruption. i am glad to say today that all the key strategic documents required as a result of the negotiations have recently been transmitted by the romanian government to the commission on time. these concern the fight against corruption, reform of the justice system and border security. the documents are currently being assessed by the commission. in another key area which we will be watching very closely, that of competition and state aid, romania has inter alia fulfilled its obligation to submit its national plan for steel restructuring, and has done this on time before the deadline. progress is also being made in the areas of police cooperation, where new laws on the gendarmerie and the national police have been adopted. romania is engaged in discussions to determine the shape of its future funding commitments regarding border management. the political determination now has to be further translated into concrete actions. based on my frequent meetings with the romanians in both bucharest and in brussels, i have a strong belief that the new government has understood the scope and the importance of the monitoring exercise, as well as the urgency to deliver concrete results in the first semester of 2005. in my view we have reason to be cautiously optimistic as regards romania’s preparation for accession. let us have a fair game. the jury is still out and it is now time to give romania the benefit of the doubt in terms of its preparations for accession as a fully-fledged member state of the european union. before concluding, let me briefly touch upon the financial implications of the accession of bulgaria and romania, to which mr smith referred in his speech. commissioner grybauskaitė has worked closely with the two rapporteurs mr böge and mrs dührkop dührkop, my former colleagues from the committee on budgetary control. the commission’s position on the matter is as follows. the amounts agreed in the accession negotiations with bulgaria and romania for the period 2007-2009 are included in the accession treaty. the financial perspective for 2007-2013 is to be broken into broad categories of expenditure for the eu-27, not on distinctions of allocations between certain groups of member states, some of which can only be very indicative anyway. the commission believes that distinguishing indicative amounts by certain groups of member states is not in line with the spirit and the letter of the interinstitutional agreement. to conclude, both the european commission and our financial assistance programmes will continue to support the efforts of the two countries to intensify their necessary preparations. the timely signature of the accession treaty is important with a view to sustaining the momentum and ensuring the successful preparation for the accession of bulgaria and romania. i count on your support in this respect.

member of the commission. mr president, the commission appreciates the hard work and close attention to detail by parliament’s committee on fisheries in preparing for this debate with regard to the two files in front of parliament this morning. the objective of the measures we are contemplating is that of safeguarding the needs of future generations from the demands of the present population. this is what we define as sustainability and we see long-term management plans as the right legislative instrument for achieving this. i am pleased to note that parliament is broadly in agreement with our thinking. as always, our shared commitment to achieving sustainability in fisheries remains unwavering. we cannot overstate this principle. our aim remains common, but our approach may be somewhat different. in this instance we have some differences concerning the details. with regard to the plan for southern hake and norway lobster we have held consultations with parties involved concerning the fisheries that catch these species, often catching them together in mixed fisheries. we agree that there should be the possibility for state aid to fishermen involved in these fisheries, but these should be applied equitably to all fishermen who may find themselves in similar situations, and should therefore be applied in the context of the european fisheries fund. we consider that the limits on tac changes should be plus or minus 15% to be in accordance with scientific advice. there is no technical basis to choose a different value. however, i accept that this limit should be applied from the first year of the plan’s implementation. we should not intentionally delay stock recovery if this is feasible within the plan. recovery should occur as soon as possible and in no later than ten years. we appreciate that there are special difficulties in the gulf of cadiz and that uncertainties are high. however, to be consistent with the precautionary approach that has been agreed in the un and in community legislation, greater uncertainty cannot be a reason to apply more lax conservation measures. we can agree to the exclusion of the gulf of cadiz from the same effort management scheme as elsewhere, if an alternative but equally effective management system is in place. after discussions with stakeholders on this point we can now agree to remove the closed areas originally proposed for nephrops, but we think they should be replaced with other closed areas that are better adapted to protecting the stock. nephrops stocks require conservation measures to restore their ability to support significant fisheries. i agree that bay of biscay sole could be moved to a management plan in accordance with its less serious biological state, but western channel sole should remain the subject of a recovery plan. legally, a management plan cannot be applied to western channel sole until it is inside safe biological limits. we are convening a scientific meeting of stecf to look at options for target fishing mortalities for sole that will be consistent with the objectives of the common fisheries policy and with international commitments at the un and the fao. therefore, we have to reserve our position until we have seen the results of this evaluation.
the rapporteur. i would like to remind you that with only one vote against, which i am very grateful to all my colleagues for, this report makes significant changes to the commission's proposal for measures to restore cod and cichlid stocks in iberian waters. the recovery target proposed by the commission for cod was based on fishing mortality, whereas my report proposes, as recommended by the scientists, the achievement of an appropriate level of biomass, supplemented by a system of limiting fishing effort by geographical areas and grouping fishing gear. the commission has already proposed a system of calculating effort based on kilowatts of power, which we consider too complicated, and we therefore propose that it be based on days at sea and that a system of co-responsibility for fishermen in the control of fisheries be introduced. the period of application, commissioner, is not negotiable for us. for this recovery plan, it is not enough to implement or decide on five years. we would be happy to see the fisheries sector recover in five years, but the ten years, as opposed to the five proposed by the commission, are intended to allow the sector to adapt gradually and more flexibly and to ensure the greatest possible stability of fishing activity, without prejudicing the final objective, which is the recovery of resources, which is desired by everyone, not just the commission. i have also modified and lightened the quantities laid down in the proposal on weighing, by-catch and other technical measures, so that the margins of tolerance will be similar to those in other existing schemes. as regards the forecasts for the cigala fishery, everyone knows today that the areas of the proposal are not adapted to the situation of the stocks or to the duration, since it is proposed that it should be indefinite. mr commissioner, according to the reports drawn up by the ieo, only one of the proposed areas has concentrations of cigala of a certain size and these are in a much more limited area than that indicated by the commission, at depths of 100 to 140 metres, so we believe that the ban, if it is introduced, should be limited both in space and in its duration, between may and august. the commission tends to forget something: the socioeconomic impact. the commission proposal, mr commissioner, is entirely concerned with conservation of resources, without any reference to the socioeconomic realities involved in its implementation, and i can assure you that if the commission proposal as it stands is implemented, it would be dramatic for the sector, because the proposed bans on cigala will in practice render all trawling in iberian waters invalid and impossible, and we are talking about multi-species fisheries in which cigala represents barely 1% of the total catches made by these fleets. i have indeed considered it appropriate to introduce a reference to the socioeconomic measures to be taken to deal with the possible loss of income that the sector may suffer, either through the new european fisheries fund, as you have said, or through any other specific instrument that the european union may create, and i am glad that the specificity of the gulf of cádiz area is recognised and that, in this sense, it has been considered more positive to dissociate it from the proposal. the exclusion of this fish from the recovery plan should not, under any circumstances, mean that measures are not being taken to enable it to be recovered and managed in a sustainable way, and in this connection you are aware that the national authorities are drawing up an emergency plan for this particular fishery. i believe, mr commissioner, that as rapporteur i have chosen the most realistic and most possible way, and i must admit that i have kept very much in mind the objective of preserving resources - which i consider to be of extraordinary importance and, as you say, ensures our future - as well as the objective of preserving a healthy, prosperous and viable european fisheries sector. that is the meaning of the report i am presenting to this house today.

member of the commission. mr president, the commission is well aware of the severity of the drought situation in portugal. it understands the concerns and is fully committed to assist portugal. my colleague, commissioner fischer boel, met the portuguese minister of agriculture, mr silva, on 6 april 2005 in relation to this issue. there are three sets of instruments that are of particular importance in assisting portuguese farmers. the first concerns market support and direct aid, where the commission has already acted. it has adopted two decisions: one on 4 march to increase the advance payments for the bovine premiums for 2004 to 80%, and another on 7 april to allow the use of set-aside land for animal feeding in the affected regions. three more decisions are currently in preparation. the first concerns a temporary derogation from the density requirements of the regulation on the conversion of arable land to extensive livestock farming. it introduces a corrective correlation coefficient to be applied to the number of livestock units recorded on the holding. another decision will extend the use of set-aside land for the feeding of animals to the whole continental territory of portugal. in this context, i also want to mention the portuguese request for transfer of intervention stocks. traditionally, the commission is opposed to such transfers in light of abundant market supplies. commissioner fischer boel has, in discussion with the portuguese minister of agriculture, accepted the particularly difficult circumstances due to the prolonged drought in portugal. she has asked the services of the directorate-general for agriculture to discuss the arrangements with portuguese officials with regard to the disposal of the transferred stocks. a third decision will authorise, under certain conditions, the advance payment of a number of premiums. these include an advance of 80% of the amount of the suckler cow premium, and 50% of the sheep, goats and dairy premium for 2005. under article 28(3)(c) of regulation (ec) no 1782/2003, the single farm payment might be advanced as well, provided that it is not paid out before 16 october at the earliest and subject to controls being carried out. the second instrument concerns rural development. when natural disasters occur, re-programming is possible. however, this possibility seems limited as we approach the end of the programming period and resources are scarce. portugal asked that farmers continue to receive rural development payments even if certain conditions cannot be met due to the drought. at the end of january 2005, the portuguese authorities requested recognition of the drought as a force majeure under article 39 of regulation (ec) no 817/2004 and to accept derogations to certain conditions concerning the agri-environment measure. application of a force majeure requires a number of objective criteria, in particular the severity of the drought and the quantification of the consequences on agriculture and the farming economy. some reports are already available and paint an initial picture of the expected consequences. on the basis of the information available, the commission has no objection to the portuguese request. however, portugal will be asked for a more comprehensive report. portugal may decide to compensate farmers through state aid for income losses resulting from severe drought. they have to notify their plans to the commission. the commission will do its best to approve such plans quickly. however, it is essential to prove that the losses due to a climatic event reached a threshold of 20% or 30%; secondly, that there is a direct link between the losses and the adverse weather conditions; and thirdly, that no over-compensation occurs. the portuguese authorities can also use the de minimis regulation on state aid. over a period of three years, up to eur 3 000 per farmer can be granted in aid without the commission being notified, provided that, among other conditions, the total amount for the period does not exceed eur 17 832 000.

it is surprising that the european union has not yet developed and implemented a short- and long-term strategy to combat drought and desertification, which is one of the main threats to economic and social sustainability in the southern and mediterranean countries. but the lack of a joint plan between the countries and the committee (agriculture and environment) is all the more striking when the european environment agency recently highlighted that the areas most negatively affected by the expected climate change are the mediterranean countries. we therefore support a policy to combat drought in portugal, and any aid to alleviate the impacts on productivity, the market or the plantations themselves resulting from this water deficit. at the same time we ask that its extension to other countries of the south be studied.
the six motions for resolutions on bangladesh are now under discussion.
member of the commission. mr president, the european commission welcomes the european parliament’s initiative to draw public attention to the serious governance and human rights situation in bangladesh. today’s debate is very timely; it is being held against the background of a law and order situation that has suffered a serious decline since the last european parliament resolution of november 2002. abuses against human rights activists, journalists and minorities are on the increase. the governance situation is at an all-time low and political violence has reached a new climax, as sadly exemplified by the grenade attack in august 2004 and the tragic assassination of former finance minister kibria in january. we share your concerns about the dysfunction of the country’s institutions, the culture of impunity, mounting fundamentalism, the human rights abuses of minorities and the escalating confrontation between ruling and opposition parties. all these factors, combined with mounting religious militancy, make us believe that bangladesh’s democratic and secular foundations are in jeopardy. the european community has been very vocal on these issues, not least in view of our development mandate and the human rights clause that provides the basis of our aid relationship with bangladesh. over the last months the european community and the member states have repeatedly called on the government to condemn the persecution of political opponents, intellectuals, journalists, ngos and minorities. the european union has reacted strongly to the attack on mrs sheikh hasina and the assassination of former minister kibria by urging the government to restore justice without delay and to give clear signals that acts of terrorism are not acceptable. we are continuously stressing our concerns about the climate of impunity reigning in the country, the confrontational politics, the mounting attacks against the tribal people of the chittagong hill tracts and the ahmadiyya community and the extrajudicial killings in ‘crossfire’ by special police forces. let me also note that the european union showed great unity on bangladesh at this year’s human rights commission in geneva, where the eu agreed to single out bangladesh as one of five countries in its statement of principle on human rights in the world. the deteriorating governance situation has compelled us to enhance donor unity. in february the european community, the world bank and the us department of state convened a meeting in washington with all major international donors to discuss how we can foster key governance reforms. the exchanges confirmed that our concerns are fully shared by the international donor community. this donor unity has allowed us to define common priorities and to convey strong private messages to the government on the poor governance and the urgent need to deliver on reforms. the gathering in washington had a clear impact on the country: it prompted the government to admit publicly the existence of an islamic fundamentalist problem. alas, the government crackdown on islamic militants is already petering out, as demonstrated by charges being dropped against a prominent islamic leader. for its part, the commission will continue closely to monitor the political situation in the country and pursue these fundamental issues through our political dialogue with the government and close donor coordination. in that context we will also increase the focus of our attention on the next parliamentary elections in late 2006 and the conditions for free and fair elections. the political dialogue will be underpinned by our offer to support pressing institutional reforms in the next aid strategy which, if accepted by the government, would contribute to a meaningful change and thus to more progress and prosperity for the people of bangladesh.

the next item is the debate on the five motions for resolutions on humanitarian aid to the refugees from western sahara.
author. mr president, i was prepared to join a list of speakers and not to start a debate. in any case, it is true that this joint resolution which we are about to adopt on the situation of the refugees in the sahara is quite self-explanatory and is bound up with a strictly humanitarian drama. in dealing with the human rights situation in the world, we will find a paragraph devoted to the situation in the sahara. and the political situation in the sahara deserves further reflection. but it is the strictly humanitarian situation that now affects us. we are talking about some 200 000 refugees who have been living in refugee camps for almost 30 years and with no other source of resources than international humanitarian aid. that's what we're talking about here today. and that is what is at stake for a number of reasons, including some strictly bureaucratic ones affecting the european commission. all of that together is about to create a real humanitarian crisis. that is what this motion for a resolution is trying to do by calling on the commission to take urgent action to prevent a humanitarian crisis of unprecedented proportions from developing. and then, it is proposed some very concrete measures, such as greater collaboration with the non-governmental organizations on the ground or greater support for those sahrawi institutions which, inside the refugee camps, are collaborating in the administration of this humanitarian aid, which, i repeat, is the only source of income for 200 000 people. there is no doubt that this resolution solves or tackles only part of the problem and that we cannot turn a blind eye to what the problem is. there is a serious problem at the doorstep of europe and sooner or later we must be able to exert all the political and diplomatic pressure on the various actors involved in the solution of this conflict so that we can as soon as possible stop having debates like this: how do we feed 200 000 people who without us will have nothing to eat.
author. mr president, the resolution we are presenting and voting on today is indeed about the increasingly deteriorating humanitarian situation in the sahrawi camps. this is a commitment made by a parliamentary delegation which visited the camps a few weeks ago, and which we are now fulfilling. aid is running out, and there is an urgent need to respond to this situation. but we must also bear in mind that the humanitarian question actually conceals the real problem, which is political. humanitarian aid is necessary because the saharawi people are forced to live in camps far from their homes and cannot lead a normal life far from their country. after 30 years of conflict, the patience is running out in the camps. there are even voices calling for a return to armed conflict if the situation is not resolved soon. this is very worrying; the european union cannot turn a blind eye to this fact. but the most worrying thing is that the solution is on the table, it exists and it's called plan baker ii. it is an imperfect plan, no doubt, but one which the saharawi people accepted, making important concessions in its approaches. and yet the other party, morocco, refuses to sign it. europe is looking to spain and therefore the spanish government must take the lead in the process of resolving the conflict. let us not forget that the saharawi population is now in the camps as a result of an unfinished decolonization, for which the spanish government is primarily responsible. i therefore encourage president zapatero to encourage spain to take up the role that portugal played in relation to timor. after 30 years of neglect, silence and broken promises, it is time for the world in general and europe in particular to stop turning a blind eye to the problem and to face it head on. it is time for the saharawi people to see their just and understandable demand for a referendum on self-determination in western sahara, in accordance with international law and the united nations charter, fulfilled. finally, i would also like to express my solidarity with the moroccan journalist ali lmrabet, who has been unjustly convicted of defamation for saying that the people living in the camps are refugees and not abductees.
author. mr president, this resolution is the fruit of the commitment that some members of the european parliament, including mr portas, mr romeva and mrs scheele, made in the tindouf refugee camps, where we spent four days, experiencing the hardships of living in the middle of the desert. we were there for a few days to see the suffering of the saharawi people, because they have no political solution, no peaceful or orderly solution to their situation. we were, like them, without water, without light. but to these tindemans' own ruthlessness, because these 150 000 human beings live in the middle of the desert without any comfort, we must add the fact that we are faltering in what is humanitarian aid. the resolution we are proposing here deals strictly with humanitarian aid, because we have seen firsthand the humanitarian difficulties facing the saharawi people because of the lack of aid. because the help they were getting is dwindling. i do not know whether any member state of the european union will have responsibility for this. france's position in this conflict is very clear... but i do not want to talk about that, because we are talking about the importance of the european union continuing to help as it has been doing to these 150 000 saharawis who are trying to find a solution. the political problems are one thing, and they will have to be solved and addressed in other resolutions. but we cannot ignore the fact that, within a few kilometres of the european union, we have 150 000 saharawis who are suffering because we are not generous enough. because by cutting off flour or reducing the food quotas we have been sending, we are contributing to the already very difficult living conditions in the refugee camps. the european union also has its responsibility as the main donor of aid from the united nations. we must also make our voice heard there.
mr president, forgetfulness is the great enemy of many situations of injustice in the world. the sahrawi people are the most important people in the world. after 30 years, these men and women are surviving in a totally inhuman situation, deprived of the most basic needs, in extremely difficult conditions. despite this, we could say that they are a clear example in terms of organization and work, which hold them together with great dignity, especially highlighting the courage of saharawi women, who have been able to build a well-structured society from nothing. we have a moral and political obligation in europe today. we are talking about a borderline situation that demands an immediate response. the saharawi people would like to live off their own resources and their own labour, but unfortunately they have to do so on the basis of our solidarity. the saharawi people have shown us their organization and their ability to manage resources. the increase in european aid and the confidence in its management by the sahrawi structures are therefore the demands we are making to this house today. we cannot forget that the cause of this humanitarian problem is rooted in a political conflict that needs to be addressed. we must be able to resolve the political question and make the referendum on self-determination for the saharawi people a reality. we must be able to find a just and final solution. peace and freedom for the saharawi people.
member of the commission. thank you for your initiative, which gives me the opportunity to express the commission’s views concerning the western sahara conflict. first of all, let me stress that the commission would like to see this conflict resolved soon and its resolution is crucial for the stability, regional integration and development in the maghreb and in the mediterranean. from a humanitarian point of view, one cannot but feel concern regarding the dramatic conditions for the thousands of sahrawi refugees, the ongoing detention by the polisario of 408 moroccan prisoners of war, the difficulties for the families divided between the refugee camps and the western sahara, and the fate of people unaccounted for on both sides. all these issues impress on us the need for an end to this crisis, which has been going on for nearly 30 years. as you know, the provision of humanitarian aid by the commission respects the principles of neutrality, impartiality and independence and is based on real needs. the commission’s humanitarian office, echo, also acts in accordance with the criteria of non-discrimination and not subjecting policies to political objectives. this means that anyone affected by a humanitarian crisis is entitled to receive aid, no matter which side of the conflict they are on. in full observance of these principles and criteria, the commission has provided humanitarian aid totalling eur 108 million to the sahrawi refugees since 1993. thanks to these continuing efforts, the commission has become the principle donor of humanitarian aid to the sahrawi refugees. the commission has never interrupted its assistance. it has, however, adapted the timing and the level of the most recent funding decisions to the situation on the ground. i would like to emphasise that, thanks to the essential role of the ‘buffer stock’, created and funded by the commission in 2000, we have been able to avoid any interruption in food supplies. the current humanitarian situation in the camps has not deteriorated. however, it remains worrying. there is a risk of deterioration when and if the possible break in the food pipeline, as announced by the world food programme, is not compensated for in a timely and sufficient manner. echo intends to propose a funding decision next month to deal with this situation. the funding for 2005 will depend both on the needs of the sahrawi refugees and on the conditions for the implementation of echo-funded projects. i would like to stress that the commission has a dual responsibility. it not only needs to address the humanitarian needs of refugees in a timely and dedicated manner but it also has to protect the financial interests of the european union. its operations in the sahrawi refugee camps are designed to carry out this dual responsibility effectively. that is why the commission attaches such importance to the proper identification of beneficiaries and full transparency of its operations. with a view to properly assessing the humanitarian needs of the sahrawi refugees, the commission is continuing its discussions with the principal agencies and organisations, in particular the algerian and sahrawi authorities, the high commissioner for refugees, the world food programme and non-governmental organisations. these ngos have played and continue to play an important role as echo’s partner in the implementation of its operations in the sahrawi camps. beyond its purely humanitarian dimension, i believe that the international community’s assistance to the sahrawi refugees helps to create and maintain conditions that are favourable to finding a peaceful solution to the conflict. more generally, i would like to state for the record that the commission and the european union’s position on the political aspects of this conflict has always been to remain impartial. the european union continues to fully support the united nations’ efforts towards finding a fair and lasting solution in accordance with international law.

the next item is the debate on the five motions for resolutions on lampedusa.
the mass expulsions of migrants carried out by the italian authorities between october 2004 and march 2005 from the italian island of lampedusa to libya are a matter of grave concern. in particular, the high commissioner for refugees denounced the return of 180 people on 17 march, stating that it was not at all clear that italy had taken the necessary precautions to ensure the return in good faith of these people to libya, a country which in no case can be considered a safe land of asylum. in this connection, we deeply regret that the italian authorities did not allow unhcr access to the lampedusa detention centre. we therefore call on the european commission to ensure that the right of asylum is respected in the european union and to put a stop to the mass expulsions. we also call on the italian authorities to respect their obligations under european union law. we therefore ask that a delegation consisting of members of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs and the subcommittee on human rights be sent to the lampedusa refugee centre and to libya to assess the extent of the problem and the way it is being dealt with and, in particular, the way people are being treated, which also means that the fate and final destination of those who have been expelled must be investigated in particular. in short, there is cause for concern that, in the area of asylum and immigration, there are increasingly frequent cases of violations of the fundamental principles to which the european union and its member states are committed. lampedusa is simply one of those examples which we should avoid repeating.

we now come to the debate on the report by mr coveney on the annual report on human rights in the world in 2004 and the european union's human rights policy [2004/2151 (ini) ] (a6-0086/2005) for this purpose we have mr almunia, who is replacing commissioner ferrero-waldner, who is in luxembourg.
president of the council. mr president, i should like to begin by congratulating mr coveney on his excellent report. i would say that it presents a very broad and comprehensive view of the human rights situation in a number of respects, as the rapporteur has just said. human rights are more than ever at the centre of the international debate. the sixty-first session of the united nations commission on human rights has just concluded in geneva. the secretary-general of the united nations released his report in march entitled "in greater freedom: toward development, security and respect for human rights for all". it has thus, in a sense, placed the question of human rights at the centre of our concern for the peaceful development of our world. that's kind of what you do in your report. you have drawn a picture of the human rights situation in the world, a picture which is uncompromising and which shows that we must continue to be concerned about human rights. it calls for even more decisive action, even more committed to the defence of human rights. the european union has always been committed to the defence and promotion of human rights; we are making it a central element of our foreign policy. in the face of the challenges of globalisation, and also in view of the continuing deterioration of respect for human rights in many parts of the world, the european union must make a further effort to promote and defend human rights, first internally with governments, but also with civil society, ngos, national parliaments and international institutions. at the heart of the defence of human rights is the commitment we must make to resolving conflicts, conflicts which are often the very source of contempt for the human person. in fact, in your report you denounce a number of cases, you draw up a sort of catastrophic catalogue of cases of human rights violations in many parts of the world. in this connection, i would like to stress the report of the secretary-general of the united nations and the reform of the united nations system, the importance of the human rights aspect in the context of the link between the reform of the united nations, better respect for the charter and the declaration of human rights. let us simply remember that the union is first and foremost a community of values, a community of values which is moreover better anchored in the draft constitution, in particular through the charter of fundamental rights. the community of values we want to be imposes on us the obligation to defend the principles of democracy and respect for human rights throughout the world. these values guide us and should guide us in our choices which are expressed through the various tools at our disposal for conducting our politics. you will understand, mr rapporteur, that i cannot answer in detail all the aspects of your report, all the extremely useful and extremely rich headings it contains. i shall therefore confine myself to a number of the questions you have raised, while giving the undertaking on behalf of the council that our services will continue to study this document and take account of the many suggestions you make in it. i would therefore like to highlight a few aspects which are of such importance that they deserve special attention, and i shall begin with the dialogue. we try to raise human rights wherever we have the opportunity and with all our interlocutors. that is why human rights are always an integral part of all agreements we conclude with partners, even if they are mainly economic agreements. we have therefore started a human rights dialogue with china to show that human rights are not a luxury for rich and developed countries, but a necessary element in economic development. we have also started human rights consultations with russia. it is also a component of the four common areas approach which we hope to put into practice at the next summit with russia on 10 may. on the other hand, as i speak, a troika of the european union is discussing the modalities for resuming the human rights dialogue with iran. in this country too, human rights are an integral part of our relationship with tehran on other important issues: respect for human rights cannot be separated from the other fundamental issues on which we are working. we know that this is a long-term task. although it is difficult, if not impossible, to quantify the results achieved through these human rights dialogues, we consider them to be an indispensable tool for advancing the cause of human rights in the various countries concerned. the need to find common ground with our partners does not, of course, exempt us from regular evaluations of these dialogues. improving the situation on the ground is the objective pursued and it is concrete results such as respect for the rule of law or the release of political prisoners that provide us with indications of the successes we achieve through such dialogues. i will also emphasize strongly the support for human rights organizations in a number of countries, which you also do in your report. it is unacceptable that in some countries the european union funds allocated to these human rights organisations are blocked by governments, something which i believe the president of parliament emphasised very strongly during a visit to one of these countries. i would also like to say a word on a subject which is very close to our hearts: respect for human rights in the fight against terrorism. this is a question of morality first and efficiency second. those who think they can weaken respect for human rights under the pretext of fighting terrorism are, in a sense, giving in to the terrible blackmail of the worst enemies of democracy, namely terrorists. so it's not a path to choose. the attacks of 11 september 2001 have indeed placed terrorism among the priorities of the european union, but we have said and reiterated recently in geneva before the commission on human rights that efforts to combat terrorism must respect human rights and fundamental freedoms. the council stated on 21 september 2001 that the fight against terrorism must be inseparable from respect for the fundamental freedoms on which our civilization is founded. at the recent session of the commission on human rights in geneva, the union actively participated in the negotiations on this subject and thus contributed to the adoption of a resolution on respect for human rights in the fight against terrorism. the resolution provides for the appointment of a special rapporteur and will thus help to strengthen the protection of human rights in the fight against terrorism. as for the cooperation you mention in your report between the personal representative for human rights, recently appointed by the secretary-general of the council/high representative for the cfsp, and the european union coordinator for counter-terrorism, it is in line with our policy on this matter and we are working to develop it. i would like to mention some other matters which are of particular importance to you. first, the rights of the child. we are still talking about human rights, but the priority should be the often catastrophic situation of children who are victims of conflict and also of poverty. i believe that the european union has a special vocation in this respect and we will have to see how we can strengthen our action in favour of children's rights. on this point too, let me remind you that the draft constitution explicitly refers to the defence of the rights of the child. i believe that we must step up our action in this direction, in terms of our development aid and in the context of the millennium development goals. there is also the question of the rights of women victims of conflict, but also the question of strengthening the european union's action against all forms of trafficking in human beings, of which women and children are generally the main victims. this is an area in which the european union must step up its action. i would also like to take this opportunity to stress the importance of freedom of information and the right to information. your parliament has made a great deal of effort to promote this right. journalists are often the victims of imprisonment, torture, harassment of all kinds and, today, hostage-taking. this is a good time to think about these journalists who have been held hostage in iraq for more than 100 days. another issue that is also discussed in your report is that of the future agency for fundamental freedoms and the risk of duplication of work resulting from the proliferation of human rights bodies. we decided as early as 2003 that the mandate of the european monitoring centre on racism and xenophobia should be reviewed and that it should be considered to become an agency. a wide public consultation was then launched by the commission. the very large number of individuals and organisations who have expressed their ideas on the future role of the observatory and its transformation into an agency for fundamental freedoms and human rights shows how concerned citizens are about human rights issues. we can only congratulate ourselves on that. following this consultation, the commission started to draft a proposal for a regulation on the basis of the many elements gathered. this proposal will then be examined in accordance with the usual procedure. so while it is premature to discuss this agency here, let me stress that, given the scale of the task, there will never be too many of us to deal with the preservation and defence of human rights. we are aware of the problems and intend to strengthen cooperation between the various bodies concerned. our aim is to strengthen all the instruments and bodies in the service of human rights in a spirit of concerted and coordinated work in order to achieve effective action and to avoid any duplication which would be an irresponsible waste of our resources. member of the commission. mr president, i would like to begin by apologising to commissioner ferrero-waldner for her absence today and also expressing my satisfaction at being able to take her place on such an essential issue in our model of society, of political and civic community and in our european project. the universal declaration of human rights begins by noting that "freedom, justice and peace in the world are based on the recognition of the inherent dignity and equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family". all of us, in the exercise of our responsibilities and in our daily and private lives, have a responsibility to promote and protect the rights of every human being everywhere in the world. the european parliament's report on human rights which we are conflict; secondly, on human rights defenders; and lastly, on the international criminal court. the commission welcomes the emphasis on children's rights in the report. in recent years, the european union has put in place an effective framework for the integration of children's rights into its policies and programmes. in collaboration with unicef, we have initiated a specific training programme on children's rights and last september we set up an interinstitutional group on this subject. the commission plays an active role in the implementation of the european union guidelines on children and armed conflict adopted in 2003: we regularly raise the issue in our dialogues with third countries and with representatives of groups involved in armed conflict. for example, during her visit to sri lanka last march, commissioner ferrero-waldner had the opportunity to place particular emphasis on the importance of eradicating the use of children in these conflicts. the commission supports a supporting and training projects in third countries. the objective of these programmes and resources is to advance the implementation of the convention on the rights of the child and its optional protocols. let me also point out that the group of commissioners for human rights places particular emphasis on this subject. my colleagues have reviewed the commission's work in this field and are currently considering how best to give priority to this issue; one of the possibilities being considered is the adoption of a communication, as suggested by mr coveney in his report. secondly, i would like to refer to the human rights defenders. in his speech to the united nations general assembly, the un high commissioner for human rights stated, in relation to human rights defenders, that they are our eyes and ears and represent our collective conscience. they are a vital source of information on developments in third countries. we, the european union, therefore depend on them, on human rights defenders, for information. that means that we have a huge responsibility to protect them, we must concentrate on improving the monitoring and transmission of information and establish a strong commitment in this respect by the missions of the european union and the commission delegations in the world. the commission is determined to play an active role in making the guidelines on human rights defenders a reality. in this respect, we give them priority in our campaign 'promoting a culture of human rights', which is one of the four pillars of the european initiative for democracy and human rights. we also place particular emphasis on supporting local human rights organisations in third countries. the programme for this and the next year of the initiative calls for more than 50 delegations of the european commission to launch a micro-project plan, which will represent more than 30% of their total budget. finally, mr president, let me refer to the international criminal court, an institution of vital importance for the promotion of international peace and justice. the commission considers the court to be one of the essential components of a well-regulated international order. it is thanks to it that those who commit mass violations of life and human dignity know that the international community will hold them accountable and, with this, we all hope that the frequency of these crimes will be reduced, but wherever they occur and wherever national systems are unwilling or unable to intervene, the international community now has a complementary system of criminal justice, executed through the court, which must deliver justice in an impartial, transparent and effective manner. this is the only way to ensure that it is regarded as a legitimate institution and that the accession of many other states to the rome statute which created the court is achieved. the european union believes that three principles of the court are fundamental. firstly, the principle of universality of the court, and in this respect we are campaigning around the world to increase the number of ratifications of the rome statute and i am particularly pleased that 77 acp countries jointly agreed last march to include a commitment to ratify the statute in the new cotonou agreement, which is to be signed shortly. secondly, we consider the principle of the integrity of the court, which is under attack by some countries, to be fundamental. for example, the bilateral immunity agreements proposed by the united states undermine the very concept of the court. the commission is also concerned about the sanctions regime imposed by the united states on those countries which refuse to sign such agreements and we continue to express our concern about these issues in our dialogue with the united states. and finally, the third principle of the court is complementarity with national judicial systems; international justice is not a substitute for national justice. that is why we support the reconstruction of legal systems in those countries where the judiciary has not been able or has not had the will to prosecute massive human rights violations. the adoption on 31 march of a un security council resolution on the situation in darfur, which for the first time refers to the international criminal court, is very encouraging. finally, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i can assure you on behalf of the commission that the breadth of countries and issues covered in parliament's report will be of great help when we start work on the european union's annual report on human rights in the near future. i would therefore like to reiterate my thanks and that of the commission to mr coveney and to the european parliament as a whole for their excellent work and to remind once again of our continued readiness to cooperate with parliament in this task. on behalf of the pse group. mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mrs klaß, and all the other members on the work done to supplement the groundwater protection provisions in the framework directive to prevent and control groundwater pollution and to establish criteria for assessing the good chemical status of groundwater bodies. we must therefore consider that, since the possibilities of purifying an aquifer are very limited, control and prevention are strictly necessary in order to prevent pollutants from being stored in groundwater. we must not forget that groundwater is the most sensitive and important water resource in the european union and, in particular, the main source of public drinking water supply. on the other hand, and given that measures to prevent or limit the ingress of pollutants into groundwater are a vital element of this proposal for a directive, it would be very important, contrary to what the honourable member who has preceded me on the floor has said, to get the amendment on article 6 which we have tabled with other honourable members approved, so that member states control indirect discharges on the basis of best environmental practices and sufficient techniques to prevent such discharges. commissioner, i would like to say that the commission, in its proposal for an annex on pollutants, has not taken sufficient account of the fact that, due to the geological nature of the existing subsurface, there are substances, such as chlorides and sulphates, which occur naturally in many aquifers in the european union and that the classification of pollutants for these salts is even questionable from a scientific point of view. i would also like to say that the proposal you have put before us is not very ambitious, since it is limited to the minimum required by the framework directive, but i am still confident that with the work of all of us we will achieve a better directive.
mr president, the first thing i would like to say is that the problem that has arisen with the use of the floor has been solely and exclusively due to a mistake in the services of the whip of my group, and therefore it is up to them to give an explanation to the colleagues who are affected. i would point out, focusing on mrs klaß's report, that farmers are probably the first to be affected by the groundwater directive we are dealing with, and yet their views have not been taken into account in the drafting of the proposal we have on the table. agriculture in many european regions ensures the existence of a vegetation mass which prevents desertification of land, a phenomenon which produces a considerable increase in natural pollutants in groundwater. the drastic reduction of this agricultural activity, as some seem to be seeking to do, would therefore run counter to the very aims of the directive we are discussing today. secondly, i would like to express my disappointment at the lack of interest shown by the committee on the environment, public health and food safety in the amendments tabled by the committee on agriculture and rural development of this parliament, in particular those calling for the element of 'quantity of water' to be taken into account in determining the factors contributing to groundwater pollution. the low-flow aquifers, as is common in many regions of southern europe, especially in the dry season, have a higher salinity and therefore higher sulphate concentrations; this salinity is, i repeat, closely linked to the volumes of water supply, a fact which has not been taken into account in the report before us. i would also like to express my opposition to the establishment of community standards which replace the concept of national thresholds with quality standards, since this would introduce a static element which is incompatible with the diversity of soils and waters existing in many european regions. farmers will also be the first victims of this measure, because the tolerance levels of some substances, especially sulphate, which are generated by nature itself in many areas, depend on the characteristics of the soils and the crops, and examples of crops, such as rice, can withstand higher sulphate levels than other plant species. the setting of community standards for such substances, which in no way endanger the health of consumers, could therefore lead to unjustified stoppages in irrigation.
