ladies and gentlemen, i would like to make a statement to commemorate the end of the second world war in europe. as you know, as everyone knows, 60 years ago today, a review of the horrors that europe experienced in that period began. the figures are staggering: 60 million dead, the systematic extermination of peoples and minorities, cities and regions reduced to rubble and ashes, economies ruined and 30 million displaced among the civilian populations of all the contending countries. and whatever the responsibility of those who started the war, the suffering of human beings is the suffering of human beings. in the pacific, as you know, the war would still continue until august 14th and it ended with those dreadful images of nuclear extermination. europe was then a continent destroyed, starved and threatened. with peace, or at least with the end of the war, on 8 may, some political leaders proclaimed that the flag of freedom was waving across europe, but today we must recognize that, at that time, the end of the war only brought peace and freedom to half a continent. the other half were victims of that new world order that was born in yalta. indeed, peace and freedom did not come for all. on 8 may, a new geography of europe was drawn up: totalitarianism - certain forms of totalitarianism - was overcome, but another, different, but equally iron and more durable, kidnapped half of europe. bipolarity was born, a long ideological conflict began, and the nuclear age terrorized the world. our continent was split in two and today, 60 years later, here in the european parliament, we can finally celebrate a europe rediscovered, not enlarged, but reunited. on 1 may we celebrated the first anniversary of the reunion we had with the countries that were kidnapped after yalta. soon we will be more and our reunification will be complete. and that gives greater meaning to this 9 may, europe day, on which 55 years ago the foundations were laid to respond to the desolation of war, to ensure that it never happened again, and which today constitutes a complete response with the arrival of the new countries that have joined the union. i would like to see today, ladies and gentlemen, a day of reflection, as we commemorate three events of a different but interrelated nature: 55 years since the beginning of the european adventure, 60 years since the end of the war and one year since reunification. it is a great opportunity to remember together our duty of memory and to make it known, especially to the younger generations who have not known war and to whom peace may seem a natural thing. but it hasn't. the streets of our cities are full of names of people and of events, of events which have shaped our history and which form part of our collective memory: the westerplatte in gdansk-danzig, montgomery square in brussels, the stalingrad metro in paris, the boulevard dresden, a few metres from here, and military cemeteries from both sides which populate the geography of europe. all this is our common memory, the memory of a continent which has now overcome what was then the subordination of the individual to the state and the contempt for law and human dignity. today our system is based on the separation of powers, on popular sovereignty and on respect for human rights. and that must be the message we must give to the whole of europe and the whole world as we celebrate the 60th anniversary of the end of the war and the beginning of the adventure of the european union: the commitment to continue fighting for the defence of the values of peace, justice and tolerance, not only for europe, but for the whole world. and let us do so by remembering that what the citizens of europe expect from their union today is no longer peace, because for europeans, peace among ourselves is already there and we all consider it irreversible. no one can imagine that we will ever again resolve our differences by resorting to arms. what europeans expect today from their union is that it should contribute to their prosperity and to their security in the face of new threats from a world which is no longer the one that was born in yalta. i therefore ask you to look to the future with the burning obligation to achieve the prosperity and security that our citizens demand of us. president of the council. mr president, i should first like to thank the rapporteur for raising this extremely important issue. we share his analysis of the importance of transeuropean networks, which is manifested in several ways: firstly, these transeuropean networks are part of a growth initiative which has been relaunched by the european council; they contribute or are expected to contribute to the competitiveness objective as defined by the march european council; they are also an essential element of the proper functioning of the internal market and, above all, they are indispensable for ensuring the territorial cohesion of the european union. delays have indeed occurred and this is all the more regrettable as a number of projects were decided under a fast-start programme. these projects were to be launched rapidly. it is precisely these issues and the reasons for these delays that have been the subject of the high level group on trans-european transport networks chaired by mr karel van miert, in particular the delays experienced by cross-border sections. to overcome these delays, the council adopted regulation no 807/2004 in april 2004, which aims in particular to increase the rate of community financing for certain projects. the obvious objective of the regulation is to ensure adequate co-financing for the projects in question; the commission is responsible for implementing this regulation and i am sure the vice-president will explain this to you. the council received a new proposal for a regulation on this subject on 27 july 2004. the proposal aims to improve the financing of the transeuropean transport and energy networks for the period 2007-13. the relevant council working party has examined the text only once. in view of the significant financial implications of this proposal, several delegations wished to wait until the discussion on the financial perspective was concluded before taking a final decision. i can say on behalf of the presidency that the implementation of this programme and these projects is of paramount importance for the reasons we have indicated. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the presidency therefore considers that the budget proposed by the commission is adequate and sufficient. the council is also examining a commission communication on the possibility of establishing a community guarantee instrument for loans for transeuropean transport network projects. i think that we will only be able to implement this set of projects if we are also able to create innovative financing methods. you have suggested a number of them, including a better distribution between the private and the public. i am sure that, on the basis of these various elements, we will be able to launch these projects as soon as possible, since this is also an important factor in the context of enlargement.

the rapporteur. madam president, thank you very much, commissioner, for your kind words, referring not only to my report but to the joint work that we have done as all the members of the committee on employment and social affairs of this parliament. ladies and gentlemen, it was a coincidence that our debate on the working time directive and the european day of remembrance on 9 may coincided. the words of our president, mr borrell, yesterday, about the relationship between our duty to remember and our duty to build a europe in which euroscepticism and anti-europeanism are defeated, still ring out in this house. our debate today and the vote tomorrow have a lot to do with our responsibilities. they have a lot to do with it, because millions of europeans are waiting for the outcome of debates in which there is great expectation, because this directive is at the heart of social europe and will be a clear sign of our will and our confidence that the european social model has a future or that, on the contrary, we are throwing ourselves into the hands of the other that comes not from the other side of the atlantic, but from the pacific itself. our debates also coincide with an important moment in the construction of europe and the ratification of the constitutional treaty in various european parliaments and peoples. and at the heart of the concerns of citizens who are faced these days with the idea of whether or not to go forward by the constitutional route is always the same question: what is europe doing to improve our living conditions? we all know that this is the key point and that it is precisely in reaffirming the european model that we unite our agenda or separate it from the agenda and the concern of the citizens. the key point, as the commissioner has said, is the opt-out. parliament wants this clause to be abolished. european laws of a social nature must apply to all countries without exception. it is not enough, commissioner, to eliminate the abuses or fraud that have been committed in the past under the old legislation. the legal basis for the directive must be abolished in all the member states, as parliament says, after 36 months or whatever is left in a subsequent negotiation with the council. why would you do that? because opt-out is in flagrant contradiction with the objectives of the directive, the health and safety of workers and fundamental principles of the treaty. because it contradicts the evidence of 10 years of experience in which, in the countries where it has been applied, the health, safety and reconciliation of family and professional life of millions of women and men in europe have been seriously undermined. because it is contrary to the charter of fundamental rights and our constitutional treaty, article 91 of which states the obligation to ensure a high standard of living in employment and a limitation of working hours. because, commissioner, we are being asked to do so by european workers, their organisations, women's organisations and, also in private, by a great many employers who want a model of industrial relations which is typically european. but what about flexibility? this parliament knows that it also needs to give a response to flexibility, because in europe we need not only better quality work, but more work. that is why we are in agreement and we will give flexibility and we will vote for the annulment, but, eye, it is a do ut des, we will not vote for the annulment if the vote is not to end the opt-out clause. we believe that opt-out is regulating a europe without rules, but we are in favour of making european rules more flexible. a higher level of flexibility is not incompatible with a high level of social protection for workers, provided that a minimum of regulations and guarantees are ensured, as the wim kok report said. we also want to respond, commissioner, to the principles that are involved in the definition of watch periods; we want the acquis communautaire to be respected; we want the court of justice's decision to be respected. the shift is work time, because the workers cannot freely dispose of their time and are in the places indicated by the employer. but we are equally sensitive to the needs of european health systems, which have serious difficulties in recruiting staff to cover these periods of watch. that is why we have sought a solution that combines flexibility and security. the commissioner, the members of the committee on employment and social affairs, we believe that both terms are compatible. those who believe they are not compatible are those who seek to perpetuate the opt-out or those who seek to define guard time as non-working time. we can make an effort, we have shown that, there is a consensus in parliament. i ask the commission and the council not to break the illusion created by this agreement, because it is the old agreement that made the european social model possible. we therefore look forward to your help, your dialogue and constructive cooperation in the months ahead.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i should like to express my great satisfaction with the draft report which parliament is voting on tomorrow, because it contains in its entirety - yes, with some modifications - each of the measures which i proposed in the initial draft. in view of the broad consensus in the committee on agriculture and rural development, i hope that this report will now receive the support of the vast majority of members of this parliament. the european people's party group has, however, tabled an amendment to the report, urging the european commission to come forward with a legislative proposal as soon as possible. the announcement by the european commissioner, mrs fischer boel, who is here, that the reform of the sector will be postponed has caused great unease among producers, an unease which i would like this european parliament to echo. the commissioner's announcement is a symptom of the low importance attached to such an important sector as fruit and vegetables, and i would remind you once again that the fruit and vegetable sector represents 17% of the final agricultural production of the european union, a fact which the commission seems to ignore at a crucial moment like this, when the financial perspectives for a seven-year period are being negotiated. the commission's attitude leaves much to be desired, in my view, and if i have understood the messages recently conveyed by the commissioner correctly, the community executive could include the reform within a sector, within a sack, of a general proposal for the implementation of a single common organization of the market in all agricultural products. in my view, this would mean mixing churras with merinas - as we say in spain - because, up to now, the fruit and vegetable sector has received a specific treatment, which has been generally positive, although it is necessary to introduce important changes on some occasions. fruit and vegetable producers were once frustrated at being treated as a separate sector, without the right to direct aid. today, however, the special scheme, based on the existence of operational funds, co-financed by the growers, has enabled them to find a means of better adapting their production to the needs of the market. although the system has its faults - what does it not have? - and although it requires some modification aimed, above all, at increasing the competitiveness of producers, it would be a mistake to assimilate fruit and vegetables to the rest of the agricultural sectors. this would mean dismantling an entire philosophy on which the progress achieved so far in the sector is based. i would like to stress the dissatisfaction which some professional organisations have conveyed to me about the delay in these legislative proposals. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial instruments are used effectively. a flexible system of crisis intervention in the hands of producer organisations would improve their role as market managers and should also serve as a bait for individual producers who have not found it profitable to join such groups. 60% of the producers are not in these groups. the draft report i have presented to the european parliament proposes precisely an alternative to the current intervention system, namely the introduction of so-called 'safe-deposit boxes', managed by the groups themselves, to finance withdrawals in times of severe crises, operations to reduce production in the event of market saturation, or even the introduction of an income insurance scheme. this well-articulated box should become the instrument which producer organizations lack today to cope with the onslaught of the market. the report also contains some measures which must be urgently put in place to deal with a problematic situation, such as the low level of association in the new member states, and it also addresses the particular problem of red fruit, for which it proposes a whole series of measures aimed at improving both the fresh and processed fruit and vegetable regime, without forgetting the need to extend the campaigns to promote products, emphasizing community origin.

h.r.h. the grand duke of luxembourg mr president, ladies and gentlemen, fifteen years ago, in 1990, on the eve of a luxembourg presidency, my father, the grand duke jean, had the privilege of addressing this distinguished house. some of you were already sitting in the european parliament at that time. i would like to pay particular tribute to them for their constant commitment to the service of europe. mr president, i am deeply moved by the kind words you have just spoken to my country. on behalf of her majesty and all those accompanying us on this journey, i thank you for your warm welcome. 1990 2005: what changes, i would even say upheavals, in that time, including in this beautiful city of strasbourg! the new and splendid building in which we are sitting, the size of the beams of this house, is a concrete expression of the historical changes that have taken place on our continent. let us remember the enormous hopes of some and the great anxieties of others in the face of the enormity of the challenges facing us in the wake of the end of communism and the reconciliation of our continent. is it not time to take stock of the progress made since then, and to acknowledge our undeniable successes in the process? in recent months, however, as we have marked the 60th anniversary of the end of hostilities, we have been reminded that the reason for our work at the baptismal font was our desire to make war between us impossible. like you, mr president, i was in auschwitz where, together with many heads of state and government, we wept in silence at the memory of the millions of innocent victims who disappeared or were maimed in the most atrocious conditions. i would also like to point out the presence - how significant - of the chairmen of the political groups in this parliament on that day. it was the duty of memory that brought us together on that day, and it is with renewed vigilance, so that history does not repeat itself, that this duty must continue to inspire our commitment to european integration. against this background, i am very pleased to be able to share with you today some thoughts which, for obvious reasons, go beyond the agenda of our presidency. mr president, my reflections lead me first to a clear recollection of what we have achieved. the road traveled in the last 15 years is full of undeniable successes, some would even say spectacular ones. europe is now stronger because it is united around common values and is able to promote them in the world. together we have been able to ward off the risk of our union degenerating into a mere free trade area. the day after german reunification, which was achieved in the wake of the single act itself and preceded by a very successful enlargement to the south, we tried together to create a single currency which today commands respect and admiration. our union has been able to expand eastward. i should like to express the emotion felt recently in luxembourg when the highest officials of bulgaria and romania signed their country's act of accession. europe has thus been able to respond to the legitimate aspirations of these peoples who have suffered so much under an ideology which for forty years has denied them the recognition of their most basic rights. intervened autonomously in the democratic republic of congo (drc). our troops have taken over from nato in bosnia and herzegovina. in afghanistan, the european presence is essential to lead the country's transition to genuine democracy. in the face of globalisation, we have always tried to make europe a centre of excellence in relation to the economic giants of america, japan, china, india and brazil. at the same time, we have been able to adopt the motto 'unity makes strength' in order to appear in the world as a credible reference in terms of democracy and solidarity with developing countries. finally, i should like to mention the enormous progress made in food security. after long and arduous negotiations, the food hygiene standards of the 450 million consumers will be the same. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, you can imagine that i could give many more examples. i would like to say that the european parliament's contribution to these successes has been decisive in many ways. your parliament has been able to achieve a prominent place in the institutional balances of our union, sometimes as an incentive, sometimes as a stimulus. in doing so, the european parliament has made its own the observation made by jean monnet in his time: 'we have no choice but to choose between the changes we will be dragged into and those we have been able to want and achieve.' the reminder of these undeniable successes and the tribute paid to the elected representatives of europe does not spare me from observing with great clarity that many of our fellow citizens, and among them many young people, feel uneasy about the construction of europe. it is clear that the freshness and enthusiasm of the new members for being part of this large family is still evident. however, the drive of the founding fathers of europe is being replaced by selfishness. the debate in the member states on the ratification of the constitutional treaty is revealing in this respect. many (applause) i would like to thank clearly, faith in this construction has been weakened. as one astute columnist observed: "the foundations of the postwar era - reconciliation, solidarity in the face of communist danger, reconstruction - have become mere ornaments". in the face of this bleak environment, our democratic structures often give the impression of being stuck and powerless. what explains these doubts, this confusion, these negative judgments? some philosophers, such as the frenchman marcel gauchet, tell us that this is due to the moment, that is to say to our time made of gigantic changes of direction. when change is relatively slow, as was the case in the 1970s and 1980s, adaptation is not very difficult. but when it produces a disruption of traditional benchmarks, such as we know in particular through globalization, it is a different matter! we have to digest the breaks, reinvent the beacons, rebuild the instruments. in short, to redefine perspectives and visions. i would like to recall a thought by michel rocard. i quote: 'one of the tragedies of europe is that it is a stewardship.' and indeed, it is necessary to agree with the former prime minister that it is saddening and therefore very unmotivating for the minds of our citizens, especially for young people, that the union is the privileged domain of money, capital, investment, standards and subsidies. it is true that these are important matters, but they are so arid that they are hardly likely to arouse much emotion. let us remember that from the very beginning of the construction of europe, nothing would have been possible without the combination of a vision of the heart and competence. with the emergence of this great europe, is it not time to ask the central question that remains the same: why do we want to live together and share all or part of our destiny? the answer is certainly not self-evident. it is 450 million human beings, with their own decisions and ambitions, with their own weaknesses and passions, but above all with their own prodigious strengths and qualities, that are the real issue. yet these human beings are supposed to share the same historical destiny on the same territory: our europe. the european adventure can only be built around peoples and nations, reflecting our great diversity. each of these nations represents a territory with its beauties and riches, but also with its scars that time has left in our memories. in identifying what should be preserved and what should be considered obsolete, the first task of our union is to reconcile the legacy of the past with the challenges of the future. it is from within itself, from its own way of advancing and building itself, that it must now invent its legitimacy. in the face of powerful development hubs, how can we overcome the risks of a decline that no one can control individually? but more importantly, how can the conditions for a new boom be created in solidarity? in these terms, the rebirth of europe - which is our collective ambition - should be the social project of the generations that are about to take over. to convince our citizens, let us remember that the well-being and prosperity of a people cannot be measured exclusively in terms of gdp. let us also be careful not to build a europe that benefits a few and at the same time is rife with situations of social exclusion, violence in all its forms, unemployment and disregard for the preservation of our environment. let us also remember that the best growth curve is of little value if it does not translate into better access to the most basic goods such as education, culture, health, social justice and above all work! the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i should like to begin by thanking all those who have contributed to the report we are voting on tomorrow. the report reflects the balance between parliament's full support for the defence of the union's interests in the current negotiations and its ambition to bring this development round to a successful conclusion, which implies the full integration and participation of the developing countries (developing countries) in the world economy. with this report, this house intends to send a strong political message of support for the progress of the negotiations, in which the commission is playing an essential role, by reiterating our commitment to the wto and its multilateral trading system, which is undoubtedly the best mechanism for promoting fair, supportive and mutually beneficial trade. this message comes at a very opportune time, given that the doha programme is at a crossroads, at a key moment in its march from which it must not retreat. following the failure of the cancun ministerial conference, the agreement of 1 august 2004 is of undoubted political importance, since it has put the negotiations on track and has also recognised the need to fully integrate the developing countries into the global economy. now, this is just a road map. the success of the negotiations depends on the firm political will of all parties to reach a substantive agreement in hong kong. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft agreement on the future of the european union. to this end, concrete and detailed commitments with dates and deadlines should be reached through a transparent, effective and inclusive negotiation process in which all wto member countries participate fully. in the field of development, we must bring the problems of poverty, malnutrition and hunger in the world to the negotiating table, with the aim of halving them by 2015, as envisaged in the millennium declaration, through a closer relationship between the wto and the other international organisations. it would also be useful for the commission to make proposals to develop trade integration mechanisms for developing countries to compensate for the losses that trade liberalisation may cause them. progress in the areas of technical assistance and capacity building and the promotion of south-south trade are also of particular relevance in ensuring the integration of developing countries into the world economy and boosting their export capacity. in agriculture, wto members must pursue their work in a balanced way on the three pillars - export subsidies, domestic aid and market access - to achieve detailed negotiating arrangements for hong kong and parallel disarmament by all wto members. as regards market access for non-agricultural products, the nama, the door should be opened to flexibility and to the application of non-full reciprocity by the developing countries, applying to them the principle of special and differential treatment. in services, revised quality offers should be presented in may and, as far as services relating to the basic needs of citizens are concerned, i do not think that liberalization should be demanded of the developing countries. ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the success of the round, the legitimacy and credibility of the wto also depend, of course, on civil society feeling that it is partaking of the benefits of international trade. in a process which has since seattle become of great social interest, it seems necessary to emphasize the role that democratic parliaments must play as an expression of citizens' feelings in international forums such as the wto and, in the case of this parliament, as a democratic control body of the union's trade policy and future co-legislator in this field once the european constitution enters into force. i would like to add a brief word to the long list of advances which this constitution represents and which justify the european acceptance of it, both in france and in other countries. ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, as the spanish poet antonio machado said, 'there is no road for the traveller, but a road is made by walking'. and it's that we're halfway between geneva and hong kong, between the nostalgia of what's left behind and the anxiety of getting there. we must come to hong kong with an ambitious and balanced proposal in which civil society and all wto member countries feel involved and satisfied with the outcome.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i congratulate mr moreno sánchez on his excellent report, which shows his vision and ability to identify common objectives in a dossier as wide and complex as the doha negotiations. the aim of this round, which was called the 'development' round from its inception in 2001, is to strengthen the basic principles of the multilateral trading framework by providing an appropriate response to the problems of developing countries. the success of the negotiations must enable them to make trade an integral part of their national development policies and, to this end, we must have sufficient flexibility to address the precarious situation of the least developed countries, to recognise the new role of emerging countries and to deal with the special impact of liberalisation processes on vulnerable countries. the rapporteur, aware of this problem, rightly considers the need to provide specific technical assistance and capacity building to developing countries; the possibility of introducing a development compartment for the least developed countries in the agricultural negotiations; the promotion of south-south trade and the need for emerging countries to continue to open their markets to the least developed countries; and he recognises as a backbone the principle of special and differential treatment, which implies non-reciprocity in trade rounds and should allow for adaptation to the profile of each developing country. its implementation should enable the international monetary fund, among other organisations, to develop the trade integration mechanism to compensate for losses that trade liberalisation may cause them. as rapporteur for the report on the generalized system of preferences, i very much welcome the rapporteur's support for my proposal to pay attention to the erosion of tariff preferences that the round may cause, and i repeat the request to the commission to draw up a special report examining its impact and the measures to be taken. the report by mr moreno sánchez is a magnificent contribution to dispelling reservations and moving forward in a round which meets the aspirations of all its members for progress.
the question i have the honour to put on behalf of the committee on international trade concerns the current state of our trade relations with china. as you know, china's accession to the wto in 2001, which parliament supported, was the result of laborious negotiations in which the european union played a very important role. there was no precedent for the entry of a trading partner whose rules were so far removed from the common system. it should be remembered that becoming a wto member was a goal pursued conscientiously by china for ten years, for which it made a series of painstaking concessions in all sectors, committed itself to fulfilling its obligations and agreed to the monitoring of such compliance. this has been stated repeatedly by chinese leaders, especially since the policy initiated by deng xiaoping. so far, forecasts of widespread conflict with china have not come to fruition. however, recurring problems arise in areas such as intellectual property protection, the fight against counterfeiting and forgery, transparency of legislation, standardisation and certification, the opening up of services, especially financial, telecommunications and transport services, and numerous non-trade barriers, for example the ccc, the famous china compulsory certification, which is almost impossible to obtain. but the essential point is that china is faced with a major contradiction: opening up its market and protecting its own industry, in a context in which rules such as the application of ilo conventions on child labour, the formation of free trade unions, etc. are not within the context of the wto, but are important, as is environmental protection, and in this connection i would like to remind you that china signed the kyoto protocol two years ago. we are in a situation right now where it seems that china is testing the boundaries of what can be acceptable. and the textile sector, to which other colleagues will refer, is an example of this, since it affects many countries and not just the european union. it is not a question of calling into question the decision taken on 1 january to liberalize the market completely, but of examining, for example, the extent to which a dumping policy can invade markets, how energy can be subsidised, how the financing policy is being implemented and whether there is preferential financing, etc. these are matters of importance. another very significant concrete example is the phonogram industry, where we are faced with a dramatic situation in europe. right now, most of the piracy, almost 70%, is in china and it's developing a lot on the internet. also, it's almost impossible to perceive copyright, because the structures don't even exist. in any case, i would like to remind you that the european union has supported china's integration into the world economy. this is a challenge for all of us and it calls for an unprecedented process of economic and social reform. china still has ten years to complete its transition to a market economy. in any case, what is certain is that, right now, china has gone from being a centrally planned economy to an economy in which it seems to be ruled by manchester capitalism with a communist mandarin. the chinese are the ones who have to take charge of their evolution, but it is important that we can have control with maximum transparency and maximum knowledge. in conclusion, mr president, we are in the final phase of the doha negotiations, which must be concluded precisely on chinese territory, with such decisive issues as the opening up of its economy, the exchange rate of its currency or stability in a part of the world with a very worrying arms race. china is also a prominent player in the club of twenty, which brings together some of the great tenors of the new world scene, and because of its history, its weight and also because the european union has seriously bet on china's incorporation into world trade, i think it makes sense to raise this question at this time, knowing that the colour of the cats does not matter to hunt mice, but that they must respect each other in order to survive together.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the report we are about to vote on in a few minutes covers or tries to cover two fundamental objectives: first, to evaluate the implementation of the information and communication strategy of the european institutions, that is to say, to look back and see what we have not done well; and secondly, to propose some effective ideas that contribute to making information and communication policy better, that is to say, to look forward and see how we can improve that policy. i would like to thank all the political groups, and especially the shadow rapporteurs - maria badía, giulietto chiesa, helga trüpel and miguel portas - for the effort they have made to enrich the report, which they have undoubtedly achieved, and to reach a broad agreement which will allow us to put to the vote a text which revolves around five basic agreements. we are basically agreed that we must ensure that information reaches every citizen, that it reaches him through the most modern instruments, namely television, radio, the internet and new technologies. it is not enough to have the answers that a few citizens who are already aware of their european identity and who already know what questions to ask are looking for. we must make europe's conscience, what it means to be european, known to everyone, and sooner or later everyone must feel the need to ask what the european union can do for them. we basically agree that to do that we must get the messages of the european institutions to the right audiences. we must ensure that the messages arouse the interest of the citizens, of each of them, in accordance with their respective concerns, because it makes no sense to spend a lot of money on saying generalities that in the end do not serve almost anything. the message that is relevant to each household must be introduced. and for that we have to decentralize information, channel it through local and regional media, relying on good professionals, real professionals who know how to help the media the way the media needs to be helped. we are basically agreed that the legitimate expectations of citizens to participate actively in the development of the european union will only flourish if we are able to reach the emotions of the citizens. the european union is no longer an ordinary international organisation with purely economic aims. it's a community of values. these values are the soul of the european union. we have to make it visible and we have to make it palatable. we are basically agreed that from now on we can do very little without the cooperation of the member states and the national parliaments. and we basically agree that we will be wrong if we do not get interinstitutional cooperation to work properly. the last point, that of collaboration between the various european institutions, has so far, during the preparation of the report, resulted in a very fluid, unusually fluid, i would say, dialogue with the european commission, and we all want it to continue to be so. but wanting it isn't enough. wishes are not enough. only the facts count. it is a fact that, with this report, the european parliament has tried to get as close as possible to the commission. the commission now has two options: either to take parliament's contributions into account in the new communication which is due to be published, or to dispense with them. in the first case, we will go forward; in the second case, we will take a big leap backwards. so, mrs wallström, the ball is in your court, but as i am sure you will be able to get it right and as i can also testify to your willingness to dialogue and agree, i am also sure that you will be able to take advantage of this opportunity for parliament and the commission to go together in the exciting task of communicating europe. i'll see you later.
vice-president of the commission. i am very pleased to address today, in this house, the vital topic of communicating europe to our citizens. mr herrero-tejedor has done an excellent job in tabling a report that poses the right questions and suggests important answers. i welcome the rapporteur’s suggestion that this plenary should have a debate on communication at least once a year. the support of europeans for the european project hinges on our communication efforts. we have all known for years – and the ongoing public debates on the ratification of our constitution show this clearly enough – that despite our common efforts to communicate, europe’s citizens still say that do not know enough about, or are not interested in, the european union, and do not understand its role and its benefits for them. less than half voted in last year’s european elections. apathy and ignorance are enemies of our democratic foundations. as our latest eurobarometer reveals, there is a clear correlation between the level of information and the support for the constitutional treaty; 75% of those who know the constitution well declared they were in favour, while the support of those who have never heard about the constitution is only 22%. the conclusion is evident: the need to communicate our projects is crucial for the future of the european union. communicating europe is a highly complex task because european construction is in itself complex; because the european project is an evolving project and because perceptions of the european project vary and are defined, to a large extent, by national history and circumstances. moreover, we should never forget that no communication can be better than the policies it wants to communicate. more than ever before, the european union needs to explain its aims and policies clearly and comprehensively. that is why the barroso commission has made communication one of its strategic priorities. the foremost priority of the present commission is connecting with citizens. however, i should like to add that this is not just the commission’s responsibility. in fact, it is very much the responsibility of all players: parliament, the council and, above all, the member states. the commission will therefore put forward a white paper on communication. it will identify options and possible solutions to the challenges that have been outlined and will be the starting point of a long-term process of structural reform and change in communication culture, involving all actors concerned within and outside the commission. the new approach will follow three strategic principles, which are also taken into account in the draft of the herrero-tejedor report that you are debating today. the first involves listening to people and taking their interests and concerns into account; the second, explaining our policies and their impact on people’s daily lives; and the third, connecting with people by communicating more and as closely as possible on topics that are of real interest to citizens. we have identified five main areas for action. the first is political commitment and ownership. commissioners will engage as key communicators about all portfolios. they will also get involved in better planning and coordination of communication activities, which will concern all levels. the commission will better integrate communication into our working culture and into policy formulation. the second involves professionalising our communications. that includes providing an effective and service-minded spokesperson service, improving research through polling and surveying and evaluating the impact of our communication activities. we must make better use of our tools and provide more and better training. the third concerns connecting with and responding to citizens. that involves adapting messages and matching national and local concerns – instead of taking a ‘one-size-fits-all’ approach – and conveying them as close to the citizen as possible. as proposed by mr herrero-tejedor, that means using contemporary tools, giving priority to those which are more likely to reach the greatest number of citizens, such as television, radio and the internet; using a language that people understand and a more decentralised implementation; using our representations in the member states as well as our relays and networks in close cooperation with parliament and the member states. our fourth focus is on adapting the means to the objectives. i believe we can all agree that communication is a human-resource- and budget-intensive activity. we will, therefore, need to allocate financial and human resources in a manner corresponding to our goals. communication will have to be considered as an in-built cost in all activities. all of that will be based on a qualitative and quantitative assessment of communication activities within the institutions. last but not least, the fifth point is that we need to work together. we need to work with the member states and with other actors. a progressive approach, leading to the possibility of forming an over-arching european union approach to communication based on real coordination and synergies between the institutions, should be established. however, we cannot forget other key actors, such as national and regional governments and parliaments, civil society and the media, focusing particularly on the regional and local media in the member states. the next step will be the white paper and the results of the broad consultation process we will launch, which will, hopefully, lead to more consistent and efficient communication with europeans, which is our common responsibility.

european union, and also to welcome the willingness shown by the commission, since, for the first time, before its presentation, this strategy has been discussed with parliament, which can thus influence its final content, rather than merely giving a response. the aim of this strategy should be, first and foremost, to keep citizens continuously and adequately informed, in order to promote their knowledge, interest and participation in the affairs of the european union. the debates taking place in the various countries in connection with the adoption of the constitutional treaty reveal the high degree of ignorance about the functioning, policies and workings of the union. the outcome of this strategy should demonstrate to citizens how membership of the european union benefits them in their daily lives. action is needed on many fronts, reinforcing the media preferred by citizens, such as television and radio, for their greater ability to penetrate households, and, in the age of the information society, it is vital to put the content of union websites in the official languages of the union and also in those with official status in the member states. european citizens have the right to full and impartial information on community affairs in their own language, on the basis of respect for and protection of cultural diversity and as a guarantee of their understanding of and commitment to the project of european integration. if we really want an informed citizenry, i think it is entirely appropriate to insist that studies on the european union be incorporated into the educational curricula of the member states, to work from the grassroots on fostering the feeling and awareness of european citizenship. the communication strategy of the union has so far proved to be insufficient and deficient, and it is therefore essential that the commission, in its next communication, which is already announced for this month, take account of the recommendations of this parliament's report in order to achieve a european union closer to the citizens.
the reality is that not only citizens, but also politicians in the member states, opinion-makers and parliamentarians know very little about what the european union is, what it does, what it is for and what decisions are taken here. and in some cases, out of ignorance or bad faith, their only message is to explain that some of the problems they have and are unable to solve are due to the european union, hiding instead the positive measures for citizens that have been taken here. i therefore believe that a communication strategy, in addition to many other things that this report says, should first of all be aimed not only at citizens but also at opinion makers and politicians in the member states, starting with the national members themselves. and secondly, it should have a clear purpose, a very specific purpose: to communicate to the citizens what is done here. it is not just, and this is where it sometimes falls, european anthems and flags and music, and the anthem of the ninth symphony. it is about conveying to the citizens what is done here and how much it benefits their lives, to counteract the negative publicity of many national politicians.
member of the commission. mr president, the commission is fully aware of the seriousness of the drought situation in spain. she understands the concerns involved and is determined to help. there are certain tools that provide opportunities in situations like this. the commission has already adopted a decision on 10 may authorising the use of set-aside land for grazing in nine autonomous communities in spain. however, the commission has not received any other specific request from the spanish authorities concerning the application of the direct aid schemes in the context of the frost and hail issue. any request by the spanish authorities to the commission - for example, for the payment of advances - will be given serious consideration. the commission's response will be based on the legislative provisions in force, taking into account the available budget. the commission has adopted a communication outlining different alternatives for dealing with risks and crises in agriculture. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the protection of the environment is based on the principle of the protection of the environment and the protection of the environment. i can say, however, that the commission, in response to a request from the european parliament, will shortly launch a pilot study on agricultural insurance schemes. in this context, i would also like to refer to the request for the transfer of intervention stocks contained in the resolution. the commission is firmly opposed to such transfers in order to avoid market distortions which disadvantage local and regional producers and traders. as regards the request for flexibility in the common organisation of the market in fruit and vegetables, which is set out in the resolution, the spanish authorities are responsible for this subject, subject to certain criteria. although there is scope for using rural development resources to provide relief to producers affected by the hail or frost, the commission has not received any such request from the spanish authorities to date. if such a request is made, the commission will examine it immediately in order to do everything possible. in this context, the possibility of reallocating funds already earmarked for rural development by channelling them into support measures such as the 'restoration of agricultural production potential' provided for under council regulation 1257/1999 could be considered. the spanish authorities could also, as in the case of portugal, consider derogating from the application of certain measures, such as agri-environmental measures, by notifying the commission of cases recognised as 'force majeure' under commission regulation 817/2004. as regards the risk of forest fires, certain preventive actions may be included in rural development measures financed by the european agricultural guidance and guarantee fund under council regulation (ec) no 1257/1999. the spanish authorities may also request the amendment of regional programmes in order to strengthen forest fire prevention measures within these programmes. it should, however, be noted that the mobilisation of additional support under the above measures can only be done within the limits of the funds available for existing programmes. as regards the mobilisation of the solidarity fund, it is true that severe drought and frost can be regarded as natural disasters and therefore fall generally within the scope of the fund. however, in order to mobilise the fund, the member state concerned must submit a request to the commission within 10 weeks of the date of the first loss. in order to be eligible for aid, the estimated cost of the total direct damage must exceed eur 3 billion in 2002 prices, or 0,6% of the gross national product of the state concerned; the lower of these two amounts shall be taken into account. this means that the loss threshold applicable in the case of spain for 2005 is just over eur 3,1 billion in current prices. the fund may only cover specific assistance measures to address emergency needs taken by public authorities, such as temporary restoration of critical infrastructure, allowing the return to normal daily activities. it is important to emphasise that the european union solidarity fund was not set up to cover all costs linked to natural disasters. in particular, the eu solidarity fund does not allow for compensation for private losses, including even in the agricultural sector. the commission has repeatedly demonstrated that it makes full use of the solidarity fund for disaster-stricken states, including the mobilisation of the solidarity fund for the prestige shipwreck. but the fact that some flexibility is sought does not mean that certain provisions of the regulation will be disregarded. the commission has also, as the honourable members will be aware, adopted on 6 april a proposal for a new solidarity fund. the proposal, which will be examined by the council and parliament, provides, inter alia, for a significant reduction in the damage thresholds for mobilising the fund, extends its scope and defines a wider range of eligible actions. the commission would be happy if this proposal were supported by parliament, since it is moving largely in the direction currently sought. finally, spain may decide to compensate farmers with state aid for income losses due to severe hail and frost. the spanish authorities are required to notify the plan to the commission. however, it is essential that:- first, they must prove that the losses due to the weather phenomenon reach the threshold of 20% or 30%;- second, that there is a direct link between the losses and the adverse weather conditions;- third, that there is no overcompensation of the damage caused. the spanish authorities can also make use of the new de minimis regulation for state aid. aid of up to eur 3000 per farmer may be granted for three years without notification to the commission, provided that, among other conditions, the ceiling applicable to spain is not exceeded.

the commission is also responsible for the implementation of the budget. mr president, mr rapporteur, i would like to thank you for your report. ladies and gentlemen, it is an honour and a great pleasure for me to speak at this crucial moment of the revision of the framework agreement governing relations between the european parliament and the commission. since my inauguration as president, i have told you of my intention to establish a positive partnership and a lasting strategic partnership with parliament. at first, we experienced periods of institutional and political tension. the willingness to cooperate of myself, margot wallström and the commission as a whole might seem to the unwary observer to be merely a reflection of our intention to avoid further friction. this interpretation proved to be misleading and shortsighted. in reality, the will to cooperate which motivates us is the result of the recognition of the institutional reality of our union. according to the treaties, it is the parliament which is the depository of the will of the peoples of europe; it is the only directly elected institution, the legitimate representative of the citizens of the member states. no other supranational institution can count on such a high degree of democracy as the european union; no other multi-state structure has recognized such an important role for representatives directly elected by the citizens; no other body has an institution that today represents four hundred and fifty million citizens on a continent finally united. the union is not an abstract entity, far away, taking decisions behind closed doors, despite the tendencies and opinions of the people. on the contrary, it is based on the will of the people and on fully democratic institutions. that is the richness of our union. this is what makes it unique among existing structures in an increasingly globalised world. we are proud of this deeply democratic character which reflects the historical tradition of our member states. we must and we want to work in this direction. this is the fundamental reason why we thought it opportune and necessary to revise the framework agreement, the most important instrument governing our relations. this review took place in an atmosphere of excellent relations under the leadership of the political authorities of our two institutions. i would like to take this opportunity to thank president borrell, the chairmen of the political groups, the chairman of the committee on constitutional affairs, mr leinen, and all those who have contributed to this important exercise in the history of our bilateral relations. the negotiations have enabled considerable progress to be made. we have agreed on a well-balanced text which meets the expectations of both parties and substantially improves cooperation between our institutions. mr leinen has already pointed out many aspects, but i would like to outline what we consider to be the five main results. firstly, we have enhanced the political dialogue between our institutions. together with vice-president wallström, i will attend on a regular basis the meetings of the conference of presidents, which will become the main forum for discussing political developments as well as the work and activities of parliament and the commission. furthermore, the timetable for the commission's legislative and work programme has been streamlined, and the process leading to the commission's legislative and work programme has become more political. in this context, margot wallström met the conference of committee chairs in february, and will do so again in july. secondly, we have strengthened openness and transparency. the commission commits itself to providing parliament with a full list of the expert groups assisting us in the exercise of our right of initiative. in addition, the chairmen of the relevant parliamentary committees may ask the commission to provide information on the activities and composition of these groups. when taken in conjunction with the existing rule on transparency relating to the comitology groups, this new provision is a very useful step. it will definitely contribute to enhancing transparency in the context of interinstitutional relations. thirdly, we have reinforced the provisions concerning political responsibility. the framework agreement enshrines the key principles of the openness, fairness and consistency of the entire hearing process. it ensures that the commissioners-designate disclose all relevant information in accordance with the duty of independence laid down in the treaty itself. in addition, we have agreed on the procedure to be followed should parliament express a lack of confidence in an individual commissioner. in such cases the president of the commission will give parliament's deliberations all the political attention they deserve. that is why we have agreed that i will either ask the individual commissioner to resign, or i will be prepared to explain before this house the decisions i have taken. this procedure safeguards the collegiality of the commission and the powers and prerogatives of its president. if new commissioners are appointed during the commission's term of office, i will ensure, together with the president of parliament, that they present themselves immediately to parliament. my fourth point concerns the improvement of our cooperation regarding the negotiation of international agreements and other aspects of our day-to-day work. we have made provision for the commission to keep members of parliament systematically informed on the conduct of negotiations on multilateral agreements. we have agreed on measures for consultation of the budgetary authority on the occasion of the announcement of new financial undertakings made at international donor conferences. we have deepened our cooperation in the field of community election observation missions. finally, we will act within the framework of the existing treaties and safeguard the competences of the other institutions, particularly the council. while the commission attaches great importance to our cooperation with parliament, one should not forget that the community method is based on a triangle. the commission is responsible for proposing legislative and budgetary proposals, and the two branches of the legislative and budgetary authority are responsible for deciding on these. as guardian of the treaties, the commission is fully committed to safeguarding this method and to paying all due attention to the balance between the institutions. with your permission, mr president, i would like to give the floor to vice-president wallström to comment on specific features of the leinen report. i sincerely hope that this house will support the revised framework agreement, thus opening a new dimension to our fruitful relationship. (applause) i would like to thank you.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, the leinen report welcomes the revised framework agreement and approves it. i am very pleased by that and i hope that this house will do the same. this morning the commission authorised president barroso and myself to approve the text on behalf of the whole commission after the positive vote that i hope will take place tomorrow. following the speech by president barroso, i wish to respond to a few remarks made in mr leinen’s report. as regards implementing powers, the commission has already made use of its right of initiative to place the council and parliament on an equal footing as regards supervising comitology decisions and proceedings with regard to instruments adopted under the codecision procedure. to this effect, the commission presented a legislative proposal in 2002, which was amended in april last year, taking into account the large majority of amendments tabled by parliament. this is the only possible legal way to change the current situation. i wish to stress that our proposal is based on the existing treaties and could be adopted without waiting for the entry into force of the constitution. the commission continues to attach considerable importance to this proposal. we are aware that parliament supports it and we hope that the council will give it all the attention it deserves. for the time being, the commission will continue to implement the current rules on comitology in full respect of the role of parliament, as laid down in primary and secondary law and in our bilateral agreements. an internal assessment is currently taking place in the commission to ensure effective and coherent application of these rules. as regards providing information to members of parliament on the occasion of negotiations on international agreements, the solution found in the revised framework agreement is the only one possible due to the legal context. as you have certainly noticed, the commission has committed itself to keeping members of parliament systematically informed. members will be appropriately informed by the commission in full respect of their role as observers. finally, we have taken note of the request made as regards ensuring proper consultation of parliament on the integrated guidelines. the latest integrated guidelines, which will be endorsed by the european council in june, cover a period of three years. from our point of view, this implies that in 2006 and 2007 the next integrated guidelines will have to be updated rather than drastically modified. for the next guidelines, the commission will have to analyse not only contributions from the member states but also data and statistics which are normally available only in december or even in january. it is a complex process. nevertheless, the european union's economy has been negatively affected by a number of events since 2000, when the lisbon council was held, which have meant that our growth has fallen far short of expectations and that we are still far from the objectives set out in lisbon. last february, the commission adopted a document entitled 'working together for growth and jobs: relaunching the lisbon strategy', which clearly stated that if europe wanted to continue to aspire to become the most dynamic and competitive economic area in the world by 2010, it had to reorient the lisbon strategy and focus it on two clear objectives: first, economic growth and second, employment. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a new regulation on the application of the principle of equal treatment for men and women in matters of employment. these guidelines are based on the premise that economic growth can make a decisive contribution to job creation and that this is the best guarantee for social benefits. i would like to thank the more than 90 amendments which have been tabled, which have been translated into 14 commitments which were adopted almost unanimously by the committee on the rapporteur. - mr president, today is indeed an important day. this overall debate puts parliament once again at the political forefront of the fight against terrorism. we are a political chamber and this is a political debate on the european measures to be taken to defend human rights and defeat terrorism, and a debate which also has a desire to do democratic pedagogy. we are convinced that, in order to be effective in the fight against terrorism, europe must also have a common policy in this area, which goes beyond ever closer and more effective cooperation between the countries of the union - of which spain and france are good examples - and of this, of the union, with third countries; a policy which responds to the concerns of citizens and which can be promoted as a model throughout the world. defeating terrorism requires, first of all, trusting in the supremacy of democracy. defeating terrorism requires being willing to use all the instruments of the rule of law, all but one more than the rule of law provides us with. defeating terrorism requires fighting impunity and overturning the legitimacy of terrorist acts. defeating terrorism requires keeping alive in the memory and in the heart the memory of its victims. terrorism, ladies and gentlemen, is totalitarianism, it is fanaticism. terrorism is aimed at destroying free and pluralist societies. terrorism is incompatible with democracy. that is why i say that only a strong, vigorous, committed democracy will be able to defeat it. in this house and in this field we have been at the forefront on more than one occasion. two recommendations were adopted here on 6 september 2001, days before the twin towers were blown up: the arrest and surrender order and the common definition of the crime of terrorism, which were adopted by the council in december of that year thanks to the fact that we, the european parliament, had done our homework in time. it is true that some countries in the union have not yet transposed them into their legislation and others have not done so properly. that is why the report i am drawing up calls for an urgent assessment, but these two decisions are an example of how much the european citizens need a parliament which is able to take the lead in political decision-making. europe is a model of democracy and respect for human rights. that is our vocation, that is the meaning of our political union. that is why, to defend and promote democracy, to ensure respect for human rights, we fight terrorism, because we know that terrorism is the enemy of democracy. we therefore propose a european policy to combat terrorism in order to guarantee respect for individual and collective human rights, the right to life, freedom of expression, freedom of movement, freedom of thought or religion: a european policy to combat terrorism in order to make collective security compatible with individual freedom and dignity. i shall not bore you with the details of each of the recommendations in the report. they're all cutting-edge, but they're all possible. all that is required is political will, and all of them are necessary. from strengthening the role of the european coordinator for the fight against terrorism to pushing for the creation of the european prosecutor. i would like to emphasize the recommendation that the european recognition of victims of terrorism be institutionalized. politically relevant is also our commitment to promote the international definition of the crime of terrorism, which is increasingly necessary if we want, as kofi annan proposed in the madrid agenda, that these crimes be prosecuted and punished worldwide. finally, i would like to draw attention to a truly ambitious recommendation: the call on the member states to promote the indelibility of terrorist offences, thus expressing the international community's condemnation of them as one of the most serious and unacceptable crimes against humanity. in conclusion, ladies and gentlemen, i know that it is a small step that we are taking today, but it is an important one. and i am proud to have helped to place the european parliament once again at the forefront of the fight against impunity for criminals and at the forefront of the defence of human rights. i thank all my colleagues from all the political groups for their contributions to this long debate. thanks to all of them, this house will be proposing proactive initiatives to the council that will change the dynamics of the past. the aim of this set of initiatives is to design a european policy capable of intervening to prevent terrorist attacks as far as possible. i am also proud as a socialist, as a basque, as a spaniard and as a european that this parliament is once again paying tribute to the memory of the victims of terrorism. the president of the government of spain, josé luis rodríguez zapatero, reaffirmed his commitment last saturday at a ceremony to award diplomas to the civil guard, saying that all the victims will always be remembered. for all democrats, that commitment, the effective remembrance of the victims, is what should make impossible a society like the one terrorists have pursued with their crimes. europe knows about totalitarianism and the importance of keeping the memory alive to prevent history from repeating itself. primo levi explained it very well in a great book. "to understand", levi said, "is impossible, but to know is necessary, and to remember is a duty".
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat terrorism, including the creation of a european union-wide network of specialised agencies. at the same time, i would also like to express my gratitude to all the members who have worked and collaborated, sometimes by discrepancy and sometimes by coincidence, on this report on the prevention and response to terrorist attacks, and i would like to thank in particular my good friend rosa díez and my good friend antoine duquesne for their collaboration and contributions to this report. in these few minutes i want to be very brief and particularly to sum up the reasons and objectives which have led me to present this report to the european parliament today. what contribution have i wanted to make to this institution today with this report? it is simply that i have been unable to learn, my limited and modest experience of what the fight against a terrorist organisation has meant for more than 25 years in my country, spain, and in the basque country. i therefore think that the most important thing today is that we reconvert the traditional way of fighting terrorism in the european union, which is usually through a comprehensive list of measures, into what i believe should be a european political project. i am sure you will ask me what the difference is between a comprehensive list of measures and a political project. i will tell you that a political project is much more ambitious than a list of measures. a political project is always the fruit, the consequence, of a priority, of an accent and, above all, of a proper and correct mentality. and above all, a political project has the capacity to be summarized and understood simultaneously by a public opinion which understands the effort of a politician to convert this list of measures into a political project. let me say that the latest results in europe confirm that we need a limited number of political projects, because there cannot be an infinite number of political projects. there must be a few political projects, which are understood by european citizens and capable of dealing with the problems of europeans. and, in my view, one of them is undoubtedly terrorism. terrorism cannot be fought generically. we cannot think of the security forces and bodies as fighting terrorism in a generic way. you're fighting a type of terrorism, a specific organization. it is true that we must always fight with the same principles of freedom, respect for human rights, and what europe means, but in each case we must be able to find a specific, concrete political project, and we must always be able to define, determine and limit the organization that is being fought; among other things, as i said before, because it is the only way to stimulate the security forces and bodies so that, when they fight an organization, they have and put all the energy possible against it. what is the main ally of a terrorist organization? the community's role in the world is not limited to the united states, but is also limited to the european community. but it always has a social support, and one of the keys to combating the terrorist phenomenon is to know islamist, radical organization, or one that claims to defend islam, or al qaeda, by its name. it is essential to call it by its name, because it is the only way to combat an organisation: to be able
