substantially in agreement, but without making a common european political project to deal with this great issue which will affect the present and the future, and which seems to be a problem of others: that the americans had it on 11 september a few years ago, or that spain specifically had it, for certain reasons, on 11 march, but that is not what, in my opinion, we must do. finally, with a remembrance of the victims and saying that they must always be at the centre of our debate, the focus of our main attention, i would like to stress once again that, on this issue, we have all the moral strength with them to tackle this fundamental question of our future from the root.
vice-chairman of the commission . mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i shall now deal with the many sensitive questions raised by the rapporteurs, whom i have listened to with great attention and whom i thank warmly for having raised matters of particular interest to the democratic life of europe. i believe that terrorism is truly the new dictatorship of the 21st century, a dictatorship that seeks to limit our freedoms and to strike at the basic rights of the people - the right to life and physical safety - and so i agree with your approach. the response is to be found in european action and strong international cooperation. this is not an emergency response: the european union must not be left in the lurch by the threat of terrorism. on this basis, just last friday in luxembourg, the council approved the action plan proposed by the commission, which contains some new and, in my view, effective proposals which will be implemented in the coming months and which are in addition to the measures already in progress. as mr oreja rightly said, these are elements of a single strategy, not a list of measures. it will be a political project on which parliament, the council and the commission can and must work together. i believe that one of the fundamental principles is that the fight against terrorism does not mean restricting people's freedom, on the contrary! it would be the greatest political mistake if the fundamental freedoms of citizens were to fall victim to terrorism, in the sense of being sacrificed or, in some cases, eliminated. the balance between prevention and repression on the one hand and the safeguarding of fundamental freedoms and rights on the other is therefore a direction on which all the reports are concentrating. i should now like to make a few brief comments on the reports presented. mr gonzález is certainly right when he stresses the importance of having an action plan available, which would in particular allow monitoring of the action taken by the member states to implement the measures decided upon. it would be a paradox indeed if, after having identified a strategy, there were no elements to monitor the implementation of the measures outlined in the strategy itself. the commission will therefore give priority to the action plan and its implementation. as many of you know, one of the key elements of the action plan approved in luxembourg on friday is the creation of a permanent monitoring instrument. the commission intends to provide a periodic report - i believe every six months - on the manner and quality of implementation of all the measures by the member states, which will of course be made public. for example, as regards certain points mentioned in the gonzález report, we are working on a communication on explosives, detonators and firearms and a second communication which will deal with radicalisation and the recruitment of terrorists. in addition to these measures, we will clearly and very quickly put forward some proposals on the problem of terrorist financing. i will return to this subject with particular reference to certain organizations which support and support terrorism. we will of course be working on the implementation of the so-called argus system, which many of you will be familiar with, which will allow - i am sure - the networking of all the existing early warning systems at the commission. the intention is to create a european network which will allow for an immediate exchange of information - in real time, i would say - between all the member states in the event of a terrorist attack. the report by mr oreja rightly emphasizes the importance of strengthening the exchange of information, cooperation with third countries and dialogue with civil society, which is a fundamental aspect, and aid and support for victims of terrorism, another aspect on which the commission will work intensively. i believe that this period of work, which parliament is inaugurating today with the reports presented, will have to take greater account of the victims of terrorism, as well as, of course, of the perpetrators of terrorist acts. i believe that the key to the success of this strategy is the principle of inclusiveness: all actors, public and private, in society must be able to participate in the democratic debate on terrorism. i believe that a proper information of the public, not threatening or dramatic, but clear, can be a reassuring answer. if we tell the citizens that there are concrete measures and that we are working on them together, i think they can be reassured that the great institutions of europe are working and will continue to work actively. as regards the protection of sensitive infrastructure, mr lambrinidis, i very much appreciated your report. one of the main terrorist threats is certainly to infrastructure, and it is in this area that cooperation between public institutions, all levels of government and the private sector is essential. the commission intends to submit to parliament a proposal for a european programme for the protection of sensitive infrastructure by the end of this year. one of the points of the programme will be to provide access to immediate and timely information, a kind of early warning, in the event of a terrorist attack. i would like to inform you that at this very moment an important seminar on this subject is taking place in brussels, with the participation of 150 representatives of the 25 member states. the meeting offered a positive answer: there is a broad consensus on the main elements of this future programme. we will be organising a second public european seminar in september, so that we can then present a real programme by the end of the year. in this context, we will provide funding of eur 1.5 million for studies on best practices for the exchange of information between member states on safety standards for sensitive infrastructure. it is clear that each member state will have to invest in the structures that exist within its territory. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. as regards the so-called non-profit sector, the commission is working on a sort of european code of conduct to address the vulnerabilities of the sector in question, which on some occasions - as has been discovered - has acted in direct or indirect support of terrorist organisations. but to do that, we ask for a great deal of collaboration from the same nonprofit sector and civil society that, like us, is interested in eradicating all those who support the actions of terrorism in any way. we are also certainly thinking of a better exchange of information between national authorities on the financing of terrorism. we are considering this and a commission communication is being prepared. there is another aspect of great delicacy: the traceability of financial transactions. it is clear that, in the absence of the tools necessary to follow the path of financial transactions, we are lacking an effective tool to hit the financing of terrorism. we therefore intend to propose to parliament and the council, before the summer, a framework regulation on information and the tools for tracing financial transactions. there are also three reports by mr duquesne, which touch on a subject which is particularly dear to me: the relationship between counter-terrorism and the protection of personal data. i think that the amendments tabled to supplement and improve the swedish proposal should be supported. these amendments take account of the important conference held in poland a few days ago and underline the importance of the right of every person to the protection of personal data, even when we are faced with terrorism. this means finding a balance: the european union must not be allowed to continue to be a victim of terrorism. i share mr duquesne's view on the role of europol and eurojust. it is important to give these bodies access to a wide range of information so that they can effectively carry out the exchange and coordination activities which are proper to europol, as is shown by the new mandate on the action of this body, received a few days ago by its new director. the principle of respect for fundamental rights is a subject which mr alvaro has raised and which i myself have raised on several occasions. the principle of safeguarding personal data must respond to real needs. personal data may not be retained unless such retention is for specific purposes and for a specific period of time, nor may access to such data be granted to any person other than the competent police and investigative authorities who are entitled to access it by law. we are preparing a measure in this respect on the basis of a legal basis which, in my opinion, is more correct than the existing one and which i explained on friday to the council of ministers for justice and home affairs, reserving the right to present a concrete text by the summer of this year. the last subject on which i would like to dwell briefly is bioterrorism. the rapporteur knows that the commission has some powers but not all. it may deal with food safety, trade in medicines, coordination between member states, civil protection and research funding. that's a lot. but it is up to the member states to take concrete measures for the operational prevention and possible reaction in the event of a terrorist attack. you know that following the 2005 bioterrorist attack with anthrax elements, a high-level committee on public health security was established with an effective cooperation programme for prevention and rapid response. the cooperation we have is working and we can tell you that there is a tool which, 24 hours a day, seven days a week, can provide early warning in the event of biological, chemical and radiological attack. many commission actions will improve the level of preparedness and prevention: we are developing simulation exercises in the event of possible bioterrorist attacks, two of which will take place later this year to concretely assess the level of prevention and rapid response. we are also developing guidelines for managing medical diagnoses in the event of agents spread by bioterrorists; we are preparing training courses together with europol and are supporting national emergency plans to ensure the availability of adequate vaccines and urgent assistance. as you know, my colleague mr kyprianou inaugurated just a week ago a major european centre for disease prevention and control. we will continue to encourage the member states on these issues. there are two final and concrete proposals i want to mention: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we have also proposed that the solidarity fund should reimburse up to one billion euro for emergency health expenditure. secondly, and lastly, i would like to mention an important initiative which we have referred to as the framework programme. this is a programme, planned and approved for the next community budget, for security preparedness and prevention. it will, of course, include funds to be allocated in the event of any bioterrorist attacks. the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights has adopted a number of amendments. mr president, mr commissioner, at this moment, the fight against terrorism, its prevention and its eradication must be the single priority objective of the policies of this european union. we must never forget 11 march, when spain and europe were cowardly and cruelly attacked for representing the paradigm of the freedoms which we in this house always try to safeguard. on that day, 11 march, the history of spain, europe and, with it, the european union changed. from that moment on, it became necessary to recognize that terrorism is not a uniform, homogeneous or monolithic reality. on the contrary, this attack showed that there are many types of terrorism; president of the council. mr president, i am very pleased to have the opportunity to address parliament this afternoon, before you vote on the resolution on the future financial perspective. the luxembourg presidency, in compliance with the budgetary powers conferred on parliament by the treaty, attaches high priority to maintaining an open and unreserved dialogue with your parliament in this area. this is one of the most important issues facing the union today. it is also taking place at a time when the european union cannot afford to fail. i would also like to express our appreciation for the work of the temporary committee on the political challenges and budgetary means of the union, which you, mr president, chaired. i would also like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done. your contribution to this complex and politically sensitive debate, if not more, is important in two ways. firstly, parliament has shown realism and has presented a coherent approach. secondly, with this report and resolution you are setting the broad parameters for the negotiations which will follow the council negotiations and which, in the end, will be just as decisive for the financial perspectives as the negotiations which will be held next week at the european council. the presidency has also been able to point out that this first round of negotiations in the council is only the first round and that the agreement of your parliament is also required to obtain the financial perspective. what is the state of the negotiations in the council? let me tell you how we see the situation in the council and how we intend to prepare for the debate on this issue, particularly at the european council next week. first of all, i would like to stress that the presidency remains committed to reaching agreement at the european council next week. nothing should distract us from the important objective of providing the union with the resources it needs to fulfil the tasks it will have to face in the coming years. the conclusion of an agreement in june is the best way to send a positive signal and the only way to determine the scale of these resources early enough to adopt and implement the various legislative instruments and programmes in due time. the union must now show more than ever that it retains its full capacity to take decisions, that it is still capable of reaching compromises in a matter as decisive for its proper functioning as the financial perspective and, therefore, budgetary policy for the coming years. you are aware of the negotiating framework method which was successfully used in the last negotiations under the german presidency and which led to an agreement in berlin. this framework has allowed us to gradually narrow down the range of possible solutions and to reach a final agreement. the latest version of this negotiating framework was adopted at the end of last week and will be discussed by the foreign ministers at the conclave to be held on sunday evening. at the same time, the president of the european council participates in bilateral meetings with his counterparts, where they discuss each other's difficulties and try to lay the foundations for a compromise acceptable to all. i would like to highlight some aspects of this latest version of the negotiating framework. i shall also make comments on certain points in your report and in the draft resolution on the financial perspective. firstly, we made it clear, even before the general affairs council in april, that a number of cuts would be necessary - unfortunately for some and inevitably for others - in all areas to balance very different views on the final overall level of expenditure. this is not entirely contrary to the thinking of your committee. the latest version of the negotiating framework includes, for the first time, figures by heading. overall, the total of €870 billion reached, which corresponds to about 1.06 per cent of the gross national income of the european union, is close to the figures discussed. although this total is lower than the commission's initial proposal, the figures for each heading nevertheless represent on average increases of between 5% and 18% in annual growth compared to 2006. so no one can doubt our determination to continue to provide the resources needed to advance the union's policies. it is also true that the very low growth of national budgets, which must not be overlooked, inevitably has repercussions on the european budget. secondly, the council debates were mainly concerned with heading 1b, i.e. cohesion policy. contrary to what some people claim, this item was not particularly affected by the reductions. we have not made this heading the adjustment variable of a minimalist budget package. in reality, the presidency shares the view of parliament: cohesion policy is an expression of the union's internal solidarity. the presidency is therefore doing everything in its power to limit the reductions in this area as far as possible. overall, expenditure under this heading in the latest version of the negotiating framework represents 0.37 per cent of the gross national income of the european union. the presidency has, however, proposed a number of changes to the mechanisms for allocating funds for cohesion policy. it did so following the debates which generally - and i must say with some difficulty - showed the desire to give priority to financing the less prosperous regions and member states. the presidency has therefore adopted a solidarity approach, ensuring that resources are directed to those who need them most. this has meant that a slightly higher percentage of cohesion funds has had to be devoted to the convergence objective and the ceiling rates have had to be adjusted so that the funds go where they are needed most. i know that some countries and regions are not happy with this approach. the presidency will continue to listen to them. however, while adjustments are always possible - and we are working on them day after day - our constraints are such that the room for manoeuvre is rather limited. thirdly, the presidency is aware that the european council in march set ambitious targets for the relaunch of the lisbon strategy. these objectives must be reflected in additional financial means. we are all committed to the objectives of competitiveness and employment. we all want to develop research in the union further. we also know that the union must accompany the social and economic reforms which we are obliged to undertake. employment remains a high priority for all of us, as does education and vocational training. the presidency has reduced the amounts proposed by the commission, but the rate of growth compared with the current period is still considerable: + 8% real growth per annum. there is hardly any national budget - i know of none - that shows such an extra effort. the same applies to heading 3a, i.e. the objective of freedom, justice and security. this objective is also a priority because it responds to the concerns of citizens in this area. in our latest proposal, it benefits from an annual real increase of 18% compared to 2006, which is equivalent to an increase over seven years of almost 200%. the growth rates for external relations, particularly in order to achieve the overall partnership objective to which the union is striving, are still 5% in real terms and we have not retained, as you have, the budgeting of the edf. fourthly, the latest version of the negotiating framework provides a little more detail on the question of resources. there is no doubt that the success of the european council will depend on an agreement on both expenditure and resources. in its search for a solution, the presidency has taken as its starting point the conclusions of fontainebleau in 1984 - i will not say, as mr juncker did, fontainebluff. as far as resources are concerned, the negotiations will only succeed if a satisfactory solution is found to the compensation in favour of the united kingdom. in this connection, the presidency proposes that the amount of the correction for this country should be equal in 2007 to its nominal average over the seven-year period immediately preceding the last enlargement and then decreased from the following year. i think this proposal is fair, because we are all committed to the solidarity effort that enlargement of our union represents. the presidency also proposed that, in line with the fontainebleau conclusions, which also address the question of budgetary imbalances for other countries, specific measures be introduced for three countries, namely germany, the netherlands and sweden, for the period 2007-13. these measures would consist of a reduction in the rate of call on the vat resource, which the presidency has proposed more generally to be frozen at 0.3%. it is clear that before a resource solution can be found, a number of other details - not always minor details and often sensitive ones - still need to be worked out. nevertheless, the presidency is convinced that this approach is the most realistic basis for a final agreement, provided that everyone has the will to achieve it and is animated by sufficient political will. these are the main points of the latest proposal which has been circulated to the member states and which will be discussed in luxembourg on sunday. that is the basis of an agreement in the council. it will then be for the council and parliament to translate it into financial perspectives enshrined in an interinstitutional agreement. mr president, commissioner, we have already spoken many times about the stability pact, and i will try to summarize some of what has been said here. my spokesman, mr radwan, said, and i agree with him, that we are in retreat. the pact i liked was the 1996 pact, signed by the cdu minister theo waigel, which was defended by his predecessor, commissioner solbes. we haven't been able to keep it. the council has noted widespread non-compliance in europe and could have done two things: either demand compliance or, euphemistically, make the pact more flexible, and that is exactly what it has done. you are here to tell us what changes need to be made to the rules of procedure to make this pact fully effective. what could parliament do? what could my group do? we could have tabled amendments trying to resurrect the old covenant, as it stood. we have not done so because, following ortega's advice, we do not like the futile effort which only leads to melancholy. we have tabled amendments, which mr karas has explained very well. what we're trying to do is keep the disaster from getting any bigger. we are trying to ensure that you apply it correctly, with reliable statistics, we are trying to reduce the margin of arbitrariness, filling in the vague legal concepts, and we are trying, in short, to ensure that the withdrawal is not a total disaster. it has been said here that europe is not doing well, and indeed it is. but if it does not go well, it is not as a result of the stability pact, but as a result of not having complied with that pact. the stability pact, budgetary austerity, in quasi-theological terms, is a virtue, a necessary, though not sufficient, condition for growth. we also need, as mrs kauppi has reminded you, those reforms which we have been unable to carry out. parliament is helping him; it is helping him to reduce the margin of discretion of governments. it's up to you to keep this from getting out of hand.
mr president, let me ask the house the following question: would we be living in the current crisis situation in the european union if there were a european union with economic growth and strong job creation, if the big european countries were offering us a different profile, if they were driving the whole of the european union forward and contributing to balancing the world economy? surely the answer would be no. there would be resources, there would be money to finance enlargement, for the challenges of the european union. but there is no economic growth, because there is no trust. and there is no trust because we are lacking firmness in implementing, in exercising policies of trust, policies of stability. that is the contribution of the stability pact. your retirement, mr. almunia, comes at a difficult time. now the next threat in the crisis of the european union is the euro. the reform of the stability pact must therefore be successful. mr karas has done an excellent job of trying to remedy a wrong, erroneous proposal of the stability pact in its basic contents. mr almunia told us this evening that the commission is satisfied with parliament's position on improving the quality of statistics and debt monitoring. i would also like to hear from mr almunia that he agrees with the limitation of the relevant factors, which are really decisive so that the stability pact is not a box that fits everything, in which, in short, we skip the rule. what we have achieved is that each country does what it understands to promote a policy of budgetary stability which, with a lack of definition of relevant factors, would be practically impossible. the example is the european union of fifteen: the countries which have done their homework in budgetary matters are the ones which have economic growth and employment today. we must not look for models outside, we must stay in the european union to look for those countries and implement those policies among us.
member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank mr karas again for his reports and all the members who have taken part in the debate for their contributions. of all the contributions, i would like to mention two, particularly those which have highlighted the success of the euro, of the single currency, and which it is worth remembering in these days when some statements seem to call into question the obvious, that the euro has brought stability, solvency, historically low prices, that the euro brings us historically low interest rates, that the euro strengthens us. we must remember this because, immediately afterwards, we must say that to maintain that strong single currency - which strengthens us as europeans in economic terms and beyond economic considerations - requires a fiscal framework and a stability and growth pact such as those defined in the treaty and developed by the regulations which this parliament is discussing today in their partial amendments. i would also like to join those of you who have reacted to the pessimism of some analyses. it is true that there are economic difficulties, that there are problems of growth and employment, that citizens feel that their needs are often not sufficiently met. but it is also true that when we look at it from the outside, or when we look objectively at the situation of the european economies, there are also elements of optimism. the day before yesterday, at the eurogroup meeting, the director of the international monetary fund's europe department informed us of the general outlines of the report he has just published, which can be consulted on the international monetary fund's website on the economy of the euro area. he began by saying that he was surprised by excessive pessimism, because, in analysing the european economy, he had observed that it had the conditions to make a full recovery. there is a confidence problem in some of the major european economies and one of the objectives of the stability pact reform is undoubtedly to give confidence and credibility to a necessary framework of fiscal and budgetary discipline. to this end, the reform is balanced, introducing some elements of flexibility but also some more demanding elements - notably in the preventive part, where it regulates regulation (ec) no 1466/97. it is a reform that requires more transparency and has therefore contributed to the adoption of important decisions to improve the quality of our statistics. in addition, yesterday, on a proposal from the commission, the ecofin council adopted some very important conclusions which reflect the improvements being made to the european statistical system and, in particular, to tax statistics. the restoration of trust also requires a clear explanation. in many of your explanations, ladies and gentlemen, i have recognized what the pact is and what the reform of the pact entails. in other cases i have acknowledged ignorance or lack of knowledge or, sometimes, simply an interpretation which does not correspond to reality: the reform of the covenant cannot be accused of repeating literally what the treaty says, because to go against the treaty is what will damage confidence. to support the treaty, to repeat what the treaty says about the reference value for the government deficit, the reference value for the government debt and all the factors to be taken into account - the treaty sets out in article 143 the relevant factors to be taken into account when analysing the situation of excessive deficit in a country - to comply faithfully with the treaty in all its dimensions, to read over with serenity and sincerity the treaty adopted to launch economic and monetary union, is one of the elements that can most help to restore confidence in the euro area and in the whole of economic and monetary union. in any case, i am convinced that this reform we are discussing today - and which i hope will come into force at the end of this month - respects the rules, introduces clarity, economic rationality, demands equal treatment and will be applied, as was demonstrated yesterday, with rigor. and what it requires of all of us is a full and complete explanation of what it means, and in doing so we will help the european citizens and the european project.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place on thursday at 12 noon.

member of the commission. mr president, the main outstanding problems which have so far prevented the incorporation of the council’s common political approach of march 2003 into the final text of the community patent regulation concerned the time limit for finding translations of the claims of the patents and the legal effect of these. efforts have been made in the council and at bilateral level to settle these points. despite substantial agreement between the member states on this issue under the irish presidency, none of the solutions discussed has won unanimous support. the commission has already invested a lot of time and effort in work on this file. while i am prepared to make one more attempt to reach agreement on the community patent in the future, i will only do so when i believe the conditions to be favourable. however, alongside the commission’s work on this issue, we also need all supporters of the community patent to speak out strongly in favour of this initiative. as to the collective management of copyright, my services are currently carrying out a thorough impact assessment in preparation for a possible community initiative. the overall aim of such an initiative will be to ensure the more transparent and efficient cross-border management of collective rights in europe. this should provide commercial users, broadcasters, webcasters or other online service providers with better access to information about the scope of the repertoire licence and the applicable terms and tariffs. a more transparent management of copyright across the european union should help stimulate more use being made of copyright content which fosters the development of new attractive services and the technology that is used to provide such services. the initiative will take due account of a consultation of stakeholders and of the recommendations of the report written by a former mep, mrs echerer, on collective management of copyright and related rights. there is no blockage in the legislative process in this area. as far as enhanced cooperation is concerned, any support from the commission for such an initiative in the field of industrial and intellectual property would depend on its impact on the economy and society and its added value compared to the existing situation. moreover, legal issues, such as those arising from the extent of existing community competence, would have to be taken into account.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, the question from the committee on legal affairs covers two aspects. the first, i would say, is the linguistic one, which has been alluded to by commissioner mccreevy, and i would point out that things may not be as simplified as in my colleague mr lehne's presentation. apart from the technical proficiency of a language which has a near monopoly, other languages were already recognised in the european patent convention, and other languages are also recognised by the office for harmonization in the internal market of the european union, based in alicante. i have the impression that there may be a limit, a certain level, below which certain languages may have a certain recognition, depending on the use of patents in those languages and the functioning of national patent offices. i therefore believe that the matter must be clarified and that, as mr lehne has said, the commission could certainly help to find a formula which would allow us to get out of this impasse. as regards the second aspect, concerning collective management companies, there is a fear that a commission proposal, for example, in the radical sense of the bolkestein directive, for total liberalization, will lead to a deprivation of the possibility of effective protection of intellectual property rights. at the moment we have a number of national systems for the protection of intellectual property and mere liberalisation could lead to the loss of protection for authors, i.e. the replacement of a system of a number of national markets, relatively protected by their national management units, by a system in which there is no protection at all, could put authors, creators and inventors in a difficult situation. i would therefore simply ask the commission, when making this proposal, not to fall into the error of the bolkestein proposal, which, as we know, has today been one of the elements used even to oppose the adoption of the european constitution in the referendum procedures, but to seek a system which makes it possible to link the need for harmonization in this field with the protection of a basic service, such as the protection of intellectual property and of artistic and literary creation.

member of the commission. mr president, let me express the commission's any my personal satisfaction with the method and the quality of the work done to tackle the challenge of developing adequate management measures for our mediterranean fisheries. it could not be taken for granted that the deadlock on this matter during the term of the previous european parliament could be overcome. the proactive attitude of this parliament, along with a general awareness of the state of fisheries resources and marine ecosystems in the mediterranean, has contributed to the achievement of a sound compromise. members of the european parliament have shown their ability to listen to the spectrum of views that have been voiced on this important question. parliament's opinion, which i hope will be adopted today, is a good starting point for the work to be carried out in the council and i hope that the european institutions will be able to deliver the new regulation shortly, in the interests of our fishermen and of fisheries and the marine environment of the mediterranean. the commission is very pleased with the close cooperation of the rapporteur, mrs fraga estévez, and the members of the committee on fisheries during our work on this important proposal. i am happy to be able to inform you that we can accept 22 of the 34 amendments tabled by the committee on fisheries and other members. nine amendments of the 22 accepted, and in particular amendments 2, 10, 11, 13, 20, 21, 22, 25 and 26 were part of a compromise package agreed with the rapporteur and approved by the committee on fisheries. the compromise is not perfect in all details. nonetheless a delicate balance of quite different views has been achieved without compromising the effectiveness of the proposal. let me turn to the other amendments tabled to the report before us. the commission can also accept amendments 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 23 and 24, which introduce new elements that either reinforce our proposal or make the timing of the introduction of certain measures more gradual. the commission cannot, however, accept amendments 1, 3, 4, 19, and 27 to 34. in particular, the concept of responsibility of nationals of member states is already enshrined in the basic regulation for the common fisheries policy and should be maintained here. amendments 1, 3 and 4 cannot therefore be accepted. with respect to amendments 19 and 33, which ask for the insertion of provisions for financial support for temporary fishing bans and for fishermen affected by the prohibition of certain fishing gear, the commission believes that these proposals are not appropriate here, either because there are already rules on these matters under community legislation and/or because these issues are to be dealt with in the framework of the european fisheries fund proposal. the commission cannot accept amendment 27, which could dilute the significance of setting a minimum landing size for the species covered by the proposed regulation. in the absence of a minimum size, there would not be any incentive for fishermen to avoid the areas of aggregation of juveniles or undersized organisms or to improve selectivity as regards fishing gear and practices. moreover, the common market for fisheries products calls for a harmonised minimum size. a strict correspondence between minimum size and selectivity of prescribed equipment is rarely possible, particularly in multi-species, multi-gear fisheries, as is the case in the mediterranean. moreover, some minimum landing sizes are set for species caught, mainly with fishing gear and practices that are not regulated in this proposal and where selectivity is essentially left to the fishermen themselves. as far as amendment 28 is concerned, the same is not clear. the deletion of paragraph 3 would mean that whitebait fisheries would be completely forbidden. the commission's aim is instead to keep them within a clear regulatory framework of national management plans. the commission cannot therefore accept this proposal. the commission cannot accept amendment 29, because a 30% increase in the height of the nets would increase fishing effort for small pelagic species, against scientific advice that calls for no increase in the fishing effort targeting this resource. moreover, since purse seines may be used to catch demersal species in coastal areas, we should avoid authorising large purse seines that could touch the bottom in coastal areas where protected habitats, such as posidonia beds, occur. the commission is however open to regulating this type of fishing gear by differentiating between purse seine fisheries for small pelagic species, demersal species and tuna. each category should follow different rules. i hope that further refinement will be possible within the council. the commission cannot accept amendments 30 and 31. it is widely recognised that management of fishing effort should be one of the main management tools in the mediterranean. establishing the maximum overall dimensions for certain small-scale fishing gear is a way to address this. the huge number of fishermen using this gear makes it indispensable to set maximum dimensions to avoid further increases in size which would result in insuperable walls of nets that impede free movement and migration for several species. small-scale fishermen should also contribute to conservation. the commission cannot accept amendments 32 and 34 for different reasons. the list of species in annex viii to council regulation 1039/98 requested by amendment 32 contains species which are either not present in the mediterranean or which can be caught by bottom-set nets and anchored floating nets in coastal areas. it is therefore undesirable to include the full list of species here. in fact the rationale of article 7(2) as mentioned in amendment 10 is to list a group of species which are caught offshore in midwater, or close to the surface of very deep waters and which, when they occur in the catch of a bottom-set gillnet or entangling net, are clear signals that such a net is a drift net rather than a bottom-set net. this provision is the only way to enforce the large pelagic drift net ban. nonetheless, the commission is open to a large list of species if there is evidence that certain species cannot be caught by real bottom-set nets but only by drift nets. amendment 34 suggesting a derogation for vessels smaller than 18 metres would gravely weaken the enforcement of the large pelagic drift nets ban. this amendment is based on the assumption that article 7(2) addresses a type of surface gillnet targeting tuna. this assumption is not correct, since such nets cannot be classified as an anchored floating net or bottom-set net as defined in article 2(9) and (12) respectively. in conclusion, may i express the confidence that, with the help of the european parliament, we can put before the council an improved commission proposal, which should facilitate its position vis-à-vis the council. all mediterranean fishermen and the marine ecosystems that they exploit need urgent and effective fisheries management. the adoption of a new, more effective and specially tailored european union conservation policy for mediterranean fisheries will also foster more ambitious steps within the multilateral framework of the general fisheries commission for the mediterranean. as you are well aware, fishing effort has been increasing in many areas and the exploitation pattern is still not satisfactory. in order to guide mediterranean fisheries towards sustainable exploitation of the mediterranean marine ecosystem, the european union, which is the biggest fishing power in the region, needs to set a good and credible example. a more effective community management framework is needed to recover the full production and productivity potential of the mediterranean in the interests first of all of our fishermen and also of other european citizens that want to benefit from the richness of the mediterranean. in concluding my speech, may i once again thank the rapporteur, as well as the chairman and members of the committee on fisheries, for their excellent cooperation on this matter. their proactive cooperation has indeed provided us with a substantial input that will help ensure sustainability for fisheries in the mediterranean.
the rapporteur. mr president, with this report, which i have had the pleasure of presenting, we have the opportunity to finally put forward a fisheries management system for the mediterranean, eleven years after that first attempt to bring order through the regulation on technical measures, regulation no 1696/94. it is therefore a key moment for the fisheries sector in this area, and for it to have come to this, i must express my full appreciation to commissioner joe borg and director-general jörgen holmquist, who have been personally involved in bringing this dossier forward, to their services, with whom i have worked day by day, and of course to my colleagues in the committee on fisheries, who have had the wisdom and generosity to give up many demands from their local sectors, sometimes under strong pressure, in order not to deprive the whole mediterranean sector of common management rules. with the involvement of all, the initial commission proposal, which, perhaps too hastily put forward, had opened up seemingly insurmountable fronts with the national administrations, with the sector and with this parliament, which, as will be recalled, rejected the proposal through the report by mr lisi. to get out of this impasse, i proposed to the commission that we work together on a common text on the points where the confrontation was greatest, in order to achieve a joint compromise, accepted by parliament and the commission, which we would present again to the council of ministers. the commission accepted this method and, after very hard negotiation and almost a year of work, it is the one we are submitting to this house today for approval. it may not be as ambitious a text as many of us would have liked; perhaps no one has been a 100% winner. but each of us has lost a little so that we can all gain, because if there was one thing we all agreed on, it was that the situation of fisheries in the mediterranean could no longer be left to the arbitrary rule of minimum regulations, which complicated rather than solved the problem. if politics is about sacrificing particular interests to achieve the common good, i think we can be satisfied with our work in approving this report, which shows that when we work together it is easier to make progress, without forgetting that when a balanced text is presented to those in power and agreed by all, it is easier to accept and therefore easier to apply. this method of working has also enabled us to eliminate leaps in the void lacking scientific and logical foundation, and some contradictions in the initial text which were at the origin of the outright rejection of the proposal. for example, greater rationality and coherence are being introduced in the regulation of the depths and distances from the coast at which fishing can be carried out in this biologically, economically and socially sensitive sea. dredges are regulated for the first time, the use of more selective nets such as the square mesh for trawling is introduced and considerable progress is made in matching the mesh size to the minimum species sizes. in addition, in the face of the commission's maximalist initiative on the seals, minimum sizes and hooks for fishing for large-sized fish, it was agreed that an attempt should first be made to get these regulations out of regional fisheries organisations such as the gfcm and iccat, since these fisheries are also carried out in the mediterranean by fleets from third countries and it is not logical to impose restrictions only on community vessels. however, if within one year these international bodies do not reach a common standard, the commission will be entitled to submit a new proposal, since we do not want to abdicate our responsibility, which derives from our strong presence in these fisheries. finally, i would like to highlight the efforts to protect species by introducing minimum sizes, with the temporary exception of hake, where we started from a commission proposal to reduce the size to 15 cm, which we have maintained until 2007, when it will return to its traditional size of 20 cm, coinciding with the proposed increase in mesh size. the size of sardines is also regulated for the first time, sizes that had disappeared from the commission proposal, such as that of clams and herring, are recovered and reasonable increases in size are introduced for other species, since the ultimate objective is to come closer, also in the mediterranean, to scientific recommendations. mr president, after having again asked for the house to approve this report and, above all, the compromise reached with the commission, i can only hope that the council will accept the new proposal in its entirety, the result of this compromise between the european commission and the european parliament. mr president, first of all i would like to say that the work done by the rapporteur - in this case mrs fraga - and the members of the committee on fisheries is, first of all, an example of collaboration, as the commissioner has pointed out, and a very positive sign for the future coexistence of the two institutions. the cooperation - which, as i say, was close and effective - between the rapporteur, mrs fraga - who has done a magnificent job - and the commission services has enabled us to arrive today at this plenary with a compromise acceptable to the majority of this house, and with a clear message to the sector, which we cannot, under any circumstances, break or cloud. and, most importantly, this cooperation allows us to unlock a situation which has become unsustainable - unsustainable for the community institutions, of course, but above all for a sea whose resources have long been considered overexploited, but which, because of its peculiarities, lives in a state of permanent exception, which it is time to end. the mediterranean is a different sea: national waters are more limited than in other parts of the community, fish stocks are trans-zonal and shared, the general characteristics of the activity are different - there is a mainly artisanal fishing fleet and a high proportion of part-time fishermen, there are many small landing sites, etc. i have only mentioned some of the features that make the mediterranean a different sea, but the objectives of the cfp are the same in the mediterranean as in other community waters: we must ensure that the exploitation of living aquatic resources creates sustainable environmental, economic and social conditions. therefore, in addition to the structural and market measures defined in the cfp which are already in place, conservation policy must be developed in the mediterranean in a similar way, as must the regulation, which must be improved and developed, the harmonisation of minimum sizes and technical measures, which must be absolute throughout the european union and effective throughout the mediterranean basin, and effective control, which must solve the problem of the sale in one member state, which is too often spain, of illegal fish from another member state, because this illegal fishing harms us both: the selling state, because it degrades resources, and the receiving state, because it degrades prices and, above all, fishermen's confidence in the management mechanisms. i therefore congratulate the rapporteur and hope that we will all come out of the vote well today.
mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr freitas, who has done an excellent job and, moreover, we have recognized this - no amendments have been tabled - and also my colleague, mrs stihler, who, on behalf of the socialist group, has done an excellent job as an alternative rapporteur. i would like to express here, however, very modestly, some opinions which may be a little bit different but which i think can add to what has not been said. firstly, the main reason why the european community is involved in the icat and the apicd is because of the presence of the european or spanish tuna fleet, as you will call it, in the eastern pacific, where it has been operating since 1975. i say this because in the explanatory statement of mr freitas' report the justification seems to be based on other grounds than the presence of our fleet in the eastern pacific. our fishing fleet in the eastern pacific and of course it has never fished with dolphins, because there is a community regulation that prohibits it: council regulation 850/98 of 30 march 1998, article 33. i would also like to say, because i think it might be useful in this house, that the apicd is being created because of a specific problem of the american fleet and, subsequently, of the mexican, venezuelan and colombian fleets, the only ones, together with el salvador, that are currently fishing with dolphins. i think that is something that we as europeans can be satisfied with. we, who have been fishing in that area - and this is an opinion - that the report should call for - and perhaps the commission can shed some light on this - the final ratification of the apac by the european union, and not its accession to this convention. i would also like to make a point on amendments nos 11 and 12. the regulation does not in any case mention a label which is safe for dolphins; that label, as such, does not exist. what the regulation does contain, in article 3, is a series of definitions, one of which is the definition of 'tuna without risk to dolphins'. i congratulate the rapporteur again, and i think that perhaps a little bit of realism is needed on the subject we are dealing with.

author. mr president, bolivia is torn between chaos and civil war. the collapse of state institutions, the absence of authority and the disorder that reigns in la paz, above all, make one fear the worst, if the worst has not already been installed. but what has happened in bolivia to bring the situation to such a head? the reasons are many: the succession of bad governments, the failure of the policies of neoliberal fundamentalism, the desperation of the impoverished and excluded masses of the system, the predatory behaviour of the multinationals and - it must also be said - the incomprehension, or worse, the indifference of the international community. the fact is that today bolivia is a failed state, ungovernable and deeply unstable whose situation may get even worse, being more difficult and costly to solve. i was in la paz and santa cruz de la sierra just a month ago, sent by the spanish government to assess the situation and propose possible initiatives. looking back at the report i wrote, i regret that things have evolved in the direction i predicted, but that was no merit, i was not a visionary; it was already obvious, as it had been for two years, that bolivia was heading towards the abyss. during that visit, i did not find in the traditional parties or in the so-called "emerging parties" and practically in any political leader, the slightest hint of sense of the state, a lucid and generous analysis for the good of the country. all or almost all of them calculated what would suit them personally: the convocation of a constituent parliament, elections for the prefects of the country's nine departments, a referendum on emerging autonomy such as santa cruz de la sierra... at that time, i found only one fundamental exception: that of president carlos mesa himself, in whom i saw a well-intentioned man, who tried to find solutions through dialogue and negotiation. but he was and is a man alone, without a party, without parliamentary support and with a motley opposition that demanded contradictory solutions from him. at that time, it had only a high level of popularity and an undoubted dominance of television communication. as he was - and has been - unwilling to repress the demonstrations and street riots, the pickets of the most radical parties and unions took over the streets and imposed their own resignation. moreover, they have vetoed the accession to the presidency of the presidents of the senate and congress, who constitutionally would be the successors of a resigned bureau, and they require that the president of the supreme court, third in the line of succession, accede to the head of state, but only so that he can call general elections in three months. paradoxically, mr president, that may be the only and best democratic way out. but perhaps not because of the demands and calculations made by the most radical, but because citizens will be able to regain the prominence that corresponds to them and that they have stolen from the street, because "the street" are minority sectors that do not count on the vast majority of the 10 million bolivians. what is the international community doing in the meantime? not much of a life. that is why this parliament has raised the question: the european union must be a global player; the european union and its member states are the first investor in development aid to bolivia. because we want the governance and stability of bolivia and because our interests are at stake, the council must instruct its ambassadors so that bolivia can find a peaceful, democratic and free way out. let it never happen again that bolivia's wealth, such as silver, rubber or wood, goes abroad or to the domestic elite, and not for the benefit of the bolivian people themselves.
author. mr president, the current situation of tension and confusion in bolivia was, i fear, predictable. we have long known that large sections of civil society, in particular the indigenous peoples, peasants, workers and the unemployed, are marginalized from the political and economic life of the country. but we in europe cannot pretend that we have nothing to do with what is happening. twenty-six of the newly privatised companies are in foreign hands, many of them european, and this has not helped to resolve the crisis or to increase the population's access to gas and water. the problem is that the european union is continually supporting privatisation processes in latin america in international bodies, without having guarantees that the minimum principles of corporate social responsibility are being met. and what happens then? that companies get credit, invest, want to make money and when there are mobilizations by local groups that have been excluded and because of the price increase as a result of privatization, then european companies decide to leave and demand, in addition, compensation for this, which further aggravates the crisis. for this reason, if the european union is to continue to have a certain credibility as a guarantor of human rights in the world, it must investigate the actions of energy companies of european origin in bolivia and elsewhere, and it must be much more demanding in respect of compliance with social responsibility standards by companies investing abroad.
author. mr president, we do not know what is happening in bolivia right now, which is experiencing some of the most dramatic times in its history. the government palace, where the presidency of the republic is located, is known by bolivians as the "burned palace". indeed, it has been burned several times throughout the country's many popular uprisings. in front of the palace, in the plaza de armas of la paz, there is a bust of president general gualberto villarroel who, in 1943, during an insurrection of the many that have been there, was killed hanging from a lantern. fortunately, according to my information just half an hour ago, the presidential palace has so far suffered no damage and the outgoing president has just made a dramatic appeal to avoid bloodshed and civil war. i think it is my duty to acknowledge, on behalf of my group, that president mesa has honoured his commitment never to use violence to suppress protest movements and i regret that such exceptional behaviour, so unusual in a country with a history like bolivia, has not been met with a response of equal height from the opposition leaders who, in my opinion, have been overtaken by events and have radicalized their statements in the last few hours. today, at this hour, in bolivia, power is in the streets. when the legislators are meeting in sucre, because it has not even been possible to access the congress headquarters in the capital, la paz, due to the blockades, the foreign embassies have activated their emergency plans for the evacuation of the country. today, as we prepare to vote and pass a resolution of support for the bolivian people, appealing to respect for the institutions and the constitutional order, i can only ask god and the quechua and aymara gods to enlighten their leaders and to bless and protect the bolivian people.
author. - mr president, freedom of expression and of the press is one of the foundations on which any democracy that is consistent with respect for human rights must be based. the european initiative for democracy and human rights therefore supports the development of pluralistic information and the strengthening of independent media, also in algeria. and you must continue to do so. in this regard, i must say that i am concerned about the current situation of the free press in algeria, especially after the reform of the penal code adopted in 2001 and, more specifically, the provisions which provide for heavy prison sentences for defamation. it would therefore be a good gesture, within the framework of the euro-mediterranean neighbourhood policy and the association agreement, for the algerian authorities to release the journalists convicted of defamation without delay, lift the state of emergency and stop persecuting the algerian private media. all this would contribute greatly to developing and strengthening the rule of law and to respecting the provisions of article 2 of the association agreement.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. mr president, my speech this afternoon is a bit incidental, because it concerns the study of the legal basis for the proposal for a regulation. the rapporteur thought at one point that he would have to propose an amendment, namely the repeal of article 22 of the convention implementing the schengen agreement, and he tabled amendments nos 85 and 70. under article 22 of the convention, aliens were required to declare their entry to the competent authorities either on entry or within three working days of entry, and the member states were required to lay down conditions and exceptions in this respect. the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs referred the matter to the committee on legal affairs, which, after studying it, came to the conclusion that the proposed amendment would require a review of the legal basis and that articles 62 (1) and 62 (2) would not be sufficient but that article 62 (3) would also be necessary, since article 62 (3) of the treaty refers to the conditions under which third-country nationals may move freely within the territory of the member states for a period not exceeding three months. that was the opinion of the committee on legal affairs. the rapporteur was subsequently able to reach an agreement with the commission on this and did not consider it necessary to continue with his amendment, so that at this stage there is no need to change the legal basis. in any case, perhaps the only value of this work is that we know that, in the case of reference to the schengen agreements, it will be necessary not only to refer to article 62 (1) and (2) but also to refer to article 62 (3).
member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. i am pleased to be able to discuss security research with you today and i thank you for the recommendations and suggestions you have made to the commission. security is an essential component of various european union policies, such as the common foreign and security policy or the area of freedom, security and justice. but security is also a prerequisite for prosperity and growth and therefore essential to achieving the economic policy objectives of the lisbon action. to meet the challenges of public safety, we need the best tools possible. a strong knowledge and technology base is also a prerequisite. to build them, we need research, both at national and european level. the commission has therefore adopted the following recommendations to the council and the european parliament a year ago: while technology alone cannot guarantee safety, safety without technology is impossible. to meet the high expectations of safety managers, users, industry and citizens, various elements must be in harmony. first, security research must play an active role in creating a social and business environment that fosters positive economic developments and enables prosperity. this research is thus a driver of growth and employment in europe. then this research must contribute to the competitiveness of the european security industry and the research programme will help to establish and develop a european market for security products. then we should also focus on civilian security issues. this type of research falls within the remit of the european defence agency, with which civilian security research liaises to address dual-use aspects of security technologies. finally, security research must be seen as a particularly sensitive sector with very specific requirements: intellectual property rights, dissemination of information, cooperation with third parties beyond the union's borders and the level of the community's financial contribution. security research is part of the 'security and space' dual focus theme in the seventh framework programme's specific programme 'cooperation'. the current proposed budget is about eur 500 million per year. the commission welcomes the fact that the parliament's report calls for a budget of one billion euros per year, as proposed by the group of personalities. in the seventh framework programme, security research will focus on the following areas: protection against terrorism and crime, security of infrastructure and supply facilities, border protection, restoring security in crisis situations. these four themes are complemented by horizontal areas: systems integration and interoperability, security and society, and research coordination and structuring. the european security research advisory board, a forum where users and the commission can consult on the design of the research programme, will be the main instrument for formulating a longer-term vision. in accordance with the report on security research, and in order to ensure good representation of the european parliament, vice-president verheugen has invited five committees to nominate a representative as an observer to the european security research advisory council. the european parliament has always supported the current preparatory action on security research, and that is a good thing. we therefore welcome the report by the committee on foreign affairs, drawn up in cooperation with the committee on industry, on which parliament will be voting. i would like to thank you for the support for security research in general in the debate on the seventh framework programme, and also specifically for the funding for preparatory measures. the commission will continue to welcome reports on the implementation of this preparatory action before the implementation of the security research programme as part of the seventh framework programme for research can begin. security research will focus on activities with clear european added value over national level. we will thus strengthen the competitiveness of the security industry at community level, contribute to the achievement of the lisbon objectives and help make our society as a whole feel and become safer. i would like to thank the rapporteur again for his work.
the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment. mr president, as a representative of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, i would first of all like to express my thanks and congratulations to mr klich on his excellent report. our contribution consists essentially in setting objectives by optimising the means, in clarifying responsibilities, in granting security research the status of a public interest 'substantial and very important issue', in giving a lot of vitality, through research, to the interoperability so necessary in crisis situations, not so much in prevention as in response and resolution of the same, and in defending the need for adequate funding, linking security research absolutely to gross domestic product, taking into account therefore the economic weight of states and not allowing research in this area to be subject to volatile fluctuations in budget availability. finally, mr president, i believe that we will have a european research programme on security within the seventh framework programme and a pluriform, technical and political advisory committee. through these research formulas we are going to improve one of our greatest weaknesses, the so-called c4isr - the command, control, intelligence and surveillance systems - and it can only be corrected through a correct application of european research policies, without links and without dependence on third parties. there is an absolute need to improve efficiency in the advancement of sensor systems, biotechnology, space and communication technologies. i therefore repeat, mr president, my congratulations to mr klich on having dealt with a report of such importance and significance.

on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i was a full member of the committee on legal affairs in the last parliament and i followed this subject, and then, as now, what i had was a great deal of perplexity, because here we are talking about the commission's legal responsibilities, based on article 232 of the treaty, which refers to the right to appeal for failure to act, but according to article 232, in order for the european parliament to claim a breach of the treaty, there must be a breach of the treaty as such. and of course, this is a directive that was not adopted by a previous british government and was then adopted by a subsequent government, which is the current government; the commission initiates an infringement procedure in accordance with article 226, the situation is changed, the directive is incorporated and then, as commissioner mccreevy has pointed out, according to the case law of the court of justice of the european union, there is no possibility of continuing the procedure before the court, because article 226 says: 'if the commission considers that a member state has failed to fulfil one of its obligations under this treaty, it shall issue a reasoned opinion on the matter, after having given that state the possibility ...' as the state complied with the commission's opinion, we have no case at this stage from a legal point of view. i have the impression, as commissioner mccreevy has said, that at this stage there is only a right of appeal to the british judicial authorities themselves, but not to the institutions of the european union. in legal terms, we could say that at the moment neither this parliament, nor the commission, nor the court of justice of the european union are the appropriate forum for raising such complaints. unfortunately, that is the wording of the treaty. we could have a different treaty, which would impose obligations on the commission in respect of things that have happened before, but the case law of the court of justice in this case is exhaustive and that was the reason why i objected to this issue then and i still object to it today. in other words, the treaty does not allow the commission to bring a state before the court of justice when the state has already complied with european union law. it is not a mathematical or immediate, automatic system, but it requires first of all a request to the state, and when the state complies the procedure is over; from then on the commission has no possibility of doing anything. i have the impression that at this stage both the answer given by the commission earlier and the one just given by commissioner mccreevy are fully satisfactory. i would recommend to those affected by the lloyd's case that they go to the british courts and pursue the appropriate actions in accordance with british law, but i think it is pointless for us to bring this procedure up here at this time; it is a huge waste of time for this parliament and, if you will, even a deception for the people affected, because they are being led down a path that will lead nowhere. and the only possibility of satisfaction is the british courts themselves; i believe, in fact, that there are already actions taken before these courts. it's the only chance of action. and that's my recommendation to the people affected for this type of claim.

president of the commission. mr president, members of this house, prime minister blair, i agree with you that it was a very interesting and useful debate. we all understand that this situation is a very special one. it should not be seen as business as usual. i understand that there is a real appetite for a frank debate. there were, of course, different views, but this debate has shown that there is a will for the search for consensus. in that search for consensus, it is important to avoid simplifications: the idea to put those who are in favour of a free market against those who are for social commitment; the idea to put political integration against economic integration. the truth is that we need economic integration and political integration. we need a consensus, but not one that ignores the need for the hard choices that europe must make. there is now a risk in europe: the risk of populism. sometimes populism on the left against globalisation and foreign competition; sometimes populism on the right, just against foreigners and against the very idea of europe. that is why it is important that all those who have some responsibility in europe – be it at national or european level – fight that populism and show, collectively, their commitment to the values that make europe a great project. ladies and gentlemen, i would also like to make another statement prompted by some of the events of this weekend. as you approach the house, you will have seen, perhaps to your surprise, that there is a large white band surrounding the outside of the house. i think this is the first time that we've used a campaign symbol in this building, a symbol of this size, and i'd like to talk to you about some of the details of what this white band means. i would like to remind you that this band is the symbol of the "world call to action against poverty" launched by the president of brazil, mr da silva, in porto alegre in january 2005. since then, more than 600 non-governmental organizations from around the world, including the most important ones, have joined this campaign and are trying to gain the support of governments and public figures. it is now our turn, the european parliament's turn, and that is why we have chosen this plenary week, which coincides with the start of the g8 summit next wednesday in gleneagles. we all agree, ladies and gentlemen, that the fight against poverty is the objective of the union's development policy and that this year presents a great opportunity to make progress in this direction, since several high-level conferences will be held on this subject during the year. you also know that the european union will contribute 46 billion euros this year to development aid, and this means that the european union is the largest donor in the world in this field. we can certainly be proud of this, but perhaps we should ask ourselves what the relative dimension of this figure is - of these 46 billion euros. the 70 euros that each european pays in the rich countries as development aid each year is equivalent to the price of a cup of coffee a week. this is the relative dimension of our effort: the price of a cup of coffee a week for every inhabitant of the rich countries; our generosity does not go beyond that. the june council approved the decision to increase eu development aid to €66 billion in 2010, i.e. from €46 to €66 would be a cup and a half of coffee. but for that, we would wait five years. i think that is an ambitious message that the european union is sending to the g8 summit this week, but we must also remember that to do that we will need to have a budget that we do not yet have. the objectives of this campaign are fair trade, debt reduction and increased aid, both in quality and quantity. i would also remind you that outside this chamber there will be a number of stands set up by ngos, and you will be able to obtain more information there until wednesday. on wednesday morning there will be a debate on africa, on the challenges of globalisation and also, of course, on this campaign against poverty, with jack straw, hilary benn and louis michel. the white ribbon is the symbol of this campaign and after the debate, all the speakers in it and myself, on behalf of everyone, will sign on a second white ribbon as a sign of our support; this ribbon will be cut and hilary benn will take it to gleneagles. but we also need the support of all of you, and that is why i ask you to sign the white ribbon at the entrance to the house as a sign of your action and your will to fight poverty, so that hilary benn can deliver a strong message from this parliament in gleneagles. but i ask you to bear in mind when you sign it that we are citizens with more powers than ordinary citizens, we are budgetary authorities, we vote on resources, we allocate resources and we approve policies; bear in mind when you sign it that in the years to come, as parliamentarians, we will have to approve the union's budget, with or without financial perspectives, and that the commitment to sign it also represents a commitment to launch from the power of this parliament a real effort to eradicate poverty in our world. thank you so much for your participation in this campaign.
