mr president, mr president trichet, mr commissioner almunia, ladies and gentlemen, i regard the annual report of the european central bank as a sign of transparency and its presentation and debate in parliament as an exercise of democratic responsibility. in 2004, the year of the enlargement to 25, the interest rates were maintained and prices were unchanged from the end of the previous year. there has therefore been a situation of stability, but also a situation of little dynamism. the economic performance of the euro area has not lived up to previous expectations: the increase in economic activity has been weak in the context of the highest global growth in the last twenty years, there has been a loss of market share in international trade and an increase in the productivity differential with the united states, while there have been no significant changes in the labour market. it is therefore necessary not only to reflect, but to make a great commitment: sustainable growth and employment are the main concerns of europeans. the reform of the stability and growth pact is a good response, replacing mechanism with rationality. at this point, mr president, we would like to emphasize the central bank's special role in providing financial conditions for all. we particularly appreciate the reference in your report to the situation of small and mediumsized enterprises and we point out that at this critical moment when confidence in the common project needs to be strengthened, you will continue to have our support in fulfilling your mission.
mr president, we consider this report a step forward in recovering the future stolen from our childhood. the trakatellis report on phthalates in toys is a victory for the health of european children, who have suffered for decades from their effects. the european parliament has succeeded after years of insistence - too many years - in upholding the precautionary principle by banning its use, a use which has probably already caused health problems for millions of children, as shown by a recent swedish study which found that, after analysing more than 11 000 children up to the age of six, the likelihood of them developing asthma and various allergies is three times higher than for unaffected children. we're talking about linoleum floors with those effects. what we have to deal with now is the debate on reach and on preventive and pro-public health research within the seventh framework programme, which should include these issues.

mr president, this misleading and ambiguous directive is the dream of patent lawyers and at the same time the nightmare of small software companies, consumers and freedom of expression on the net. because we are dealing with a directive rejected by more than 90% of the small software companies on the continent. we are dealing with a monopoly directive - indeed a monopoly directive - because it is an anti-liberal directive. it is a directive that powers a world of its own of the rockefellers and morgans of the early last century. it is a world that does not benefit european small businesses, whose numbers are increasing, often in the less developed parts of europe, such as extremadura in spain, where hundreds and hundreds of new software companies are developing. these companies are threatened, as are those developing in poland and in all the enlargement countries. there's been a lot of lies told here. it has been said that we are against patents on technical software: that is not true. we are for, obviously, when it comes to the physical world, the forces of nature: a washing machine, a car... no one is against these patents! but we are against patents which are a real threat to the flow of information and innovation. a lot has been said about innovation. unlimited free patenting has been confused with innovation, two things that have nothing to do with each other. what we're defending is the right to develop software, to develop industry. and this directive is going to put curtains and many obstacles to real innovation on the ground of this continent called europe. i think we deserve a software world, a business world, a consumer world, that is open to real innovation.
mr president, the previous speaker, mr gargani, has expressed concern about the balance in the position we take on this proposal for a directive. i believe that it is precisely the rapporteur, mr rocard, and mrs berger, in their amendment no 53, who have highlighted the objectives of this balance, saying that 'the conditions for granting patents and the methods for enforcing them must be carefully defined, in particular in order to keep within reasonable limits the inevitable consequences of patent systems, such as the restriction of creative freedom, legal uncertainty and the adverse effects on competitiveness'. the amendments tabled by mr rocard and mrs berger seek to maintain this balance, firstly, with regard to what exactly is computer-applied invention: we are not discussing computer inventions here. computer inventions - computer programs - are already protected by a 1991 community directive which established intellectual property rights, or copyright, if you will. and that directive is in force. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we must take great care not to mix one thing with another and thus prevent the exercise or development of computer-based creation. in concrete terms, amendment no 50, tabled by mr rocard and mrs berger, is very important in maintaining the right to interoperability of computer programmes. the fact that a patent may exist on some aspect of the computer program should not prevent the free creation or use of computer programs for further development. that interoperability clause, which is defended in amendment no 50, is also defended in a slightly different text - amendment no 68 - by mrs mann, mrs mccarthy and mrs roth-behrendt. in short, it must be avoided in any case that the development, experimentation, manufacture, sale, licensing and import of software which makes use of a patented technique for achieving interoperability can be considered as infringement of a patent. in short, the amendments tabled by mr rocard and mrs berger are aimed at maintaining the possibility of creation in this area and, if possible, projects such as the linex project, developed by the junta de extremadura in spain, can go ahead in the interests of creative innovation in the european union.

which some of us know well because we live it day by day - for example, that member states may submit national plans throughout the whole programming period or that the article on equal opportunities for men and women be strengthened and that this vision of gender equality be integrated into fishing activities, and, as regards aquaculture, the extension of aid to mediumsized enterprises, not just micro and small, and that it may be possible to finance the improvement of the working conditions and safety of workers in the sector. the consensus reached on the eligibility criteria is also important, as low employment and declining fishing activity make it logical to remove the reference to municipalities with fewer than 100 000 inhabitants. the two most controversial points, the renewal and modernisation of ships and engines and joint ventures as an alternative to scrapping, have also been saved in a positive way, thanks to the good negotiating spirit that has existed. my group is in favour of allowing the fleet to continue the process of renewal and modernisation, provided that this does not lead to an increase in capacity. we have an obligation to keep the fishing industry in the european union alive and well by guaranteeing a living wage and living conditions for the workers in the sector and by preserving resources, but we also have an obligation, commissioner, to save lives at sea. my region, galicia, knows this very well, as in the last two years it has lost many of its people at sea, because of construction problems, because of structural problems in the boats. we cannot allow this to continue and we must continue to support the renewal of the fleet.
author. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all, as chairman of the committee on international trade, i would like to welcome commissioner kovács and tell him that we would be delighted to have him in the committee on international trade for a first debate on the subjects we are dealing with together. i'm telling you directly, in this very intimate environment that we're in right now, at this time of night. i also want to express my satisfaction and that of my commission for the adoption of the gsp regulation in april, although it is regrettable that it was not adopted on time to benefit the countries affected by the tsunami. and, with regard to the rules of origin, although it is true that parliament has no power of codecision or consultation on the regulation implementing the customs code, by virtue of the council decision of 1999 laying down the procedures for the exercise of implementing powers conferred on the commission, we are entitled to be regularly informed about the procedures carried out in committee. this would mean that, as with the directorate-general for trade, from which we received the documents of committee 133 on time, the directorate-general for taxation and customs union would send us the draft implementing measures, the results of the votes and the minutes of the meetings. this is in accordance with the powers conferred on us by the regulation, which are not strictly those relating to trade matters but also to economic and trade relations with third countries. we are therefore interested and ready, commissioner, to consult our respective agendas in order to develop the logical relations of debate, dialogue and control with your portfolio. as regards the content of the reform proposal, we consider that the range of issues raised from the point of view of simplification, flexibility and control is significant; i will refer to them very briefly. as far as simplification is concerned, we welcome the removal of a long list of conditions imposed on exporters and the extension of the certificate of origin solely on the basis of the value-added criterion. in this connection, we would like to receive as soon as possible any impact studies or simulations that have been carried out, showing the economic impact of the establishment of value-added thresholds on trade and the beneficiary countries. as regards flexibility, we believe that allowing regional accumulation between countries in the same region will promote economic integration between them, which is part of our basic philosophy and can also have beneficial effects. finally, as regards control, we must propose the establishment of new control mechanisms so that there is no accumulation of excessive bureaucratic and administrative procedures which could discourage the use of mechanisms for the use of preferences. at a time when the debate on the achievement of the millennium development goals and the fight against poverty is very lively, both in this parliament and in the un, the osce and the g8, we believe that this is the most appropriate time for a reform of the rules of origin which opens up our markets and benefits the countries which need it most. that is the purpose of this question and we would like to know what the commission's criteria are at this point.
member of the commission. mr president, the communication of 16 march 2005 defines general orientations for the future of the rules of origin in preferential arrangements. it is a three-pronged approach, which should be seen as a package: firstly, simplification and appropriate relaxation of the substance of the rules; secondly, improved procedures for their implementation and enforcement; thirdly, a secure environment for legitimate trade, in particular through a targeted monitoring of the functioning of the arrangements. while the orientations should be applied progressively to all arrangements, their priority focus is firstly on the arrangements devoted to the development of each gsp. the commission considers that formal simplification could be achieved by placing the current numerous and complex rules for determining the origin of products that are not wholly obtained in a country by a single, across-the-board method based on value criteria. that method also offers the flexibility, through the setting of the value threshold, to adjust the origin requirements according to the desired results in terms of market access and development for beneficiary countries. it would apply both for determining what sufficient processing is when materials not originating in a country or in a cumulation zone are used, and for allocating origin, but in the context of cumulation, using different value thresholds. let me take the opportunity to address your second question. the need for relaxation has, taking into account my preliminary remarks, to be considered against its desired effect, not only in terms of growth of exports under the gsp, but mainly on the actual development of the beneficiary countries. in that context the criteria to be taken into account in order to define the value thresholds lie in the impact of the new rules on development. the use of a value-added method is therefore a starting point. the commission is launching studies to measure its impact on certain products that are key commodities for developing countries, such as textiles, agriculture and fisheries –until now the determination of their origin has not been based on value – and which are sensitive for the community in tariff and market terms. the study will help in defining the criteria and in verifying whether a value-added method with the appropriate thresholds for both sufficient processing and cumulation is actually in line with the principles of simplification and development-friendliness. should this study demonstrate that the value-added approach would not deliver the expected results for certain sectors, the commission will adopt another approach to better achieve these objectives. referring to your first question, the commission is ready to explain in more detail to representatives of parliament. however, the terms of reference of the study are how the products and countries will be selected for the simulations and the steps to be followed in evaluating its results. with regard to the definition of thresholds, that will be part of the process of drawing up and adopting the commission regulation to amend gsp rules of origin. parliament will be involved, in accordance with the comitology procedure. however, once the commission is in a position to formally start the examination of the draft regulation within the customs code committee, the draft will be made available to parliament. with regard to your third question, the commission has carefully considered the idea of allowing global cumulation between all gsp beneficiary countries. that goes far beyond the cross-regional cumulation. cumulation of origin, to have a real impact, should be an additional opportunity to source materials from countries that are real economic partners, with lower constraints than from other countries. expanding sourcing possibilities to all developing countries would result in denying the very concept of cumulation, assuming that most of the supplies used by developing countries to manufacture products to be exported to the eu under the gsp come from other developing countries. such a global cumulation would, in fact, replace the normal origin requirements. the main beneficiaries of such a situation would again be the biggest exporting countries and not the poorest and more vulnerable ones, whose interests would be better served by appropriate value thresholds. to make an impact, cumulation and its facilitation must remain targeted in groups of countries with mutual and balanced economic interests. as highlighted by the communication, that does not exclude extending existing cumulation zones or merging existing groups such as asean and saarc. however, that must correspond to needs expressed by the groups of countries themselves and it must be supported by the necessary instruments for administrative cooperation in origin matters. the commission remains at the disposal of parliament to keep it informed of the further development of this important file. i should like to say to the chairman of the committee on international trade: i am at your disposal and the disposal of your committee whenever you invite me to participate in your proceedings.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, as rapporteur for the report on the generalized system of preferences and follow-up rapporteur for the reform of the rules of origin, i would like to stress the importance of the preferences recognised by the union being effectively applied and actually benefiting those to whom they are addressed. the main concern of parliament is to ensure that this objective is achieved and, therefore, in sharing the objectives of its communication, i would like to raise a few questions. as regards simplification, i would first of all like to stress that special treatment is needed for the least developed countries and that lower thresholds and the possibility of de minimis rules in their favour are recognised. at the same time, the setting of value-added thresholds as a single criterion requires addressing certain side problems, because this requirement can be very costly for companies in less developed countries, which would need quite sophisticated accounting and auditing systems. if this criterion is linked to the net cost of production of the various countries in terms of exchange rates, wages and commodity prices, the complexity of the system can be increased and exclusionary effects can be generated in the least developed countries with cheap labour. as regards the flexibility of the rules of origin, i would point out the need for countries enjoying the same preferential treatment, even if they belong to different geographical or commercial regions, to be able to accumulate among themselves. we believe that this would be a coherent rule and at the same time it would be necessary to recognise the possibility of bilateral cumulation with the european union itself, so that finished products in a beneficiary country containing materials from the community could also benefit from the preferences. as regards the monitoring measures, i reiterate the need for impact studies and simulation exercises, and i ask you to listen to the views of civil society and to monitor the monitoring of the system, and to keep parliament duly informed.

president-in-office of the council. mr president, it is a very great honour for me to be here today. it is the first occasion on which i have addressed this great body. thank you very much for the particularly its chairman, mr dimitrakopoulos, for its report and for the presentation this morning. apologies for my pronunciation. i did ancient greek at school, but of course that was written rather than oral. the disagreements within the european union over military action against saddam's regime in iraq are a matter of record and we all acknowledge that strongly held views remain on both sides. given the strength of feeling, i am particularly grateful to your committee for the way in which it has looked forward for a future for iraq rather than backwards to rehearse the arguments over it. since the end of military action, the european union has recognised its strong and common interest in supporting the new iraq that is now emerging. i think we all condemn those who want to determine iraq's future through extremism and violence. we condemn all killings and kidnappings, but, given the nature of this body, we particularly condemn the recent kidnapping of the egyptian ambassador in iraq, mr ihab al-sherif, and the attacks on other diplomats from arab countries. we are determined to see the success of a peaceful, stable and democratic iraq, which responds to the needs of all its citizens. just over a year ago, the european council endorsed the commission's communication setting out medium-term objectives for the development of the eu's relationship with iraq. that strategy is bearing fruit. last november, the council presented a package of european union assistance to iraq's then prime minister, dr allawi. that included a longer-term commitment to starting negotiations on a third country agreement and to promoting eu trade and political cooperation with iraq; a reminder of the commission's offer to implement the generalised system of preferences and financial support. experts from the commission worked with the united nations and the independent electoral commission of iraq, and helped to make a success of iraq's first democratic elections on 30 january this year. several members of the european parliament also observed those elections. the general affairs and external relations council in february agreed to build on this package of assistance with further support for iraq's political process, including the drafting of a new constitution. it agreed on a new community aid package of eur 200 million and the launch of an eu integrated rule of law and police training mission for iraq with offices in baghdad and brussels. that mission began training iraqi police, judiciary and penitentiary officials yesterday and is making a valuable contribution to the iraqi government's efforts to increase its authority and to entrench the rule of law. overall, the european union is today delivering an impressive and comprehensive programme of assistance to the government and people of iraq as they seek to build a peaceful and democratic future. last month, along with commissioner ferrero-waldner, the high representative, javier solana, and the president of the general affairs council, jean asselborn, i visited baghdad. in my view, and i hope commissioner ferrero-waldner shares this view, it was a very important visit, symbolising the european union's commitment to the new iraq. there the commissioner reiterated the commission's intention to open an office in baghdad as soon as possible, so as to strengthen the eu's dialogue and technical assistance. at the international conference on iraq in brussels a fortnight ago, hosted jointly by the united states and the european union, representatives from 87 countries and international organisations gave a similar and strong message of support to the new iraq. let me just respond in opening to one absolutely key point. i will make my first apology for referring to the rapporteur as the chairman. if this is regarded as a slight on my very good friend elmar brok, the chairman of the foreign affairs committee, i apologise to him too. mr dimitrakopoulos rightly said that the security situation was the key to everything else and the security situation is serious. there is no disguising that. he also intimated that the sooner the iraqis were able to take control of their own security the better. let me say, as one of what were the two formal occupying powers in iraq, the united states and the united kingdom, and someone with his own personal responsibility for the war, we share this aspiration. leave aside the arguments of the past. all of us believe that the quicker the iraqis are able to take responsibility for their own security the better and the quicker the coalition forces will then be able to leave. the security situation is poor. the better news is the increase in the training and ability of the iraqi security forces. now there are 168 000 individuals in the iraqi security forces overall. more and more of them have a proper capability and are being used. we are well aware that under security council resolution 1546 the mandate for the foreign forces in iraq will come to an end in december this year, unless it is renewed in some way, and that in any event, as 1546 makes clear, we the coalition forces are only there at the invitation of the iraqi government. were the iraqi government to ask us to leave, we would leave immediately. on the issue of whether there could be a united nations 'blue-hatted' force, i have no difficulty with that in principle. the only issue is encouraging other countries to come forward. whether we can achieve that remains to be seen. however, on the overall objective of coalition forces being reduced and then leaving and the iraqis taking full control for themselves, we are absolutely in agreement. to sum up, the united kingdom will look during its presidency to pursue a growing relationship between the eu and iraq, building on what we have already achieved. i welcome the committee's endorsement of the goal and particularly their call for the commission to open its office in baghdad and for the eu to send an observer mission to the elections to be held in iraq in december. i greatly welcome the committee's suggestion that the european parliament should build on its relationship with the iraqi transitional national assembly. i look forward to today's debate

water, and also on creating jobs, because what is most important is that people themselves are able to feed their families. of the eur 200 million committed we will soon have finalised eur 145 million, to be channelled through the world bank’s international reconstruction fund facility for iraq to meet basic needs. the forthcoming donor conference in amman will then offer an opportunity for the iraqis themselves to take the lead, based on the last conference in brussels, in setting up a real donor coordination mechanism. they already announced it at the conference and we would like to work with them. in addition to reconstruction aid, the international community also needs to do more to reduce or reschedule iraq’s debts. the commission will be pushing eu member states on this, because we think it is fundamental. it is a prerequisite that neighbouring countries especially contribute more and more, because they will really play a central role in shifting the balance in the region. these countries need the assistance and cooperation of their neighbours. the neighbours have made this commitment in principle, but now we have to see whether it can be put into practice. iraq is an extraordinary country with a great but turbulent past. it is now the inspiration for a new era of international cooperation. we know that the agenda that we have set out is very ambitious, but i think we can deliver if we just stay the course. the iraqi people have shown tremendous courage and resilience, particularly in turning out in such large numbers to vote, but also in their everyday lives against a background of violence and intimidation. they deserve compassion, but also solidarity and financial and other assistance. that is what we have to do on moral and also political grounds. president-in-office of the council. mr president, i wish to say, for the second time this morning, what an honour it is to address the european parliament. i greatly value the dialogue i have had with parliament and its committees, not just over the last four years as britain’s foreign minister but over the previous four years as britain’s home secretary. indeed, i have been serving in the british government long enough to recall our previous presidency, seven and a half years ago, when i had the privilege of chairing the justice and home affairs council. i also wish to congratulate parliament on its initiative today to support the ‘make poverty history’ campaign. it is a sign of your strong commitment to global development in what is a vital year for africa and for the poorest nations worldwide. mrs morgantini has submitted to me some detailed questions. i have already sent her a detailed answer to those questions and i shall make sure they are more widely available. in my speech i shall be answering many of the points she raised. over the last few months, the headlines in europe have often been about disagreement and difficulty. the voters in two founder member states have brought into sharp relief questions of profound concern to all europe’s citizens. how can the european union better deliver to them the prosperity and security which we all seek in a rapidly changing world? some of the answers to that question will concern the european union’s internal policies, including future financing. the united kingdom, as tony blair said to parliament just two weeks ago, takes its responsibilities as eu president very seriously. we will work hard to reach agreement on the financial perspective by the end of the year. alongside this, we will seek to conduct the wider debate on europe’s future direction and priorities in an open and inclusive way, respectful of the different viewpoints in this parliament and amongst europe’s governments and citizens. yet if we are to respond fully to people’s hopes and fears for the future, it is just as important that the eu strengthen its actions in the wider world. one of the most striking developments of the last few years has been how much we have done already in the european union to rise to that challenge, on a basis of very broad agreement. a few years ago, europe’s nations were severely divided, as we were reminded in the previous debate over iraq. yet today we are taking strong common action in support of peace in the middle east, sudan and the democratic republic of the congo. we have a comprehensive programme of engagement with the new iraq. we are leading the international community in the difficult but vital process of engagement with iran. the story is the same on security and defence. just a few years ago the debate on esdp revolved around the location and staffing of a small planning cell in a suburb of brussels. but today an eu force is working with nato in bosnia on the ground. eu missions there and in macedonia are training police. we are also training iraqi police and judiciary. we have two european missions in the democratic republic of the congo. we are assisting the african union force in sudan. so, today, the european security and defence policy is not a piece of paper: it is making a real difference to thousands of lives across the globe. i want the united kingdom’s presidency – and the years ahead – to be a time in which we build on these achievements and further strengthen the european union’s influence and power as a force for good in the world. nowhere is that more important than in africa. africa today is poorer than it was 25 years ago. half of the population south of the sahara lives on less than a dollar a day. africa’s share of world trade is one third of its level in 1980. the total national income of sub-saharan african countries is less than the developed world – the eu, the united states, japan and a few other countries – spend on farming subsidies. a major breakthrough is needed if we are to achieve the millennium development goals. at the current pace, it will take sub-saharan africa more than 100 years to meet the targets for primary! education or reducing infant mortality. for three of the goals – those for hunger, poverty and sanitation – the situation in sub-saharan africa is getting worse day by day. meanwhile, life expectancy in africa today is just 42, less than the age of most people in this chamber. it is predicted that in some african countries life expectancy will be under 30 in five years’ time. twenty million africans have already died of aids, now the continent’s biggest killer. three-quarters of those living with hiv worldwide are in africa. nelson mandela said: ‘like slavery and apartheid, poverty is not natural. it is man-made and can be overcome and eradicated by the actions of human beings’. mandela was right. africa has all too many examples of how the actions of human beings prevent other human beings from building better lives for themselves. in darfur – as hilary benn, my colleague and friend, the secretary of state for international development in the united kingdom – and i have both seen for ourselves, the government-backed militia has killed many thousands of people. millions have had to flee their homes. in zimbabwe, the government has already trampled over democracy and basic human rights and has ruined an economy that was once amongst the strongest in the whole of africa. the government in zimbabwe has now turned on the poorest and the most vulnerable in that country, driving hundreds of thousands from their homes and destroying their livelihoods. the problem of zimbabwe is not one of intrinsic lack of resources or of climate but one of very bad governance. the european union has been right to send a firm message that the government of zimbabwe’s behaviour is wholly unacceptable. we have done so through new extended and restrictive measures against the mugabe regime, and through a firm condemnation of the latest abuses. but amongst all this gloom, let us remember that the picture in africa is far more complex than it at first appears. in the 1970s you could count the democracies of africa on the fingers of one hand and still have two fingers left: there were three. today there are more than thirty democratically elected governments across the continent. only a few years ago, armed conflicts were ablaze across africa, but today sustainable peace is taking root in countries such as burundi, liberia, sierra leone and angola. the organisation of african unity used to preach non-interference in its members’ internal affairs. in contrast, its successor, the new african union, is founded not on non-interference but on non-indifference. it is taking as its inspiration what the european union has been able to achieve in a continent that was once itself characterised not by the peace and stability we now enjoy, but by conflict, war and bloodshed. through the new partnership for africa’s development, nepad, african leaders have agreed to a peer review mechanism which many developed world governments, many governments in europe, would find uncomfortably intrusive. nor is the economic situation in africa as uniformly negative as it sometimes seems. some countries, such as mozambique and ethiopia, have achieved growth rates of around 7%, a level sufficient to lift large numbers of people out of poverty. the continent has enormous resources, both physical and human, and these positive factors should give us real cause for hope. africans want a better future and we in europe, with our international partners, must continue to deliver the support to enable reform in africa to take root and in turn help africans to change the situation for the better. so we have made this year a year of action and we have already achieved a great deal. last month’s european council is currently famous for its disagreements on the european union budget, but i suggest that our children will better remember it as the council which decided to double european aid to africa over the next five years. that was the enduring legacy of that council and, with luck and work, the temporary problems over the european budget will indeed be temporary. we are also resolved to make that aid better coordinated and more effective, building on the agreements made at the oecd meeting in paris this spring. we have to ensure that the aid does not compound bad governance and enrich the corrupt, but rather that it is used to drive up standards of governance and help the poorest, for whom it is intended. the g8 has agreed 100% debt relief for all highly indebted poor countries and the g8 leaders who assemble today in gleneagles and meet today and tomorrow will discuss further support. at the united nations summit in september, we are going to review the millennium development goals and strengthen international action to achieve them. however, we have to do more. under our presidency, the united kingdom will work to deliver a european strategy to support africa’s successful development. the strategy needs to be comprehensive and ambitious; it should go beyond financial support and show how africa will invest in people, in good governance, in growth, peace and security. as part of this strategy, we have to deliver better access to developed markets for the world’s poorest countries, so as to make the doha development agenda a reality, and we should start with this december’s meeting in hong kong. the european union, the united states and other rich countries must honour their commitments to abolish export subsidies and do so to a clear and explicit timetable. we have to recognise, too, the central importance of peace and stability in africa. already there are thousands of refugees in darfur who are safer. why? thanks to financing from the european union peace facility for the african union’s mission there. through the facility, we can increase our support further by supporting the african union and organisations like the economic community of west african states, ecowas, which itself has played such an important role in tackling conflict in west africa. the peace facility really has been a success, but the money allocated to it is running out and we need to agree adequate long-term countries in africa, who themselves are wanting us to make use of these mechanisms within agreements like the cotonou agreement. the great live 8 concerts that took place across europe and across the world that this time the aid effort to africa will work. let us hope that it will. let us hope that the developed nations actually deliver the aid they are promising, but let us also understand this: the process will only work if governance in africa is improved and corruption there is cut down. in our action in africa and across the world, the european union can draw on three great strengths. firstly, the eu’s intrinsic power and influence. when we speak together we can set the international agenda. we are doing so on world trade, but i have seen that too in leading with javier solana, with joschka fischer and now with philippe douste-blazy in the difficult iran dossier. the strength of the european union when it is united is phenomenal. the strength we have is the strength of our global connections. there is hardly a country anywhere in the world that does not have some special tie of history or friendship with one or other of the european union’s member states. the latest enlargement, last may, added further to that network of partnership and trust and our global reach is mirrored in this parliament and in your strong international engagement. the eu is today building stronger relationships with neighbours such as russia and new strategic partners such as china and india, which are going to hold such important summits with the eu during our presidency. obviously we will wield greater influence with such strategic partners when we act together. the third, and perhaps most important, strength is the strength of the european union’s values. soft power in foreign policy has been defined as making others want what we want. the european union’s enlargement is one of the most striking and powerful examples of that soft power in action. the magnetic pull of the eu’s success, its values and institutions, have helped to transform first southern, then central and eastern europe and the prospect of eu membership is now spreading reform and stability to turkey and across the western balkans. others here perhaps know the western balkans better than i do, but all of us who know the western balkans know that in reality the only thing that is helping to push those divided communities towards some prospect of peace and security is the european union, its values and its strength. the june european union council recognised this in reaffirming its intention that the eu should fully implement its existing commitments on enlargement, including opening negotiations with turkey on 3 october. meanwhile, our neighbourhood policy is helping to promote our values further to the east and to the south, including to ukraine and to the mediterranean countries, with which we will also host summits during the uk presidency. those values are the bedrock of the transatlantic relationship, the world’s greatest alliances of liberal democracies, essential in tackling the global challenges of the future from terrorism and proliferation to poverty and climate change. through these assets – our own strength, our global connections and the power of our values – the european union today has even greater potential to increase its strength as a force for good across the world. i look forward to working with you all towards that goal during our presidency. member of the commission. mr president of the european parliament, mr president of the council, ladies and gentlemen, when i applied for the development and humanitarian aid portfolio, i knew that africa would be at the heart of my action and commitment. a commitment inspired by a sense of indignation and urgency: africa remains, even today, isolated from the world, on the fringes of our consciousness and far from the benefits of globalization. it is also based on the rational recognition that the context has changed and that the opportunity is now emerging, perhaps unique, to make africa a more prosperous, stable and better governed continent. in this context, europe can and must make a difference, because today we can create the conditions for poverty eradication and there are no longer any excuses for not doing so. africa has changed. the africans themselves have decided to turn their backs on fate and take their destiny into their own hands. the energetic and effective action of the african union in darfur, togo and côte d'ivoire, for example, has given a new dimension to the principle that african responses to african crises must be found. this action, based on strong regional organisations, opens up new and hitherto unforeseen prospects for peace, stability and security. moreover, the african union is supported by strong leadership that is now outlining a promising vision. if africa has changed, so has europe. europe is increasingly asserting itself as the spokesman for a world of greater solidarity, more justice and a more multilateral system. in 2005, the year of development, europe must make its voice heard as the leading donor of development aid and can, in this capacity, push the international community towards a concrete and voluntary approach which would prevent the millennium development goals from soon becoming synonymous with broken promises. i am also very pleased to note that the european council - as i have just said - has followed the commission's proposal, which will effectively double official development aid by 2015 and double aid to africa by 2010. finally, the world has changed. the events of recent years have shown us how the existence of failing states can be a source of instability, can create safe havens for terrorists and criminals. the intensification of globalisation at all levels also makes it necessary to intensify solidarity. i believe that development policy is now the preferred instrument for humanizing globalisation. i can't think of a better one. what is unique about globalization is that it did not, as some would have us believe, come about through a political decision hidden in a shelter somewhere. globalization has not been truly orchestrated; it is a spontaneous process, welcomed by some, feared by others, but over which, and this is the point, no authority, whether national or international, seems to have direct control. i am sure there are those who believe that it can do a lot and that it has many more advantages than disadvantages. the intensification of globalisation at all levels must of course be met by the intensification of solidarity at all levels. what does globalization mean for people who don't have access to water, for young people who don't have access to education, for children who are dying of diseases that we could cure? while some may dream of a return to models that unfortunately flourish in the déjà vu, i think it would be wrong to believe that people do not want globalization or that they want to go backwards. what we europeans want is a globalisation that benefits everyone, that is a positive lever for all humanity, without exclusion. in this context, nothing is more urgent than making globalisation work in africa and for africa. it is true that the liberalisation of markets in this context is only virtuous where the state has the capacity to enact rules to contain deviations from them and to ensure that the general interest is respected. as you know, to take advantage of the opportunities offered by globalization, governments need to ensure a macroeconomic framework. they must also create the effective and predictable conditions for this macroeconomic framework and must of course also ensure governance in a framework favourable to economic activity. they must also encourage and support a vigilant civil society that ensures a fair and balanced redistribution of wealth and other services such as access to justice, administration, health and education. from this point of view, and particularly for africa, i believe that a very special, focused effort must be made in the fight for equality between men and women. for all these reasons, i think it is useful to define a common european strategy. not just for development, but also for africa, a strategy that can respond to the new geopolitical situation in africa; we are also working on a strategy with our african partners to capitalise on this new momentum globally. the african union has become a key political partner, a real engine of change for the continent. at the same time, i think it is worth pointing out that this construction cannot stand on its own. the house of the african union must be built on solid regional building blocks. there will be no continental integration without a strong, ambitious and recognised regional organisation. an ambitious political partnership between the european union and the african union is therefore more necessary than ever. what should this wedding be about? i do not have an exhaustive answer, but i will limit myself to four possibilities which i would like to propose as working hypotheses. you know that i will come at the end of the year with not only a statement on development, an update of the development policy which we will of course have discussed and will discuss together, but also a real master plan for africa. the first is governance. the primacy of governance, which is obviously not contested by anyone, as we have said, africa is not poor, it is unfortunately badly governed. and yet, africa is starting to move. governance efforts are being made at different levels. over the past five years, more than two-thirds of sub-saharan african countries have had multiparty elections, some more free and fair than others, and several changes of government have taken place in a democratic and peaceful manner: most recently, the elections in burundi. i hope that in the drc in march we will also be able to make significant progress. i would also like to recall that 23 african countries have ratified the statute establishing the international criminal court. it is good to say that, although some of the democratic powers in the west have not yet done so. the most striking fact of recent years is that africa has given itself a vision, a mission and principles. in terms of governance, this fact, embodied in the institution of the african union and reflected in the vision of nepad, represents a break with the past and the practices of the past. this vision and these principles have not remained at the declarations of intent stage, since with the african peer review mechanism, africa now has a unique tool to accompany africans by africans. this mechanism deserves our full support. the second axis is infrastructure and networks. we will all agree that without trans-african networks, without infrastructure, there will be no development. the european union itself is proof of this. the european union has shown the relevance of this reality. increased efforts are needed to improve and ensure the sustainability of infrastructure networks and to accelerate growth and promote trade. the commission therefore proposes to develop a europe-africa partnership plan on infrastructure and networks. through this partnership we will support the development of trans-african networks which are essential for interconnectivity and the flow of knowledge on the continent, trans-european telecommunications networks, railways, airlines, infrastructure for de-icing, which are also very important: ports, airports, waterways, everything related to energy and water. in parallel with this infrastructure partnership, we should innovate in terms of financing mechanisms based on the participation of the private sector and other donors. i shall come back to this in the statement on the edf in a few months' time. thirdly, of course, trade. all actors recognise the central role of trade in economic growth. africa's share of global exports has fallen by almost 60%, which corresponds to a loss of $70 billion a year, or the equivalent of 21% of the region's gdp, more than five times the $13 billion that returns to africa each year through development aid. we obviously have to reverse this trend. as you know, we are currently negotiating economic partnership agreements with six regions, four of which are in sub-saharan africa. peter mandelson, the trade commissioner, is negotiating these deals. this is without doubt the most ambitious trade process ever negotiated between the north and the south. for the first time, the european union is financially supporting the negotiating effort of its partners. for the first time, trade agreements are being negotiated with the sole objective of developing our partners. for the first time, these agreements are based on and for the regional integration of our partners and for the first time our financial and technical cooperation can be used for reforms, budget support, actions to improve the capacity to increase supply, the construction of an attractive environment for investment and trade. the last axis is culture. culture is a key dimension of development which, in my view, has been far mr president, it has been a quarter of a century since willy brandt presented his report on north-south relations. since then, the problem of poverty has not only not been solved but, in many cases, has worsened. in fact, the latest report on world poverty shows that there is only some progress in china, in some countries in south-east asia and in some specific cases in latin america. in africa the data are disconsolatory, so we must welcome this british initiative, which is not opportunistic in my opinion - it was already announced, at least two years ago, by minister straw and his prime minister. after 40 years, dozens of wars and millions of deaths have left the african continent exhausted. there are no magic recipes in the fight against poverty and we have only two certain facts: firstly, poverty, contrary to what some people think, is not an economic but a political problem, and its solution requires, first and foremost, political decisions; secondly, to succeed, economic growth must be ensured - without growth, there is no wealth to distribute. from there, these days we hear millions of voices around the world calling for the application of the classic recipes: increased official development assistance, debt forgiveness and fair trade. these are three necessary but insufficient measures. political and social leaders in poverty-stricken countries must demand much more, especially in terms of strengthening civil society - their societies - transparency and good governance, which can increase investment in health, education and gender policies. in africa there are more than 100,000 armed children, whose faces some of us have known. if we are to make progress on the target of halving poverty by 2015, these points i have outlined are on the line that must lead us to success.

i think we have introduced a number of new aspects. firstly, there has been a strong emphasis on natural resource management in this project. this project is of great pedagogical importance for teaching environmental governance and management. in addition, the institutional presence has been emphasized, that is, the municipalities and regions as local authorities who have, precisely, to revalue their resources. and in this connection i would also like to highlight another element: the introduction of landscapes worthy of respect which have not been integrated into the natura 2000 list, such as some rivers, but which can be important shared spaces. and there is also another novelty: the concept has been introduced and the idea of international projects and cross-border projects has been reinforced. why would you do that? because natural areas are often precisely in border areas, high in the mountains; the case of rivers is very clear: it is logical that one day a life could be made of a river, because rivers cross many countries. i should also like to say something else: we have created a market spirit for natura 2000. we believe that in this case we should follow the american policy of creating wetland banks, natural area banks, so that the states can compensate the owners by creating a kind of ownership exchange area for the natura 2000 area. and in this way, companies and many others who have to take initiatives on the territory will also be able to contribute financially to compensate, under the 'polluter pays' principle, for their passage through these protected territories with active, positive policies for the conservation of the natural environment, financed by private entities and institutions. so this is not just another life programme, it's a consensual project guided, i think, by a great deal of common sense, and for that i congratulate everyone.

the next item is the debate on the report by mr duarte freitas, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council regulation laying down specific measures for agriculture in the outermost regions of the union (com (2004) 0687 - c6-0201/2004 - 2004/0247 (cns)) (a6-0195/2005).
mr president, first of all i would like to thank mr freitas for the work he has done as rapporteur, which i consider very satisfactory. i would also like to thank the commission of our union for the work it is doing for the benefit of the outermost regions. i think mr michel has made that very clear. it is a success story: over the last 14 or 15 years the outermost regions have benefited from special treatment under the poseidon, poseima and poseican programmes, which have enabled four million citizens, spread over islands in the central atlantic, the caribbean and the indian ocean, to enjoy a decent standard of living commensurate with their needs, and regions which used to export population to now maintain it and, in some cases, even import it. in other words, there has been a marked improvement in the living conditions in these regions. it has been done by a fairly reasonable procedure, which consists in allowing agricultural surpluses from the rest of the union to enter our territory and even allowing the importation of products to other parts of the world, and on the other hand preventing these imports, which are necessary to maintain living conditions, from destroying agriculture and other elements of the local economy. the commission's proposal is aimed at making the system we have in place more flexible. as the commissioner has said, 56 micro-measures were needed which did not really fit the nature of this type of organisation. the amendments tabled by the committee on agriculture and rural development are aimed at making the mechanism more flexible and should also be welcomed. i would like to point out - perhaps for those who are not aware of the situation - that the reason for these special features and flexibility of the outermost regions is their absolute inability to compete on the union's markets, that is to say, aid to farmers in the canary islands or réunion or madeira or the azores will not in any way affect the rest of the european union, since the conditions of competition are the same and, on the contrary, i would say that they will facilitate the development of the economy in the rest of the union, by having markets of a certain purchasing power which benefit the whole of the european union. i therefore hope that this house will give a massive vote in favour of the report by the committee on agriculture and rural development and that these measures will continue to work for our benefit and that of the rest of the territory of the european union.
mr president, we are discussing today a regulation which will go unnoticed among the serious problems which concern us today in the union, but which is of vital importance for the agricultural sectors of the outermost regions and, in many cases, a matter of survival. i would like to highlight two aspects of the project we are discussing: firstly, the maintenance of the financial leaflet, which was approved in the last reform in 2001, which is no small thing in the present times; and secondly, the decentralisation of management which gives the regional authorities the power to introduce the necessary flexibility in accordance with the needs of the agricultural sectors at any given time. in other words, there is no plan to change the intensity of aid, but rather to have a more flexible instrument for management, as mr duarte freitas points out in his amendments nos 4 and 21. the rapporteur's amendment no 27 aims to give legal cover to imports of c sugar in certain outermost regions, especially the azores, the canary islands and madeira. this is not a problem without obstacles, but i hope that the commission will be able to analyse and understand it in order to find the most appropriate solution. commissioner michel made a reference during his speech, which was elliptical in the sense of political correctness, to the management of the specific supply arrangements in the islands - i am referring in particular to the canary islands. believe me, mr michel, the canaries would like both the local authorities and the commission services to ensure maximum transparency in the management of the res, this specific scheme for supplying the islands.
the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force. many of those we met expressed concern at what they saw as a replacement of the still-unfinished peace agenda by an emerging economic and trade liberalization agenda. in this context, the vulnerability of many groups is notorious and therefore worrisome. the groups most affected by the present situation include indigenous groups, social movements and human rights defenders and, as the resolution we are debating and voting on today shows, women and children, especially the poorest. example one: according to the human rights defenders protection unit of the national human rights movement, between january and may there were 76 attacks against human rights defenders, including raids on premises, attacks and murders. during our visit, several of the assaulted and threatened groups told us about their experiences. they also deplored the impunity enjoyed by those responsible for these events, due to the lack of investigation by the authorities. example two: the data on structural and direct violence suffered by guatemalan women are alarming, but the judicial and legislative responses seem insufficient. irregular adoptions and allegations of forced pregnancies or child abduction are just one symptom, among others, of the weakness of the guatemalan rule of law, especially in relation to poor women and indigenous communities. the commission should therefore be urged to set the following priorities in the future eu strategy for guatemala 2007-2013: social cohesion, the right to food, rural development and reform of the land tenure and use system. the strategy must also be drawn up with the greatest possible participation of the groups concerned. only by involving the different actors in the process will it be possible to ensure that the implementation of the strategy has the local support necessary to make its objectives a success.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rights of children are respected, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report. according to official figures we obtained there, in 2004, 3,824 guatemalan children were the subject of international adoptions and that figure, for a country of just over twelve million inhabitants, shows that something is wrong there. adoption of a child costs between 25 000 and 30 000 us dollars, of which the donor mother receives only 2 or 3%, i.e. less than 400 euros. this means that the total amount obtained by this phenomenon of mass donations amounts to the second item of the country's total exports. they are, in general, children of single mothers, many of them girls, between 13 and 14 years old, mostly indigenous, and victims of drugs and/or prostitution in many cases. numerous guatemalan governments have tried over the past few years to pass a law that would develop the hague convention on adoption, but have been unsuccessful. the guatemalan congress has not been able, probably under external pressure, to pass such a law. now, the guatemalan government expects that in the coming weeks a law will be passed to put an end to this situation; for this reason, my group intends to send a very clear message to the guatemalan authorities, telling them that they have our full support for their congress to finally pass a law that will put order into this really intolerable situation.

let me now make a statement referring to the events of this summer. as you will recall, on 7 july, at our last session before the holidays, we were shocked by the terrorist attacks in london, which, as we feared at the time, had caused a very large number of victims. the terrorist threat to europe continues and is a problem to which the events of july and those which followed will force us to attach particular importance. but this summer has also been marked by other tragic events: the persistence of terrorism in iraq, terrible natural disasters and accidents that have caused grief in many families around the world - particularly here in europe and, now, very especially, in the united states. you should know that, throughout this summer, whenever one of these events has occurred, your president has, on behalf of the european parliament, immediately expressed our solidarity and addressed himself to the authorities of the countries affected by these tragedies. every time they have happened we have let our voice be heard. and today i think it's good that we all join together, globally, in the grief of the families of the victims of these events, of those who have lost their loved ones in the deadly conflicts that affect the planet. the united states deserves special mention, for it is suffering today from a drama of surprising proportions that is moving the whole world. the number of victims will, it seems, be very high, the displaced persons number in the thousands and the economic damage and the wound to the social structure are very great. in iraq, every day terrorism kills, drop by drop, numerous people. there is enough rumour, as happened a few weeks ago, for a panic movement on a bridge in baghdad to cost over a thousand lives. dramatic accidents involving civilian aircraft and helicopters have killed more than 400 people in indonesia, greece, venezuela, peru and the baltic sea, and also in afghanistan, where european military personnel - member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the extreme weather events of this summer have left a trail of destruction in many countries of europe and in the united states. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would therefore like to express my condolences and our solidarity with the victims of these disasters and accidents on behalf of the college of commissioners. the worst drought in 60 years has hit the iberian peninsula and, combined with high temperatures, has contributed to the spread of fires in southern europe. along with the fires, floods swept through central and eastern europe, and hurricane katrina struck the southern united states. floods and forest fires are recurring phenomena in europe. this year we had more serious consequences but what happened is not something that surprises us. it is therefore necessary, in anticipation of such disasters, that policy makers have designed measures to facilitate prevention where possible and use all available resources to deal with such crises in the most effective way. to enable the european union to respond effectively and in a coordinated manner to major emergencies, the community civil protection mechanism was established in 2001. this mechanism coordinates the means of assistance available in the member states. it also assists in the conduct of preparedness exercises and the design of hypothetical scenarios and simulations to identify any gaps and problems in the civil protection systems of the member states. it shall also promote cooperation and interoperability between the emergency services of the member states. when, at the request of the portuguese government, the mechanism was activated, the european union was able in less than 24 hours to organise the deployment and intervention of a number of firefighting vessels and helicopters from france, italy, spain, germany and the netherlands to support the portuguese firefighters, and with the help of this aid, and because of the more favourable weather conditions, it was possible to put out the fires within a few days. so in this way the situation was brought under control and today at 12 noon we had only five fires whereas on 22 august we had over 50. the facility was also used to provide assistance to bulgaria and romania, the two countries most affected by the floods. many member states have offered help by sending crews, pumps, disinfectants and other means through the european union's civil protection mechanism. these days, the european union is making a significant contribution and participating in the united states' efforts to deal with the tragic devastation left behind by hurricane katrina. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the aid granted to the victims of the earthquake in the united states is not used to finance the destruction of the civilian population in the country. the european aid package consists of contributions from the member states, ranging from material aid to equipment and the deployment of experts and other specialists. the commission has already sent experts and other material to the united states. the community civil protection mechanism has become a necessary tool for coordinating european aid. the response to this summer's events, as well as to the tsunami at the end of last year, has shown that the mechanism is working satisfactorily. however, there is room for improvement. in april 2005, the commission therefore proposed a package of measures to strengthen the european union's response capacity in the field of civil protection. these measures include proposals to improve the transport of aid and to enable the european union to lease specialised equipment from third countries, such as additional firefighting aircraft. this is precisely the kind of measure that will best protect european citizens - and not only - from future disasters. the package of measures to strengthen civil protection is now being examined by the council. i am sure that the european parliament supports our proposals and stands in solidarity with our efforts. the civil protection can only cover the first, immediate phase of an emergency. other means need to be used to deal with the consequences of disasters and to prevent them; the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the commission has a number of such instruments. i will mention some of them. rural development programmes offer support for a wide range of forestry activities with funds for fire prevention and restoration of damaged forests. the forest focus regulation is the latest instrument we have at our disposal for monitoring and implementing forest fire prevention measures. the financial framework for forest focus for the period 2003-06 is eur 65 million, including eur 9 million for fire prevention. as regards floods, the commission has proposed the establishment and implementation of a coordinated european union action programme on flood risk management. in accordance with the council conclusions of december 2004, the commission has taken the political initiative in this respect. the european union solidarity fund may provide support to countries affected by major disasters to assist them in their reconstruction efforts. romania and bulgaria have already requested the commission to mobilise the solidarity fund. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let me close by saying that i am sure that the european parliament will support our proposals and will take this opportunity to turn its commitment to solidarity into further action. it is our duty to those affected by the recent disasters.

i am grateful to mr weber for his willingness to engage in dialogue and seek agreement. i believe, honestly, that democracy is basically a regime of public opinion and that therefore the quality of it depends on the quality of what we have come to call freedom of expression, which is a right that not everyone understands well. for me, freedom of expression is first and foremost the right of every citizen to choose the news channels he prefers. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the media are not allowed to be controlled by a few people. i would like to make a few specific points from these considerations, which are very general in my view, which i would like to put into practice in the not too distant future. we must fight all initiatives which undermine freedom of expression and therefore we cannot allow interference with the content of programmes. let us refrain from doing so. in my view, we should not tell commercial television stations how they should manage advertising on their networks, because advertising is fundamental to commercial television. they have to respect the ceiling set by the law, but we should not tell them how to distribute it, because they know perfectly well how to make the engine of their commercial survival profitable. mr weber, we must set a political objective - and this is where we most disagree - to put an end to a concept which i consider to be perverse: that of public service. this concept makes sense insofar as radio spectrum is limited and governments therefore have to regulate it through a system of administrative concessions, which in the end end end up being intimidating. but mr weber, you have acknowledged that we are moving towards a world in which television has to be redefined, in which television is the conventional television we know, but it is also internet television, mobile television and television because of all the new technologies. it is therefore not a scarce commodity, and we must limit state interventionism. i would like to see this concept of public service not attributed to commercial television in the not too distant future. and i would therefore like to see us agreeing on a redefinition of the role of public television, which is fundamental, as long as it respects the principle of subsidiarity, that is to say, making those programmes which viewers want to watch and cannot watch on commercial television. mr weber, that is the principle of subsidiarity which i defend. in conclusion, mr president, i believe that technologies are changing, that they are therefore changing perspectives, and that it is our responsibility to make the most of the new 'television without frontiers' directive so that it can be an opportunity to improve the quality of democracy. that's why i want to express my wish that we will do well.

member of the commission. mr president, first let me express my thanks and appreciation to the rapporteur, mr becsey, for his objective analysis of the commission's proposal. i am pleased to note that his report corresponds fully with the views of the commission. let me say a few words about the commission's proposal. in the communication on the vat strategy presented in 2003, the simplification of tax obligations was identified as one of the key areas for future work. in particular, a proposal for a directive on this issue was scheduled for 2004. the objective of simplifying business obligations in the field of vat is in line with the request made by the european council of 25 and 26 march 2004 to identify areas for simplification. as mr becsey rightly says in his report, cross-border businesses need to comply with the tax rules of every member state in which they undertake their activities. that implies that such businesses are faced with enormous administrative burdens, which discourage companies – especially small and medium-sized enterprises – from cross-border business. those burdens obstruct the smooth functioning of the european single market. one of the ways of attaining the lisbon agenda objectives, in particular that of promoting economic growth, is to reduce cross-border administrative burdens and compliance costs in order to facilitate community-wide activities by businesses. the commission's proposal fully meets the objective of reducing such administrative burdens. the commission proposes the establishment of an optional one-stop system, whereby taxable persons can fulfil their vat obligations in the member state of establishment. it will harmonise the scope of the goods and services to which member states may apply restrictions on the right to deduct. it will extend the use of obligatory reverse-charge mechanisms for certain business-to-business transactions carried out by non-established taxable persons. furthermore, it reviews and updates the scheme for small and medium-sized enterprises and simplifies the distance-selling arrangements. finally, it will provide for the exchange of information between member states, which will be facilitated by the electronic system for the exchange of information. for your information, the proposal has received a positive reaction from the european economic and social committee. the committee has acknowledged that, in the current environment, the unanimity rule for decision-making applies; the commission should opt for a pragmatic approach. the united kingdom presidency has indicated that it will give these proposals a high priority, and discussion on this proposal commenced in the council during july. two more meetings will be devoted to the subject in september. so far, the council has concentrated its discussions on a general overview of the commission's proposal. i appreciate that the council's approach has been globally positive.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, commissioner kovács, ladies and gentlemen, vat is the most important indirect tax in the various member states and also a key figure in the european tax system, making a major contribution to the union's budgets. the development of the lisbon strategy calls for improved tax rules to foster growth and employment; reducing administrative burdens can boost the internal market and stimulate business activity, in particular by encouraging the participation of small and medium-sized enterprises in the internal market and benefiting consumers. the european socialists are in favour of simplification, modernisation, uniform application and intensification of the fight against tax fraud. to advance these objectives, we believe that lessons must be learned from experience and the opportunities offered by new technologies must be seized. for these reasons, we have very much welcomed the commission's proposals on simplifying crossborder debts and refunds, harmonizing the categories of deductible expenditure and administrative cooperation in the context of the single window. the final result of mr becsey's report is in this direction and is meritorious, even if it is clouded by the inclusion of an amendment, no 9, which modifies the commission's provision to recognise the member states' right to grant exemptions to small and medium-sized enterprises whose turnover does not exceed eur 100 000. the alternative wording of the resolution has, in our view, opened up a debate on its timeliness and appropriateness, which has led to a lack of consensus among the various groups. i hope that we will soon be able to come together again on this point, so that we can move forward firmly in favour of the objectives of the european union in a sensitive area such as the one raised by the commission's proposal.
