mr president, defining and specifying what the political role of the european union and its institutions should be in the fight against terrorism is, in my view, an absolutely urgent objective for this presidency of the european union. this is not a europeanist argument, but a fundamental necessity for each of the countries affected by the terrorist phenomenon. it is necessary for the deep sense of the union to emerge, it is necessary for all of us, for all europeans, and it is necessary because if the european union does not know how to play a role in the fight against terrorism, the question will arise: what is the european union for? if there is no unity in the face of fear, and that is the european union, what is the european union for? and that will obviously mean not only a failure for the european union but also a waste for the european nations, who will not know how to use the union's courage to combat a phenomenon such as terrorism. the european union must be an essential political element in the fight against terrorism, especially for the ministers of the interior. i know that these ministers have many urgent matters, they need many instruments and tools, but i believe that one of the first urgent matters in this european council before you is that you, the ministers of the interior and justice, should be able to promote a european political project and find a usefulness and effectiveness for the european union in combating terrorism, because you are the ones who will need the union most in the coming years. i am talking about a political project of the european union, not an exhaustive list of measures which, in the end, we are not able to communicate. it is clear that we must support the union's measures on biometric data, to which mr clarke referred, or certainly data retention or certainly what the ministers of the interior need, but we must put the emphasis on the political dimension, on the dimension of a european political project. in this parliament we spend a lot of time talking about technical and legal measures, but very little time on the political effort that the european union requires to combat terrorism. we cannot continue to build the house by the roof; we must give the european union's action the indispensable political dimension. and where can we find the european political project? i mean, in the face of islamist terrorism, the terrorism of those who claim to defend islam, the terrorism of al qaeda, the important thing is that we understand that it's an emerging phenomenon, about which we don't know almost everything: the cadence, the timing, the way in which they are choosing the nations where they commit the attacks. we don't know. we need a european political project based on information and intelligence to understand the phenomenon and diagnose the organization we are facing. we must be able not only to take action but also to make sure that the european citizens know and understand what we are doing. we do not spend time or political effort saying what we are doing and european citizens do not know what the european union is doing. they only see the national police forces; the european union does not exist to combat terrorism, they do not recognize us, they do not see what we are doing. that is why it is so important to make an effort to have national police information forums that are spearheaded by the european institutions, we need a european information centre, where the security forces can access databases such as eurodac, sis or vis and, in short, ladies and gentlemen, we need a political dimension. you don't fight against terrorism. to say that we are fighting international terrorism is to say nothing. we are fighting an organisation and that is why i am concerned that those responsible for the european institutions do not dare to name the organisation we are fighting. i do not care whether we are talking about al qaeda, islamist terrorism, radical or fundamentalist groups, or groups claiming to defend islam, but terrorism has in its diffuse character its main accomplice and therefore the european union must, without a doubt, face up to a problem of this nature, adopting all the instruments of the rule of law and, of course, from our unequivocal respect for what the defence of human rights means.

mr president, i admit that in the fight against terrorism i am not neutral. i fully support the approach and priorities which minister clarke has expressed to us today on behalf of the british presidency. i therefore want to take advantage of your presence here and that of commissioner frattini to stress the need for action, for us to take the political initiative. fighting terrorism is more than chasing and arresting criminals and comforting victims; it is more than police cooperation and solidarity. it is not a question of reducing the operational powers of the ministries of the interior or justice; it is a question of responding effectively and responsibly to the threat posed by terrorism to democracy. terrorism is a choice: a vile, cowardly and cruel choice. their actions are not predetermined by any ideology, any religion, any social or political situation, and nothing can justify it. an effective policy must be able not only to identify and bring to justice those directly responsible for the crimes, but also to act on their roots and on those who legitimize their acts, because terrorists are not only those who plant bombs, but also those who, for example, inculcate hatred in young people born and educated in democracy, a hatred that fanaticises them and leads them to murder their neighbours and to terrorize millions of innocent citizens, as was dramatically shown by the london attacks or, for 27 years, by the eta attacks in spain. europe needs a clear voice that citizens can identify as our political position on this matter. the citizens of europe, and the terrorists too, must realise that we are not resigned to living with terror; the citizens must know that we are prepared to take all the necessary decisions and to use all the instruments of the rule of law to guarantee their security, to make their freedom effective and to defeat the terrorist strategy. in a democracy, security is an instrument in the service of freedom. we all know there can be security without freedom, but there is no freedom without security. only a pluralist, democratic and secure society can guarantee the full exercise of freedoms. both rights are inalienable and we must make them compatible. that is why, in addition to showing my support for the measures announced, i call for a common, transparent and consensual european anti-terrorism policy, so that democracy can be strengthened, so that citizens can regain confidence in their institutions and so that terrorists can lose all hope.
mr president, i think it is a question of identifying the problem correctly. the response to this identification is a sustained attack on our democracy, and so i do not think it is useful in a democratic society to put freedom and security on the same scale: in the face of an exceptional and very serious situation, special measures must be taken, temporary and legally based, but with determination, without complexes and without concessions. there is another hidden side to this debate, which i want to mention. this is the much-discussed problem of data storage. it is not said, but i say that behind all this there are pressure groups and there are unacceptable economic situations. it is worth adding, mr president, that economic interests and security cannot be set against each other, much less be disguised as an alleged encroachment on public freedoms, even if only temporarily. mr president, i am firmly with the victims, with the british people and their government, and i support them wholeheartedly; i am with the democratic judges and police. i would like to conclude, mr president, by saying something i know very well: they hear us, they have procedures for hearing us; we do not want to know what they say, but when they say it and to whom they speak. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are not in disneyland, we are in a democratic and determined fight against terror.
mr president, after september 11, 2001, the united states, under the pretext of maximizing security, led an underground, and for a time secret, sui generis war. it is a matter of what we might call 'the relocation of torture', brought to the fore recently by the kidnapping, in the middle of a milan street, of an egyptian citizen, allegedly carried out by the cia. the italian prosecutor ordered the search and capture of thirteen americans involved in the kidnapping of the suspected terrorist, sent to egypt to be subjected to special treatment. cairo acknowledged receiving it through extraordinary procedures. such procedures are called, in cia jargon, 'extraordinary rendition', which is equivalent to outsourcing torture: they kidnap a person suspected of having connections with terrorism and send him to a country, usually arab, specialized in such art; secretly, and without respecting any right, he leaves american territory, so that the patriotic values, which repudiate, fortunately, such behavior, are not violated, since the interrogations take place on foreign territory. the commission has replied to the question put on these issues by three socialist colleagues that, as these are abductions carried out by a third state on the territory of member states, it is impossible for it to act. i understand that, but the union has close links with the states involved in the scandal i am referring to, and so i think it would be helpful if the council, even if there is no community competence, were to make it quite clear that europe is acting in international relations in a different way.

witnessed another important step forward following the publication of iraq’s constitution as recently as 28 august 2005. we congratulate the iraqi people on reaching this important milestone in the political process. drafting the constitution has, of course, been difficult. all of iraq’s communities have worked together to draft this constitution and there have been compromises on all sides. but founding tenets of the new iraq. no law can be passed that contradicts those tenets. all iraqis are held equal before the law, regardless of gender or, indeed, of religion. freedom of belief is protected in the constitution. all extremist groups are prohibited. the new iraq pledges to respect its neighbours and its international obligations. the oil of iraq is owned by all the iraqi people on the draft constitution in the october referendum. broad public support for the constitution will help ensure a stable future for iraq. the iraqis have succeeded in drafting this constitution despite the actions of terrorists who are trying to destroy the country’s desire for that peaceful future. the council recognises the many challenges still ahead for iraq, particularly in terms of the security of its people. the european union is working to build up the capacity of the iraqi security forces and the judiciary through its integrated rule of law and police training mission. on iran, however, we are deeply concerned by that country’s unilateral resumption of activity at the uranium conversion facility in esfahan on 8 august. this is in clear breach of successive iaea board resolutions and, indeed, the paris agreement iran entered into just last november. the iaea board resolution, which was adopted by consensus on 11 august, is a clear and united signal from the international community of its wish that iran return to suspending all conversion activities without delay. we also regret that iran has chosen to reject, without serious consideration, the european side’s detailed proposals presented on 5 august. these are the most far-reaching proposals for relations between iran and europe since the revolution. they would lead to a new relationship based on cooperation. i would like to reiterate that the european side is not asking iran to give up its civil nuclear programme. the european proposal specifically offered support for that programme, but there is no civilian operational need for iran to develop fuel cycle capabilities. putting its fuel cycle activities on hold would not affect iran’s ability to develop a civil power and research programme; yet allowing them to continue would bring iran closer to the ability to produce fissile material for a nuclear weapon. we remain committed to a diplomatic solution. we hope iran will reverse its decision and re-suspend uranium conversion activity. the key to resolving this issue is for iran to take the confidence-building steps requested of it by successive iaea board resolutions and restore the suspension. as part of our wider engagement with the region, november’s euro-med 10th anniversary summit in barcelona will be a critical opportunity to help the european union’s mediterranean partners to meet the challenges of the 21st century. the barcelona process needs to modernise and move towards a more results-orientated process, with much more focus on reform. in other words, it needs to address the concerns of the peoples on both sides of the mediterranean. the 1995 declaration was a landmark and much of it remains valid today. but it still requires much in the way of implementation. this includes the need to address obstacles to progress on governance, human rights, market openness and foreign investment. we want to see medium-term targets adopted at that summit outlining the kind of region we all want to see in five years. we cannot achieve these aims without peace in the region. without peace, we will not achieve the zone of stability and prosperity that is our shared objective. but lack of peace should not also become an extra barrier to progress elsewhere. we would do well to heed the demands of the people across the region for more transparent government, for economic reform and for social and cultural awareness. we believe that there is a new determination in the region to address the challenges facing its people. we are determined to work hard to ensure that the barcelona process plays a full role in addressing the challenges facing citizens across the euro-med region. the summit would be a unique opportunity for us to demonstrate that our partnership is relevant to our peoples and can deliver results on the issues that matter to them. our partnership can help achieve a step change in regional development and indeed modernisation, through action on good governance, economic reform and education. delivering results in these key areas, against specific targets and commitments, will help drive forward regional progress.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, honourable members, it is my pleasure to be able to address you today on the middle east peace process at a time when there is a renewed feeling of momentum and hope. after five years of the second intifada, the past six months of calm have witnessed a downturn in violence and terrorist acts and the israeli withdrawal from the gaza strip and removal of settlers from certain parts of the northern west bank has passed off smoothly. the professionalism of both sides is to be commended. but real challenges lie ahead. by this i mean firstly putting in place the conditions necessary so that the israeli withdrawal creates an opportunity for ordinary palestinians to improve their daily lives. secondly, the implementation of the roadmap in full, and thirdly, the creation of a viable palestinian state at peace with its neighbour, israel. the commission recognises that for the recent disengagement to be considered a success it must bring tangible and immediate improvement to the lives of ordinary palestinians. the commission has therefore launched a eur 60 million package as an immediate response to the withdrawal. this consists of a eur 40 million infrastructure facility geared to labour-intensive, fast-disbursing projects to restore essential services in the west bank and gaza; eur 12 million assistance to institution-building to help the palestinians assume governance responsibilities following disengagement, and a package of eur 8 million focusing on social services, as well as east jerusalem. the commission is also working closely with the european investment bank to identify common projects in the infrastructure sector. i would like to mention here the fact that we have already in place the european neighbourhood policy and that we have already agreed common action plans with israel, the palestinian authority and jordan and that the commission is absolutely convinced that in the context of the european neighbourhood policy europe can play an important and helpful role in overcoming the problems of the region. this assistance will not, however, achieve its desired results unless israel and the palestinian authority tackle such important issues as movement of people and goods between gaza and the west bank and the outside world, the greenhouses, operation of the border terminals, the dismantling and removal of settlers' homes and movement of people within the west bank. it is for this reason that the commission is providing financial, political and human resources support to the quartet special envoy james wolfensohn, whose contribution to the disengagement has been remarkable. the special envoy has succeeded in fostering dialogue with the palestinian authority and israel on each of these issues. however, only one – the greenhouses – has been settled in full. the commission is helping in this. we are, for example, ready to fund a new presence at border crossings as a confidence-building measure, if the parties so request. the commission is also keenly aware of the need to maintain the israel-palestinian authority customs union so as to avoid possible trade disruption and to do what it can to promote interregional trade and investment. the second challenge for the peace process is implementation of the roadmap. the disengagement has clearly been traumatic for israel, but it has not caused the much-feared rift in israeli society. on the palestinian side, president abbas was able to keep the palestinian factions in check. it is now for the international community to help move both sides forward in parallel, helping the palestinian authority to make progress on tackling incitement and the dismantling of terrorist infrastructure and pressing israel to bring to a halt the creation of new 'facts on the ground', which threaten to undermine future final status negotiations. settlement activity in and around jerusalem and the route of the separation barrier are the two most pressing issues. the third challenge is how to promote the creation of a viable palestinian state, for which the implementation of the roadmap is a necessary condition. there is already renewed impetus for palestinian reform, institution- building, stemming from the intention of the palestinian authority to establish a medium-term plan for economic development and from the g8 political commitment to raise up to eur 3 billion each year for the next three years in order to fund this plan. in the coming weeks, the commission will be putting forward proposals for a comprehensive and coherent medium-term strategy for the european union's relations with a future palestinian state, including better coordination of eu positions and financial assistance. we need to see how best we can promote the political and economic viability of a future palestinian state through targeted assistance in support of reform and institution-building. it is clear that efforts must be geared towards the promotion of human rights and democratic principles, the rule of law, improved security and increased effectiveness of public administration.
the truth is that the evacuation of the settlements in the gaza strip is finally good news in a context where we have only heard of hatred, death, endless suffering and desolation. today it is up to the palestinians, and i would like to quote their leader, mahmoud abbas, to follow the democratic path they have chosen, to control extremist movements and to consolidate their institutions; israel, on the other hand, should also refrain from building new settlements and together, through dialogue, seek, as commissioner verheugen has just pointed out, the viability of two states, secure, with recognized borders on the basis of united nations resolutions. it is clear that there are other problems which remain to be resolved, and they are perfectly outlined in the road map: the problem of east jerusalem, the refugee problem and the conflict between israel and syria. and this at a time when the political situation presents the resignation of mr netanyahu as a member of the government to contest the leadership of the likud with prime minister sharon, and on the horizon of the palestinian elections, where the european union will be present with an observation mission, led by our colleague véronique de keyser, to whom i wish to express my best wishes. i therefore welcome, mr president, the statement made by the presidency-in-office of the council that the european union must play a fundamental role in achieving a just and lasting peace in the region. the european union is the main donor to palestine; it is a partner of israel, egypt, jordan, lebanon and also of syria in the future association agreement, and it is clear that it has a key role to play in political and economic reforms in the region. i therefore welcome the initiatives presented by the european commission as a first step in the context of this package of 60 million to rebuild the infrastructure of the region and to consolidate the palestinian authority in the gaza strip.

mr president, gender policies must be transversal and must permeate all the political, social and institutional dimensions. i think this report is a good example of this in relation to medical and health practices. i therefore congratulate the rapporteur, mrs svensson, as others have done. as several studies indicate, men and women are treated unequally in prescribing, treatment and medical and healthcare costs. to give examples mentioned in the report, women are victims of specific violence, genital mutilation, diseases such as osteoporosis, breast cancer and eating disorders, sexual exploitation and prostitution and insecurity in the workplace. these are specific issues that deserve specific treatment. among the reasons for our positive attitude to this report, i would like to highlight the insistence on the need for the states and the commission to adopt this gender perspective in their policies. that is why i also welcome the words of the commissioner at the beginning.
i would like to refer specifically to two diseases mentioned in the report: chronic fatigue and fibromyalgia. two invisible diseases, because of the difficulty of diagnosis and the lack of resources for research and treatment. it is estimated that 90% of those affected by these diseases are women. we are therefore clearly faced with two gender diseases. it is urgent to investigate the origin and causes of these diseases, to investigate further the treatments and to compare the results. to this end, it is essential to increase the resources devoted to research, improve the training of health professionals, organise information and social awareness campaigns, carry out studies on their social, legal, labour, economic and health impact, and promote and develop new techniques for early diagnosis and for the dissemination of prevention habits already in place. i would therefore ask the commission to carry out a study comparing the extent to which treatments are applied and their effects, both physical and psychological, in each of the member states, in order to find a solution to these diseases. it is essential to include a gender perspective in the formulation and implementation of health policies. fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue are not the only illnesses that affect mostly women. other diseases of the sexes mentioned more frequently in this debate, such as breast cancer and osteoporosis, are somewhat more advanced in terms of prevention, diagnosis and treatment, but in all cases further active progress is needed, further research and the public authorities' effective guarantee of the health of men and women.

author. mr president, china is again the subject of debate in this house, and i fear that this will not be the last time we address the subject. the growing relations between the european union and china are a great opportunity for both sides, and i dare say, for the world in general. however, this relationship cannot be based solely on the improvement of trade relations between the two parties. if the european union is to have a credible policy towards china, it must be much clearer in demanding that china radically improve its human rights policy. the eu-china human rights dialogue is a good instrument for this, but i fear it is being clearly underused. there are several problems that china is not tackling responsibly, given its increasingly interdependent role in the world: freedom of association, freedom of expression, freedom of the press and even religious freedom. i am one of those who believe that government and public institutions should be secular in character and that it is fundamental to strive for the separation of political and religious powers, but i also believe that true secularism must guarantee freedom of religious practice in the private sphere. i am therefore concerned about the constant complaints from different groups about the difficulties they have in practicing their religion in china. just as i am opposed to a state financing or supporting one religion in a special way over others - ladies and gentlemen, we should indeed give our warmest welcome today to the observers from bulgaria and romania who are already sitting in our parliament. their presence reminds us that in may last year the fifth enlargement of the european union was left unfinished while romania and bulgaria were waiting to complete the accession process. it is also good to remember that our parliament gave its opinion in accordance with the treaty of accession of these countries, which is being ratified by the member states, and i think we can all say today that we hope that the date of accession will indeed be the date envisaged, 1 january 2007. i am sure that no one will spare any effort, that we will all do everything in our power, including romania and bulgaria, to make this a reality. i would like to say to our new colleagues today that we look forward to their contributions to our debates and wish them the greatest success in their parliamentary work. but, ladies and gentlemen, the arrival of our bulgarian and romanian colleagues comes at a particularly difficult time for the european union. the institutions are functioning normally on a day-to-day basis, nothing unusual is happening in the normal life of the union, but the european project is suffering from an identity crisis which we should not hide. some of the voices we have heard in recent days say that the european union could do without a vision of its future, and that it would be enough for the union to improve the functioning of its markets and to continue to expand. for some, this would be enough. however, in my opinion, the problem is deeper. the problem is the political dimension of the european project and its geographical dimension. today both the political and the geographical dimensions are at an impasse and the european parliament must play a powerful role in helping to break out of it. our institution must make a powerful contribution to getting out of this situation. ladies and gentlemen, a little over a year ago i set out the priorities of our parliamentary work. but, believe me, we could hardly have imagined then, in september last year, what our present circumstances would be. we could hardly have imagined the situation we find ourselves in today. i therefore think that we should review what has happened this year and re-examine our objectives for the parliamentary year which is now beginning. let us ask ourselves collectively what we have achieved from what we set out to do a year ago and how we are going to approach the parliamentary year which is now beginning at this critical stage of european construction. we also welcomed new colleagues a year ago. a year ago we welcomed colleagues from 10 new member states and then we wondered, in the joy of reunification, whether we would be able to work together, to bring together such different parliamentary cultures; whether we would be able to overcome the challenge, unique in the world, of working in 20 different languages, which are not yet enough to reflect the linguistic diversity of the union. i believe that after a year, a year of intense activity in every respect, we can say that this challenge has been met and that the parliament of the enlarged union is functioning satisfactorily. i want to thank you all for your contribution to this success. i also announced to you a year ago my determination to conclude the complex and sensitive issue of the statute for members. you will recall that everyone agreed that this was a priority, and i was very encouraged to try to find a solution to it. well, today we can say: mission accomplished. thanks to the invaluable contribution of the luxembourg presidency, the council agreed in july to the text adopted by parliament, which i will sign next wednesday. this is a very important agreement for our institution, the absence of which has long been a poison to our public image. i would now like to point out that, from the point of view of our operating rules, we have to set ourselves two objectives: the regulation on parliamentary assistants and the reform of the financial regulation so that the union can manage its resources more effectively. there is a broad consensus on this. without prejudice to sound management, the union needs a financial rule to enable it to function more effectively. we already have a draft which the commission has sent us. and i propose that we set ourselves the objective of having this new financial regulation come into force together with the 2007 budget. a year ago, too, the inauguration of the new commission was looming, and then, as you will remember, we went through a period of turbulence. but today i think we can say that the european parliament has gained in maturity, in legitimacy, in credibility and in visibility in public opinion. and that our cooperation with the commission is based on solid foundations. after that hectic inauguration, we negotiated a framework agreement between parliament and the commission. an agreement which will enable us to make substantial progress in the field of information and democratic control. i congratulate myself on that, too. and in its implementation, the conference of presidents will receive mr barroso in two days' time to learn firsthand the approaches that the commission has announced for this course. it is also a year since the tragic end of the beslan hostages overshadowed our plenary session. i therefore stressed the need to promote the european area of security and justice by actively promoting an anti-terrorist strategy. but a year later, the terrorist barbarism is still active. london was the latest casualty on european soil, but iraq is every day. the terrorist threat is greater today and it will not go away anytime soon. it will test the capacity of european society to deal with it in a way that respects our democratic values. the balance between freedom and security will therefore be a permanent part of our debate. it was already the case in the last plenary session when we heard minister clarke, and it will continue to be the case in the future. on the other hand, we are all aware that terrorism blurs the distinction between internal affairs and foreign policy and that today, whether we like it or not, it appears to be directly linked to immigration problems. we must therefore fight terrorism together with our neighbours and partners in the islamic world, especially in the mediterranean and the middle east. ladies and gentlemen, let me pause here for a moment to say that one of the great questions for the future of the european union is its relationship with the muslim world. perhaps the most important. i propose that we use the euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly, which now presides over the european parliament, to develop this relationship in a positive way, avoiding the terrorist threat and the tensions generated by immigration from turning into islamophobia, which commission sent parliament the financial services action plan which envisaged the rapid implementation of some 40 measures in the financial services sector. we were told then that the ordinary legislative procedure was too slow to adapt to the speed of the financial markets. i would like to say that in the vast majority of cases the fault for this delay was not parliament but the council. the next step is taken in the report called lamfalussy, by the person who directed its preparation, which, in order to provide a solution, to adapt the speed of the procedure to the speed of the markets, proposed splitting the rules into two levels. the first level is general principles, basic guidelines. the second level is the specific legal rules. level one, codecision. level two, total exclusion from parliament. we were asked to renounce the prerogatives that constitute privileges, the basic rules of any european parliament. the european parliament was right to express its misgivings. we simply wanted to be in the same position as the council. in case of overreach, in case the president did not comply with the content of the mandate, we wanted a revocation, which is called a call-back. it was not possible at the time, because the treaties did not allow it, and we were waiting for the constitution. we are in a transitional situation, a 'transitional sub-scale', and that is why i am appealing here to the expiry clause to which mr radwan has referred. until then, it will be necessary to reach an agreement which harmonizes the two objectives: speed in the legislative procedure and respect for the powers of parliament, powers which, as in the case of any parliament, have been withdrawn with difficulty over time. finally, i would like to justify our misgivings by recalling a spanish politician, known for his skill and ability to cheat the rules, who said: 'you make the law, let me make the regulation'. that is the danger we are concerned about.

and financial contribution under the eec-comoros agreement. as the honourable members know, the community has a longstanding relation with the comoros in the fisheries area. the first fisheries agreement with the country dates back to 1988. although it is the smallest tuna agreement, it is of importance due to the strategic location of this fishery in the indian ocean as well as for the fishing possibilities obtained. the new protocol, which was initialled on 24 november 2004, covers a 6-year period from 1 january 2005 to 31 december 2010. the protocol grants fishing opportunities for 40 tuna seiners and 17 surface longliners and has a financial contribution of eur 390 000 per year. the agreement is one that is of mutual benefit to both parties and contains a number of new elements including the following. firstly, an exclusivity clause, which prohibits the existence of private licences or other private arrangements outside the scope of the agreement. secondly, a vms requirement to reinforce checks on vessels operating in comorian waters. thirdly, the social clause applicable to local seamen signed on by community vessels. fourthly, rules on taking on board observers and, fifthly, adjustment of the share-out of the cost of the agreement between the community and shipowners from a ratio of eur 75/25 per tonne to eur 65/35 per tonne, which is already applied in other tuna agreements in the pacific. this increase of the shipowners' share of the cost will gradually be applied to all tuna agreements in the community as was called for in the reform of the common fisheries policy. i believe that these new elements introduced in dialogue with the comoros authorities and according to the principles set out in the new fisheries partnership agreements will ensure that the comoros agreement contributes to responsible and sustainable fisheries in the comoros. this work includes the establishment of annual and multi-annual objectives, the distribution of the part of the financial compensation – 60%, the aims to be attained and criteria and procedures in order to allow for an evaluation of the yearly results obtained in accordance with article 7 of the protocol. let me now turn to the amendments. on amendment 1, the commission is of the opinion that this is not necessary, given that the procedure for the adoption of the new framework agreement – parliament. therefore, the commission considers that these amendments are not necessary. on amendment 4, may i recall the basic community provisions concerning the mandate of the commission to mr president, commissioner, i would first of all like to congratulate mr sterckx, mr jarzembowski, mr savary and mr zīle on their reports on the liberalization of rail transport networks and services in the european union, quality of service, the qualifications of drivers and the rights and obligations of passengers. for our part, and with regard to the development of the community's railways, we fully agree to support the opening up of transport services in general and rail passenger transport in particular to private competition, but we do so on the basis that the road infrastructure will be in the hands of independent managers, so that all potential users of the networks can have equal access to them. we therefore call for the opening of international rail passenger services to be brought forward to 2008 and accept that individual member states may postpone the liberalisation of the rest of national, regional and local passenger services until 2012. we believe that this opening should be done in an orderly manner and without jeopardizing the existence and economic viability of pre-existing public services. we do not want to harm citizens or the urban, metropolitan or regional transport services which currently exist under the aegis of public institutions. we have argued that, if the relevant objective economic analyses carried out by the regulatory bodies of each member state so advise, they may limit the right of access of an international service to a particular infrastructure on a regional section or restrict the right to pick up and drop off passengers at stations on that section. we will also defend reciprocity of treatment, so that those states which open up to private rail services in advance may temporarily restrict this right to companies in which railway groups based in other states do not have similar conditions for free access to railway infrastructure. in other words, if a state does not open up its networks to competition, its companies will not be able to operate in other open-up states. finally, we believe that private railway service contracts should be for a period of five years, which can be up to ten years if they use specialised infrastructure and require significant investment. a longer period could only be allowed in very specific cases of large-scale and long-term investments, requiring the inclusion of a multiannual amortisation plan covering the periodicity, investments, divestments, amortisations and the way to deal with such a large initial economic outlay. we believe that the opening up and liberalization of passenger services with all the guarantees of quality, safety and qualification of drivers, as well as with adequate regulation of passenger rights, will provide the citizens of the union with the necessary mobility for the progress and sustainable development we are pursuing as a future objective.
mr president, commissioner, i come from a country and a region which, because of its history and geography, is particularly sensitive to the need to achieve optimum diversification and rebalancing between the different modes of transport, with particular regard to rail. the madrid-paris talgo and the high-speed lines, which have been extremely well received by spanish citizens, bear witness to this love and openness to the modernisation of the railways. but let us not forget what it has cost us, and what it still costs us, to get out of the isolation of the single track, of the different track width, to overcome our complex and difficult topography and to face a future of central permeability of the pyrenees, which is increasingly urgent to reduce congestion at its extremes, crucially in the transport of goods. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we know - and the chairman of our committee, mr costa, has said it with authority - that the competitiveness of the railways lies not only in other rebalancing measures but, to a large extent, in the infrastructures, in the interoperability of the systems and in the specialized staff; in short, in investments and support. that is why we are lending our support to the transeuropean networks. i also do not think it is serious to fall into a kind of yo-yo regime: first we liberalize and deregulate and then we intervene again. and that is what has happened with the commission's proposal for quality standards in the transport of goods. we must recognize the courage and worth of mr zīle, who has worked as best he could under the circumstances which make this proposal a good candidate for the exercise of better regulation, which president barroso and commissioner verheugen are so secretive about. as an alternative rapporteur, i must admit that i was completely astonished to learn that neither customers nor companies wanted this type of legislation. perhaps we should, commissioner - and i think you are creative enough in that sense - try to invent other instruments which are really useful in making rail freight transport more attractive, not only to the litigators but especially to the users. no, you cannot legislate on freight rail as you would on other products, like socks. as regards the sterckx and savary reports, i would warmly welcome their timeliness and urgency and the excellent signal to the public. on the one hand we are looking for good european professionals who are capable of driving trains throughout the union, and on the other hand we want to establish, clearly and courageously, the rights and duties of travellers, with particular attention to travellers with mobility problems, a situation which will one day affect us all. finally, as regards mr jarzembowski's report, which is always so impulsive and sure of its objectives, and which all too often coincides with those of europe, i must say that it does not seem realistic to me to want to overrun the commission's proposal, and to mix it up with an interinstitutional battle which, by striving for the best, can jeopardise a good achievement. we would have preferred to have accompanied the commission's realistic and nuanced proposal with a comfortable majority that would have sent a clear signal to all the partners. he has preferred to provoke, by his exaggerated proposal, a contrary reaction from a significant part of this house. in any case, i still believe that the commission's proposal for opening up is the most pragmatic and realistic, provided that it is part of a global framework for building a european transport area, in which rail competes on equal terms with other means of transport. and that's achieved through modernization and investment.

mr president, commissioner, mr president-in-office of the council, i would first of all like to congratulate the energy commissioner on his swift reaction to the extreme and recent volatility of oil prices through this plan, the main lines of which he has set out to us today and with whose conceptual basis and concrete measures i fully agree. the price of crude oil has risen by 50% in the last year and this increase is reflected in a significant deterioration in the competitiveness of our economy. thus, many governments are under strong pressure to reduce oil taxes on certain transportation sectors. but as the commissioner has rightly said, that is not the solution. in addition to creating market distortions and problems with state aid rules, it opens the door to possible increases in consumption and future increases in the price of the barrel. we must adopt the measures that the commissioner indicated in the plan: a strong push towards the use of renewable energy and improved efficiency, an increase in refining capacity, the fight against speculative movements, consideration of nuclear energy as an indispensable option in the security and supply strategy and the promotion of the use of biofuels. we are debating a crisis today, but we must draw from it enough strength to design our future intelligently. i would not like to end without asking the council, whose representative is at this moment contemplating a role with great interest, to give very serious thought to the effects of an intolerable reduction in the funds devoted to research and technological innovation in the seventh framework programme in circumstances such as those we are now experiencing.

president-in-office of the council. mr president, two weeks ago at the 2005 world summit, our heads of state and government met to decide how the international community, through the united nations, should tackle the world's most pressing problems: the interrelated challenges of development, security and human rights. the decisions they took after two years of debate and consultation, now enshrined in the so-called outcome document, set the united nations agenda for the years ahead. the challenges to the world's security and prosperity have been starkly and comprehensively set out by the united nations secretary-general kofi annan's high-level panel on threats, challenges and change, by professor jeffrey sachs, head of the united nations millennium project, and by kofi annan himself in his in larger freedom report. all concluded that until we took urgent action to address poverty, disease, environmental degradation and social injustice, we would not be able to prevent or resolve conflict. we would not be able to build peace, and without peace and security, development cannot take hold. neither is possible without respect for human rights. these, as all the members of this parliament will know, are not new concepts. indeed the united nations was created 60 years ago to build peace and security throughout the world. but the world is very different 60 years on. through technology and communication, countries are more closely bound together than ever before. that means too that the impact of conflicts and disasters is increasingly global in its reach. we all, therefore, have an overriding interest in working together to secure peace and build prosperity. some, i know, were disappointed and frustrated by the results of the world summit. many felt that the commitments made did not go far enough. reaching a consensus amongst 191 nations was never going to be easy. we know that only too well from our own experience with 25. so we should take heart from the fact that the far-reaching commitments made by g8 leaders in july to increase aid, to reduce debt and to expand trade have essentially been safeguarded at the united nations summit. as kofi annan, the secretary-general said, and i quote directly, 'taken as a whole, the [un summit] document is still a remarkable expression of world unity on a wide range of issues'. our task now is to ensure that the agreements are implemented. as my prime minister, tony blair, said in new york, if we start implementing with urgency the agreements on doubling aid, on opening up trade and establishing fair-trade rules, on debt relief, on hiv/aids and malaria and on conflict prevention and stopping genocide, we would have more democracy, less oppression, more freedom, less terrorism, more growth, less poverty. i am proud that the european union was at the forefront of efforts to reach consensus on all of the issues under debate. we had many priorities for the summit across the four so-called clusters of development, peace and collective security, human rights and the rule of law, and strengthening the united nations. i believe that the conclusions reached at the summit set us out on the right path towards improvements in all of these areas, as long as the momentum is sustained and as long as we act now. the interest and commitment shown by members of this parliament towards improvements in these areas is truly admirable and was demonstrated in the expertise of the european parliament delegation who attended the summit, led by co-chairmen nirj deva and michel rocard. the summit secured firm and unambiguous commitments from both donor and developing countries on what is needed to reach the millennium development goals. it strengthened the partnership between developed and developing countries set out at monterey and consolidated all the achievements of this year so far. it broadened the consensus around the commitments established back in july at the gleneagles summit to 191 countries, in particular the need to accelerate progress towards the millennium goals in africa and to make international progress once again on climate change. it also agreed, as set out clearly in the outcome document, that development must be sustainable and take account of its impact on the global environment. under the uk's presidency, the european council has continued to press for more international action to increase development aid in the fight against poverty and deprivation. we, the european union, are already easily the world's largest aid donor: 80% of the extra usd 5 billion of aid pledged at the g8 summit in gleneagles will come from europe. we have also made a historic commitment to double aid to africa by 2010. we have spearheaded the important agreements reached this year to reduce debt and launch global immunisation programmes against illnesses and diseases in the poorest countries. there has of course been criticism that not enough progress was made on trade, back at that summit in july. but it will ultimately be through the doha development round that the international community can and must deliver real gains for poor countries by abolishing export subsidies and reducing all barriers to trade, including trade-distorting domestic support. we will work as hard as we can to ensure that political leaders focus on getting results at the wto ministerial meeting in hong kong in december and indeed focus on these issues before the december hong kong ministerial meeting. as my prime minister has said, if we end up with a failure in december, that will echo right round the world. to make progress on development we need peace and security. as kofi annan set out in his document, in larger freedom: 'we will not enjoy development without security, we will not enjoy security without development, and we will not enjoy either without respect for human rights.' the summit agreed to establish a new peace-building commission, which will bring together united nations member states, un agencies and the international financial institutions to close a critical gap in the un's ability to help countries emerging from conflict to make that vital transition to long-term stability and avoid relapsing into war. you know, as members of this parliament, that the european union is committed to meeting the summit deadline of establishing the commission by the end of this year. more could have been said in the summit document regarding terrorism. the strong condemnation of terrorism 'in all its forms and manifestations' was certainly a welcome political statement. but we must now work on fulfilling our pledge to conclude the comprehensive convention on terrorism by september 2006. that will mean agreeing on a legal definition of terrorist acts, something that all of our governments have a real interest in securing. despite the summit's failure to reach agreement on measures for non-proliferation and disarmament, i can assure parliament that we will continue to work to move forward the agenda on these important issues. ensuring respect for human rights lies at the very heart of the united nations mission. we are fully supportive, therefore, of the creation of a new human rights council to replace the maligned commission on human rights. we must urgently agree on its size, its mandate and composition so that it can begin its work and ensure that human rights are once again at the core of all un activity. perhaps the decision of greatest significance to emerge from that summit was the agreement on 'the responsibility to protect' – a political commitment that the international community has a duty to act when states cannot or will not protect their populations from the worst atrocities: genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. it is an important recognition that in today's world we cannot fail to act when vulnerable populations face these terrible atrocities. we must also work to strengthen the united nations secretariat, to make it a more effective and efficient body. we should begin by encouraging kofi annan to use the executive powers he already holds to effect change from within the organisation. but we, as member states, also have a key responsibility to ensure that the united nations is structured and equipped to meet today's and tomorrow's challenges. the european council welcomed the commitments to reform the main un bodies, including the general assembly, the economic and social council and the security council. if the un is to be effective it has to work collectively with all of its members. that means winning their support. un organisations must therefore be representative, open and efficient. we will continue to work on improving the effectiveness of the general assembly and ecosoc in particular. we particularly welcome the mandate given to the secretary-general to consider longer-term reform of the un's development, humanitarian assistance and environment organisations so that their work is better managed and better coordinated. to be effective the united nations must have the resources that it needs, but it cannot afford to waste funds on inefficiency and duplication of effort. the european union fully supports the long-standing principle of budgetary discipline. we are therefore seeking to adopt a budget for the next financial year that will enable the secretary-general and the united nations to deliver what its members ask and expect, including under the new mandates agreed at the summit in new york. the key to the success of that 2005 millennium review summit and the un's reform programme in general is, of course, implementation. some of the proposals will be explored in the committee of the general assembly, in session from now until the end of this year. others will be taken forward independently. the european union will again be at the forefront of this process. we, as united nations member states, are responsible now for turning words into action. particular. torpedoing them was to appoint bolton as the us representative to the united nations and to submit 750 amendments to the draft final text, long worked, negotiated and agreed by the international community, to empty it of any content. by the way, it is sarcastic that when the americans finally have to make a few concessions, it is all parabians and expressions of gratitude that they have not carried their latest remake of apocalypse now to the last consequences. secondly, i acknowledge that the european union's role at the summit has been relatively dignified and positive. it has also been reasonably effective when its member states have acted in a coordinated and coincident manner. thirdly, i would like to stress that the best example of this is what has undoubtedly been the most valid aspect of the new york summit: with regard to the millennium development goals, no progress has been made, despite the efforts of some to back down. the european union acted firmly and at least the commitments and timetable agreed five years ago were kept. fourthly, the failure of the essential reform of the united nations is regrettable, a point which is just as illustrative as the previous one, but in a negative way. here our member states came up with different approaches and the union was unable to take a stand or exert any influence, and thus became partly responsible for this failure. fifthly, we are pleased that the summit has supported the strategy of the alliance of civilizations, which was taken up by kofi annan, by adopting a european initiative such as that proposed by the prime ministers of spain and turkey. and sixthly, we are glad that europe has helped to keep the united nations afloat, saving it from the shipwreck that some had prepared. but it is not enough to keep the united nations afloat; it is essential to relaunch the organization once and for all. the european union's efforts must be directed towards this objective, but to do so, our union will need to be more than just floating. i would like to end with a quote from an african politician: 'this world is not exciting and even disgusting at times, but it is frightening to think what it would be like if europe were not acting as a factor of rationality, balance, a certain coherence and, at times, solidarity.'
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i took as a basis the commission communication on a strategic partnership between the european union and india of june 2004 and the excellent and well-documented response of the government of india in its strategy paper of august 2004. i have taken note of the various events which have since taken place in india and europe and, of course, the fifth bilateral summit in the hague last november, the cornerstone which officially launched the strategic partnership and which grants india the status of a privileged partner, similar to that accorded to other important countries. finally, i followed up as much as possible the preparations and meetings leading up to the 6th bilateral summit in new delhi on 7 september this year, which gave the green light to the expected joint action plan for the strategic partnership. i think that in certain areas of the report i go further than the commission and the council and there may be a dissonance between my position and theirs at times, but it is more by omission than by concrete action on their part. however, i believe that if my report is adopted in the plenary tomorrow, it will be fair to say that the three institutions of the union mentioned - parliament, the commission and the council - fully share the desire to promote, strengthen and enrich, for the mutual benefit, the relationship with the largest democracy on the planet. we cannot forget that we are talking about a country, india, which is effectively the largest democracy on the planet. it is also worth recalling, and i do so in the text, that some of the objectives set out in the council communication and the recent joint action plan require specific funding, which, if we are to be serious, must not be avoided. otherwise, political dialogue is of little use. in this chapter i propose that parliament express its support for the priority given to political dialogue in the strategic partnership, while stressing that the achievement of the millennium development goals and the effective fight against poverty must remain the central elements of the union's strategic engagement with india. the latter is itself a political act, because without political will to approve the appropriate financial resources, no development objectives can be achieved. india is about to complete a great developmental task that has already been undertaken. i am starting from the fact that it and the union share the view that trade, investment and free competition are key factors in development, but also that, for development to be harmonious and equitable, fundamental social requirements that strengthen economic and social cohesion, the environment and consumer rights must be taken into account. i therefore ask new delhi to take a very close look at these factors. the day before yesterday, i would like to comment to you. an editorial in an influential british newspaper said that the honeymoon between the government of india and the private financial sector was over and accused the government of india of allowing the leftist allies - and i quote - in the government coalition to block the promised reforms. despite this, the newspaper acknowledges that the indian economy is booming, growth may exceed 7 percent this year, business profits are increasing, the it sector is strengthening, the stock market is buoyant and capital continues to enter in huge proportions. however, the newspaper said, the indian government cannot take credit for any of these achievements, which it said were due to "nothing less than good luck, past reforms or the efforts of the private sector". frankly, i find the influential newspaper whimsical. i was unaware that good luck was an active determining factor in the economy. the fact is - and i end with this - that india is moving forward, as is its strategic relationship with the union. my five-minute speech is all i can do. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i would just like to remind the government and the people of india of the following: the death penalty must be abolished, the un convention against torture must be ratified, india must join the international criminal court and it would be a good idea for india to join the treaty on the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons, as, of course, pakistan and israel have done.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, commissioner, first of all i would like to thank mr vatanen for the enormous amount of work and dedication he has put into this report, and i would also like to express, once again, my frustration at the potential and the high expectations which mr vatanen's report has aroused in me. he, in his report, and you can see, does not make a mistake in the diagnosis, he even acknowledges it, emphasizes it and presents it in a way as dramatic as the figures are. the problem is therefore not expressed in its full magnitude. it also points out that there is a great discrepancy between the safety rates of the various member states, but i believe that this discrepancy does not exist in the diagnoses and also in the most useful instrument: legislation, setting limits and deterrent coercion. the great frustration is to see that what we are proposing today for the european union, for a union in which, as the commissioner has rightly said, citizens expect a strong signal and added value, precisely in what each member state has wisely been imposing, there are great differences and sometimes enormous deficiencies, as regards legislation on speed limits, blood alcohol limits and the use of seat belts. in this sense, we believe that the time has come to take this step and the socialist group has tabled an amendment in which we ask the commission, after evaluating the recommendation, specifically in the case of blood alcohol limits, to also offer us the necessary legislative measures applicable to these three fundamental aspects, which all european citizens and all member states recognize. but they also recognize that there are problems. and in those coordination problems is where the greatest weakness lies. we therefore ask the commission to be understanding and to accept our amendment.
mr president, commissioner, it is a fact that the total opening up of textile trade on 1 january has led to an avalanche of chinese products. the commission proposed limiting these imports and, as a result, the june agreement was reached. but, taking advantage of the time needed to finalize this agreement, some european importers accumulated a large amount of goods. the new agreement of 5 september 2005 is a contribution to the solution of the problem, which, at the point it had reached, did not benefit anyone. but that agreement cannot be described as satisfactory, because it has given an image of lack of rigor. there are those who proclaim, right here, right now, that the textile industry should have adapted faster because it knew what was going to happen 10 years ago. but let me predict that if we do not deal with these challenges in an orderly way, today we will be talking about textiles, but tomorrow we will be clamoring for cars or for products of information and communication technologies. the choice is not between free trade and protectionism, but between growing trade, but fair, transparent and with social and environmental minimum standards. in conclusion, i would like to draw your attention to a fact that is causing alarm in the sector. alongside the large known distribution chains producing in china with stable prices, unknown firms have appeared declaring abnormally low prices, which do not even cover the cost of the raw material of the product. for example, the prices of trousers entering the union can range from eur 6 to eur 0,43, both of which are trousers produced in china. these practices account for about 40% of imports from china in my country. i suspect, commissioner, that we are dealing with a case of fraud, in which the value declared at customs is being used to reduce the importer's tax bill, both in relation to the community tariff and to vat. i would therefore like to know what decisions the commission is going to take in this respect.
on behalf of the green group, mr president, this is certainly a fundamental problem. on the one hand, the different conditions of production and therefore of prices explain the existence of international trade, but on the other hand, a completely free trade between economies operating with very different labour costs, as is the case of china and the european union, contains several elements that distort the rules governing competition. what should we say to that? firstly, as consumers of chinese products, we in the european union have a greater responsibility, since we are china's largest trading partner, even ahead of the united states. secondly, china's development and opening up to the world is good news and should be celebrated. but thirdly, that such opening must be done within a framework of respect for minimum and common standards, which guarantee a fair and fair game in trade relations, and that the benefits of such opening and exchange benefit the weakest parts of the production system, that is, workers, while also ensuring respect for international environmental standards. the key is therefore not to promote free trade but to promote fair trade. this means setting new rules for business between countries, including quotas based not on price but on production conditions, establishing traceability rules to ensure compliance and, above all, regulating the practice of large, increasingly mobile multinational companies, which often follow the logic of the race to the bottom, seeking to produce in places that pose fewer social, labour and environmental demands.

mr president, the ceasefire declared by the maoists in nepal is indeed now a new window of opportunity which, if properly used, can help to resolve the armed conflict in that country. to do this, as recommended by the international crisis group, requires a change in the international community's current approach, especially with regard to the monarchy. throughout the seven months since the royal coup, violence has increased markedly, as have kidnappings, torture, unjustified arrests, disappearances, etc., committed by both government forces and maoists. the government, for its part, has entered a spiral of corruption and inefficiency. and not only that: it cannot properly manage the conflict and with regard to the general affairs of government and state it is also failing. the persecution of leaders of democratic parties, the arrest of journalists during pro-democracy demonstrations and the harassment of trade union groups have only made the situation worse. in this context and in the face of the maoist declaration of ceasefire, as well as the first steps taken by the seven-party alliance to push for a political process to resolve the armed conflict, king gyanendra should respond with a government ceasefire and should initiate constructive talks with the political groups and the maoists, with the ultimate aim of restoring democracy in nepal. the government should also release political prisoners still in prison and ensure respect for human rights and freedom of expression, especially by the nepalese security and military forces. in the meantime, the council and the member states must ensure that the suspension of military aid is maintained, in strict compliance with the code of conduct on arms exports. finally, we must demand that the nepalese government re-establish the office for aiding tibetan refugees in kathmandu, in cooperation with the unhcr, as is customary.
member of the commission. mr president, seven months have passed since the royal takeover in nepal, but the political and human rights situation in the country has not improved. on the contrary, the human rights situation remains critical and it is estimated that the conflict-related death toll has risen considerably since 1 february. it can also be observed that a number of measures introduced under royal rule are contrary to the guarantees of freedom of expression and association in the 1990 constitution, pointing towards a return to the pre-1990 panchayat system of governance. as was to be expected, the royal nepalese army has failed to control the insurgent threat and incurred heavy losses, most notably on 7 august when the maoists overran an army base in kalikot. the maoists, on the other hand, do not appear to have been weakened since february, although they lack wide popular support. nevertheless, there are some positive developments as well: a memorandum of understanding was agreed at the un commission of human rights in april this year to launch a human rights monitoring mission and to set up four regional offices of the office of the high commissioner for human rights in the country. the european commission is planning to support the mission with a contribution of eur 5 million, which is 30% of the total mission budget, and the first results are encouraging. it becomes increasingly apparent that the 1 february coup has unleashed many genies from the bottle: demands for republicanism and total democracy are now permeating nepalese society from all sides and it remains to be seen whether the much advocated 'twin pillars' of constitutional monarchy and multi-party democracy are the only viable option for nepal's future. the forthcoming eu troika visit to nepal, planned from 4 to 6 october, will assess the developments since the last visit in december 2004 and aim to offer public support for the moderate voices in the democratic middle ground working towards the eu's goal of a sustainable peace based on the principles of civilian, accountable and democratic government. working closely with the european union member states and especially the successive european union council presidencies, the commission remains committed to pursuing all efforts, whether they are diplomatic, political, or developmental, that might facilitate the peace process and the return to democracy in nepal.

member of the commission. mr president, the commission attaches great importance to the preservation of the multi-ethnic character of vojvodina. the commission has the authority to investigate thoroughly any ethnic incident and effectively promote good inter-ethnic relations. we appreciate that the authorities have condemned the ethnic incidents that have occurred and we concede that these incidents do not amount to any form of gross violation, nor are they backed by the belgrade authorities. nevertheless, we are convinced that the authorities have often been late and negligent in investigating reported incidents. the fact that the perpetrators of violent acts and harassment are neither identified nor brought to justice creates a climate of impunity, which unfortunately can foster further incidents and increase the feeling of frustration and insecurity among the minorities. in this respect, the law enforcement agencies and the judiciary are often failing in their duties. let me stress that this is a sign of a much wider problem. there is an urgent need in serbia to reform the police, to make it professional and accountable, and to reform the judiciary, which needs to become efficient and truly independent from undue political pressure. these reforms are key for the protection of the rights, not just of minorities, but of all citizens. in line with the recommendations issued by the european parliament after the fact-finding mission of last january, we have urged the authorities to take concrete measures in the field of police and judicial reform. this includes the need for more adequate representation of the minority communities in these institutions. nobody needs a police or judiciary based on ethnicity, but it is certainly true that a better and more qualified presence of personnel coming from the minority communities could improve their functioning, by facilitating communication with citizens in their mother tongue. it would also increase the trust placed by citizens in the state. if we look at the incidents that have been reported, very often they involve youngsters. this shows that there is an urgent need for the authorities to take measures in the field of education, as recommended by the european parliament. schools can play a key role in preserving the cultural richness of a region like vojvodina and in helping young people take full advantage of that richness, rather than withdrawing into nationalist isolation. we know that often the youngsters involved in or supporting these incidents are the children of people displaced because of the wars of the last decade. the influx of displaced persons has sometimes changed the ethnic composition of the regions. there is no simple solution to this issue and we should seek to prevent people who belong to the serbian community but are often themselves in a very precarious situation, including from a socio-economic point of view, from turning their frustration into violence. the authorities still have much to do. it is also important for cooperation between serbia and montenegro and its neighbouring countries to be intensified in the context of their bilateral agreements. this is particularly true of the agreement between serbia and montenegro and hungary. we appreciate the initiative of holding a european parliament hearing on the situation of the minorities in vojvodina on 13 october. this will offer an excellent opportunity to discuss the issue directly with both the authorities and the representatives of the minority communities. for its part, the commission is continuing to monitor respect for the rights of the various ethnic communities in vojvodina, as well as in the rest of serbia and montenegro. in the feasibility report issued last april the commission concluded that serbia and montenegro were adequately meeting the criteria – including the political ones – for the opening of stabilisation and association agreement negotiations. at the same time, the commission drew the authorities' attention to a number of issues, including respect for human and minority rights. respect for these rights is indeed an integral part of the political criteria for the stabilisation and association process and it is an essential element of the stabilisation and association agreement. the way a country treats ethnic minorities and the quality of the relationship among them are important indicators of democratic maturity. a country aspiring to come closer to the european union needs to show such maturity. during the stabilisation and association negotiations process, the commission will continue to monitor respect for human and minority rights, as well as the other requirements related to the stabilisation and association agreement. in this regard, let me stress that we would be failing in our duty if we looked at the situation of only one minority in one region of serbia, however important it may be. we need to pay due attention to all minorities and in particular the most vulnerable ones, such as the roma. the progress report on serbia and montenegro due to be published next month by the commission will also review respect for human and minority rights. at the same time, the commission will continue to support vojvodina with financial assistance, although there is no specific programme targeting the province as such. vojvodina has benefited as much as the rest of serbia from eu assistance. let me mention just a few examples. a contribution of eur 40 million was made to the reconstruction of the sloboda bridge, which will be opened in october. the support given to small and medium-sized enterprises amounts to eur 8 million worth of credit. in addition, the two neighbourhood programmes with hungary and romania were launched in january 2005. i am confident that strengthening the relations between the eu and serbia and montenegro, through the conclusion of the stability and association agreement, will help consolidate democracy and the rule of law, which will also be to the benefit of the ethnic minorities. thank you for your attention.
