member of the commission. ladies and gentlemen, let me first of all thank your assembly and in particular the committee on women's rights and gender equality for the preparation of this report. poverty and social exclusion, of which women are victims, are extremely important issues. as your report really shows, the feminization of poverty is a persistent trend in european societies. women make up the majority of the unemployed and longterm unemployed and are far more likely than men to work part-time. it is clear that women continue to face violence in both the public and private spheres. in addition, some 500 000 women are trafficked for sexual exploitation in europe each year. these two phenomena are most often the result of the poverty in which these women are forced to live. your report reaffirms that women's employment remains the key to their economic independence and one of the main factors in removing the trappings of poverty and social exclusion. employment has a direct impact on the status of women in society as a whole. european employment actions are a fundamental mechanism for achieving equality between women and men. an integrated approach is important to increase the employment and vocational integration capacity of women. this approach must focus on the needs of women and identify the interests of certain groups of women who are most at risk of social exclusion. examples include single mothers, migrant women and women from ethnic minorities, disabled women and elderly women. between 1997 and 2004, female employment rose from 50.6% to 55.7%, mainly due to the economic growth europe experienced during this period, although not too high. employment is thus increasing, but marked inequalities and numerous forms of gender discrimination in employment still persist. in general, it is women who face unemployment more often. they also largely represent jobs that are less well-paid, less stable and associated with less social protection. at the same time, they continue to bear the bulk of the responsibility for the care of children and other dependants. the objectives set out in the context of the open method of coordination to combat social exclusion underline the importance of taking gender equality into account when developing the implementation and monitoring of national action plans on social inclusion by member states. the national action plans, the key tools of the european method, are evaluated every two years. the mainstreaming of gender equality in all areas of gender mainstreaming is a general obligation that should, in theory, be applied to all national measures linked to the achievement of the objectives. for convenience, the common indicators of poverty and exclusion are systematically presented separately for men and women. in addition, the visibility of the social inclusion process and the involvement of stakeholders on the ground is ensured through financial support under the community action programme against exclusion. in conclusion, i would like to highlight three priorities for the future. first, gender equality must be made the primary objective of the social protection system by strengthening the social rights of atypical workers. secondly, we need to strengthen policies to increase quality childcare and care for dependants of all ages so that men and women have real choice in reconciling work and family life. finally, the gender dimension in policies and measures to combat poverty and social exclusion needs to be strengthened in order to prevent the feminization of poverty. ladies and gentlemen, i would like to draw your attention to one area that shows how much we all care and how little can sometimes be achieved by legislation alone. the fact that there consistent approach is the duty of the day.

member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank the european parliament, its committee on the environment and in particular the rapporteur, mr blokland, for the work they have done on this report at second reading. one of the main objectives of the proposed new regulation on shipments of waste is to ensure that the european union is aligned with the international requirements for shipments of waste, both at oecd and un level, i.e. the basel convention. the other main objective is to address the problems arising in the implementation, administrative management and enforcement of the existing regulation. the new regulation therefore also seeks to contribute to greater clarity and better legislation on shipments of waste. the council held discussions on this subject during the italian and irish presidencies. at first reading, the commission amended its proposal and adopted in full, in part or in principle 43 of the 103 amendments proposed by parliament. the council's common position incorporated 41 of parliament's amendments. the common position is an important step forward in improving the clarity of the regulation and its provisions, always in line with the objectives pursued. i would like to stress that our aim is to see this matter dealt with as quickly as possible. we need this new regulation to improve the clarity and application of the rules governing shipments of waste and to comply with the european union's international commitments. the commission did not, however, accept the common position on three specific issues, which it explained in a statement, by means of a communication to the european parliament, on 1 july 2005. these are the legal basis of the regulation, the objections of the member states to the shipment of waste destined for recovery and a provision to exclude animal by-products from the scope of the regulation. the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection has voted in favour of 90 amendments to the common position. the commission considers 74 of them to be fully or in principle acceptable, but cannot accept 16 of the amendments. the preservation of the internal market is a matter of fundamental importance to the commission. today, waste for recovery is freely moved between member states, provided that strict environmental protection rules and the principle of proportionality are respected. a thriving european recycling market helps to reduce the environmental impact of the use of natural resources. the free movement of waste for recovery is already established by the existing regulation on shipments of waste, the provisions of the treaty of the european communities on the free movement of goods, and the case law of the european court of justice. the changes proposed by the council common position would create serious obstacles to the internal recycling market and are not acceptable to the commission. the proposed amendment no 35 could prevent possible problems in the internal market. it provides for maximum time limits for objections to shipments of waste for recovery under national standards. such objections may be raised only until the date of entry into force of specific community legislation,and at the latest 4 years after the entry into force of this regulation. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be able to take a decision on the application of the directive on the recycling of waste.

mr president, commissioner, flu pandemics have been documented in europe for over a century and it is known that the three subtypes of the a virus we have had are of avian origin: h1 in 1918, h2 in 1957 and h3 in 1968. they all had a bird origin and they all mutated. since 1997, it has been known that the h5 subtype is highly virulent, capable of transmitting to humans and producing a highly deadly influenza, but that transmission, until now, is only by contact with sick birds or their droppings. the h5 virus has spread between wild and domestic birds, and migratory birds are carrying it everywhere. in addition, it has been transmitted to mammals such as pigs and cats. there is therefore a broad consensus among experts and health agencies that the a h5 virus could adapt to human transmission and produce a new pandemic. i believe that the commission, within its powers, has been acting responsibly and transparently so far. their skills may need to be increased if a pandemic or emergency period comes. i would like to stress the importance of setting relevant standards for the member states to follow, and coordinating and monitoring their compliance, and of calling on the media to report accurately but without creating unnecessary social alarm. i believe that we need to strengthen the wildlife surveillance network, which is intimately linked to most emerging diseases. finally, i believe that the resources for r & d within the european union must be increased to provide a scientific and medical response in the shortest possible time, should the need arise.
mr president of the republic of chile, mr president of the chilean congress and senate, ladies and gentlemen, we have the privilege today of welcoming the president of the republic of chile, mr ricardo lagos escobar, who is also accompanied by the presidents of the two chambers of the chilean parliament. mr ricardo lagos is a person of exceptional importance in the political landscape of latin america. mr president, allow me to welcome you warmly on behalf of the european parliament. when ricardo lagos was 45 years old, he left a quiet and comfortable life at the united nations to rent a small office in santiago, chile, and start working for democracy in his country, then in full military dictatorship. he worked, fought and traveled throughout chile; he was arrested, but returned to the struggle to end the regime of general pinochet. his work has been persevering in repealing the authoritarian enclaves of a constitution signed by a dictator, and a month ago he managed to carry out the reform of that constitution, which is now signed by a democratic president. in the collective memory of chileans and of all democrats in the world, i think there is a fond memory of the image of ricardo lagos on a television programme, who made history, looking at the camera with his finger raised, confronting pinochet and opening the way for millions of chileans to vote "no" in the 1988 referendum, with which pinochet wanted to perpetuate himself in power. i think that's the most symbolic image of the transition to democratic openness in chile. (applause) because of his faith in chile and in democracy, he supported a christian democrat, patricio aylwin, as president of chile, and in that government he was minister of education and he tackled a profound reform of education in his country. then he met another christian democrat, president frei, who had been his opponent in the presidential elections, the minister for public works. he is a good example of cooperation between christian democrats and socialists at a time when the country needed it to move towards democracy. that was when i had the opportunity to meet him: he, minister of public works in his country, and i, in mine. from your hand, my dear friend, i began to know your wonderful country, from the volcanic deserts in the north to the alpine landscapes in the south, to the southernmost. and finally, in march 2000, he was elected president of the republic of chile, a country that, as early as 1812, at the dawn of its independence, drafted its provisional constitutional regulation, which read as follows: "every free inhabitant of chile is equal in rights (...). the foreigner ceases to be a foreigner if he is useful; and every wretch who seeks refuge in our soil will be the object of our hospitality and help. no one will be prevented from entering the country, nor will they be allowed to leave when they wish. apply these words to ceuta, melilla or lampedusa, and you will see the raging news that is happening in europe today. (applause) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, chile, in the aymara language, means 'the place where the world ends' and, indeed, at the border of the bio-bio river the world ended, because there the spanish conquest was stopped in the face of fierce araucanian resistance. but today chile is a fully integrated country in the world, open, dynamic and democratic, which has signed with the european union the most comprehensive association agreement that the union has signed with any other country that does not aspire to be a member of the union. since then, chilean exports to the union have increased by 35% and our overall trade has almost tripled. that shows the mutual benefit that our partnership brings. i would like to welcome you, mr president, and acknowledge that it is a privilege for this parliament that you have wanted to come here when you are about to end your presidency, a presidency which you leave with an approval rating of over 65%, which is surprisingly positive, not only in latin america but also in europe. that is why, mr president, believe me, we are all very pleased to hear from you the lessons we can learn from the great chilean experience towards democracy. president of the republic of chile. i thank you very much, mr president, for your kind introduction, ladies and gentlemen, members of this parliament, friends: 15 years ago i came before you to talk to your heads of staff as one of the leaders of the opposition to the dictatorship in chile. today i stand before you as president of the republic of a democratic country, after 15 years of successful exercise of a broad political and social coalition in government. chile has changed a lot since those dark years. we have managed to recover our civic life and our democratic institutions. we have doubled the output and globalized our economy. at the same time, we reduced poverty by half, reformed education, health and justice, and, with public and private resources, we have embarked on the most ambitious infrastructure and housing plan: today, one in four homes in chile has been built in the last 15 years. and i think because we've made these changes at the same time, we now have a high level of social cohesion and our population supports our integration into the global society. we have always looked to the experience of europe. for more than half a century you have managed to combine democracy, a market economy and high social cohesion, compatible with macroeconomic balances and a welfare state or, better, a social safety net. we have a common cultural heritage and historical ties that bind us together. the support which this house has given to the democratic recovery in chile is something which chileans have a vivid memory of. in difficult times for our country, members of this parliament at the time travelled to chile, took part in our assemblies, supported our civil society and showed their solidarity with the democratic cause. we can only be grateful to remember these facts. and we ask you to value the significance of what has been achieved. europe's role was, is and always will be invaluable. history - our history - would be different this day with the valech report, on imprisonment and torture in those dark years. i do not know of any other country in the world which has dared to set up a commission to hear the statements of 35 000 people who were arrested and tortured, of whom 29 000 were recognised as victims by the commission. we have been able to recognize the moral conscience of our society. we have faced the task of bringing truth and justice to human rights violations. chile today enjoys, as president borrell said, a firm and robust democracy. the authoritarian constitution has been amended. the workers have regained their rights. chile today has unemployment insurance, labor reforms and a new, more effective labor justice system. the role of women is increasingly recognised; there is important and comprehensive legislation on family duties and rights. environmental protection is part of the collective imagination and has been embodied in important public policies that were recently analysed by the oecd. today, in chile, new generations, raised and trained in democracy, are pushing the boundaries and deploying their creativity in all areas. today, seven out of ten young people in higher education are the first generation in their families to go to university. that is the magnitude of the change we have introduced in chile: it is a more libertarian, more solidary, more progressive, more open to a world in which we want to leave our mark. that's right, we've reduced poverty from 40 to 18 percent, and destitution from 12.9 to 4 percent. we have a competitive economy, low corruption rates and satisfactory human development indicators. however, we are not satisfied; much remains to be done. we need to change the social provision to make it fairer and more equitable. we still have a chronic inequality in the distribution of income from work. the income gap between the richest 20 percent and the poorest 20 percent is, on average, 14 times. but if we introduce the elements of social policy, this difference is reduced to seven times. the virtuous balance must be struck between social protection and the conditions for maintaining competitiveness. and so we look at europe in a different way than you do. the european debate is sometimes our debate, 'i am aware of the moment in which i am speaking in this parliament and i do not want to go into subjects that are peculiar to your debate' but i would like to point out here today that although chile has often presented itself as a neoliberal model, nothing is further from the truth. we understand that the so-called washington consensus, which talks about liberalizing markets, privatising certain companies, deregulating and having balanced budgets, is something chile has done and at the right time. but what is not in the washington consensus is the need to have, with that growth, concrete public policies directed at the most disadvantaged sectors; concrete public policies to create a social safety net, without which no country is able to compete in the world. (applause) countries that are not able to have a minimum of social cohesion within their societies, in the long run, face an internal conflict within their society, which prevents outward competition. so what we've done is a tremendous effort to grow and we've grown. but this growth has been reflected in social policy, in education; we've done the most profound health reform, and let me tell you -- god, how hard is that? -- because health reform is dealing with a set of vested interests. i told the doctors friends we have in chile, "you, my friends, are all socialists in the morning, when you work in a public hospital, but you are all capitalists in the afternoon, when you serve your private clients". and when they threatened to strike, i said, "okay, but they're going to strike in the morning and in the afternoon". it's obvious, right? (applause) so, it's hard to do health care reform, because the only ones who are not organized are the patients in hospitals, and the only ones you have to speak up for are them. the reform therefore implies a tremendous shift in favour of primary health care. today, in chile, with respect to 25 pathologies - which will then be 56 pathologies, representing 80% of the medical interventions in hospitals - we can guarantee three things: a quality institution, a time limit for being cared for and, if the person has no resources, the resources are put by the fifteen million chileans. the process of reform was long, but it is part of social cohesion, which is essential. we understand your debate, on health, on the subject of forecasting; i want to point out that the average age in chile is very similar to the average age you have in europe, there are only a few months difference, and, therefore, having to deal with a social forecast of an aging population is very important for us. at the same time, we have been able to achieve a good macroeconomic situation and i would like to point out that chile fully meets the maastricht requirements. in other words, your debate is sometimes our debate too. and that's why we're following you closely, that's why we want to learn from what you've done as well. why not say it? europe is in many ways an important paradigm in the world today and sometimes you, immersed in its debate, do not realise that you are also an example of the kind of society that is being created in the world today. it is true, we know that to continue to grow equitably in the future and not be trapped in a scheme of exporting raw materials and low job creation and welfare, we have to make a strong investment in innovation, science and technology. we've quadrupled our efforts, but we're creating an innovation fund fund funded by a very small portion of the income that copper produces. copper is a non-renewable resource, which generates a lot of revenue for chile. that big windfall will be a fund for the future through science and technology. and in this respect, then, we have european cooperation. the agreement we have with europe is an agreement which also allows us access to the provisions you have in this area. we also want to perfect our integration into the world economy. we are convinced that countries progress when they take the whole planet as a possibility. we should not be frightened by globalization. in our case, globalisation has opened up new possibilities, even for small economies far removed from the major international centres. of course, no automatic mechanism is going to reduce the inequalities, instability and crises that globalization brings. but we need to have rules and institutions that are able to give a channel to the globalization process. if we are to achieve them, we must affirm the capacity of a global policy, which is emerging today, to give direction to society. i want to be frank here: we are concerned about globalisation taking giant strides, without the multilateral institutions which have to set the rules for the globalisation process moving as fast. (applause) and here we see europe, a crucial player in making the rules of trade fairer, in creating global public goods, in reorganizing international agencies and in macro-economic coordination among the world's major economic powers. who do i turn to when in south-southern chile the ozone layer is decreasing and the sun's rays are stronger as a result of gas emissions in the northern hemisphere? some people do not like the kyoto agreements; i have told the leaders of those countries that this is all right, but tell me, where am i going to complain about what is happening in the world? because what happens in my country is a problem outside my country. (applause) and here, i want to share with you something that seems central to us: for a country like chile, multilateralism ends up being local politics. that is why we believe in the united nations, of which we are a founding member. that is why we believe that the security council is the only body that has the legitimacy to use force in the name of humanity. (applause) so, at a time when our country was a member of the security council, we said no to an invasion of iraq if the decision was made outside the security council. member of the commission. it is very difficult to make a blanket statement; obviously we have a ban on driftnets with a very large span because of the negative effect they can have on the sustainability of fish and their impact on bycatch cetaceans. there we have a total ban on the use of driftnets. with driftnets that are much smaller in size and where there is no risk of cetacean by-catches, the commission’s position is more open. if, on the basis of scientific study, it can be concluded that driftnets do not create undue pressures on the sustainability of salmon or any other fish stocks and there is no risk of by-catches of cetaceans, then we take a more open approach. that is why, because of the reports and criticism in ireland, we have commissioned the study to see what the situation is and how the management of the stock is proceeding. if we see that there are undue pressures on sustainability then we will take the necessary remedial action. perhaps it is somewhat misleading to point the finger at one particular type of net. there could be other types of net that are not classified as driftnets but that, in particular circumstances, could have an even more negative impact on the sustainability of fisheries. therefore the task of the commission is to restore sustainable fisheries where they do not exist and where we are fishing sustainably – which is the exception, not the rule – to maintain sustainability.
member of the commission. it is the responsibility of the member states to ensure effective control, inspection and enforcement of the rules of the common fisheries policy, which include a prohibition on the use of driftnets targeting highly migratory species. it is, on the other hand, the responsibility of the commission to evaluate and monitor member states' compliance with this obligation. for a number of years, the commission has monitored member states closely to ensure they are taking the necessary measures for proper control and enforcement of the driftnet prohibition. although in the atlantic the situation has proved to be satisfactory, in the mediterranean serious problems persist. the last inspections carried out by commission inspectors this summer confirmed that driftnets were currently being used in italy, france and spain. the commission has already launched infringement proceedings against these member states. reasoned opinions were addressed to italy and france and a letter of formal notice to spain. the opinions and the letter from the commission challenged the lack of proper control and enforcement by the competent authorities of the member states concerned as regards the prohibition on driftnets. the commission is also examining closely, on the basis of the information at its disposal, national legislation which is not, or seems not to be, in conformity with the community probation on driftnets. to cite an example, in the infringement procedure against france the commission challenged the compatibility with community legislation of a french decree allowing the use by french fishermen of the thonaille, a driftnet targeting bluefin tuna. this legislation was recently annulled by the french conseil d´état, which, in its decision, used the same arguments as the commission had used in its reasoned opinion. i would also like to stress that, although the commission is aware of the assertion that almeira's surface longliner fleet has suffered a 40% reduction in catches, as stated by the honourable member, there is no scientific evidence that such a reduction has actually occurred and that this is caused by the unfair competition attributable to non-spanish fleets. representatives of the spanish fleet concerned have been asked to provide the data to support their allegation. in any case, i can confirm that the commission will take all necessary steps in accordance with the rules of the ec treaty and of the common fisheries policy to ensure that member states comply with the community legislation prohibiting driftnets.
madam president, i would like to thank the commissioner for his sincerity. it is well known, as the commissioner has very well shown, that driftnets are still being used in the mediterranean. there is a sense of helplessness among fishermen who comply with the regulation, but there is something more serious than all that. this summer it was found that of the 37 vessels found with driftnets prohibited by environmental organizations, 18 had already received subsidies for their conversion. i think that this problem cannot be left to the member states alone. i think the commission must act and it has done so with some states, but this is clearly not enough. the regulation cannot be allowed to be flouted and certain practices allowed at the same time as subsidies are granted. we really hope for a response to your intervention.

the commission's vice-president mr president, the report by mr mauro on which we have just been debating is a very good report. i would like to thank mr mauro once again, as well as the members of the committee on budgets, the committee on transport and the committee on industry, research and energy for their support of the commission's proposal. the reactions today show how much you care about this subject. this makes perfect sense, since in an enlarged europe - and i am very sensitive to those who have spoken on behalf of the new member states - transeuropean networks are one of the key elements for european integration, the internal market and the lisbon strategy. there is a broad consensus between our two institutions on the objectives to be achieved. i hope that the final decisions on the new financial perspective will take full account of this priority and avoid disappointments, such as those mentioned by mr savary, who very rightly pointed out that it was probably a bit risky to put forward a proposal even though we did not have the financial perspective. but i will answer mr savary, as i have answered all of you, that it seems to me that parliament and the commission must do everything possible to ensure that the financial perspective is tailored to the needs of the europe you have both described so well. the budgetary envelope is now being discussed. as i said at the beginning of the debate, the proposal sets an overall budget of eur 20.690 billion in commitment appropriations for the period 2007-13, including eur 20.350 billion for the transport component and eur 340 million for the energy component. the commission welcomes your full support for this approach to transport. i note, however, that in line with the work of the temporary committee on the new financial perspectives and the resolution adopted by your parliament, it is proposed to reduce the proposed budget for the ten-energy (see amendment no 34). i would point out that this would be less than the current 155 million for the period 2000-06, even though the union now has ten new member states. if parliament were to confirm this possibility, the tens-energy could hardly have an impact on the development of energy networks at a time when the global energy context is pushing us to strengthen gas and electricity infrastructures, which directly contribute to our energy security. the amount requested is also justified by the need to support, in a few well-justified cases, investments beyond the study phase. the commission, i repeat, therefore wishes to maintain the proposed amount. i would like to return to the possibility that you are planning to finance up to 50% of projects which allow the crossing of natural barriers. these are amendments nos 19 and 20. the commission proposal provides that this type of project may be financed up to 30% of the total cost of the project, while the exceptional maximum rate of 50% - exceptional, i say - should be reserved for the crossborder sections of priority projects. experience shows that some member states concentrate their financial resources on the sections of priority projects located on their own national territory, whereas for cross-border sections, there are generally significant delays. by increasing the rate of community financing for this type of section, the commission wishes to exert a leverage effect to facilitate the implementation of these projects. that is why the commission is not in a position to accept your amendment to extend the maximum rate for cross-border sections to natural barriers. let us be clear: the budget of €20.3 billion proposed by the commission for the tens-transport will not allow 50% to be used everywhere. we will only be able to give a boost to a few crossborder projects, because it is really in the community's interest to carry out these projects. if we stick to the concept of natural barrier, this could also apply to sections of projects within the member states, for example where a geographical constraint, a mountain, a river or the sea, requires the construction of a work of art. of course, there are costs involved, but, to my great regret, we do not have sufficient resources to implement this provision, if it were to be adopted. i understand that, since i myself come from a mountain country, but i think we really must stick to the maximum rate for the cross-border sections of the priority projects. thirdly, i would like to make a comment on amendment no 22 and the principle of non-cumulative community aid. if we were to remove this principle of non-cumulative community aid, we would be in contradiction with the financial regulation applicable to the general budget. but of course this does not mean that the different sections of the same project cannot be financed under the various community financial instruments and that for each of these sections the structural funds or the cohesion fund cannot be used successively! you also want the multiannual indicative programme to be submitted to the council and the european parliament for approval. the definition of the multiannual indicative programme is an implementing measure, since the european parliament and the council have already defined the priorities in the guidelines for the trans-european transport and energy networks. the allocation of financial resources through the multiannual programme should be based on technical assessments of the state of progress of projects, among the priorities set by parliament and the council. as regards environmental considerations, i confirm the commission's commitment to fully respect existing requirements, while avoiding the introduction of the entire list of provisions in the legislative texts into the regulation. it is clear that the transeuropean networks must be a model for the environment. i was astonished, mr president, when i said that mr henin - he has now left, fortunately - was completely wrong, because the meeting to which i was invited gave me the opportunity to explain that the all-terrain vehicle has major drawbacks for the environment and for future mobility in europe. i therefore defended the interests of rail freight at this meeting, contrary to what mr henin said, and i would remind you that the majority of the corridors in the transeuropean networks are for rail. i would also like to say that we are naturally very keen to encourage the introduction of the european railway signalling system, ertms, because it is through this system that we ensure interoperability throughout the european railway system. i do not want to go into more detail at this time, mr president. i repeat that this proposal is an ambitious proposal for supporting transeuropean networks. it is a key element for european integration, the internal market and the lisbon strategy. i think that parliament's support for this proposal is essential. i am very clear that now is the time to send a strong message to the council, mr president. the excellent report by mr mauro will certainly contribute to the proper development of the codecision procedure. some of you have just mentioned the failures of the essen programme. i believe that today we have made a number of arrangements, in very close cooperation with your committee on transport and tourism, so that these priority projects can be carried out with the assurance that a number of deadlines will be met. i think that all this obviously depends very much on the financial perspectives, but what we can say tonight is that, thanks to parliament, thanks to the commission, if the financial perspectives, mr president, are what europe needs, we will be able to implement these transeuropean networks effectively this time, which will undoubtedly be a decisive element for the single market, for mobility in europe. i thank you again and i thank parliament for all the attention and interest it has liberty of explaining some of the main amendments, but we shall submit this list to you so as not to delay the closure of this debate. for the commission's position on parliament's amendments, see annex 319 to the commission's proposal.

everywhere, one finds sports drinks. food additives are the result of constant technological progress, which not only allows us to enjoy higher quality food products, but also offers greater food safety to consumers. however, improper use must be prevented and reviews kept up to date, so that ignorance and media pressure do not negatively influence consumer confidence and damage the image of food containing these additives, which is not a drawback but an improvement in food safety. finally, i would like to point out that i do not agree with the amendments tabled by the green group, and in particular those which call for the commission to submit a report reviewing all existing authorizations for additives. this amendment duplicates the requirements of the council framework directive 89/107/eec on food additives, which, in its annex ii, specifies that all additives shall be under a state of permanent observation and shall be evaluated whenever necessary.

member of the commission. madam president, last month nearly 7 million afghans went to the polls to elect a parliament for the first time in 36 years. this was the culmination of a political transitional process agreed in bonn four years ago. i visited afghanistan at the beginning of september to look at the election preparations and see for myself the practical impact our assistance is having on the ground. i was also able to discuss all the challenges ahead and the next phase of the stabilisation process with president karzai and his ministers, as well as with afghan civil society and the united nations. i would therefore like to take this opportunity to say a few words about the elections, the preparations for the post-bonn period and future eu-afghanistan relations. the european union has supported afghanistan’s recent election in a number of ways. it is no exaggeration to say that the election could not have taken place without the european union, including contributions by the member states. we funded 40% of the election budget, contributing eur 159 million. we have also sought to improve transparency by deploying an eu election observation mission, headed by mrs emma bonino who is present today. this has followed the process since july. it also benefited from the cooperation of an observer delegation from parliament, led by mr salafranca sánchez-neyra, who is here today as well. i think we can say that the eu eom was the single largest international observer group in the country. its presence was extremely important. in its preliminary statement, the eu eom reported that the election day itself had been largely peaceful, the process up to that point had been generally well administered and the elections marked a step forward for afghanistan’s democratic development. nevertheless, it also noted a number of concerns, for instance with the whole campaign environment, the choice of voting system and the complaints mechanism. i understand that in some provinces fraud and irregularities have come to light during the counting phase. the election observation mission has urged the electoral authorities to deal diligently with these concerns. i would like to congratulate mrs bonino for her team’s excellent work so far. i look forward to the final report, which will include an overall assessment of the entire election process, as well as recommendations to improve the conduct of future elections. mrs bonino will be travelling to kabul again before the end of the year to present the report to election stakeholders. what comes next, after the bonn process? afghanistan has come a long way since the fall of the taliban. i am proud that the european commission’s assistance has had a tangible impact. we have pursued a combination of visible reconstruction, lasting capacity-building and improvements in the day-to-day lives of the afghan people. we are on track to deliver the eur 1 billion we pledged in tokyo for the period 2002 to 2006. if we think back to the chaos, devastation and repression in afghanistan four years ago, it is clear that the country has made progress. five million children are back in school, one-third of them girls. eighty per cent of children have been vaccinated against measles and polio. roads, schools and clinics are being built and many of them are already working. however, the situation is still fragile and the improvements are not yet fully sustainable. it is clear that the country still has a long way to go. more work is needed, particularly on good governance, the rule of law, security, counter-narcotics and development. i therefore very much welcome the idea floated by the united nations at the end of august of a major international conference, hopefully early in 2006, to draw up the ‘post-bonn compact’ between afghanistan and the international community. the european union will again be an important participant in the conference. what should the compact do? it should focus particularly on afghan ownership and sustainability. lasting stabilisation will not be possible unless the afghan side is willing and able to take greater responsibility for the transition process and for making it sustainable. the bonn agreement showed the value of clear-cut targets and timetables to ensure momentum. so we should aim to incorporate clear benchmarks in the post-bonn compact. some form of joint afghan-international monitoring of progress would also be useful. the post-bonn compact should be a two-way street: it should contain clear-cut commitments from the afghan side and commitments from the international community to stay engaged financially, politically and militarily. finally, i turn to the role of the european union. the european union and its member states have been playing an important role in afghanistan. together we accounted for one-third of the usd 12.5 billion in grants pledged at the tokyo and bonn conferences. eu member states are currently contributing 80% of the troops in isaf. the eu special representative in afghanistan, francesc vendrell, has been doing excellent work politically. under the auspices of the british presidency, we are currently discussing with president karzai’s government a joint declaration on an eu-afghan partnership. it would be an important political signal of continuing eu commitment to afghanistan. it would also make clear our expectations, the kind of further progress we want to support in afghanistan in fields such as governance, development and human rights. my hope is that this can be concluded in the weeks ahead so that it would be in place ahead of any post-bonn conference and could help to shape discussions there. finally, i believe that the european union is both entitled and obliged to play a major part in ensuring the success of the post-bonn compact. the commission will, in any case, remain engaged.

madam president, the mediterranean region is very important for the member states and for the european union as a whole. it is clear that the countries on the southern shore do not have the same level of political development and/or economic prosperity. however, most of these countries are faced with various deficiencies, to a greater or lesser degree: political deficiencies, poor democratic development and limited pluralism; economic deficiencies, because we are facing outdated economies, unable to generate employment for a growing population and without sufficient attractiveness to attract the necessary foreign investment; and social deficiencies, high poverty and social inequality, illiteracy, discrimination against women - as has been said here - , poor capacity of their public institutions, with negative consequences in the fields of health, education, the economy, border control, and much more. the mediterranean region should therefore be a priority for the union, not only because of the many historical, political, economic and social links between the countries on both sides, but also for other reasons, such as security, including the threat of terrorism, or the challenge of immigration. cooperation between the two sides of the atlantic is therefore indispensable and must cover a very wide range of activities. cooperation has to work in both directions, i repeat, in both directions. the problems of these neighbouring countries affect us, our future is shared; it is impossible to create a wall between the north and the south of the mediterranean, and even less so in today's globalised world. we must therefore deepen our relations with these countries, encourage them and help them to overcome the shortcomings to which i referred earlier. that is why the report we are going to adopt tomorrow insists on the need for modernization at the political, economic, social and institutional levels and also at the level of human rights. in this respect, i welcome the commissioner's words and the importance she attaches to these issues. there is a need - and i think we should all agree - for a reform momentum on the south bank. the european union cannot be concerned only with the stability of these countries; stability cannot, in the end, become the alibi for immobility. if we insist on the need for reform in our countries, how can we not insist on the need for reform in your countries? these countries must evolve. otherwise, the problems will increase, and the political and economic crises - and also in the field of immigration and security - will only grow, and in the end, non-reform will be the one that brings instability. hence the importance of the barcelona process and the european neighbourhood policy. they must be the union's fundamental instruments, firstly to demonstrate to these countries the priority they occupy in our external action and, secondly, to help them, to demand that they also cooperate loyally with us in solving the problems that affect us and, finally, to encourage them to reform. a reform that can bring prosperity, freedom and ultimately more stability to these countries and, therefore, to the whole mediterranean basin. i would like the next barcelona summit to rise to the challenge and i would of course like to conclude by thanking mrs jäätteenmäki for her efforts.

madam president, the euro-mediterranean process is ten years old and the first conclusion is that if it did not exist, it would have to be invented urgently, simply and simply because, as our rapporteur jäätteenmäki's report says, despite its shortcomings, it has been a success. it was impossible to imagine that the structural and historical problems of the mediterranean countries could be solved in a decade. but we've gotten down to business, and some of those problems are starting to be solved. i therefore believe that the objective of a free trade area by 2010 should be more than an end goal, it should be a milestone to continue, which should be complemented by many other things. the euro-mediterranean process must be deepened and reformed, the fundamental idea behind it must be underlined and, in this case, the potential achievements must be turned into a tangible reality. the international situation also tells us that the euro-mediterranean process is the best way to promote cooperation. other strategies, based on aggression and threat, do not work. however, the premium of going forward, which is at the basis of this euro-mediterranean process, is proving its usefulness. for example, i chaired the european parliament's delegation of observers to the parliamentary elections in lebanon, a euro-mediterranean partner; member of the commission. mr president, i should like to thank you for this opportunity to share with you our current thinking on the new import regime for bananas. needless to say, we are very disappointed at the second arbitration award issued on 22 october 2005. the current import regime for bananas was agreed at doha in 2001. on this basis we obtained a waiver from our wto obligations for granting a preference to our acp partners. it was also agreed at the time that we would move to a tariff-only system not later than 1 january 2006. for this purpose we opened negotiations with our main trading partners for modifying the concessions in our schedule on bananas and went through arbitration as foreseen in the annex to the doha waiver. the relevant benchmark set out in the annex to the doha waiver is whether the rebinding of our tariff on bananas maintains market access for most-favoured-nation suppliers. following a first negative award on 1 august 2005, the arbitrator determined in a second award issued on 27 october that the european community had failed to rectify the matter with its proposal for a new most-favoured-nation tariff rate at eur 187 per tonne. this was a very disappointing result. our calculations were done in an objective and transparent manner and were supported by thorough economic and legal analysis. the aim has always been to ensure a neutral modification of the import regime with a most-favoured-nation tariff that provides equivalent market access conditions to let in american suppliers – as the current quota regime does – and keeps an equivalent level of acp preference. throughout this process we had consultations with our trading partners but there were no common positions from their side that could have been the basis for a negotiated solution. where does that leave us now? the arbitrator’s award does not indicate what could be an appropriate tariff level. in deciding on the import regime for bananas there are a number of considerations that need to be taken into account: most importantly, our responsibility to all the different stakeholders. we have considered the interests of community producers and the management of the common market organisation for bananas with a view to its future reform. we have our commitments towards the acp partners in the cotonou agreement to maintain their tariff preferences. in the light of all the above, we need to move to a tariff-only system from 1 january 2006 and we must move quickly as our operators need legal certainty. at the same time, i am fully aware of our responsibilities towards all stakeholders, which we take very seriously. the commission will therefore be making a proposal very shortly on the level of the tariff starting from 1 january 2006.

mr president, the 2001 agreement with the united states and the latin american countries, to which the commissioner referred earlier, and with which we thought we could end the banana war, now entails a radical change in the community's import regime from january 2006, a change which the european sector will have to face with a high degree of uncertainty. in 1993, the union decided to establish its own import regime and a common organization of the market for bananas, which is completely different from the common organization of the market for the rest of the fruit and vegetables sector. the introduction of a too low border tariff. the root of the problem is, in short, an accounting adjustment on which the future of the banana sector in the european union depends. the lower the duty, the president of the court of auditors. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. on behalf of the members of the european court of auditors, i thank you for inviting me to the debate on the court's 28th annual report for the financial year 2004, which i presented to the committee on budgetary control last night. i am pleased to be present, in my first year as president of the court, at the launch of the annual discharge procedure for the implementation of the eu budget. the annual report is based largely on audits of the accounts and of the legality and regularity of the accounts carried out by the court. the results of the court's audits of economic viability, on the other hand, are generally published in the form of special reports. the 2004 financial year was marked by the accession of 10 new member states, which increased the appropriations for payments from eur 98 billion in 2003 to eur 105 billion in 2004. thanks to better planning and management, the use of funds was considerably increased compared with previous years. at eur 2.7 billion, the 2004 surplus was much lower than in 2003, only about half as high. i would now like to comment on the main points made in the court's statement of assurance, also known as the das, starting with the statement of assurance on accounting reliability. for the financial year 2004, the court concluded that the consolidated financial statements give a true and fair view of the revenue and expenditure for that financial year and of the financial position at the end of the year, except for the item 'other debtors'. as in the past, the accounting system used for the preparation of the 2004 annual accounts is not suitable for a complete recording of assets and liabilities in the balance sheet. however, the commission has made significant progress towards the introduction of accurate accounting by the 2005 financial year. however, at the time of the examination, the court considered that further progress was needed as the figures needed to establish the opening balance sheets for 2005 had not yet been validated by the commission's authorising officers. if appropriate measures are not taken by the end of this year, the reliability of the 2005 accounts may be affected by the deficiencies identified by the court. as regards the legality and regularity of the underlying transactions, the court of justice stated in its statement of assurance that: for the financial year 2004, the court concluded that the monitoring and control systems put in place were effective and that the underlying operations were legal and regular as regards revenue, commitments, administrative expenditure and the pre-accession strategy as part of the payment appropriations estimates. with regard to the other appropriations for payments for agricultural expenditure, structural operations, internal policies and external policies, the court is again not in a position to give a full statement of assurance. the monitoring and control systems have not yet been fully established, have not yet been effective and payments continue to be marked by significant errors. for the first time, the court can report that the efforts of the commission and the member states in implementing the integrated administration and control system (invekos) have had a positive impact, covering 59% of agricultural expenditure. invekos is a very effective tool, when used properly, to limit the risk of irregular expenditure to an acceptable level. i now wish to go into more detail on the specific assessments for each area of activity in the context of the declaration of assurance. in the case of revenue, the court found that the revenue operations were lawful and regular. however, systemic weaknesses have been identified in the gni own resources both at the commission and at the member state level. as in previous years, the court has again found evidence that, overall, expenditure under the common agricultural policy remains marked by significant errors. while the court found that the invekos works effectively when applied correctly, agricultural expenditure not covered by the invekos or not applied appropriately is at a higher risk of irregularities due to weaknesses in the control systems. in the field of structural measures, the court again found weaknesses in the management and control systems in the member states for all the programmes included in the sample. the court found weaknesses in the member states' controls, such as the lack of implementation or documentation of controls, the lack of verification of eligibility criteria or the lack of evidence of the provision of the co-financed services. the declarations of expenditure of the member states, on the basis of which the commission makes payments, are subject to a high rate of error. the court examined a sample of 167 projects and identified a wide range of problems. this included a large number of cases where ineligible expenditure was reported. in the case of internal policy areas managed directly by the commission, the court found that, despite progress in some areas, the monitoring and control systems did not function adequately and that there was a high error rate in the underlying processes. a common cause of error is complicated regulations. in this case, the risk of error is likely to remain high unless the legal framework is changed and procedures simplified. this situation, which is not a significant improvement on previous years, was mainly due to the fact that too high costs or ineligible costs were declared or to the lack of supporting documents, such as proof of the actual provision of paid services. in the case of external policy expenditure, the court noted that the systems had been improved and that there were few errors in the underlying processes at delegation level. however, weaknesses in internal control systems and a relatively high error rate were again identified at the level of the organisations responsible for implementing the project. the court's overall judgment on the pre-emption strategy was positive, as the underlying transactions were essentially lawful and regular. the monitoring and control systems at the level of the commission's central services, delegations and certifying bodies are generally reliable and function well in practice. however, at national level, the court identified weaknesses in the systems of implementing bodies in bulgaria, romania, turkey and other sapard countries. in the area of administrative expenditure, the underlying transactions were substantially legal and regular and the monitoring and control systems functioned generally adequately. what are the main conclusions to be drawn from this? the court found that the majority of the estimates of payment appropriations were again marked by substantial errors of legality and regularity at the level of the underlying transactions. this is due to inherent risk-bearing operations and the fact that the monitoring and control systems are not sufficiently effective in limiting the risk of irregularities to an acceptable level. however, improvements were noted in the systems, in particular invekos, the main monitoring and control system for agricultural expenditure implemented by the member states. this is also the case at commission level, where the reform process of the administrative and financial system launched in 2000 has produced good results. however, much remains to be done, particularly at member state level. the legislation, rules and procedures for spending are still often too complicated. a large proportion of expenditure is inherently risky and is based solely on declarations by the beneficiaries. finally, the european union itself has grown considerably and changed considerably since the introduction of das in 1994. in these 11 years, annual expenditure on payments has risen from eur 60 billion to eur 100 billion, while the number of member states has increased from 12 to 25. the scope and complexity of management has therefore increased, involving an increasing number of authorities and organisations. the need for more effective monitoring and control systems is therefore increasing. in its opinion no 2/2004 on the single audit model, the court proposed the creation of a community internal control framework covering all levels of administration community institutions, member states and beneficiary countries . the court's opinion on the single audit model was a contribution to the political debate on improving the management and control of community funds. the commission took a step forward by adopting a so-called roadmap for the creation of an integrated internal control framework. this roadmap will provide the basis for extending the reform to all forms of management of funds, in particular at the level of shared management with the member states; the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. the court welcomes this initiative by the commission for a roadmap. as the eu's external auditor, the court will closely monitor progress and assess the impact of these changes on the financial management and control of eu finances over the next few years. in connection with another issue, namely the position of the court on future financing, management and control in the field of the common agricultural policy and structural measures, it should be noted that this position should be taken into account in the final formulation of this important legislation. the provisions on the retention of supporting documents provided for in the present draft regulation on structural operations would make it impossible for the court to examine some of the expenditure concerned. the court is aware of the need to continuously improve itself and make the best use of its resources in a constantly changing union. our aim is to promote the interests of the european union as effectively and efficiently as possible. it is sometimes argued that the court should not provide additional ammunition to those who have an interest in discrediting the union. however, i am firmly convinced that the interests of citizens are best represented by an objective and independent external audit body that makes clear and balanced statements based on objective facts. recent events the rejection of the draft constitution by voters in two referendums in two member states and the difficulties in reaching agreement on the financial perspective for 2007-2013 are seen by some as a sign of a lack of trust in the european union and its institutions among citizens. i am firmly convinced that the legitimacy of the union can only be guaranteed if our institutions function smoothly and if management is of high quality, both at the political and executive levels. the member states also have to live up to their responsibilities for the management and control of a large part of the eu budget. the european court of auditors has a key role to play in this: it must provide an independent, professional and objective picture of financial management and help shape change in the interests of citizens. (applause from the centre)
vice-president of the commission. mr president, i should like to thank the president of the court, mr weber, for the fair presentation of the 2004 annual report and the members of the parliament for giving me the opportunity to give the commission’s first reaction. the court’s report is fair and balanced: it says that the commission is having success in implementing tangible improvements in its management systems, but that many areas still need to be improved. the commission welcomes the court’s positive opinion on the reliability of the accounts, which faithfully reflect the revenue and expenditure of the communities for the year and their financial position at the year end. the court has only one reservation, which has been resolved through the introduction of the accrual-based accounting system in 2005. this means that the accounts met their primary objective and that the accounts have been drawn up according to the provisions of the financial regulation in force. the court gives a positive assurance on the accounts, on revenue, on commitments, on pre-accession aid, and on administrative expenditure. it is also satisfied with edf development aid, some eur 2.4 billion outside the budget. the court also notes two key improvements since last year: in a large part of the common agricultural policy and in aid to candidate countries to the eu. the system used to check much expenditure under the common agricultural policy – the integrated administration and control system (iacs) – is considered an effective control system in limiting the risk of irregular expenditure, when properly applied. this system will be applied to an even greater percentage of agricultural expenditure in the coming years. so simplifying greatly, in addition to the several positive assurances i have already mentioned, the court is now reasonably satisfied with the systems of control and spending in an increasing part of the eu budget, roughly estimated to represent one third of the budget. this is tangible and quantifiable progress towards a positive statement of assurance. the conclusions of the court have not always been fully understood by the general public and the media. i liked very much the remark in the president of the court’s speech that makes it clear that the court’s qualified opinion on certain areas cannot be interpreted as meaning all transactions of the 2004 payment budget are affected by error, nor can it be interpreted as an indicator of fraud. we must all understand the comprehensive nature of this large budget discharge exercise. this procedure shows that the commission is accountable to directly elected members of parliament. this may be the eleventh consecutive non-positive statement of assurance, but i hope it is clear from my initial remarks this does not imply that we are not making progress. members of parliament have pointed out repeatedly that the commission alone cannot ‘produce’ a positive das. the 2003 discharge resolution gave very valuable guidance on how to further improve, and we are working to do that. as you know, this commission has proposed a ‘roadmap to an integrated internal control framework’, looking for support in parliament and council. while i am very grateful for parliament’s support on the roadmap, the ecofin council’s statement of 8 november was not as radical as the commission had hoped it would be; political declarations at national level were not accepted. but a cascade of operational management declarations by payment and similar agencies is not an impossible goal, though a national synthesis report for each sector, similar to that which the commission draws up on the basis of the annual activity reports of its directors-general, will be more difficult to achieve. we will go ahead with our proposals. our action plan towards an integrated internal control framework will be published next month. it is based on the results of the ‘gap assessment’ between the control framework in place for all types of budgetary expenditure and the general principles defined by the court in its opinion no 2/2004 on a single audit. we hope that the legislation being finalised for the new series of programmes in the years after 2006 will reflect the new thinking. the proposed revisions to the financial regulation and the implementing rules also reflect this thinking. court sampling reveals substantial errors that we are of course concerned to reduce to a minimum. to do so, we are focusing and seeking assurance on the procedures for managing the risk of irregularity. this is the way to ensure, within a limited resource base, that the costs of extra controls provide added benefits in terms of reducing risks of error. i would especially mention here two quotations from the speech made by the president of the court: ‘in structural matters, the court found weaknesses in the management and control systems in the member states across all programmes’; and the second quotation: ‘in the area of internal policies the court notes that the errors often stem from complicated rules’. certainly i agree with these remarks. need for simplification of rules was repeated yesterday at the meeting of the committee on budgetary control but, if i look for the individuals who are responsible for the large number and complexity of the programmes and rules, i find hardly anyone. everybody talks about the need for simplification but, when business goes into detail, it is not so simple any more. a large part of the complexity often comes not from the officials but from clients, policy makers, politicians in member states and members of the european parliament. the changes are often resisted by the same players. i use this opportunity to call on all policy makers, when the creation of another goal, plan and programme is under consideration, to look critically at aspects of fiscal management and the need to control and audit these programmes. there is a lot more to be said, but the budget discharge process is now only at the beginning and within the coming months members of parliament will have all the answers to their questions. parliament and the commission will work together to finalise the process of discharge of the 2004 european budget.

member of the commission. the issue of taxes on air traffic has been much debated lately, but it has been among the instruments considered in the search for new sources of funding for official aid to developing countries, in line with the un millennium development goals. the honourable member is no doubt aware that the council has been actively considering the issue and that the commission has produced several staff working papers on the technical aspects at the request of the council. two types of tax instruments have been considered: the taxation of aviation fuel and a levy on airline tickets, also known as a departure tax. from the internal market point of view, the legal setting is not the same for those two types of taxes. taxes on aviation fuel are covered by community legislation in the form of the energy tax directive, 2003/96/ec. although aviation fuel is, in principle, exempt from taxes, the member states may choose to tax fuel for domestic flights. they may also tax fuel for flights between member states, provided they agree bilaterally to do so. however, in practice there is no scope to tax fuel used by third-country carriers operating in the ec. as regards a levy on airline tickets, there are no specific community provisions. member states are therefore free to apply such levies on the obvious condition that they comply with their commitments under the ec treaty. the honourable member has asked whether the commission is considering ways to prevent such taxes on air travel becoming obstacles to the internal market. i would first like to stress that the fact that a product or service is taxed does not mean that its free movement is obstructed. there is an obstacle to the internal market only if a tax is heavier on transactions between member states than on similar transactions within a member state. the commission will make full use of its powers to enforce the treaty against any discriminatory taxes on air travel, as it does for all other taxes. however, i understand that the discussions between member states at this stage focus mainly on airline ticket levies. in this respect i must stress that, in the absence of community rules, this is first and foremost a matter for the member states themselves, acting within their fiscal sovereignty. nevertheless, the commission has argued in its staff working papers that there are good reasons to prefer a common approach to ticket levies. the commission has also declared that it is willing to work on the technical aspects with the member states that intend to pursue this option. that would help to ensure compatibility with treaty obligations. i should like to point out that the commission is continuously monitoring the functioning of the internal market. taxes of the kind mentioned in the honourable member’s question are still rare. should the commission identify a structural problem linked to the taxation of air travel, be it fuel taxes or ticket levies, it could ultimately make use of its right to propose appropriate legislation.

member of the commission. in response to your first question concerning tourism, increased taxation of air travel could in theory lead to a reduction in air travel demand. however, the increase in the price of the air ticket must be viewed in the context of the overall cost of a travel package – i.e. travel, accommodation and leisure spending – of which it is usually a minor part. the possible impact on tourism should also be set against the overall trend of a very strong growth in tourism demand. there are therefore good reasons for thinking that the overall impact on tourism will be moderate. in answer to your second question about remote and peripheral regions, the increased cost of air travel may have a greater impact on regions that are highly dependent on air transportation. however, as air ticket taxes are primarily a matter for member states, those who choose to apply such taxes will have latitude to design their taxes so as to provide correctives to take into account the special circumstances of remote regions and the social needs of their inhabitants. the commission has stated that it is prepared to work with member states, as i have already said, on the technical aspects of airline tickets. this could include looking at various correctives for remote and peripheral regions within the framework of community rules.
